271.title: Audio recorder
271.content: Audio recorder records an audio bus to a 16-bit WAV file. Set File pattern, enable Record, then disable it to close the take and receive its Filename. %n and %t keep numbered or dated takes.

272.title: Beat following
272.content: Beat Tracker extracts tempo and beat phase from audio or incoming control events. Unlike the metronome above, it follows an external performance; connect its outputs deliberately to tempo, speed or other controls.

274.title: Audio Examples
274.content: Start with a sound you want to transform, or a phrase you want to perform. These scores connect sound-making to the timeline: an effect can become a section of a piece, a pattern can be recalled on cue, and a live phrase can become a loop.

275.title: Choose a starting point
275.content: . | Transform a recording: Audio Effects puts granular piano and a bell through a shared effects chain. For a more radical change in texture, Granular synthesis approaches compares continuous clouds, rhythmic grains and tiny loops. | Build a sound without samples: Faust synthesis moves between resonant percussion and plucked strings. Pure Data integration shapes a noise texture with timeline curves. | Change a melody without rewriting it: MIDI effects and arpeggiation varies note order, rhythm and scale. Scala tuning and Wavecycle separates tuning from the oscillator’s timbre. | Perform an arrangement: Arranging synth patterns with triggers recalls bass, bells and drums on cue. Sequencing audio effects creates contrasting sections from one drum part. Live audio looper captures your input over a drum backing. | Keep channels independent: Multichannel audio and per-channel controls gives channels different delay times, then plays the separate signals next to a combined mix. | . See Audio plug-ins for host-format requirements, Audio utilities for channel routing, and Audio effects for built-in processing. A plug-in or external patch used by an example must also be available on the computer opening it.

277.title: Audio Looper
277.content: . The process named Looper (audio) records the audio it receives at in into a loop and plays it back at out. Each overdub is kept as a layer of its own, so it can be undone, and every take is written to a file that can be placed in the timeline as a regular sound clip. The MIDI looper works the same way with notes and controllers, and the value looper with any stream of values.

278.title: Modes
278.content: Mode chooses what the looper does: . | Mode | Behavior | . | Play | Plays the loop. | . | Record | Records an empty loop. On a loop that has something in it, overdubs it, as on a looper pedal: to record a new loop, Clear it first. | . | Overdub | Records a new layer on top of the loop while it plays. On an empty loop, it is a recording, as Record makes, which then gives way to overdubbing. | . | Stop | Outputs no loop. The loop is kept. | . Mode is the state of the looper: it always shows what the looper is doing, or what it is about to do on the next grid point, whatever changed it: an action of the Switches tab, a recording ending after its bars, a full loop, Capture, a file loaded. Every control is a port with an address, so the looper can be driven by OSC, MIDI or a footswitch mapping as well as by the mouse. A cable or an automation that sends the same mode on every tick asks for it once, when it changes: when the looper changes Mode itself, at the end of a recording for instance, the cable does not ask again and the mode does not flip back.

279.title: Record, Overdub and layers
279.content: |   | What it is for | What it does to the loop | How layers are cut | . | Record | Making a loop. | Makes the loop: it is as long as the recording, or Record bars bars. On a loop that has something in it, Record overdubs: Clear first to make the loop again. | The recording is the first layer. | . | Overdub | Playing over the loop. | Adds what is played on top of the loop, each round fading the layers under it by Feedback; with Past the end on Extend, makes it longer. | One layer from when it starts to when it stops; with Passes on Per cycle, one each time round; New layer cuts one where it is pressed. | . | Play, Stop | Listening, or not. | Nothing. | None. | . A recording ends in one of three ways, and After record says what it gives way to whichever it is: its Record bars running out, the loop reaching Max length, or Rec / Play / Dub. Setting Mode to another mode during a recording ends it into that mode.

280.title: Timing
280.content: Quantize makes a mode change wait for the next point of a grid, so that a loop starts and ends in time. Every action waits for it as well, except Undo, Redo and Clear, which act at once, and selecting a layer. Dragging the knob goes through the values of a unit; clicking its readout chooses the unit: . | Unit | Values | The grid | . | Free time | None, or up to 8 seconds | Every that many seconds, counted from the loop’s start once there is a loop. None changes at once. | . | Note value | 1/64 to 4/1, straight, dotted or triplet | A note value, whatever the signature: 1/4 is a quarter note (the default), 1/1 a whole note, four quarters, which is not a bar in 3/4. Shorter than a bar, the grid starts again on every bar line. See quantization. | . | Bars | 1 to 16 bars | Whole bars of the current signature: 3 bars is a phrase of three bars. | . | Loop | 1/4 loop to 8x loop | The loop itself: Loop waits for the loop to come round to its start, 2x loop for every other time, 1/2 loop for its start and its middle. | . Loop follows the loop as it plays: its length whatever it is, on the bar grid or not, its speed and its direction. An overdub that makes the loop longer waits for the end of the loop as long as it is so far. A stopped loop goes by where it would be had it kept playing since it was recorded. Before there is a loop, while it is empty or being recorded, Loop waits for the length the recording will have: Record bars bars, or one bar when Record bars is 0 (2x loop is twice that). Record bars makes a recording end on its own after that many bars, into what After record says. With Record bars at 0, a recording lasts as long as wanted, until the mode is changed. Late stop (ms) handles a recording that is asked to stop a little after a grid point, for example a footswitch pressed just after the downbeat: the recording ends on that grid point instead of a whole grid step later, and playback carries on in time. When it gives way to an overdub, what was played since the grid point is the start of the overdub. The default is 120 ms; 0 turns it off. Start from chooses where the loop is read from when the mode changes: . | Choice | Behavior | . | Loop start | Every change of mode reads the loop from its beginning again. | . | Where it was (default) | Playing, overdubbing and stopping carry on from where the playhead is: Play, Overdub and Play again stay in time. | . | In phase | As Where it was, and a loop heard again keeps to the timeline, see Start from In phase. | . A recording always starts at the loop’s start.

281.title: Footswitches
281.content: The Switches, Layers and Speed tabs have buttons made to be mapped to footswitches, MIDI notes or OSC messages: Switches holds the one-button actions and the transport, Layers holds Undo, Redo, Clear, Layer and what acts on the selected layer, and Speed holds Speed, Reverse and Follow tempo with Toggle reverse, Half speed and Double speed. Capture is in the Length tab, next to Capture bars. Play, Stop, Record and Overdub set Mode, exactly as setting it by hand does. The others say what Mode cannot: “the next thing”, “a new layer”, “from the start”, “this layer”. What they change waits for the next point of the grid, as a change of Mode does, and Late stop applies to them; the controls they change (Mode, Layer, Reverse, Speed) show what they changed them to. | Action | What it does | . | Rec / Play / Dub | One button for everything: records an empty loop; while recording, ends the recording into what After record says; overdubs a playing loop; while overdubbing, does what After overdub says; plays a stopped loop. | . | Play / Stop | Plays a stopped loop; stops it in any other mode. Does nothing on an empty loop. | . | Play, Stop, Record, Overdub | Set Mode to that mode. Record on a loop that has something in it overdubs it, and Mode shows Overdub. Record while recording, or Overdub while overdubbing, does nothing. | . | New layer | While overdubbing, ends the layer and goes on overdubbing in a new one on the grid, without the playhead moving. Does nothing otherwise. | . | Retrigger | Goes back to the start of the loop on the grid, in the same mode: an overdub goes on from the start in the same layer. While recording, starts the recording again, its bars and its tempo counted from there. | . | Undo, Redo, Clear | At once, see Layers. | . | Previous layer, Next layer | Change Layer, the selected layer, at once, from the oldest to the newest. The view outlines it. | . | Mute layer, Erase layer | Mute, unmute or erase the selected layer, on the grid. | . | Solo layer | Mutes every layer but the selected one, on the grid. Pressed again on that layer, the layers get back the mutes they had, unless a mute or an erase changed them in between. Pressed on another layer, solos that one. | . | Toggle reverse | Turns Reverse on or off, on the grid. | . | Half speed, Double speed | Set Speed to x1/2 or x2, or back to x1 when it already is, on the grid. | . | Capture | See Capture. | . Layer moves to each new layer as it is added, so Mute layer, Erase layer and Solo layer act on the newest layer unless Previous layer stepped back. When layers are merged, erased or brought back, Layer keeps naming the layer it named: the merged one when it named one of the two merged. Rec / Play / Dub and Play / Stop act on the mode the looper will be in once what waits for the grid is taken up. Pressed twice before the grid point, each press is taken up on a grid point of its own: on an empty loop, two presses of Rec / Play / Dub record one grid step and play it. Setting Mode, or pressing Play, Stop, Record or Overdub, replaces whatever was waiting. Three settings choose what the one-button actions do: . | Setting | Choices | . | After record | What a recording gives way to when it ends, by its bars, a full loop or Rec / Play / Dub. Play (default) hears the loop at once, the usual choice. Overdub goes on overdubbing from the very frame the recording ends on: nothing played across the end of the loop is cut, for pads and sustained textures. A recording made by Overdub on an empty loop always gives way to overdubbing. | . | After overdub | What Rec / Play / Dub does while overdubbing. Play (default) goes back to playing, as single-switch loopers do. New layer goes on overdubbing in a new layer, as New layer does, for building a loop layer by layer with one switch. | . | Stop at | When a stop is taken up. Grid (default) waits for the next point of the grid, as any change of mode. Loop end lets the loop play to its end, for ending a song on a whole loop. Now stops at once, ignoring the grid, for a stop that must not wait. | .

282.title: Layers
282.content: Each overdub pass is a layer of its own. The view shows one lane per layer. | Undo removes the last pass. Pressed during an overdub, it drops the pass in progress and overdubbing carries on in a new one. Pressed during a recording, or Clear, starts the recording again at once, its bars and tempo counted from there. Undoing the first recording empties the loop. | Redo brings back the last pass undone. A new overdub after an undo replaces what redo would have brought back. | Clear empties the loop and forgets every pass. | Feedback is how much of the loop is kept each time an overdub goes round it. At 1 nothing fades; below 1, older passes fade a little more at each round. Undoing a pass gives the passes under it back the level it took from them. | . Past the end chooses what an overdub does when it reaches the end of the loop: Wrap goes round the loop again; Extend makes the loop longer by its length, each time the end is reached, and the passes under it play again over the new part. The extended loop ends when overdubbing stops: on a one-bar loop, overdubbing for four bars makes a four-bar loop, and a shorter overdub after that leaves it as it is. Stopping just after the loop grew, within Late stop, does not add the last length. Undo gives the loop its length back. Max layers, 2 to 32, is the number of layers kept apart. At max layers says what a pass does once there are that many: . | Choice | Behavior | . | Merge into newest (default) | The pass is merged into the newest layer when it ends: the oldest layers stay as they are. Undo right after takes the pass out of the newest layer again; once another pass starts, the merge is final. | . | Merge oldest | The two oldest layers are merged into one, and that undo step is lost. | . | Replace a muted layer | The pass takes the place of the oldest muted layer, or of the newest layer when none is muted. Undo right after takes the pass out and puts the replaced layer back where it was, muted as it was; Redo replaces it again. Once another pass starts, the replacement is final. | . A muted layer that is merged is left out of the merged one, and lost. Erasing a pass . Any pass can be taken out of the loop while it plays, not only the last one: . | in the view, with the x at the right of its lane, on the next grid point. The view shows a lane per pass, up to 32, sharing its height between them; with more passes than that, the oldest share the first lane, which has no x. | with Layer and Erase layer, in the Layers tab: Layer says which pass, counting from the oldest one, and Erase layer erases it on the grid. Layer 1 is the top lane of the view when every pass has a lane of its own, and the file ending in -layer1 of a take written as layers. Both are ports, so a footswitch or an OSC message can erase a pass. | . The passes over the erased one stay where they are and the loop keeps its length, even when the erased pass had extended it. The passes under it get back the level its feedback took from them, as when it is undone. Undo and Redo go on with the passes left, and what Redo would bring back is kept. Erasing is not itself undone by Undo. Erasing the pass being overdubbed is the same as Undo: the pass is dropped and overdubbing carries on in a new one. Erasing the only pass empties the loop, as Clear does.

283.title: Takes and the timeline
283.content: When a recording or an overdub ends, the loop is written to a WAV file: 32-bit float, with its tempo and length in bars stored in the file, and marked as a loop. A click on Send, the button at the top right of the looper’s view, places the last take in the timeline as a looping sound file, in a new box starting where the take was recorded, below the looper’s box. This is one undoable action. The take can also be dragged into the timeline, or anywhere a sound file can be dropped: dragging from the Send button, which has a grip for it, drags what Send would place, the files Export says. Dragging a lane drags that layer alone, its own file, which lands as a box of its own. A muted layer is dragged as well: it was chosen. When the last take has no file of that layer, because Export is Mix or the layers changed since, the file is written when the drag starts: the lane says Preparing meanwhile, and the drag goes on as soon as it is there. Sent or dragged, a take or a layer plays the way the loop did when it was written: its stretch mode follows the Follow tempo the looper was playing with. Timestretch gives the take the melodic time-stretch mode, Timestretch percussive the rhythmic one, Repitch and Repitch fast the matching repitch modes. With Off, the take is not stretched: it plays at the speed it was recorded at, and its box and its loop are as long as the recording itself, at the tempo where it is placed. A change of Follow tempo applies to the loop from the next start, and so to the takes made after that. The stretch mode can be changed afterwards in the sound file’s inspector. A take dropped from a file browser has no such information, and gets a stretch mode chosen from its name, as any sound file. While a recording or an overdub goes on, the last take does not have it yet. A press on Send then asks for a take of the loop as it is heard at that moment, the pass in progress included as far as it went, without stopping it; the button says Saving until the take is written. A click places it as soon as it is there. A drag from the button starts with the next move of the mouse once it is there, if the button is still held; let go before, the take is the one the next drag or Send gives. A lane dragged meanwhile gives its layer as far as it went. When the score is paused, nothing is being taken in any more, and Send and the drags give the last take there is. When the score stops while a recording or an overdub goes on, the overdub’s layer is closed as any, and Mode then shows Play: when the score plays again, the loop plays, and nothing is recorded over it until Record or Overdub is asked for again. The looper goes with the score’s stop, and its view has nothing to ask of it any more: so the score’s stop leaves a take of its own, with the mix and a file for each layer, whenever the last take does not have them all as the loop is, which it does not after a recording or an overdub that went on until the stop, or with Export on Mix. It is written even though the looper is gone by then, and the view keeps it, saying Stopped with the score: each lane still drags its layer, and Send and the drag from its button still place what Export says, whatever it is changed to once the score is stopped. Export chooses what Send places, and the files the take written when a recording or an overdub ends has: Mix (default), the loop as it is heard; Layers, each pass in a file of its own, as it is heard in the loop; or Both. Sending a take places those files in one box named after the take, a slot each, the mix first; dragging it from the Send button drops the same files. A take that Send or a drag asks for, or that the score’s stop leaves, has all of them, so that Export can be changed afterwards. While the score plays, a Send for files the last take does not have, Export having been changed since it was written, asks for a take that has them, as during a pass. Takes of a saved score go into a Takes folder next to the score. Takes of a score that has not been saved yet go into score’s data folder, where they stay until removed. File > Project files > Consolidate project… copies the takes a score uses next to it. File > Project files > Remove unused files… finds the takes the score no longer uses only with Look through the whole project folder checked: by default it looks only in the folders score sorts media into (Audio, Video, …), and the Takes folder is not one of them. It then moves them to an Unused folder of the project, or deletes them.

284.title: Loading a file
284.content: Dropping a sound file on the looper replaces the loop with it, up to Max length, and plays it: Mode shows Play. Loop file is the port this sets: it is not in the looper’s own view, but it is in the inspector, and a file path sent to it, by a cable or an address, loads the file the same way. A file at another sample rate is converted. A mono file goes to every channel.

285.title: Capture
285.content: Record starts taking in when it is pressed, or on the next grid point. Capture works backwards: it takes what was already played, recorded or not, from the input the looper keeps. You play first, and decide afterwards that it was worth keeping. | With no loop, Capture makes one: the last Capture bars bars of the input become the loop, and it plays at once. Mode shows Play, so Stop stops it. | Over a loop, Capture adds what was played over the last round of the loop as a new layer on top, as if that round had been an overdub pass. Each part of it lands where it was played in the loop, and the loop keeps its length: Capture bars does not apply, one round is taken. A stopped loop is taken as going round where it would be had it kept playing, as In phase has it, and it plays from there. The layer is like any other: Max layers and At max layers make room for it as for an overdub pass, the layers that are muted stay muted, it is faded at its ends, moved by the latency, and the layers under it fade by the Feedback once, as for one round of overdub. A take is written as for any pass that closes. | . Capture is undone like a pass: Undo takes the captured layer out, Redo brings it back. On an empty loop, Undo empties the loop as it does after a first recording, and Redo brings it back. Pressed shortly after a point of the grid, within Late stop, Capture ends on that point, as a late stop would. Capture does nothing while a recording or an overdub is going on. Capture and Capture bars are in the Length tab. Capture needs Keep last (s), in the Memory tab, the number of seconds of input the looper keeps at all times. It is 0 by default, which keeps nothing and uses no memory: Capture then does nothing. It also takes no more than Keep last holds, so a loop longer than Keep last is captured in part.

286.title: Monitoring
286.content: Passthrough chooses when the input is heard: . | Choice | Behavior | . | None | The input is never heard. | . | Record (default) | The input is heard while recording and overdubbing only. | . | Full | The input is always heard, mixed over the loop. | .

287.title: Memory and latency
287.content: . | Max length (s), default 60, is the longest loop. A recording that reaches it ends into what After record says; the view shows the loop as full. | Channels, default 2, is the number of channels recorded. | Latency (ms) moves what is recorded earlier in the loop, to make up for the time the input takes to reach the looper. | Engine latency adds the input and output latency the audio driver reports, for a performer playing from the sound card along with the loop. JACK and PortAudio report it; with other drivers, set Latency by hand. Leave it off for input made inside score, which has no such delay. | . The memory for these is reserved when playback starts, so changes to Max length, Max layers, Channels and Keep last apply from the next start.

288.title: Tempo changes
288.content: Follow tempo, in the Speed tab, chooses how a loop follows the tempo of the score, with the same methods as sound files: . | Choice | Behavior | . | Off (default) | The loop keeps the speed it was recorded at, and no longer falls on the bars after a tempo change. | . | Repitch, Repitch fast | The loop is resampled: it keeps to the bars, and its pitch goes up and down with the tempo. | . | Timestretch, Timestretch percussive | The loop is time-stretched: it keeps to the bars and to its pitch. | . A change of Follow tempo applies from the next start of playback, as the time-stretching is set up then. Following applies to a loop that is playing. A loop being recorded or overdubbed plays at its own speed, and a tempo change is heard from the next round of the loop. Mode changes and the end of a recording after its bars always follow the tempo of the score. A take is written with the tempo the loop was recorded at, so a clip made from it follows the tempo of the score like any sound file.

289.title: Reverse and speed
289.content: Reverse and Speed, in the Speed tab, play the loop as a tape would be. | Reverse plays the loop backwards, from where the playhead is. Turned off, the loop plays forwards again from there. Nothing is changed in the loop: reversing is only how it is read. | Speed plays the loop at x1/4, x1/2, x1, x2 or x4. The pitch follows the speed: at x1/2 the loop is an octave down and takes twice as long, at x2 an octave up and half as long. | . An overdub writes where the playhead goes, as on tape. What is played over the reversed loop sounds reversed once the loop plays forwards again; what is played at x1/2 sounds an octave up, and twice as fast, at x1; at x2, an octave down. Speed and Reverse change how the loop is read, not the score’s time: Quantize, Record bars and Late stop go by the score as before, and a loop keeps its length. A recording is always made forwards at x1: it is what makes the loop. With Follow tempo, Speed applies on top of the tempo: at x2, a loop recorded over two bars plays in one bar whatever the tempo, its pitch up an octave even when time-stretched. Past the end set to Extend only extends an overdub going forwards: backwards, the playhead reaches the start of the loop and goes round. The view’s playhead has an arrow pointing the way the loop plays, and the header says when it plays backwards or at another speed than x1. Phase goes down from 1 to 0 while the loop plays backwards.

290.title: Comping
290.content: There is no comp mode: comping is overdubbing with layers cut where wanted, then keeping the best. | Overdub, and cut the takes into layers: New layer on each new attempt, or Passes on Per cycle, in the Play tab, for a layer each time round the loop, or After overdub on New layer for Rec / Play / Dub to do it from one switch. The playhead goes on all along. | Listen to each: Previous layer and Next layer select one, Solo layer hears it alone, Solo layer again hears them all again. | Keep the best: Mute layer mutes a layer, Erase layer removes it. The m and x of a lane do the same in the view. | . | Passes | Behavior | . | Whole (default) | An overdub is one layer, from when it starts to when it stops, unless New layer cuts it. | . | Per cycle | An overdub that goes round the loop several times makes a layer of each round, cut on the start of the loop. With Past the end on Extend, a layer is cut each time the loop grows by its length. | . A layer cut by New layer or Per cycle is closed like any: faded at its ends, and written in a take. It has its own lane, and can be undone or erased on its own. A muted layer is kept but not heard, as if it were erased: it takes nothing from the layers under it with its feedback, and it is drawn dimmed. Muted layers are left out of the mix of a take; a take written as layers still has a file for every layer, the muted ones included, as they would be heard, so that the rounds can be spliced in the timeline.

291.title: Start from In phase
291.content: With Start from set to In phase, the loop stays in phase with the timeline. Playing and overdubbing carry on from where they were, as with Where it was; and whenever the loop is heard again after being stopped, it starts where it would be had it kept playing since it was recorded: . | after Stop, then Play or Overdub; | when the score is played again, from wherever it starts; | when the score jumps to another date while the loop plays. | . The position comes from where the loop was recorded on the timeline. Without Follow tempo, it is counted in the score’s time: a loop of a second stopped for half a second comes back half a loop on. With Follow tempo, it is counted in quarter notes, so the loop comes back on the bars it was recorded on even after a tempo change. Speed and Reverse are taken into account: the loop comes back where it would be at its speed, going its way.

292.title: Presets
292.content: The library has presets for the usual ways of looping. Each one sets every setting of the looper but Channels, which is the input’s, so loading one after another leaves nothing of the one before. They are quantized to the bar unless said otherwise. | Preset | What it is for | . | Song form | Record, Play, Overdub and Play again, for verses and choruses. Quantize is Loop: the first recording ends on a bar, then every change waits for the loop to come round, and a stop lets it play to its end. | . | One footswitch, song form | The same from Rec / Play / Dub alone, a stop also letting the loop play to its end, with a Late stop of 250 ms for a foot that is a little late on the downbeat. | . | One footswitch, layering | Rec / Play / Dub records, goes straight on overdubbing, and each press after that starts a new layer. Play / Stop stops. | . | Comping, a layer per press | Each press of Rec / Play / Dub while overdubbing starts a new take in a layer of its own; mute the ones to drop, and once there are 16, a new take replaces a muted one; takes are written as a mix and as layers. | . | Comping, a layer per round | One overdub, a layer each time round the loop, for trying a part again and again; takes are written as a mix and as layers, to splice the rounds in the timeline. | . | Four bars, then play | A recording of four bars, then plays it. | . | Four bars, then overdub | A recording of four bars, then goes on overdubbing. | . | Free loop | No grid, no Record bars, no Late stop: the loop is as long as it was played for. | . | Ambient decay | Four bars, then overdubbing with no gap and Feedback at 0.7, so that older layers fade away; the input is always heard. | . | Half speed | The loop plays an octave down and twice as long; what is overdubbed sounds an octave up once played at x1. | . | Played backwards | The loop plays backwards, and overdubs over it sound reversed once it plays forwards. | . | Grows as you overdub | A bar long recording, and Past the end on Extend: overdubbing over several bars makes the loop that long. | . | In phase with the timeline | Start from In phase: a loop played again after a stop, or when the score starts or jumps, is where it would be had it kept playing. | . | Capture what I played | Keeps the last minute of input, which Capture needs: press it to make a loop of the last four bars played, or, over a loop, to add its last round as a layer. | . | Takes for editing | Export on Both: takes are written as a mix and as a file for each layer. | .

293.title: Outputs
293.content: Phase goes from 0 to 1 as the loop plays, to drive anything that should follow the loop, such as video.

294.title: Older scores
294.content: Scores and presets made with older versions of the looper load with the settings they had. Controls renamed since keep their values: . | Loop is now Mode, Quantif is now Quantize, and Bars is now Record bars. | Post-action is now After record, with the same choices, and Restart is now Start from: Always is Loop start, Recording is Where it was. A score older than Restart gets Start from’s default, Where it was, where the looper of the time read the loop from its start on every change of mode: set Loop start for that. | Takes is now Export. | Quantif was a list of note values, read as fractions of a bar: a score or a preset made with it gets the grid it waited for. None is None, Whole is 1 bar, and the other values are the same note values: 4th is 1/4, Dotted 8th is 1/8. In a signature other than 4/4, these note values are now note values, a quarter being a quarter, where they used to divide the bar. | Sync is gone: a looper saved in a sync group plays on its own, and keeps its other settings and its cables. | . These change what an older looper does: . | Record on a loop that has something in it overdubs it. It used to record a new loop in its place: clear the loop first for that. | Stopping the process or the score stops the looper: what was being recorded or overdubbed is closed as a pass and written as a take, the playhead goes back to the loop’s start, and a recording or an overdub gives way to Play, which Mode shows; any other mode is taken up again when the score plays again. The looper used to stay in the mode it was in, the playhead where it was. | Overdub on an empty loop records it, then goes on overdubbing; it used to only pass the input through. | . The settings added since come up at their defaults, and these change what such a looper does: . | Layers: each overdub is a layer of its own, with undo. Past 8 layers (Max layers), a pass is merged into the newest layer when it ends. | Channels is 2: a looper used to record as many channels as its input had. Set it for an input of more channels. | Max length (s) is 60: a recording that reaches it ends into what After record says. The looper used to grow its buffer for as long as it recorded. | Take files: every recording and every overdub writes a WAV file, in a Takes folder next to the score, see Takes and the timeline. | Late stop (ms) is 120: a recording asked to stop within 120 ms after a grid point ends on that point. Set it to 0 to end on the next point, as before. | .

296.title: Audio Effects
296.content: . A piano fragment can become a pitched pattern, a distorted pulse or a wash of echoes. Here it shares an effects chain with a bell that you strike by hand, so the same processing is heard on two very different sources.

297.title: Signal chain
297.content: MIDI notes change the granular piano’s pitch; the bell is played live, independently of the sequence. Both pass through drive, a lowpass filter and a modulated delay before reaching two parallel reverbs. Built-in effects, Airwindows and embedded Faust code work together; no separately installed VST is required.

298.title: Try it
298.content: . | Open the ZIP directly in score. The piano recording is included and credited in the patch to Signature Sounds. Use a build with Granola, Faust, Airwindows and BarrVerb; configure audio output at a low listening level. | Start playback, then press the Faust bell’s gate control. Listen to the difference between the repeating piano and a single bell strike passing through the same chain. | Increase delay feedback cautiously to hear repeats persist. Slow the sample-and-hold LFO so each change in delay time is audible on its own: the modulation reshapes the echoes, not the original notes. | Mute one reverb at a time to hear BarrVerb and Airwindows kCathedral5 separately, listening to the space around an attack and the tail after it. | Edit the piano-roll notes while leaving the effects unchanged, then replace the piano with your own source. | . ossia score can load effects from VST, VST3, LV2, CLAP and JSFX plug-ins as well as Faust. Once available in the process library, they can be used alongside the processors in this example. Download this example . Try this on web .

299.title: Learn more
299.content: . | Audio plugins - Complete guide to VST, VST3, CLAP, LV2, JSFX plugins | Faust - Writing and using Faust DSP code | Audio Effects - Built-in audio effect processes | Supported protocols and formats - All supported audio plugin formats | .

301.title: Audio-reactive point geometry
301.content: . A point cloud expands into noisy deformation as the sound level changes. Smoothing makes the movement follow a gradual envelope instead of jumping at every fluctuation. RMS measures the audio input’s level. Its smoothed output drives NoiseField’s deformation amplitude; separate LFO modulation keeps the noise evolving. A color stage makes the generated positions visible in the native point-cloud renderer.

302.title: Try it
302.content: Select a working input in score’s audio settings, allow microphone access if prompted, and start playback. Make a short sound, then hold a steady one. Adjust RMS Gain and Gate so the deformation responds to the levels you intend to use. Lower Exp Smoothing Alpha: the cloud reacts and settles more slowly. The slow noise evolution can continue even when the audio response is quiet, so listen and watch for those two sources of motion separately. No recording is included. If you do not have a microphone, connect a sound-file process to RMS instead. Compute-shader support is required; increase gridSize cautiously because it increases the generated geometry. Try this on web . Download this example .

303.title: Audio-reactive volume
303.content: . A green fractal volume becomes more or less dense-looking with the audio envelope while the viewpoint slowly orbits. The sound changes how the volume is viewed, not its geometry. A compute shader generates a Menger fractal as a three-dimensional texture. The viewer samples that texture along viewing rays to form the image. Smoothed RMS level drives the viewer’s density, while two LFOs drive its viewing angles; the audio does not regenerate the fractal’s structure.

304.title: Try it
304.content: Enable a working audio input, allow microphone access if prompted, and start playback. Raise RMS Gain until quiet sounds make the volume visibly thinner and loud ones make it dense, then lower smoothing Alpha so the density lingers after each sound. Change the Menger generator’s iters or zoom separately. These alter the volume being sampled, whereas the audio changes its apparent density in the viewer. No audio file is bundled; connect a sound-file process to RMS if needed. The embedded volume generator requires compute-shader support; this is a native volume-texture example, not a Qt Quick 3D scene. Try this on web . Download this example .

305.title: Audio-Reactive Visuals
305.content: Generated percussion and live sound animate a geometric pattern, while echo and analog-style distortion turn its movement into trails. A smoothed zoom follows the overall envelope, and a trace threshold reacts separately to the microphone.

306.title: Two analysis paths
306.content: A Stereo Mixer combines the synthesized percussion with live audio for level analysis. RMS converts that sound into a control signal, and OneEuro smoothing makes the zoom follow it more gradually. A second RMS analyzes the microphone independently to control the trace threshold. The steady rhythm shapes the overall motion while a voice or instrument interrupts the image. Turning down the microphone in the mixer does not silence its separate trace-control path.

307.title: Setup
307.content: Use a build with Faust and its standard physical-modeling library for DjembeMIDI. Select a working audio input for the microphone branch; the percussion is synthesized and needs no recording.

308.title: Try it
308.content: . | Start playback and turn Stereo Mixer inputs 1 and 2 down one at a time to hear each source being analyzed, then increase RMS Gain. | Adjust OneEuro smoothing until the zoom follows individual accents, then until it moves gradually. | Adjust the second RMS’s Gate while making quiet and loud sounds: below the gate, the microphone no longer affects the trace threshold. | . To use recorded audio instead, connect a sound-file process to the microphone paths you want to replace. Try this on web . Download this example .

311.content: Parameter movement can give a static sound, light or image a sense of phrasing. Start by deciding whether you want to generate movement or shape movement arriving from elsewhere. | Device modulation shows regular oscillation, repeating steps and wandering noise side by side. It also shows why sending individual changes differs from reading a parameter’s current value. | Smoothing and filtering trades steadiness against responsiveness on generated noise, then calibrates the result to the range a destination needs. | . 313.title: Automation (float)
313.content: . The Automation (float) process allows to control single value parameter using a breakpoints function.

314.title: Basic editing
314.content: Create new points on curve . Multiple points can be added on an automation. To add a point, double-click in the automation slot to create a point under the mouse cursor. You can also create a new point using Ctrl+click(Win / Linux) or⌘+click(Mac) in the automation’s slot. Remove points from curve . To delete a point from an automation, click on a point to select it, then from its contextual menu select Remove. Multiple points and attached segments can be selected and removed at once using the Remove contextual menu entry. Edit points . To edit a point value of position in time, select it using the mouse and move it along the x axis to adjust in position in time, or along the y axis to adjust its value. You will note that when selecting a point, its value gets displayed next to the mouse cursor . For fine control, you can also use the dedicated number boxes from the inspector. Click on a point to select it and display its inspector then use the value number box to adjust to the desired value. Adjust segment’s curve . Power type segments (default) can be added a curve factor. To do so, click a segment and use Shift+Drag. Dragging the curve upward add a log-like curvature to the segment, while dragging downward add a exp-like curvature.

315.title: Segment shapes
315.content: Segments between two points can be set to various predefined shapes. To do so, click a segment and from its contextual menu, choose the desired segment shape in the Type category. Shapes include: . | Power (default) | Linear (a slightly optimized version of Power with zero curve factor) | Standard Easing curves | . | backIn | quadraticIn | quarticIn | sineIn | exponentialIn | . | backOut | quadraticOut | quarticOut | sineOut | exponentialOut | . | backInOut | quadraticInOut | quarticInOut | sineInOut | exponentialInOut | . |   |   |   |   |   | . | bounceIn | cubicIn | quinticIn | circularIn | elasticIn | . | bounceOut | cubicOut | quinticOut | circularOut | elasticOut | . | bounceInOut | cubicInOut | quinticInOut | circularInOut | elasticInOut | . |   |   |   |   |   | . | PerlinInOut |   |   |   |   | .

316.title: Freehand function
316.content: Automation’s function can be hand-drawn using Alt+Drag in Automation editor. Drawn function will get optimized and transformed onto a beak-point function on mouse release so you can edit various points individually.

317.title: Advanced edits
317.content: Lock between points . By default, moving a point in the automation is limited horizontally by previous and next points’ position in automation. This can be turned on and off using the Lock between points option in the automation contextual menu. When off, points can be freely moved along the whole automation’s slot. Suppress on overlap . When Lock between points option is unset, crossing adjacent points can be handled in two different ways. By default, crossing an adjacent point in automation will remove this point. This can be turned off using by unsetting the option in the automation’s contextual menu. When off, moved point will get inserted at its new position without removing other points in automation.

318.title: Tween mode
318.content: Tweening allows an automation to ramp smoothly from the running value of an address which was assigned to, during the first segment. This means that, assuming an OSC address /foo, if tweening is enabled, no matter the visual “start value” of the first point of the automation curve, the actual first point during execution will be taken from the value of /foo when the score reaches that part. This allows smooth transitions from a live control, to a scripted one.

335.title: Beat Tracker
335.content: Beat Tracker estimates tempo and maintains a beat clock from live audio or incoming beat events. It does not change the timeline until its outputs are connected to the desired controls.

336.title: Inputs and setup
336.content: Source selects Audio, Events, or Audio + Events. Audio arrives at In, with channels summed to mono. In Events mode, send pulses to Beat: integers and floats are interpreted as beat numbers, while impulses and other values mean an unnumbered beat. Events per beat accommodates subdivisions, such as 24 pulses per beat for MIDI clock. For audio, select Band, set Gate (dB) above background noise and constrain Min BPM / Max BPM with Limit BPM range. Transport tempo hint helps choose between half-time and double-time interpretations. Clock filter, Whitening, Lookahead (ms) and Offset (ms) refine detection and output timing.

337.title: Outputs and performance controls
337.content: . | Tempo is the estimated BPM; connect it to an interval’s Tempo inlet to drive tempo. | Speed is a playback-rate multiplier that corrects phase as well as tempo; use it with a synchronizer or Speed inlet instead when following position matters. | Phase and Bar phase run from 0 towards 1; Beat index counts beats and Next beat (s) predicts the next beat. | Beat, Downbeat and Onset emit timing events. Confidence, Locked and Valid let the patch decide whether to trust the result. | . Use Tap to establish tempo while unlocked or reset phase while locked; Resync declares the downbeat without changing tempo. x2 and /2 correct tempo-octave mistakes. Nudge -/+ correct alignment. Hold freezes tempo but still follows phase; Follow off freezes the clock and stops analysis. Set Beats per bar to the intended meter. Sparse, ambiguous or silent audio can lose lock. Monitor Confidence and Valid and provide a suitable manual fallback rather than assuming continuous reliable tracking. See Analysis for onset and other audio descriptors.

342.title: Breaking the timeline
342.content: In previous steps of this Quick Start guide, we used score to write simple scenario use cases following a timeline-based approach pretty similar to the one found in usual DAW software. While such an approach allows us to write very precise temporal developments of a scenario, it may also hit some limits in live performance situation or installation where a much more flexible approach is required. score offers a number of features to bridge the gap between different approaches and thus combine timeline-based workflow and cue-based workflow. One of them is the use of trigger points.

343.title: Enabling triggers
343.content: Introducing trigger points in your scenario allows us to keep organizing things in time while allowing interactive triggering of elements: when executing the scenario, parts of the scenario starting with a trigger point will be put “on hold” until they get triggered. When triggered, following automations and states will get executed at the speed and duration specified in the scenario. To add a trigger point, simply select a state on the scenario, then from its inspector, toggle on the trigger icon. When turning on the trigger, you can see a T-like icon appearing on top of the selected state. You can also note that a dashed line appears on top of the preceding automation slot. This indicates that the duration of the preceding automations is now undefined: preceding automations will get executed up until the trigger is, well… triggered. In the example above, the scenario start with a simple fade-in. Notice that it gets executed as the scenario play-head goes across the automation slot. While the scenario play-head continues its progression, you will notice though that the green progression bar at the top of the automation stops as it reaches the trigger point. Execution of the following automations is then on hold until the trigger point is triggered by a mouse click. From then, execution follows its course until the next trigger point in the scenario. Here again, execution is put on hold until trigger point is clicked by mouse.

344.title: Triggers remote control
344.content: In the example above, we used the mouse to trigger the followup of the scenario execution. While convenient for demo purposes, you are more likely to rely on other inputs in creation situation such as some controller gear. You may use any parameter from your device as an input for trigger points. To set an input for a trigger point, just grab the desired parameter in the Device explorer and drop it on the trigger icon. In the example above, we use as an input one button of a Korg nanoKontrol Midi controller. When done, you will see in the inspector the address of the dropped parameter in the address field. You may also drop the parameter on the address field of the trigger point inspector. When playing your scenario, part of your scenario will now get triggered as you press the dedicated button on your controller.

345.title: Buffer queue
345.content: Buffer queue stores incoming Input messages in a bounded queue. It is a control-value buffer, not an audio delay. “Queue” and “Buffer queue” refer to this same process.

346.title: Controls and output
346.content: . | Max length sets capacity. When full, a new message replaces the oldest stored value. | Data chooses Oldest, Newest, or Whole buffer (an ordered list) on Output. | Mode chooses Every tick, On input, On change, When full, On input, when full, On change, when full, On bang, or On bang, pop oldest. | Bang requests output in every mode. Pop removes what was sent: one selected value, or the entire buffer for Whole buffer. The special On bang, pop oldest mode removes the oldest value after each output even with Pop off. | Hold Clear to empty the buffer and discard arrivals. An impulse clears it for one processing tick. Lock prevents new messages being queued without preventing output. | . On input reacts to arrivals even when Clear or Lock discards them. On change reacts to queue additions and clearing, not to the removal caused by Pop. Every tick and When full can therefore repeatedly send stored data without new input. For batches, choose Whole buffer, On change, when full, and Pop. For manual playback, choose Oldest and On bang, pop oldest, then connect a trigger to Bang. See Value delay for delayed echoes rather than explicit queue management.

347.title: Buffers to geometry
347.content: Buffers to geometry wraps GPU buffers in a geometry description. It does not infer a mesh layout from the bytes: formats, offsets, strides and draw settings must agree with the upstream producer. The output is Geometry, not a scene hierarchy.

348.title: Buffer and attribute setup
348.content: Connect buffers to Buffer 0–7. Each of the eight attribute slots has these controls: . | Control | Meaning | . | AttrN buffer | Input buffer number, 0–7. -1 disables the attribute. | . | AttrN offset | Byte offset from the beginning of the connected buffer view. | . | AttrN stride | Byte distance between records. 0 uses the selected format’s tightly packed size. | . | AttrN format | Component representation: Float, Half, unsigned/signed integer, short or normalized byte formats with the available component counts. | . | AttrN semantic | Attribute meaning, such as position, normal, texcoord0 or color0. Custom attribute names are preserved for consumers that understand them. | . | AttrN instanced | Advance this attribute per instance rather than per vertex. | . Several attributes can refer to the same interleaved buffer. Their offsets differ but their record strides must match.

349.title: Draw settings
349.content: | Control | Meaning | . | Index Buffer | Buffer 0–7 containing indices, or -1 for no index buffer. | . | Index Format | UInt16 or UInt32. | . | Index Offset | Byte offset into the connected index-buffer view. | . | Vertices | Geometry draw count. Set it to match the intended draw; the process does not derive it from buffer size. | . | Instances | Number of instances, starting at 1. Supply enough records for instanced attributes. | . | Topology | Triangles, TriangleStrip, TriangleFan, Lines, LineStrip or Points. | . | Cull Mode | None, Front or Back. | . | Front Face | CounterClockwise or Clockwise winding. | . | Position, Rotation, Scale | XYZ translation, Euler rotation in degrees and per-axis scale. | .

350.title: Example: tightly packed XYZ positions
350.content: . | Use Array to buffer from Geometry and buffer utilities to convert [0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0] to Float32. | Connect its output to Buffer 0. | Set Attr0 buffer to 0, Attr0 format to Float3, Attr0 semantic to position, Attr0 offset to 0 and Attr0 stride to 12 bytes. | Leave other attributes and Index Buffer at -1. Set Vertices to 3, Instances to 1, Topology to Triangles and Cull Mode to None. | Inspect Geometry with Geometry Info before connecting it to the Render Pipeline. | . For interleaved Float3 positions followed by Float3 normals, use a 24-byte stride for both attributes and offsets of 0 and 12 bytes respectively. The data format describes the existing bytes; selecting another format does not convert them.

This page describes the current named-semantic version; use it for new patches unless an existing layout specifically requires v1. For extracting or reorganizing existing geometry, see Extract buffer and Repack attributes.

354.title: What is bytebeat?
354.content: Bytebeat is a minimal approach to programming synthetic sounds using arithmetic and bit-level properties of numbers. Expressions turn a time counter t into an audio waveform. score’s Bytebeat process compiles these expressions as C++; it is not a JavaScript interpreter or a separate general-purpose language implementation. Guides and other implementations: . | Countercomplex’s blogpost which introduced Bytebeat | The absolute beginner’s guide to coding Bytebeats! | Greggman’s implementation | Radavis’s implementation | .

355.title: Expression evaluation in score
355.content: Enter one expression per line, not a complete C++ program. Each non-empty expression line is evaluated independently; the generated wrapper converts each result to signed char, sums the converted values and divides by 128 times the number of expressions. Multiple lines are mixed together, not evaluated as consecutive statements in a script. The generated signal is copied to both output channels. t is an integer-based counter. In the current implementation it is the output sample counter divided by four using integer division, so it advances once per four output samples. Formula comments mentioning 8, 11, 22 or 32 kHz describe their original context, not a per-expression sample-rate setting in score. Common operators include arithmetic +, -, *, /, %; bitwise &, |, ^, ~; shifts <<, >>; comparisons; and the conditional expression condition ? a : b. ^ means XOR, not exponentiation. Use parentheses when combining operators. See the C++ language reference for the underlying syntax. C++ versus JavaScript semantics . Many published Bytebeat formulas target JavaScript players. They are inspiration, not a promise of source compatibility: . | C++ integer division truncates; ordinary C++ % operates on integers. JavaScript number arithmetic, coercions and floating-point remainder do not carry over unchanged. | In score’s current wrapper, expressions containing / or % select an integer-backed helper type for t. Its overloaded division and remainder return zero for a zero divisor in the guarded operations. This is not a JavaScript numeric model, and it does not make every expression safe: operations that use ordinary C++ values, invalid shifts and other undefined behavior still need care. | JavaScript bitwise operations apply their own numeric conversions and shift-count rules. C++ shifts require a valid count for the operand width; do not assume formulas such as t >> t have portable behavior. | Names such as w, b, r and n in the archive are not predefined score variables. JavaScript-style assignments do not implicitly declare C++ variables. JavaScript array literals such as [1,2,3] are not C++ array expressions; string indexing in C++ yields a character value rather than JavaScript’s numeric string coercion. | If the SDK supplies <cmath>, the wrapper includes it, allowing C++ mathematical functions. A JavaScript formula may require adapting a call such as Math.abs to an appropriate C++ abs / std::abs overload. The current wrapper also provides a limited Math compatibility object when these headers are available, but it is not JavaScript’s Math object. | . The current Math helper exposes max, min, abs, pow, sqrt, floor, ceil, round, sin, cos, tan, sinh, cosh, tanh, asin, acos, atan, asinh, acosh, and atanh; constants are E, LN10, LN2, LOG10E, LOG2E, PI, SQRT1_2, and SQRT2. Its functions use the wrapper’s integer-based type: sqrt is an integer square root, floor / ceil / round return their already-integer argument, and trigonometric results are converted back to that type. pow uses repeated integer multiplication for positive exponents. Do not expect JavaScript floating-point results or undocumented Math methods. The Bytebeat implementation defines the wrapper, helper operators and output conversion. These are score-specific behavior, separate from the ISO C++ language definition.

356.title: Safety and availability
356.content: Bytebeat uses the native C++ JIT runtime. Its code is unsandboxed and runs inside score; numeric helpers do not provide memory isolation or protect against blocking code. Compile only trusted expressions, save your document and start playback at a low audio level. The historical collection includes explicitly loud formulas and formulas needing adaptation; successful compilation does not establish safe execution or a safe listening level.

359.content: . For the language explanation, C++ versus JavaScript semantics, and the complete attributed formula collection, see Bytebeat expressions.

360.title: Usage
360.content: Bytebeat code can be edited when pressing the small “window” button on the process. Each line of code can be treated independently. This process compiles native C++ expressions, not JavaScript. It requires the C++ JIT runtime; SDK header availability controls access to mathematical functions. Code is unsandboxed: save your document, use trusted formulas and start playback at a low audio level.

363.title: Calibrator
363.content: . This process allows to calibrate an input signal to extract the “significant” part of the signal, when it is impossible to define an accurate range of values at the time the score is being authored: for instance, consider a temperature sensor. Its range as defined in the Device explorer could be between -30°C and 70°C. However, the daily variations could be sometimes around 15°, sometimes around 25°… with most of the range being unused. The Calibrator object outputs values between 0 and 1, by computing over time the actual minimum and maximum of the input values and scaling between those. In addition, it allows to access a few statistics on the input signal. The effective range can further be adjusted and shaped. To get its output, simply connect to the “Scaled” output. In this example, the input of the calibrator is connected to the sensors:/temperature sensor, which has a range of 0-100°. But if the inputs of the process only vary between 10° and 30° while the installation is runnning, the scaled output will be 0 for 10° and 1 for 30°.

364.title: Example: showing the raw camera feed
364.content: In this example, we perform the following steps: . | Add the camera input through the device explorer. | Likewise, add a window device in which the camera is going to be rendered. | Add a “passthrough” video effect, to connect the camera input to the window output. | Set up the passthrough ports. | Press play and enjoy ! | . The passthrough effect can be found in the user library, in the folder Presets/GLSL_Shaders/utility.

365.title: Technical information
365.content: Camera capture uses the platform’s available input mechanisms and FFmpeg conversion/decoding paths. Supported camera modes depend on the device, driver and score build; camera access may require operating-system permission. Default Camera selects an available camera and suitable mode when connected. Select a named camera and mode to fix the device, resolution and frame rate. Texture outlet inspectors preview the rendered result. Window Capture and NDI also offer previews in their capture settings.

366.title: Window and screen capture
366.content: Builds with capture support register Window Capture as a separate video input. Its Mode choices are Window, All Screens, Single Screen and Region, with unsupported modes disabled by the current backend. Select the window or screen, or set Region X, Region Y, Region Width and Region Height. Refresh updates the available sources; Frame Rate and Preview help configure the feed. On Wayland, choose the capture source in the system picker when capture starts. On macOS, grant Screen Recording permission in System Settings → Privacy & Security, then refresh. Windows and X11 use their own capture backends. Route Window Capture to a texture inlet just like a camera; it is not the Window output device.

367.title: GPhoto2 DSLR
367.content: Builds with GPhoto2 support expose GPhoto2 DSLR for compatible cameras. Camera Model and Port identify the camera; its live-preview images feed the texture graph and camera-reported configuration entries become typed device parameters. This needs the libgphoto2 runtime and a camera with supported preview/configuration operations, not merely USB connectivity. See GPhoto2 DSLR device for discovery, runtime libraries and the configuration tree.

368.title: V4L2 support
368.content: V4L2 is the Linux video subsystem API. The v4l2loopback kernel module allows for a lot of useful things. Grabbing the screen with v4l2loopback . $ sudo modprobe v4l2loopback $ ffmpeg -f x11grab -framerate 60 -video_size 3840x2160 -i :0.0+0,0 -f v4l2 /dev/video0 . Forwarding an external video file to score through v4l2loopback . $ sudo modprobe v4l2loopback $ while 1 ; do ffmpeg -re -i ./test.mp4 -f v4l2 /dev/video0 ; done .

369.title: Special camera support
369.content: Microsoft Kinect . Support for Kinect cameras has been implemented through the Freenect library. It requires building score from source with the Freenect libraries. Shared video sources . Use the dedicated Spout devices on Windows, Syphon on macOS, or PipeWire video on Linux. These are available input/output paths in compatible builds, not camera-driver modes. GStreamer and Libav provide additional streaming inputs.

370.title: Camera device
370.content: . Score supports using camera inputs in its VFX graph. The camera can be used as the input of a texture port.

371.title: Blending native scene cameras
371.content: . Move between an oblique view of a chessboard, an overhead view and a distant narrow-angle shot with a single two-dimensional control. Blending cameras turns a collection of composed shots into a playable viewpoint. Three native Camera processes feed Camera Switch. Nodes converts the position of its Input Point into blend weights, so moving across the control changes the camera before the scene is rendered. This blends viewpoint parameters rather than crossfading three rendered images.

372.title: Try it
372.content: Open the ZIP directly in score; the chess model is included. Start playback and move Nodes’ Input Point toward each of its three nodes, then travel slowly between them. Watch both the viewing angle and framing change. For a direct cut instead of a continuous move, use Camera Switch’s selection mode and Index. If you replace the model, adjust all three cameras’ Eye and Target values to its scale. The model and rendering shader are included; this uses the native scene pipeline, not a Qt Quick 3D controller. Try this on web . Download this example .

373.title: Camera input
373.content: . Keep a performer or installation visitor visible while sound changes the color, blur and distortion of their live image.

374.title: Image and treatment
374.content: Audio analysis turns microphone level into controls for the shader pipeline. Smoothing makes some changes gradual; peak detection resets the distortion on sharper accents. Movement in front of the camera changes the source picture, while sound changes what happens to it.

375.title: Setup
375.content: Select an available camera in the Camera device settings and a working audio input in the audio settings. Grant camera permission where required and close applications that hold exclusive access to it.

376.title: Try it
376.content: . | Start playback and move silently in front of the camera, then make sound while staying still: movement changes the picture, sound changes the effects applied to it. | Adjust RMS Gain to suit your input, then lower the smoothing for abrupt responses or raise it for lingering transitions. | Change peak detection’s trigger and reload thresholds. Clap a few times, then make a sustained sound, and watch when the distortion resets. | . Without a microphone, connect a sound-file process to RMS. The recording replaces the analysis source, not the camera. Try this on web . Download this example .

378.title: CAN device
378.content: The CAN device receives CAN bus frames and decodes their signals using a .dbc database. It is useful for bringing sensor or machine telemetry into a score without writing a packet decoder. It requires a build with CAN support and a Linux SocketCAN interface. It is receive-only: writing an address does not transmit a CAN frame, configure a sensor, or implement CANopen control services.

379.title: Set up the bus
379.content: . | Connect a supported CAN adapter and configure its SocketCAN interface outside score, including the bitrate appropriate to your hardware. The device dialog does not configure the bus bitrate. | Choose Add device → CAN in the Device explorer. | Select the Interface and a DBC file describing the incoming messages. The interface list contains the interfaces present on this machine; you can also type a name when preparing a document before connecting its adapter. | Check the database summary: it reports message and signal counts, the effective hexadecimal message identifiers, and parser warnings. | Expand the device and use its signal addresses as inputs to your score. | . DBC files in the library can also appear in the CAN device picker. Selecting a database does not create or bring up a CAN interface. A virtual SocketCAN interface such as vcan0 can be used instead of physical hardware for development.

380.title: Settings
380.content: | Setting | Meaning | . | Name | Device name used in score addresses. | . | Interface | SocketCAN interface, for example can0 or vcan0. There is no assumed can0 when none is detected. | . | DBC file | Database used to construct the signal tree and decode frames. Keep this file available when moving the project. | . | Node id offset | Added to each database message identifier. For a database describing CANopen node 1 with identifiers 0x181, 0x281, an offset of 1 targets 0x182, 0x282. This changes frame matching, not the hardware’s node ID. | . | 32-bit ints are floats | Workaround for vendor databases that describe IEEE 754 float payloads as 32-bit integers. Leave disabled unless the database is known to require it; explicit float/double declarations are unaffected. | . | CAN FD | Allows payloads larger than eight bytes; classic frames remain supported. The interface and bus must also support the traffic being received. | . | Filter to database | Enabled by default. Requests per-socket kernel filtering to the database’s message identifiers. | . Several score devices can share an interface with different databases or node-ID offsets. This is useful for several identical sensors on one bus.

381.title: Address mapping
381.content: A DBC message becomes a container; each signal becomes a parameter beneath it: . CAN:/MessageName/SignalName . The decoder uses the database’s byte order, signedness, scaling, offsets and multiplexing information. Scaled and floating-point signals become float parameters; suitable unscaled integers remain integers, and a single unscaled bit becomes a boolean. Descriptions and domains come from the database where available. Only unambiguous supported DBC unit strings receive score units; an arbitrary vendor unit is not automatically converted. Standard and extended identifiers are distinguished even when their numeric values match. Unsupported or malformed database content is reported through warnings; the presence of a tree is not proof that every vendor-specific DBC extension was understood. If values do not change, check the interface state, actual frame IDs, node offset, frame format and database before changing signal scaling. See also Working with devices and Mapper device for combining decoded signals.

388.title: Classifier
388.content: . The Classifier process provides real-time machine learning classification capabilities using RapidLib algorithms. It’s similar to tools such as Wekinator but integrated directly into score’s processing pipeline. It is very close to the Regressor process: the difference is that Regressor interpolates while Classifier outputs the exact input value that was set during training.

401.title: CoAP Device
401.content: . CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) is a specialized web transfer protocol designed for use with constrained nodes and networks in the Internet of Things (IoT). It is a standard internet protocol closely related to HTTP in behavior and operations, but with much more efficient communication optimized for resource-limited devices.

402.title: Overview
402.content: CoAP is designed for: . | Constrained devices with limited processing power and memory | Lossy networks with high packet loss and low bandwidth | Battery-powered devices requiring energy-efficient communication | Machine-to-machine (M2M) communication in IoT ecosystems | Embedded control systems and sensor networks | . Key CoAP features: . | UDP-based for low overhead (default port: 5683) | RESTful architecture similar to HTTP but optimized for constraints | Built-in discovery mechanism via /.well-known/core | Observe pattern for real-time data subscription | Block-wise transfers for handling large payloads | .

403.title: Supported Transports
403.content: ossia score supports all standard CoAP transports: . UDP (Default) . | Lightweight, connectionless communication | Best for battery-powered and resource-constrained devices | Port 5683 (5684 for DTLS secure connections) | . TCP . | Reliable, connection-oriented communication | Better for stable network connections | Useful when message ordering is critical | . WebSocket . | CoAP over WebSocket transport | Browser compatibility and firewall traversal | Integration with web-based systems | .

404.content: Basic Configuration . | Add CoAP Device: Right-click Device Explorer → Add Device → CoAP | Configure Connection: . | Host: Target device IP address (e.g., 192.168.1.100) | Port: CoAP port (5683 for UDP, custom for others) | Transport: UDP, TCP, or WebSocket | . | . CoAP’s discovery mechanism then automatically finds available resources which get exposed as ossia device explorer nodes.

Discovery Problems . | Check /.well-known/core endpoint responds correctly | Validate link format syntax in discovery responses | Try manual resource addition if auto-discovery fails | Verify content-type headers in discovery responses | .

408.title: Combining lists and selecting routes
408.content: . Should several signals travel together, or should only one control a destination at a time? Three moving waveforms make the difference visible.

409.title: Overview
409.content: Combine packs the three values into a list; Spread separates them again. None of the signals needs to be chosen over the others. Mux instead selects one input, and Demux sends its input to one selected output. The displays show these operations locally, without media or external devices.

410.title: Try it
410.content: Start playback in nodal view and watch the Signal displays. | Change Mux’s Current index between 0, 1 and 2. The output follows the chosen waveform; the sources themselves do not change. | Change Demux’s Current index while a waveform is moving. Watch new values arrive at a different display. Unselected displays may retain their history, but receive no new messages. | Follow the Combine and Spread branch. Change one LFO and find its corresponding output after the list is separated: all three signals remain available together. | Add another signal and adjust the inlet and outlet counts to match. Decide whether the new signal should be another selectable source or another component of the group. | . Download this example . Try this on web .

411.title: Combine and Spread Signals
411.content: . Group two independent movements so they can travel together without losing their identities. An LFO supplies a repeating rhythm and an automation curve supplies a drawn shape. Combine packs them into an array for a shared processing stage; Spread separates them again for different destinations.

412.title: Try it
412.content: Start playback and watch the combined display next to the two individual traces. Edit the automation curve and watch the second component change while the first continues its rhythm. Then change the LFO rate to vary only the first component. Its quantification is enabled, which explains the steps in that trace. The array holds control values, not audio channels. No external device is needed to explore this routing pattern. Download this example . Try this on web .

414.title: List of command-line options
414.content: Getting the list of options . $ ossia-score --help . Loading a score on startup: . $ ossia-score filename # For example: $ ossia-score /home/oscar/my-score.score . Playing a score on startup . $ ossia-score --autoplay filename # For example: $ ossia-score --autoplay /home/oscar/my-score.score . Playing a score on startup after some delay . This is useful if for instance the score has audio plug-ins that take some time to load, such as orchestral plug-ins with large sound banks. $ ossia-score --autoplay filename --wait delay_in_seconds # For example: $ ossia-score --autoplay /home/oscar/my-score.score --wait 5 . Loading score without showing the GUI . $ ossia-score --no-gui . (note: this is not very useful without specifying a file to load). Loading score without showing the “do you want to restore” pop-up dialog . This is useful if you are quitting score for instance by killing the process, as score will register that as a crash, which will cause the pop-up to show up next time. $ ossia-score --no-restore . Timeline rendering . --opengl enables OpenGL rendering of the main timeline; --no-opengl disables it. The timeline defaults to non-OpenGL rendering. These switches do not select the video/GPU processing backend. --vector-gui favors vector drawing where available (sharper when zooming, potentially slower); --no-vector-gui favors cached pixmaps. These are GUI rendering choices, not audio or video quality settings. Running a startup script . ossia-score --no-gui --wait 2 /path/to/project.score --script /path/to/setup.js ossia-score --no-gui --script 'console.log("ready"); Qt.exit(0);' . --script can be repeated. An existing file path takes precedence over inline JavaScript; .mjs files are imported as ES modules and an exported initialize() function is called when present. Other script files are evaluated as JavaScript. Quote inline code so the shell does not interpret it. Scripts run after the document has loaded, or against a new empty document when no score was supplied. --wait N adds a non-negative, whole-second delay before startup scripts and autoplay. There is also a short startup scheduling delay; this is not a precise synchronization clock. Supplying --script bypasses the start screen and normal session restoration. A missing/unreadable script exits with status 2; an evaluation or module-initialization error exits with status 3. A successful script does not automatically quit: use Qt.exit(code) when a batch task is finished. Autoplay and scripts are both scheduled after startup; do not rely on their relative order to finish setup before playback. See Scripting for the scripting environment. Local device ports . ossia-score --local-osc-port 16666 --local-ws-port 19999 project.score . These set the default local score device OSC and OSCQuery WebSocket ports. Defaults are 6666 and 9999 respectively. Command-line options take precedence over SCORE_LOCAL_OSC_PORT / SCORE_LOCAL_WS_PORT, then the built-in defaults. Existing document device settings can have their own ports; edit the score device in the Device explorer to change those. Give independent running instances non-conflicting ports. These options are supplied by the engine plug-in, so the core --help output does not list them. Custom QML applications . --ui /path/to/App.qml loads a custom UI without the normal editor and disables restoration. --ui-debug /path/to/App.qml loads it while keeping the score editor visible for debugging. A score file can also be supplied; add --autoplay explicitly if it should play. For packaging a UI, score and assets together, see Custom applications. Developer compilation commands . With the JIT plug-in and matching SDK available, --compile-node /path/to/Object.hpp compiles an Avendish object and --compile-addon /path/to/addon compiles a supported source add-on. They register the result and exit rather than installing a binary package. See Plug-ins with Avendish for the required source shape and platform constraints.

415.title: Complete recommended command line to launch a score on startup
415.content: On Linux: . $ /usr/bin/ossia-score --no-gui --no-restore --wait 5 --autoplay "/path/to/your/score.score" . On macOS: . $ /Applications/Score.app/Contents/MacOS/score --no-gui --no-restore --wait 5 --autoplay "/path/to/your/score.score" . On Windows: . > "c:\Program Files\ossia score\score.exe" --no-gui --no-restore --wait 5 --autoplay "c:\path\to\your\score.score" .

416.title: List of useful environment variables
416.content: Set environment variables before starting score. The examples below use POSIX shell syntax; Windows users can use set NAME=value in cmd.exe or $env:NAME="value" in PowerShell. | Variable | Effect | . | QSG_RHI_BACKEND=opengl | Select the initial graphics processing backend. Recognized values are opengl, vulkan, metal, d3d11 and d3d12; the platform, Qt build and driver must support the requested backend. Metal is macOS-specific and Direct3D is Windows-specific. This is separate from timeline --opengl. | . | SCORE_OPENGL_FORMAT=gles | Request OpenGL ES for OpenGL context probing; gl requests desktop OpenGL core profile. This chooses the API family, not a numeric GL version, and cannot add missing driver capabilities. | . | SCORE_LOCAL_OSC_PORT=16666 | Default local device OSC port, unless overridden on the command line. | . | SCORE_LOCAL_WS_PORT=19999 | Default local device OSCQuery WebSocket port, unless overridden on the command line. | . | SCORE_PRETTIFY_JSON=1 | Write indented JSON when saving JSON documents, useful for reviewing diffs. The option is checked for presence: unset it to restore compact output. It is not a command to reformat arbitrary files. | . | SCORE_DISABLE_ALSA=1 | Disable ALSA device enumeration on Linux. | . | SCORE_DISABLE_AUDIOPLUGINS=1 | Disable startup scanning of external audio plug-ins, including VST, VST3, LV2 and CLAP where compiled in. | . | FAUST_LIB_PATH=/some/path | Override the default location of the bundled Faust libraries; see Faust. | . For example: . QSG_RHI_BACKEND=vulkan SCORE_PRETTIFY_JSON=1 ossia-score project.score . score consumes QSG_RHI_BACKEND during graphics setup and removes it from the process environment after applying it, so independently embedded Qt runtimes in audio plug-ins do not inherit an incompatible backend request. Select only a backend available in the application’s graphics settings.

417.title: Command line API
417.content: You can launch ossia score from the command line or shell scripts with various useful options.

418.title: Common practices
418.content: The following pages will guide you through recurring patterns and snippets that apply to various use-cases common in the creation of media artworks. For instance, how to spatialize sound beyond stereo, how to organize a score in scenes, how to play cues, what are the possibilities for live-coding in score… .

419.title: Bitfocus Companion Device
419.content: . Bitfocus Companion provides modules for controlling streaming, broadcast and AV equipment. score can host Companion modules directly, exposing their actions, feedback and variables in the Device explorer.
