A separate Companion application or Stream Deck is not required for this module-hosting workflow. Compatibility depends on the individual module, its runtime requirements and the target equipment; a module in the package is not a guarantee that every Companion feature is implemented by score.

420.title: Requirements
420.content: Software . | ossia score with Companion package installed from the package manager in the settings | Compatible software or hardware controllers you want to use. | . Package Installation . | Open the Package Manager from the settings | Search for “Bitfocus” in the remote packages list | Install the Bitfocus Companion Modules package. | Restart ossia score | .

421.title: Device Setup
421.content: 1. Add Companion Device in score . | Right-click in Device Explorer | Select Add Device | Choose Bitfocus from protocols | Select the actual device or protocol in the list. If the list is empty, check that the package is installed. | Configure the selected module’s connection fields, such as host, credentials or product. These fields are supplied by the module, not a universal Companion server address. | .

422.title: Available Controls
422.content: The tree is generated from the module’s definitions. Categories are singular in addresses and appear only when the module supplies them: . | Address shape | Use | . | Device:/action/actionId | Send a pulse to execute an action. | . | Device:/action/actionId/optionId | Set an option consumed by that action, using the option’s type and available choices. | . | Device:/feedback/feedbackId | Read the latest result reported by the module’s feedback subscription. | . | Device:/feedback/feedbackId/optionId | Configure the feedback subscription. Changing an option updates the subscription. | . | Device:/variable/variableId | Read a variable published by the module. | . Use the actual IDs shown in the tree; action descriptions may be more readable than their address names. For a multi-option action, set its options first, then send the pulse to its parent action address. For an action with exactly one exposed option, writing that option also executes the action; avoid an extra pulse unless you intend to execute it twice. Feedback is data, not a rendered Companion button. Boolean feedback becomes a boolean parameter; other feedback may carry values or style data. Variables and feedback are supplied by the module and should not be treated as generic writable remote settings. A module may publish no feedback until it has connected, or may change its definitions after configuration.

423.title: Host and project requirements
423.content: The package contains the modules and may provide their Node.js runtimes. score selects a packaged runtime matching the module’s requested major version when available, otherwise it looks for node (node.exe on Windows) on the executable search path. Missing runtime or module dependencies can prevent connection. The module configuration is saved with the device. Keep the corresponding module package installed on machines that open the project. Treat projects and exported device files containing connection credentials as sensitive; do not assume that export removes secrets. This is not an import of Companion button pages, layouts or an entire Companion project. Build score states and processes around the exposed actions and values. The module owns the address tree, so manually adding arbitrary children does not add new module functionality.

424.title: Related Documentation
424.content: . | OSC Device - Direct OSC communication | Control Surface - UI control surfaces to control specific modules in the timeline. | Remote Control - score remote control | .

425.title: Compute-rendered Clifford attractor
425.content: . An accumulating field of points reveals a Clifford attractor as its shape slowly changes. The image shows both the current form and traces of earlier ones.

426.title: Modulation and fading
426.content: Slow LFOs vary the attractor parameters while the compute shader draws points into the image. Brightness shapes their visibility, and fading determines how much of the earlier drawing remains. Fast fading with slow modulation shows one distinct form; slow fading with faster modulation layers several.

427.title: Try it
427.content: . | Start playback and observe a full sweep of the slow modulation before changing it. Alter the LFOs instead of manually adjusting an inlet they already drive. | Raise brightness to make new points more visible, then change fadeRate to set how quickly old ones disappear. | Raise pointsPerThread for a denser drawing; past a point, the image barely improves while the frame rate drops. | . Use a graphics backend with compute support. No external image or geometry is needed; this patch is a visual experiment, not a performance benchmark. Try this on web . Download this example .

428.title: CSF Compute Shaders
428.content: The Compute Shader process runs CSF shaders: score’s compute-shader extension of ISF. Use CSF when a fullscreen fragment pass is not the right model: image processing, storage images, GPU simulations, particle systems, geometry generation, geometry filters, buffer writes, volume generation, and indirect draw preparation. A CSF file is a GLSL compute shader with a JSON header. It can be dropped from the file explorer or user library. Controls, GPU resources, input and output ports are built from the header.

429.title: Using the process
429.content: Drop a CSF file into the score, connect its generated resource inlets, and send image outputs to a video output. Geometry outputs need Model Display or Render Pipeline before they can be displayed as an image. For geometry with its own topology, set the downstream Render Pipeline Mode to Geometry. The CSF language reference contains a minimal image filter, every resource and pass field, buffer layouts, geometry macros, expressions and built-ins. Shader cookbook provides image, geometry, indirect-work and audio recipes. Go directly to a relocated section: . | Minimal file | Header fields | Resource types | Images | 3D image | Persistent image | Sampled textures | Storage buffers | Uniform buffers | Geometry resources | Generator or filter | Geometry fields | Attribute fields | COPY_FROM | Indirect draw | Auxiliary buffers and textures | SSBO auxiliary | UBO auxiliary | Texture auxiliary | Custom types | Passes and execution models | Execution model types | Indirect dispatch | Expressions | Built-in uniforms | Image formats | Patterns | Image filter | Geometry filter | Particle feedback | .

430.title: Runtime requirements
430.content: Compute and storage images require a compatible device and backend. Integer storage formats require Qt 6.10 or newer as well as device support; earlier Qt versions can fall back to RGBA8 without preserving integer semantics. See Graphics pipeline. Keep the bounds checks in the reference examples when changing image dimensions or geometry counts.

431.title: Related Processes
431.content: . | ISF Shaders: Fullscreen fragment shaders and post-processing. | Render Pipeline: Draw CSF-generated or filtered geometry. | Model Display: Display geometry with a built-in renderer. | Lightness Computer: Convert texture outputs to pixel arrays. | .

433.title: Computer vision
433.content: Computer vision utilities provide classical image filtering and analysis, blob and contour processing, and feature and motion analysis through the optional CV add-on. See Add-ons for availability and graphics requirements. For model-based detection and pose estimation, see AI Recognition.

435.title: Console panel
435.content: Open the console with Ctrl+Shift+C(Win / Linux) or⌘+Shift+C(Mac). Enter JavaScript in the input line and press Enter to evaluate it in the application context. Results appear above the prompt; evaluation errors are shown with ERROR:. The console can inspect and edit the current document, not just calculate values. var selected = Score.selectedObject(); if (selected) console.log(Score.path(selected)); console.log(Score.documentName()); .

436.title: Completion and history
436.content: The prompt offers completion for Score, Util and Device; Ctrl+Space requests completion. Up and Down browse command history, which is saved across application restarts. | Shortcut in the input line | Action | . | Ctrl+A / Ctrl+E | Move to start / end. | . | Ctrl+B / Ctrl+F | Move backward / forward one character. | . | Ctrl+U | Clear the line. | . | Ctrl+K | Delete from cursor to end. | . | Ctrl+W | Delete the previous word. | . | Ctrl+T | Transpose neighboring characters. | .

437.title: Editing safely
437.content: Use Score.withMacro(function() { ... }) to group document changes into one undo step; inspect Score.canUndo() and Score.undoText() before undoing. Device writes, filesystem operations and shell commands are not automatically undoable. Console scripts have the application’s permissions: paste only trusted code. See Scripting for library scripts, startup scripts and menu actions, and the editor scripting reference for Score, Util, View, devices and protocols. The Javascript process uses a separate execution engine, so a console variable is not automatically available in its tick. The JavaScript/QML language overview explains the runtime differences.

439.title: Context-Free Art
439.content: Generate images from a Context Free design grammar (CFDG): named rules compose and repeat shapes rather than processing a camera or movie frame. See the Context Free / CFDG language reference for grammar structure, shape adjustments, syntax versions and the upstream manual. This is not a real-time process. For continuous image processing and feedback during playback, use ISF Shaders.

440.title: Context Free and CFDG
440.content: Context Free generates an image from a context-free design grammar (CFDG). Rules replace a named shape with other shapes until the result consists of drawable primitives. score exposes this language through Context-Free Art; image generation is not a real-time shader operation.

441.title: Language reference
441.content: The official Context Free manual covers the language. Its reference sections include: . | Startshape: the root shape from which generation begins. | Shape rules: definitions, parameters and weighted alternatives. | Shape adjustments: relative position, scale, rotation, color and opacity. | Expressions: arithmetic, functions and random expressions. | Control flow: loops, conditions and transformations. | Version 2 syntax: the older grammar used by many existing designs. | . Choose the syntax matching your program; do not combine the older rule form with newer shape syntax indiscriminately. The upstream manual also describes the standalone application’s capabilities, not a promise that score exposes every renderer or export option.

442.title: Reading a grammar
442.content: The essential elements are a starting shape, definitions for named shapes, primitive shapes such as squares or circles, and adjustments attached to each invocation. A child inherits its parent’s drawing state with those adjustments applied. Reusing a shape definition therefore creates related forms at different sizes, positions and colors without duplicating the drawing instructions. Recursion is a way to elaborate a form, not a timeline loop. A recursive branch that continually reduces its scale eventually becomes too small to draw; a design that keeps producing large visible shapes can require much more work. Establish a modest static design before trying a more expensive grammar during a performance.

443.title: Relation to other languages in score
443.content: Use EisenScript for rule-based 3D geometry. The two languages share ideas but have different syntax, transformation rules and termination behaviour. For per-frame image effects and GPU feedback, use ISF instead of treating CFDG as a fragment shader.

444.title: Impulse metronome
444.content: . The simplest possible metronome, synchronized to its parent interval. Will send an impulse on each beat.

445.title: Free metronome
445.content: . A desynchronized metronome. It can ignore the parent interval’s tempo and will instead beat at its own unrelated speed, a bit like the [metro] objects in Pure Data or Max/MSP. If “Quantify” is set on “Free”, then the raw frequency in Hertz will be used as tempo source. Else, the parent tempo is used. The rate can be chosen with the musical division selector. See Free Metronome for the current time-chooser-based version and legacy behaviour.

446.title: Messages, routing and storage
446.content: | Task | Processes | . | Send a manual trigger or hold a repeated trigger | Bang and Button | . | Gate, select or distribute values | Spigot, Mux and Demux, Switch | . | Count arrivals or walk through a sequence | Counter, Enumerator | . | Retain and release messages | Buffer queue, Value delay | . | Join asynchronous values | Rendezvous | . | Store indexed data | Tables | . | Combine or choose inputs | Value Mixer, Multi-choice | . | Parse text and binary values | Regex, String / byte conversion, Value serialization | . Where a process uses musical or absolute durations, see Time Chooser. “Every tick” means every execution processing block, not every beat or graphics frame.

448.title: String tool
448.content: Send UTF-8 Text to apply ASCII trim, optional Slice (Start and Length in Unicode codepoints), literal Find/Replacement, ASCII Case, Reverse, Rotate left, Repeat and padding. Min length, Max length and Max bytes bound the result. Negative slice Start counts from the end; Length -1 retains the remainder. The output is Text, with failures on Error. Reversal works on codepoints, not grapheme clusters, so combined characters can separate.

449.title: Split string
449.content: Splits Text into Parts using a literal Delimiter. An empty delimiter splits Unicode codepoints. Keep empty retains empty fields; Max parts and Max bytes bound processing. Invalid UTF-8 or exceeded limits are reported on Error.

450.title: Join string
450.content: Joins a string list on Parts using Separator, emitting Text. Max bytes bounds output; invalid UTF-8 and limit failures go to Error. This is literal joining, not CSV quoting. Use Value serialization when nested values or typed fields need a defined interchange format.

451.title: File operations
451.content: These processes work with raw string data. Async execution keeps file operations on a worker; Sync can block execution and should not be used for slow storage during a real-time performance. Observe Busy, Success and Error rather than assuming a request completed immediately.

452.title: Read File
452.content: Select Path and trigger Read. Mode chooses Whole, Range, Stream or Autostream. Whole reads a bounded file; Range uses byte Offset and Count; Stream requests chunks; Autostream delivers chunks as execution advances. Maximum bytes bounds reads, and Timeout bounds stream worker requests. Outputs include Data, Bytes, Lines, EOF, Busy, Success, Error and Timed out. Async Autostream may temporarily lack a chunk on startup or with slow sources; it is not an uninterrupted real-time streaming guarantee or a FIFO session.

453.title: Read File Line
453.content: Select Path, trigger Open, then send Next for each line. Rewind restarts the cursor and Close ends it. Maximum line bytes bounds a line. Line, Line number, Bytes, Open, EOF, Busy, Success and Error expose results and status. LF and CRLF are supported, including blank lines.

454.title: Write File
454.content: Each raw-string arrival on Data performs the selected Mode at Path: Ignore does nothing, Write replaces the file, WriteRange overwrites a byte range while preserving surrounding bytes, and Append adds data. Offset and Count apply to WriteRange. Line ending chooses None, LF or CRLF; Maximum bytes bounds writes. Bytes, Lines, Busy, Success and Error report results. Equal consecutive messages are distinct writes; retained values are not automatically replayed. Save paths support %n (available numbered name) and %t (date/time). To append several chunks into one file, use a fixed resolved path rather than a fresh-name template for every write. For sampled device data with address columns and playback, prefer CSV recorder.

456.title: Controlling score remotely with OSCQuery
456.content: A score can be controlled through OSC and OSCQuery with the Local device. See also the WebSocket remote control protocol.

458.title: Control surface process
458.content: . This process allows to control remote parameters defined in the Device explorer from the central timeline / nodal view. To add an address, drag’n’drop it from the explorer to the process’s central area. This will add it as an automatable and controllable parameter for the duration of the execution of that process, with a meaningful user interface widget depending on the metadata associated with the OSC node (unit, data type, range…). Note that like every other score process, it will only have an effect during the execution of the score.

459.title: Remote control API
459.content: The control surface process provides remote control features, through the system discussed in Remote Control. When such a process starts executing, the following message is sent: . { "Message": "ControlSurfaceAdded", "Path": "/path/to/the/surface", "Controls": [ ... list of control objects... ] } . When the process ends, the following message is sent: . { "Message": "ControlSurfaceRemoved", "Path": "/path/to/the/surface" } . Controls . A control object defines a given control and has the following format. { "Custom": "The name of the control", "Domain": { ... domain object ... }, "Value": { ... value object ... }, "id": 1234, // the identifier of the individual control "uuid": "af2b4fc3-aecb-4c15-a5aa-1c573a239925" // the identifier of the control kind } . The remote can send the following message to change a parameter in score: . { "Message": "ControlSurface", "Path": "/path/to/the/surface", "id": 1234, // the id of the individual control that changed "Value": { ... the value object ... } } . Value object . The Value object has the following format: . { "TYPE": VALUE } . Where TYPE can be any of Int, Float, Bool, String, Char, Vec2f, Vec3f, Vec4f, Tuple, Impulse. For instance, valid values are: . { "Float": 1.23456 } { "Int": 127 } { "String": "hello world" } { "Vec2f": [0.5, 1.54] } { "Bool": true } { "Impulse": 1 } { "Tuple": [ { "Float": 1.234}, { "String": "hello" } ] } . Domain object . The Domain object has the following format: . { "TYPE": { "Min": THE_MIN, "Max": THE_MAX } } . where TYPE is the same than above. The most common cases are of course Int and Float as it does not really make sense for bools, etc. Example to have a slider that goes from -10 to 100: . { "Float": { "Min": -10 "Max": 100 } } . It is also possible to define a domain through a set of acceptable values instead of a range: . { "TYPE": { "Values": [ ... array of acceptable values ...] } } .

461.title: C++ native code
461.content: score compiles C++ into native code for the C++ JIT process and Texture generator. These are two different host interfaces, not standalone programs with a main() function. Bytebeat expressions use the same JIT infrastructure through a generated expression wrapper.

462.title: Language and runtime requirements
462.content: The authoritative language definition is the ISO C++ standard; cppreference is a useful, non-normative language and standard-library reference. The current score JIT uses C++23 with GNU extensions (-std=gnu++23). The callbacks and graph-node types below are score APIs, not part of standard C++. The JIT plug-in requires LLVM 20 or newer and compatible Clang development libraries when building score. It is omitted from fast-development builds and builds without these dependencies. Texture generation additionally requires the graphics plug-in. Install the matching score SDK headers for code using score and libossia interfaces; standard-library header availability also depends on the installed toolchain and SDK. Windows JIT and run-time add-ons use llvm-mingw, the official Windows toolchain. MSYS2 CLANG64 is the development alternative; MSVC is only needed for exceptional Qt WebEngine builds. Match the application version, architecture and compiler ABI rather than mixing headers from another score installation. See SDK setup.

463.title: Native-code safety
463.content: This is unsandboxed native code running with the same privileges as score. A crash, invalid memory access or blocking operation can affect the whole application. Only compile trusted code, save documents before experimenting, and keep allocation and blocking I/O out of real-time processing. Successful compilation is not a safety check.

464.title: C++ JIT factory
464.content: The entry point must retain its C linkage, name and signature: . extern "C" ossia::graph_node* score_graph_node_factory(); . The factory returns a newly allocated graph node; score takes ownership. It may create a node to inspect its ports as well as a node for execution, so do not return a stack object or a single shared raw pointer. The node’s declared inlets and outlets determine the process ports: there is no fixed universal list of controls. The supplied example derives from ossia::nonowning_graph_node, declares a value inlet and outlet, and multiplies incoming values by two while preserving their timestamps. Its processing override has this signature: . void run(const ossia::token_request& t, ossia::exec_state_facade st) noexcept override; . Start from the example supplied by your installed version and the current process implementation, which includes the complete factory example and port mapping. The callback is a libossia graph-node method, not an Avendish processor call operator. Recompilation may change the interface; check cables after modifying the ports.

465.title: Texture-generator callback
465.content: Texture generator accepts C++23 code exporting this callback: . extern "C" void score_rgba(unsigned char* rgba, int width, int height, int t); . | Parameter | Meaning | . | rgba | Writable CPU pixel buffer: four consecutive unsigned bytes per pixel, in red, green, blue, alpha order. | . | width, height | Current texture dimensions in pixels. Write only within the width * height * 4 byte buffer. | . | t | Integer render-call counter, starting at zero for a renderer and incremented on each callback invocation; not elapsed seconds or an audio sample counter. | . Pixels are laid out row by row; pixel (x, y) begins at 4 * (y * width + x). The callback is invoked for rendered frames, and the buffer is uploaded as an RGBA8 texture. Texture data is retained across frames while the buffer is reused, so a callback can update only part of an image. Do not rely on previous contents after a resize or renderer recreation, or retain the buffer pointer beyond the call. Rendering happens on the CPU, not in a GLSL shader. Large textures therefore increase the work your callback must complete. Use a smaller fixed render-target size if rendering is too slow. The process page retains the complete example, preset images and downloadable score. Implementation references: callback compilation, callback type, and pixel buffer and frame invocation.

466.title: Avendish is a separate workflow
466.content: For a reusable processor with declarative controls and ports, use Plug-ins with Avendish. Avendish describes a processor as a C++ type, with its own port contracts and package metadata. It does not use either callback above as its authoring interface. The developer command --compile-node file.hpp compiles an Avendish object into a registered add-on; it is not the low-level graph-node entry point used by the C++ JIT document process. Source add-ons and prebuilt add-ons are packaged and installed through the development workflow, rather than pasted into a document’s C++ JIT or texture editor. See also the command-line reference.

467.title: C++ JIT
467.content: This process compiles C++ into a native processing node while score is running. Open its code editor from the process’s window icon or inspector, edit the supplied program and use Compile to rebuild it. The canonical C++ native-code reference documents the factory ABI, compiler requirements and native-code restrictions.

468.title: Workflow and ports
468.content: Start from the supplied example, which declares a value inlet and outlet and multiplies incoming values by two while preserving their timestamps. The node’s declared ports determine the process interface; there is no fixed universal list of controls. See the C++ JIT factory reference for its entry point and graph-node contract rather than pasting a standalone C++ main() program. Connect the input to a value-producing process and the output to a monitor, mapping or device destination. Recompilation can change the port structure, so check cables after changing the interface. Compilation errors appear in the editor/log; verify compilation before starting a performance.

469.title: Availability and safety
469.content: This is native, unsandboxed code with the same privileges as score. A crash, blocking operation or invalid memory access in a node can affect the whole application. Keep allocation and blocking I/O out of real-time processing. If the process is unavailable or SDK headers cannot be found, check the language and runtime requirements.

470.title: Avendish is a separate workflow
470.content: For reusable processors with declarative controls and ports, use Plug-ins with Avendish. Its --compile-node command is not this document process’s entry point; see the workflow distinction and command-line reference.

471.title: CPU data bending
471.content: Turn a live camera feed into visibly damaged imagery while keeping the original beside it for comparison. Three Bendage treatments break up the same picture in different ways. Try this on web . Download the example .

472.title: Try it
472.content: Install the Bendage add-on, select an available camera in the Camera device settings, and grant capture permission where required. Start playback: JPeg, Safe Word and Xlippy appear next to the original image. Move in front of the camera: your movement stays readable in some treatments and disappears in others. Adjust an undriven effect control by hand, then lower the LFO frequency for slow deformation or raise it for rhythmic disturbance. Micromaps set how far that modulation travels through the effect controls; narrowing their ranges can preserve more of the source image. These effects process images on the CPU, so keep the input resolution modest. Without a camera, connect a movie or generated texture to all three effects and Grid’s first input so the comparison still uses one shared source.

473.title: CSF language reference
473.content: This is the canonical shader contract for the Compute Shaders process. For GLSL syntax, generated declarations and portability, see GLSL runtime reference. For worked tasks, see Shader cookbook. CSF is score’s compute-shader extension of ISF, not part of the standard ISF specification. Its JSON header describes GPU allocations and dispatches; its body uses Vulkan-compatible GLSL. Shared controls and sampled inputs follow the ISF input contract, while the resource, buffer and geometry interfaces below are score-specific.

474.title: Minimal file
474.content: /*{ "ISFVSN": "2.0", "MODE": "COMPUTE_SHADER", "RESOURCES": [ { "NAME": "inputImage", "TYPE": "image", "ACCESS": "read_only", "FORMAT": "rgba8" }, { "NAME": "outputImage", "TYPE": "image", "ACCESS": "write_only", "FORMAT": "rgba8", "WIDTH": "$WIDTH_inputImage", "HEIGHT": "$HEIGHT_inputImage" } ], "PASSES": [{ "LOCAL_SIZE": [16, 16, 1], "EXECUTION_MODEL": { "TYPE": "2D_IMAGE", "TARGET": "outputImage" } }] }*/ void main() { ivec2 p = ivec2(gl_GlobalInvocationID.xy); if (any(greaterThanEqual(p, imageSize(outputImage)))) return; vec4 c = IMG_LOAD(inputImage, p); IMG_STORE(outputImage, p, vec4(1.0 - c.rgb, c.a)); } .

475.title: Header fields
475.content: | Field | Required | Description | . | MODE | yes | Must be "COMPUTE_SHADER". | . | PASSES | yes | Compute dispatches to run each frame. | . | RESOURCES | no | GPU resources, ports, and controls. Preferred CSF spelling. | . | INPUTS | no | Alias accepted by the parser; useful for shared ISF-style conventions. | . | TYPES | no | User-defined struct layouts used by buffers and geometry attributes. | . | DESCRIPTION, CREDIT, CATEGORIES, ISFVSN | no | Metadata. | . RESOURCES and INPUTS are parsed with the same resource vocabulary. In CSF examples, use RESOURCES to make the compute intent clear.

476.title: Resource types
476.content: Each resource has NAME and TYPE. Type names are case-insensitive in practice, but lower-case matches most score examples. | Type | Meaning | . | image | Storage image when ACCESS or FORMAT is present; otherwise sampled texture input. | . | texture | Read-only sampled texture. | . | cubemap | Read-only sampled cubemap. | . | storage | Structured SSBO. If TYPE is omitted, storage is the default. | . | uniform | std140 UBO. Read-only, small data. | . | geometry | GPU geometry port with per-attribute buffers. | . | float, long, bool, event, point2D, point3D, color | UI controls and uniforms. | . | audio, audioFFT, audioHist | Audio textures. | . event inputs accept an impulse as well as true, and fire for one rendered frame. Use an event for a simulation reset rather than a permanently enabled boolean.

477.title: Images
477.content: A CSF image resource can be read, written, or read/write. { "NAME": "outputImage", "TYPE": "image", "ACCESS": "write_only", "FORMAT": "rgba16f", "WIDTH": "$WIDTH_inputImage", "HEIGHT": "$HEIGHT_inputImage" } . | Field | Description | . | ACCESS | read_only, write_only, or read_write. | . | FORMAT | GLSL image format such as rgba8, rgba16f, rgba32f, r32f, rgba32ui. | . | WIDTH, HEIGHT, DEPTH | Size expressions. DEPTH creates a 3D image. | . | DIMENSIONS | 2 or 3. Alternative way to declare 3D images. | . | IS_ARRAY / ARRAY | 2D texture array image. | . | LAYERS | Array layer count expression. | . | CUBEMAP / IS_CUBE | Cubemap storage image. | . | PERSISTENT | Ping-pong image history; the previous frame is available as <name>_prev. | . | GENERATE_MIPS | Generate mipmaps after the dispatch. Valid for 2D images. | . | VISIBILITY | Binding visibility when the resource is shared with graphics stages: compute, fragment, vertex, or vertex+fragment. | . | COMPOSITE | How the published image composites when consumed directly: over, add, multiply, screen, replace. | . Use the portable image helpers when orientation matters: . vec4 c = IMG_LOAD(inputImage, ivec2(x, y)); IMG_STORE(outputImage, ivec2(x, y), c); IMG_STORE_LAYER(arrayImage, ivec3(x, y, layer), c); . Integer storage formats such as rgba32ui require Qt 6.10 or newer, plus device support. With earlier Qt versions, unsupported format names fall back to RGBA8; that fallback does not preserve integer shader semantics. See Graphics pipeline for sizing and backend restrictions. Raw imageLoad / imageStore also work, but they do not apply score’s coordinate-origin fixups. 3D image . { "NAME": "volume", "TYPE": "image", "ACCESS": "write_only", "FORMAT": "r32f", "WIDTH": 128, "HEIGHT": 128, "DEPTH": 128 } . Dispatch with EXECUTION_MODEL: { "TYPE": "3D_IMAGE", "TARGET": "volume" } and write with ivec3 coordinates. Persistent image . { "NAME": "state", "TYPE": "image", "ACCESS": "read_write", "FORMAT": "rgba32f", "WIDTH": 1024, "HEIGHT": 1024, "PERSISTENT": true } . state is the current writable image. state_prev is the previous frame’s read-only image. PERSISTENT with write_only is invalid because there is no meaningful previous read path.

478.title: Sampled textures
478.content: A read-only sampled texture is declared with TYPE: "texture", or with TYPE: "image" when no ACCESS / FORMAT is present. { "NAME": "lookup", "TYPE": "texture", "FILTER": "nearest", "WRAP": "clamp_to_edge" } { "NAME": "volumeTex", "TYPE": "texture", "DIMENSIONS": 3 } { "NAME": "sky", "TYPE": "cubemap", "MIPMAP_MODE": "linear" } . Sampler fields are the same as ISF: WRAP, WRAP_S, WRAP_T, WRAP_R, FILTER, MIN_FILTER, MAG_FILTER, MIPMAP_MODE, BORDER_COLOR, COMPARE, ANISOTROPY, LOD_BIAS, MIN_LOD, MAX_LOD.

479.title: Storage buffers
479.content: storage declares an SSBO using std430 layout rules. { "NAME": "particles", "TYPE": "storage", "ACCESS": "read_write", "PERSISTENT": true, "LAYOUT": [ { "NAME": "count", "TYPE": "uint" }, { "NAME": "pos", "TYPE": "vec4[]" } ] } . Fields: . | Field | Description | . | ACCESS | read_only, write_only, or read_write. | . | LAYOUT | Struct fields. Last field may be a flexible array with []. | . | SIZE | Flexible array length when needed. | . | PERSISTENT | Ping-pong buffer history; previous frame is <name>_prev. | . | VISIBILITY | Graphics-stage visibility when shared: compute, fragment, vertex, vertex+fragment, or none. | . | BUFFER_USAGE | Special usage: indirect_draw or indirect_draw_indexed. Allows empty LAYOUT. Indirect dispatch needs no special usage: point EXECUTION_MODEL TYPE: "INDIRECT" at an ordinary storage buffer (see Indirect dispatch). | . Access fields as members: . uint n = particles.count; vec4 p = particles.pos[i]; .

480.title: Uniform buffers
480.content: uniform declares a std140 UBO. Use it for small read-only data such as cameras, counts, and constants. { "NAME": "camera", "TYPE": "uniform", "VISIBILITY": "vertex+fragment", "LAYOUT": [ { "NAME": "viewProjection", "TYPE": "mat4" }, { "NAME": "position", "TYPE": "vec4" } ] } . For writable or large data, use storage instead.

481.title: Geometry resources
481.content: A geometry resource publishes or consumes GPU-resident geometry. It is the bridge from compute to Render Pipeline and Model Display. { "NAME": "geo", "TYPE": "geometry", "VERTEX_COUNT": 36, "INSTANCE_COUNT": "$USER", "TOPOLOGY": "triangles", "ATTRIBUTES": [ { "NAME": "position", "SEMANTIC": "position", "TYPE": "vec4", "ACCESS": "write_only", "RATE": "vertex" }, { "NAME": "normal", "SEMANTIC": "normal", "TYPE": "vec4", "ACCESS": "write_only", "RATE": "vertex" }, { "NAME": "translation", "SEMANTIC": "translation", "TYPE": "vec4", "ACCESS": "write_only", "RATE": "instance" }, { "NAME": "color", "SEMANTIC": "color", "TYPE": "vec4", "ACCESS": "write_only", "RATE": "instance" } ] } . Generator or filter . | If VERTEX_COUNT is present, the CSF creates its own geometry buffers. | If VERTEX_COUNT is omitted, the CSF acts as a geometry filter and adopts upstream geometry sizes. | . Set TOPOLOGY explicitly when producing points or lines. The topology travels with the generated geometry, but the downstream Render Pipeline Mode must be Geometry to follow it automatically. An explicit raster PIPELINE_STATE.TOPOLOGY overrides that control. A buffer of three positions alone does not tell a renderer whether you intend one triangle or three points. Geometry fields . | Field | Description | . | VERTEX_COUNT | Vertex count expression. May use $USER, scalar inputs, texture sizes, or other geometry counts. | . | INSTANCE_COUNT | Instance count expression. | . | TOPOLOGY | triangles, triangle_strip, triangle_fan, lines, line_strip, or points. | . | FORMAT_ID | Optional format tag stamped on the output geometry. | . | PERSISTENT | For filters, read/write attributes work on persistent upstream buffers instead of a fresh per-frame copy. | . | INDIRECT | Allocate GPU-written indirect draw commands. | . | AUXILIARY | Structured buffers or textures that travel with this geometry. | . | ATTRIBUTES | Per-vertex and per-instance attribute buffers. | . Attribute fields . | Field | Description | . | NAME | GLSL attribute name. | . | SEMANTIC | Semantic used by downstream renderers. Defaults to NAME. Standard examples: position, normal, color, texcoord, tangent, velocity, instance_draw_id. | . | TYPE | GLSL type such as float, vec2, vec3, vec4, uint, mat4, or a type from TYPES. | . | ACCESS | read_only, write_only, read_write, or gather. | . | RATE | vertex or instance. Defaults to vertex. | . | REQUIRED | false allows missing upstream attributes to use a fallback. | . | COPY_FROM | Forward an attribute from another geometry without shader writes. | . ACCESS: "gather" means read/write plus foreign-index reads. Use it for neighbour loops, N-body interactions, stencils, and any shader that reads indices other than its own invocation. It forces separate _in and _out buffers so reads see a stable snapshot. Access attributes with macros: . vec4 p = ISF_READ(geo, position)[idx]; ISF_WRITE(geo, position)[idx] = p + vec4(0.0, 0.01, 0.0, 0.0); uint count = uint(ISF_READ(geo, position).length()); . For read_write, ISF_READ expands to the input/snapshot buffer and ISF_WRITE to the output buffer. COPY_FROM . Forwarding is useful when an output geometry combines computed attributes with unchanged data from another input. { "NAME": "normal", "TYPE": "vec4", "COPY_FROM": { "GEOMETRY": "source", "ATTRIBUTE": "normal" } } . The forwarded attribute is not bound for shader reads or writes. Indirect draw . "INDIRECT": { "COUNT": "$USER", "DRAW_COUNT": true, "INDEXED": false } . INDIRECT allocates an indirect-command buffer associated with the geometry. The shader fills draw commands and optionally a draw-count buffer. The runtime uses GPU indirect drawing when available and compatible fallbacks otherwise. Use ISF_INDIRECT(geo) and, with DRAW_COUNT, ISF_INDIRECT_COUNT(geo) in GLSL. When allocating a capacity of commands, initialize inactive slots to zero and guard indirectly dispatched work against the live count. Some backends use bounded dispatch or draw fallbacks rather than native GPU-count execution. Shader cookbook shows the corresponding corpus recipe, plus geometry forwarding and audio input examples.

482.title: Auxiliary buffers and textures
482.content: Geometry can carry extra data besides attributes. SSBO auxiliary . "AUXILIARY": [ { "NAME": "physics", "ACCESS": "read_write", "SIZE": "$USER", "LAYOUT": [ { "NAME": "totalEnergy", "TYPE": "float" }, { "NAME": "velocity", "TYPE": "vec4[]" } ] } ] . UBO auxiliary . "AUXILIARY": [ { "NAME": "scene_counts", "TYPE": "uniform", "LAYOUT": [ { "NAME": "drawCount", "TYPE": "uint" } ] } ] . Texture auxiliary . Auxiliary textures travel with the geometry and do not create score input ports. "AUXILIARY": [ { "NAME": "base_color", "TYPE": "texture", "FILTER": "linear" }, { "NAME": "shadow_atlas", "TYPE": "image", "DEPTH": true, "COMPARE": "less" }, { "NAME": "history", "TYPE": "storage_image", "FORMAT": "rgba16f", "ACCESS": "read_write", "WIDTH": 1024, "HEIGHT": 1024 } ] . Auxiliary texture TYPE values include image, texture, cubemap, image_cube, storage_image, storage_cube, storage_image_array, and storage_3d.

483.title: Custom types
483.content: TYPES declares reusable struct layouts. "TYPES": [ { "NAME": "Particle", "LAYOUT": [ { "NAME": "position", "TYPE": "vec4" }, { "NAME": "velocity", "TYPE": "vec4" }, { "NAME": "life", "TYPE": "float" } ] } ] . Use type names in storage layouts and geometry attributes.

484.title: Passes and execution models
484.content: CSF shaders run one or more dispatch passes per frame. "PASSES": [ { "LOCAL_SIZE": [16, 16, 1], "EXECUTION_MODEL": { "TYPE": "2D_IMAGE", "TARGET": "outputImage" } } ] . | Pass field | Description | . | LOCAL_SIZE | Workgroup size [x, y, z]. Defaults to [16, 16, 1]. | . | EXECUTION_MODEL | Dispatch strategy. | . PASSINDEX is the current pass number. Execution model types . | Type | Dispatches over | Required / useful fields | . | 2D_IMAGE | Width and height of target image | TARGET, optional STRIDE_X, STRIDE_Y | . | 3D_IMAGE | Width, height, depth of target image | TARGET, optional STRIDE_X/Y/Z | . | PER_VERTEX | Vertex count of a geometry | optional strides | . | PER_INSTANCE | Instance count of a geometry | optional strides | . | 1D_BUFFER | Elements of a storage buffer | TARGET | . | MANUAL | Fixed workgroup count | WORKGROUPS | . | USER | User-controlled workgroup count | creates X/Y/Z dispatch controls | . | INDIRECT | Workgroups read from a storage buffer | TARGET, WORKGROUPS fallback ceiling, optional OFFSET | . STRIDE, STRIDE_X, STRIDE_Y, and STRIDE_Z reduce dispatched workgroups. Strides can be integers or expressions. Indirect dispatch . { "LOCAL_SIZE": [64, 1, 1], "EXECUTION_MODEL": { "TYPE": "INDIRECT", "TARGET": "dispatchArgs", "WORKGROUPS": [1024, 1, 1], "OFFSET": 0 } } . TARGET is a storage buffer containing a {x, y, z} uint triplet. WORKGROUPS is the fallback ceiling used when the backend cannot dispatch indirectly; the shader must still bounds-check.

485.title: Expressions
485.content: Many fields accept expressions: . | Variable | Meaning | . | $inputName | Value of a scalar input. | . | $USER | Dedicated user integer slider. | . | $WIDTH_name, $HEIGHT_name, $DEPTH_name, $LAYERS_name | Texture dimensions. | . | $VERTEX_COUNT, $INSTANCE_COUNT | Counts of the first geometry. | . | $VERTEX_COUNT_geo, $INSTANCE_COUNT_geo | Counts of a named geometry. | . Supported operators include +, -, *, /, %, comparisons, &&, and ||. Supported functions include abs, sqrt, sin, cos, tan, exp, log, ceil, floor, round, min, max, pow, clamp, lerp, step, and smoothstep.

486.title: Built-in uniforms
486.content: | Uniform | Type | Description | . | TIME | float | Playback time in seconds. | . | TIMEDELTA | float | Time since previous frame. | . | PROGRESS | float | Timeline progress from 0 to 1. | . | FRAMEINDEX | int | Frame counter. Starts at 0. | . | PASSINDEX | int | Current pass index. | . | RENDERSIZE | vec2 | Render size in pixels. | . | DATE | vec4 | (year, month, day, seconds). | . | SAMPLERATE | float | Audio sample rate. | . | gl_NumWorkGroups / isf_NumWorkGroups | uvec3 | Actual workgroup count for the current dispatch. | .

487.title: Image formats
487.content: Common image formats: . | Category | Formats | . | Float / normalized | rgba32f, rgba16f, rgba8, rg32f, rg16f, rg8, r32f, r16f, r8, rgb10_a2 | . | Signed integer | rgba32i, rgba16i, rgba8i, rg32i, rg16i, rg8i, r32i, r16i, r8i | . | Unsigned integer | rgba32ui, rgba16ui, rgba8ui, rg32ui, rg16ui, rg8ui, r32ui, r16ui, r8ui | . Format names are case-insensitive, but lower-case GLSL qualifiers are the safest spelling.

488.title: Patterns
488.content: Image filter . /*{ "ISFVSN": "2.0", "MODE": "COMPUTE_SHADER", "RESOURCES": [ { "NAME": "inputImage", "TYPE": "texture" }, { "NAME": "outputImage", "TYPE": "image", "ACCESS": "write_only", "FORMAT": "rgba8", "WIDTH": "$WIDTH_inputImage", "HEIGHT": "$HEIGHT_inputImage" }, { "NAME": "gain", "TYPE": "float", "DEFAULT": 1.0, "MIN": 0.0, "MAX": 4.0 } ], "PASSES": [{ "LOCAL_SIZE": [16, 16, 1], "EXECUTION_MODEL": { "TYPE": "2D_IMAGE", "TARGET": "outputImage" } }] }*/ void main() { ivec2 p = ivec2(gl_GlobalInvocationID.xy); if (any(greaterThanEqual(p, imageSize(outputImage)))) return; vec2 uv = (vec2(p) + 0.5) / vec2(imageSize(outputImage)); vec4 c = texture(inputImage, uv); IMG_STORE(outputImage, p, vec4(c.rgb * gain, c.a)); } . Geometry filter . "RESOURCES": [ { "NAME": "strength", "TYPE": "float", "DEFAULT": 0.1, "MIN": 0.0, "MAX": 2.0 }, { "NAME": "geo", "TYPE": "geometry", "ATTRIBUTES": [ { "NAME": "position", "SEMANTIC": "position", "TYPE": "vec4", "ACCESS": "read_write" }, { "NAME": "normal", "SEMANTIC": "normal", "TYPE": "vec4", "ACCESS": "read_only" } ] } ], "PASSES": [ { "LOCAL_SIZE": [64, 1, 1], "EXECUTION_MODEL": { "TYPE": "PER_VERTEX" } } ] . void main() { uint i = gl_GlobalInvocationID.x; uint n = uint(ISF_READ(geo, position).length()); if (i >= n) return; vec4 p = ISF_READ(geo, position)[i]; vec3 normal = normalize(ISF_READ(geo, normal)[i].xyz); ISF_WRITE(geo, position)[i] = p + vec4(normal * strength, 0.0); } . Particle feedback . For particle simulations, use read_write or gather attributes plus a feedback cable from the geometry output back to the geometry input. The runtime allocates snapshots / ping-pong buffers so reads see the previous state and writes produce the next state. Use gather when each invocation reads neighbours: . { "NAME": "position", "SEMANTIC": "position", "TYPE": "vec4", "ACCESS": "gather" } .

489.title: CSV Recorder
489.content: . The CSV process records and replays device parameters matching an address pattern expression. Each matched address becomes a column; each sampling time becomes a row. For instance, in the screenshot above, the following configuration would recreate a CSV file on each playback of the score called /tmp/save.csv with content such as : . timestamp,/0/co2,/1/co2,/2/co2 0,0.5429007,0.6073362,0.3612722 63,0.5429007,0.6073362,0.3612722 127,0.5429007,0.6073362,0.3612722 191,0.5037621,0.42720786,0.28013167 255,0.6991433,0.42720786,0.47998703 319,0.8627539,0.42720786,0.36869702 383,0.9684921,0.42720786,0.8776827 447,0.9994888,0.42720786,0.36079046 511,0.95079887,0.42720786,0.80060333 575,0.8301902,0.42720786,0.39480355 639,0.65690416,0.42720786,0.7897841 .

490.title: Controls and replay
490.content: Interval sets the sampling interval with a Time Chooser. The recording samples current parameter values at that interval; it is not a log of every intervening message. Timestamped uses the first column for timestamps in milliseconds. Mode selects recording, Playback or Loop. During playback, column addresses must resolve to parameters in the current device tree. Separator selects comma, semicolon or pipe. The comma option is currently labelled Colon in the control, despite writing ,. Strings containing separators or quotes are escaped, and the player reads quoted strings and pipe-separated data back. Match the separator to the file when importing.

491.title: Filenames and takes
491.content: File pattern accepts %t, replaced by the current UTC date/time with colons changed to underscores, and %n, replaced by an available number in the resolved destination directory. A path ending in capture-%n.csv keeps separate takes; a fixed filename can be overwritten when recording starts again. For playback, select the actual recorded filename rather than a template that generates a new name. Keep the destination directory writable and the recorded device addresses available for replay. For audio rather than device values, use Audio recorder.

493.title: Cues, loops and exclusive playback
493.content: . Perform a sequence of visual and sound cues without deciding every transition in advance. The visual section recalls looks, repeats a movement and eases from the current setting; the audio section either layers clips or allows only one at a time.

494.title: Visual cues and transitions
494.content: Open the ZIP directly in score and start playback. A shader image responds to color, intensity and blur cues. No external OSC application is required. | Alternate Send cue 1 and Send cue 2. Each one jumps straight to a stored color. | Trigger Play once, then Repeat. Let the repeating automation run through several cycles before triggering its end: it keeps going for as long as you wait. | Fire the independent intensity cues in any order, then play the connected sequence, which enforces its own order and timing bounds. | Set the blur manually before trying Tween 1, Tween 2 and No tween. Look for the initial jump: Tween starts from the current value, which matters when a live operator may have changed the image. | . The preview uses score’s native ISF graphics. If adapting the cues to an external OSC application, the saved device listens on UDP 9997 and sends to 127.0.0.1:9996.

495.title: Audio cues and loops
495.content: Configure audio output and begin at a low level; the sounds are included. In Scenario-nonexclusive, trigger several sound intervals and listen to the layers accumulate. Repeat the same choices in Scenario-exclusive: starting one interval stops the others in that scenario. Use non-exclusive scenarios to build a texture and exclusive ones to replace one section with another. Loop switches use the root interval’s bar quantization. Request a switch just after a bar starts, then near its end, and listen to the common boundary at which each request takes effect. The performer chooses what comes next while quantization preserves the musical transition. The annotations also introduce root start and stop states for initialization and shutdown cues. Try ordinary Stop, then Stop and reinitialize, and watch which settings return to a known look instead of keeping their last values. Download this example . Try this on web .

496.title: Cues
496.content: Cues are an essential part of interactive shows: they allow to record a set of controls and messages that will be applied at a single point in time: OSC or DMX messages, MIDI control changes, etc. In score, cues are messages that are contained inside states.

497.title: Creating a cue
497.content: Cues are created by drag’n’drop, from a set of Device explorer nodes, to the score. It is possible to add messages to a cue by dropping on it. Existing messages to a given address will be replaced by the value that is being dropped.

498.title: Updating a cue
498.content: If you want to replace the parameters of a cue with their current value in the explorer, you can click on the state. The state inspector has a “Snapshot” feature which will update all the values stored in the cue, with their current live value. | The first icon with the camera, “Snapshot” (Ctrl+L(Win / Linux) or⌘+L(Mac)), takes all the parameters currently selected in the Device explorer and copies them to the cue. | The second icon, with the circled camera, “Refresh” (Ctrl+R(Win / Linux) or⌘+R(Mac)), takes all the parameters inside the saved cue, and updates them to their current “live” value as shown in the device explorer. | .

499.title: Playing a cue
499.content: Cues will be played automatically when the score execution reaches them: .

500.title: Playing a cue manually
500.content: It is possible to play a cue through the “Play” tool in the user interface.

501.title: Playing a cue with an external control
501.content: It is possible to entirely control when a cue is going to be sent, by adding a trigger on it and let it “float” in the scenario. Such a floating cue can originally be created by double-clicking on the scenario (or drag’n’dropping directly from the Device explorer, and removing the created interval afterwards). Then, one needs to add a trigger (through the inspector or by pressing T when the state is selected), and configure it for out-of-time playback. Here is how this would work: . The set-up on the triggers look like this: . Notice in particular that the two buttons, “Auto-Trigger” and “Start on play”, are checked. It would be possible for instance to trigger the cue when a MIDI CC reaches a specific value or similar. See Breaking the timeline for more information on triggers.

502.title: Curl Noise Geometry Filter
502.content: A loaded angel sculpture twists into a fluid-looking form, leaving traces as it moves. The model needs no rig: the deformation and the trails are separate stages. The Curl noise geometry filter displaces vertices on the GPU during rendering. An LFO produces changing noise-scale values; exponential smoothing softens the transitions before they reach the filter. A procedural sine warp gradient colors the result, and Long Exposure retains earlier rendered images. In order: Object loader loads Models/angel.obj, the Curl noise filter displaces it, Model display renders it, and Long Exposure sends the image to Window:/. This is a vertex-shader deformation, so the filter does not require compute-shader support. It is different from Scene Graph Filter, which selects scene objects rather than deforming their vertices. See 3D scene pipeline for that distinction and Geometry and buffer utilities when adapting mesh attributes.

503.title: Try it
503.content: Open the ZIP directly in score and start playback; the angel model is included. Lower Curl noise’s intensity to recover more of the original silhouette, then increase it to make the swirling displacement clearer. Speed up the scale modulation for restless motion, or raise the smoothing for gradual shifts. Adjust Long Exposure’s absorption and discharge separately: these change how long the image holds each movement, not the geometry itself. To try another sculpture, choose it in Geometry Loader. The original model source is ModelsOBJ. Try this on web . Download this example .

504.title: Learn more
504.content: . | Object loader - Loading 3D models | ISF Shaders - Interactive Shader Format for GPU effects | LFO - Low-frequency oscillator for animation | Model display - 3D mesh rendering process | Graphics pipeline - How rendering works in ossia score | .

505.title: Custom applications
505.content: Package score with a QML interface, a score and its media as a standalone application. Start from the custom application template: replace qml/Main.qml and score/app.score, then edit the application name and metadata in its workflows. The template’s packaging workflow uses an existing score release. Its full-build workflow builds score with selected features before packaging.

506.title: First package
506.content: Run from the score source checkout with Bash: . bash tools/create-app.sh --help bash tools/create-app.sh \ --qml /absolute/path/to/App.qml \ --qml /absolute/path/to/ui-assets \ --score /absolute/path/to/project/App.score \ --output /absolute/path/to/packages \ --name "My Installation" \ --app-organization "My Studio" \ --app-domain "example.org" \ --app-identifier "org.example.installation" \ --app-version "1.0.0" \ --platform linux-x86_64 . --qml, --output and --name (also called --app-name) are required. Omit --score for a UI-only application. Use absolute paths: platform scripts change their working directory. Repeat --qml for additional files or directories, listing the main QML file first. Directory contents are merged into the package’s qml directory. With --score, the scripts copy the score’s sibling files and directories, except hidden files. Keep the project in its own folder and collect its media as described in Project files.

507.title: Base distribution and targets
507.content: --release TAG selects a GitHub release (default: continuous). --local-installer PATH uses a local distribution instead. | --platform | Base distribution | Output and host requirements | . | linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64 | AppImage | AppImage and launcher shell script. The script executes the input AppImage and architecture-specific packaging tools: use a compatible Linux host. | . | macos-intel, macos-arm | .app or .dmg | .app bundle and DMG; requires macOS tools including hdiutil and PlistBuddy. | . | windows, windows-arm64 | Windows installer .exe | ZIP containing the application and native launcher. Requires Bash, 7z/7za, a Windows-targeting C++ compiler and a ZIP tool. | . | wasm | WASM release ZIP, or local build directory/ZIP | Static web directory and ZIP, not a native executable. | . Without --platform, the script detects the host. Repeat it for multiple targets when the host has the required tools. On Windows, use llvm-mingw’s clang++ or MSYS2 CLANG64 for the native launcher. For WASM, pass a release ZIP or a local directory containing ossia-score.js, ossia-score.wasm and its accompanying files. Serve the generated <safe-name>-wasm directory over HTTP. See Building for WebAssembly for browser and hosting requirements.

508.title: Startup and debugging
508.content: The native launcher starts score with --ui and the main QML file. A supplied score loads at startup; add --autoplay to start playback. Additional native command-line arguments are forwarded to score. Launch with --debug to show both the custom UI and score editor (--ui-debug). In a browser, use ?debug.

509.title: Branding and icons
509.content: | Option | Purpose | . | --app-organization, --app-domain | Application organization and domain. | . | --app-identifier | Bundle identifier, especially for macOS distribution. | . | --app-version | Application version metadata. | . | --app-description | One-line description. | . | --app-copyright | Copyright metadata. | . | --app-png | Linux PNG icon. | . | --app-appdata-xml | Linux AppStream metadata file. | . | --app-icns | macOS ICNS icon. | . | --app-ico | Windows ICO icon. | . Native launchers set SCORE_CUSTOM_APP_ORGANIZATION_NAME, SCORE_CUSTOM_APP_ORGANIZATION_DOMAIN, SCORE_CUSTOM_APP_APPLICATION_NAME and SCORE_CUSTOM_APP_APPLICATION_VERSION. Application and organization names give the app its own settings. On Windows, provide an ICO file to apply the icon and version resources. WASM does not use the native launcher environment or native icon metadata.

510.title: Environment and per-OS overrides
510.content: --app-environment /absolute/path/to/app.env supplies environment settings to native launchers: . export MY_INSTALLATION_MODE=gallery . Linux and macOS source the file as Bash. Windows accepts literal assignments with an optional export prefix, but not shell expansion or commands. If adjacent files exist, the orchestrator appends the matching overlay after the base file: . | app.env.linux | app.env.macos | app.env.windows | . The overlay overrides the common values. End each file with a newline. WASM does not use these environment files.

511.title: Qt resources
511.content: --app-qrc /absolute/path/to/resources.qrc invokes rcc from PATH and places resources.rcc beside the native executable, or at /resources.rcc in the WASM preload manifest. WASM also accepts the RCC environment variable. The current scripts omit rcc’s binary-output flag. To supply a binary resource bundle manually, run rcc --binary resources.qrc -o resources.rcc and place it beside the native executable; score registers it on startup.

512.title: Enabled add-ons
512.content: The packaged app uses the add-ons in its base distribution. To select add-ons in a source build, set SCORE_ENABLED_ADDONS to comma-separated directory names from src/addons; SCORE_ENABLE_ADDONS is also accepted. Leave it unset to include all discovered add-ons. Pass the resulting distribution with --local-installer.

513.title: GitHub Actions
513.content: ossia/actions provides: . | package-custom-app: packages a release with app-name, qml-files, optional score-file, release-tag and platforms. | custom-score-build: builds score with cmake-options or cmake-cache. Pass its artifact-id output to the packaging action’s score-build-id input. | . For example, in a Linux job after checking out your application: . - uses: ossia/actions/package-custom-app@master with: app-name: My Installation qml-files: qml score-file: score/app.score release-tag: continuous platforms: linux-x86_64 . The template workflows include native and WASM packaging jobs and artifact uploads. To build WASM from source, use an ubuntu-24.04 runner and set target-platform: wasm on custom-score-build, then platforms: wasm on package-custom-app.

514.title: Signing and distribution
514.content: On macOS, set MAC_CODESIGN_IDENTITY to sign the app and DMG. Notarization also uses MAC_NOTARIZE_TEAM_ID, MAC_NOTARIZE_APPLE_ID and MAC_NOTARIZE_PASSWORD. In GitHub Actions, supply the corresponding certificate and notarization inputs from repository secrets. Windows packaging produces a ZIP without Authenticode signing; Linux produces an AppImage.

515.title: Procedural PBR material
515.content: . A cube takes on a changing surface as animated textures alter its color, roughness, normals and emission. The textures feed separate maps on PBR Mesh, while a moving light reveals their effect on shading. The native scene renderer produces the lit image; bloom then spreads its bright areas into a glow. Changing the material and adding glow are separate operations.

516.title: Try it
516.content: Start playback and lower Roughness: highlights from the moving light become sharper. Raise Metallic to tint the reflections with the base color. Then adjust Emissive strength and Bloom threshold separately: one changes the material’s brightness, while the other controls which highlights spread into the image. Change the light modulation to see the same material under a different movement. The cube, textures and shader code are all generated or stored in the score; no external model or image is needed. Try this on web . Download this example .

517.title: Custom UIs
517.content: It is possible to create custom control UIs for a given ossia score through QML and QtQuick, a GPU-accelerated UI language part of Qt. Use a custom application UI for an installation, or give an individual Javascript process its own control interface. QML interfaces can use the editor API, Qt Quick Controls and score port bindings without putting editor operations in execution callbacks. It is recommended to be familiar with QML, Qt Quick (for instance by going through the QML Book) and ossia score’s scripting before making your own UI.

518.title: UI objects
518.content: The QML custom UI API documents PortSource, PortSink and AddressSource, including playback requirements and undo behavior. This tutorial uses these bindings to connect a control panel to a running score.

519.title: Running with a custom UI
519.content: A whole-application UI can be passed as a command-line argument: . $ ./score --ui path/to/my/ui.qml path/to/my/document.score .

520.title: Per-process interfaces and placement
520.content: For an individual Javascript process, save a companion effect.ui.qml alongside effect.qml, then open it with the process’s custom-UI action. Code and UI can be edited independently in the script editor. Choose Window, Side panel or Central placement as appropriate for your workspace. See the complete ScriptUI example and port lookup API, including the numeric control inlet required by the example, and the view API for scripted placement. Messages and persistent state . Use the message bridge and persistent-state API to exchange messages with the execution script or save UI state in the document and presets. The UI and execution script are separate objects, not a shared set of QML properties.

521.title: Imported QML forms
521.content: To reuse a trusted exported QML form, see Imported QML forms for the complete ImportedUi example, root-item requirements, mappings and diagnostics.

522.title: Graphics and texture previews
522.content: For choosing visual controls, drawing with Qt Quick Canvas or showing an existing texture through TextureSource, see Graphics and texture previews. Native process-control declarations are not visual widgets for a custom layout.

523.title: Basic example
523.content: Give a performer a small control panel instead of the full score editor. This example pairs a shader-zoom dial with live numerical readouts and a second dial for an external OSC destination. It shows how a custom interface can expose just the controls and feedback needed to operate a piece. Download the example score. Try this on web . Save the QML below as custom-ui.qml beside the downloaded score, then launch: . $ ./score --ui custom-ui.qml custom-ui.score . The interface starts playback automatically. Open the score’s Window output and turn the first dial to change the shader’s zoom. The labels read a changing LFO amplitude, a monitored output value and a device address, so you can compare direct control with feedback from the running score. The last dial writes to OSC:/bar, configured to send to a receiver on the local machine at UDP port 9996. Use an OSC monitor or another application listening on that port to observe it; the dial does not control the shader. No OSC receiver is needed for the shader and local readouts. Change the device’s destination if your receiver is elsewhere, and allow local UDP traffic if required. In the QML, PortSource connects a widget to a named process control, while AddressSource connects it to the device explorer. The names and addresses below match the downloadable score. When adapting the panel, change the bindings to match your own processes and devices rather than just relabelling the widgets. import QtQuick import QtQuick.Controls import Score.UI as UI Rectangle { color: "white" width: 640 height: 480 Component.onCompleted: Score.play(); Column { Label { text: "Operating a control:" } Dial { UI.PortSource on value { process: "some_shader" port: 1 } } Label { text: "Reading the value of a control inlet:" } Label { UI.PortSource on text { process: "LFO" port: "Ampl." } } Label { text: "Reading the value of any outlet by adding a value display:" } Label { UI.PortSource on text { process: "Value display" port: 0 } } Label { text: "Reading the value of any address:" } Label { UI.AddressSource on text { address: "OSC:/foo" sendUpdates: false } } Label { text: "Setting the value of any address:" } Dial { UI.AddressSource on value { address: "OSC:/bar" receiveUpdates: false } } } } .

525.title: Data visualization and sonification
525.content: . Follow the same data by eye and ear: a changing curve builds a history of points on screen while controlling synthesized sound. Try this on web . Download the example .

526.title: From data to control values
526.content: An imported greenhouse-gas data column plays as an Automation. Statistics expose its mean, variance and consecutive differences, while smoothing turns variation into a more gradual control signal. Calibrators map statistical changes onto the ranges of the color and delay settings. The GPU history retains earlier points through a delayed feedback connection. The sound is synthesized from the curve, not a recording of the phenomenon being measured: both sound and image are interpretations shaped by the chosen mappings.

527.title: Setup
527.content: Open the ZIP directly in score. The data curve is already imported, so the original CSV is not required. Use a compute-capable graphics backend and Airwindows for TapeDelay2; the history shaders are embedded and use score’s native rendering.

528.title: Try it
528.content: . | Start at a low listening level. Watch the history grow and match changes in the sound to the curve and statistical displays. | Increase smoothing: short fluctuations fade from the sound, leaving the slower trend. | Lower point size to pick out individual points, or raise it to see the overall shape of the history. | Import your own data as a replacement curve and reconsider its mappings: a meaningful range for one dataset need not reveal another. | . Keep the delayed feedback connection when adapting the visual history; it carries the past values that make the accumulating view possible.

529.title: Data processing
529.content: You may want to enlarge a small movement, wait for two participants, move a signal across many destinations, or generate variation without a performer. These examples show the results in plots and value displays; connect them to sound, light or images afterwards.

530.title: Choose a response
530.content: . | Make a signal fit its destination: start with Math expressions and structured objects. Change the scale and offset of a signal, then extract single fields from a larger message. | Control when a response happens: try Mapping and event utilities. Filter repeated input, retain a short history, or wait for fresh events from two sources. | Treat many destinations as an ensemble: open Address pattern tools. Distribute a list of values or move a signal through a group instead of wiring every destination individually. | Let a signal evolve by itself: use Delayed value feedback, where one coefficient decides whether a recurrence settles or keeps varying. | . For a short first exercise, open the feedback example and change its coefficient from 3.68 to 2.5. Watch the trace settle, then restore the original value to bring back the irregular motion. The example displays the control signal and produces no sound.

531.title: Distance-Based Amplitude Panning (DBAP)
531.content: DBAP calculates loudspeaker gains from the distances between one source and a list of speakers. It produces control data, not audio. Use Matrix Spatialization to apply the gains to a mono sound source. Two processes are available: DBAP (2D) takes XY coordinates; DBAP (3D) takes XYZ coordinates.

532.title: Inputs and output
532.content: | Port | Value | . | Source | One XY or XYZ position | . | Speakers | List of speaker positions, in output-channel order | . | Blur | Additional distance term that broadens the gain distribution | . | Roll-off | Relative-distance exponent control, from 0 to 100; default 6 | . | Output | Flat list of gains, one per speaker | . Source is the first inlet; Speakers is the second. Use the same coordinate system for both.

533.title: Gain calculation
533.content: For each speaker, the distance is the Euclidean source-to-speaker distance with Blur squared added under the square root. A small offset avoids division by zero. The gain is the inverse of this distance raised to Roll-off × 0.166096. The gains are then normalized so their squared sum is one. Increasing Roll-off concentrates the distribution on nearby speakers; increasing Blur makes it broader. This normalization does not provide overall distance attenuation when a source moves away from the array.

534.title: Connecting a source
534.content: . | Send speaker positions from Multi-Cursor Manager to Speakers for a 2D layout. | Send the source position to Source. Path Generator produces a list of positions: with one trajectory, use Array Flattener to turn its output into a coordinate pair or triple. | Connect Output to Matrix Spatialization’s Weights. | Connect a mono audio source to Matrix Spatialization’s Input, set Audio outs to the speaker count and Channel offset to zero. | Route the resulting audio channels to the loudspeakers. | . Use a separate DBAP instance for each independently moving source. For a regular grid, see GBAP.

536.title: Temporal Patching (Delayed Mode)
536.content: . Let a sound return in another form after its original passage has moved on. Here, effects start later than their source but receive earlier source material, creating staggered transformations instead of joining the sound currently playing.

537.title: Overview
537.content: Delayed cables retain the source material and deliver it relative to each effect’s start. Moving an effect interval therefore changes when that treatment appears in the composition. The entrances are composed on the timeline, independently of the source’s own lifetime.

538.title: Try it
538.content: Configure audio output and start at a low level. Bytebeat generates the source, so no sound file is needed; Bytebeat, Faust and Airwindows support are required. | Listen to the direct sound, then to the Low, Medium and High effects as they begin. Follow how earlier material reappears through later treatments. | Let the source stop automatically, but leave the effects active. Listen for the remaining delayed material and tails, then use the effects’ end triggers to close the passage. | Move one effect interval farther from the source and replay: its entrance moves later, but it still begins with the same early source material. | . See glutton mode, where a newly active effect receives the currently playing source without replaying its earlier material. Live input is optional; use headphones if adding a microphone to avoid loudspeaker feedback. Download this example . Try this on web .

539.title: Learn more
539.content: . | Audio routing - How audio propagates through the timeline | Audio plugins - VST, Faust, JSFX effect formats | Audio device - Configuring audio input/output | .

541.title: Depth cameras
541.content: The Depth Camera Input device streams color, infrared, depth images and point clouds from depth cameras into ossia score, along with their inertial sensors and settings. It is available in the desktop builds since 3.9.0.

542.title: Supported cameras
542.content: | Camera | Linux | Windows | macOS | . | Orbbec Femto Mega / Mega i / Bolt | yes | yes | color and infrared only¹ | . | Orbbec Gemini 330 / 335 / 336 / 345, Gemini 2, Astra 2, DaBai | yes | yes | yes | . | Kinect v2 (Xbox One) | yes | yes | yes | . | Kinect v1 (Xbox 360) | yes | yes | yes | . | Azure Kinect DK | yes | yes | no² | . | Intel RealSense D400 / D500 / L500 / SR300 | yes | yes | yes | . | Luxonis OAK-D, OAK-1 and OAK-4, including PoE models | yes | yes | yes | . | Oak3DVision Oak CDK / QCDK (time-of-flight) | yes | no³ | Intel Macs only³ | . ¹ The Femto Mega and Bolt compute depth with an Orbbec depth engine that is not available for macOS. The Gemini and Astra cameras compute depth on the device and are not affected. ² Microsoft never released an Azure Kinect SDK for macOS. ³ The vendor only ships prebuilt binaries for Linux, Intel macOS and 32-bit Windows. Orbbec Femto Mega cameras and Luxonis OAK PoE cameras also work over Ethernet.

543.title: Installation
543.content: The device itself ships with ossia score. The camera drivers come as a single Depth cameras package to install from score’s package manager, then restart score. Linux: install the udev rules . The cameras are accessed over raw USB. Without the matching udev rules, the camera is not accessible and score reports no camera, exactly as if nothing was plugged in. The package contains the rules for all supported cameras: . sudo cp ~/Documents/ossia/score/packages/depth-camera/udev/*.rules /etc/udev/rules.d/ sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger . Then unplug and replug the camera. Azure Kinect: install Microsoft’s SDK . The Azure Kinect depth engine cannot be redistributed. Install the Azure Kinect Sensor SDK system-wide, or place libk4a and its libk4a1.4/libdepthengine subfolder in the package folder. If it is missing, score’s log says so. USB 3 . The Azure Kinect DK, the Kinect v2 and the RealSense D400 series need a USB 3 port. On USB 2, the Kinect v2 and Azure Kinect do not show their cameras at all, and RealSense cameras fall back to very low frame rates. A USB-C cable does not guarantee a USB 3 port.

544.title: Adding the device
544.content: In Add device, choose Depth Camera Input in the Video In category. Each installed camera family appears as its own category in the browser, listing the cameras it can see; selecting one fills in its address. Leave the address empty to use the first camera found. The address can also be typed, for instance to reach a camera by serial number or over the network: . orbbec:sn:CL8L1234ABC Orbbec camera, by serial number orbbec:net:192.168.0.12:8090 Femto Mega over Ethernet freenect2:sn:012345678901 Kinect v2 freenect:index:0 Kinect v1 k4a:sn:000123456789 Azure Kinect realsense:sn:040322070203 RealSense . If the requested camera is not present, the device does not connect rather than silently using another camera.

545.title: Streams
545.content: The device has one node per enabled stream: . | Node | Type | Notes | . | rgb | texture | Color image. Not available on time-of-flight cameras without a color sensor. | . | ir | texture | Infrared image (on a time-of-flight camera, the amplitude image). | . | depth | texture | 16-bit depth image. | . | pointcloud | geometry | Connect it to a 3D process, such as a model display or any geometry input. | . | imu/accel, imu/gyro, imu/temperature | vec3f / float | Inertial sensors, when the camera has them and the Accelerometer / gyroscope option is enabled. | . Point cloud positions are in metres, right-handed, with +X to the right, +Y down and +Z forward. Accelerations are in m/s² (including gravity) and angular velocities in rad/s. Textures can be processed with shaders and the computer vision objects, and the point cloud can be used in 3D scenes.

546.title: Camera settings
546.content: The settings that each camera’s SDK allows to change appear under a controls node, grouped by what they affect: for instance controls/color/exposure, controls/depth/laser_power or controls/sensors/temperature. They are ordinary parameters with their real type and range: they can be automated, mapped or controlled over OSC. Read-only values (temperatures, measured exposure) are under sensors/, and rarely needed actions such as rebooting the camera are under advanced/. On Luxonis OAK-D Pro cameras, depth/laser_power turns on the dot projector, which is off by default and needed to measure depth on plain surfaces.

547.title: Alignment, resolution and frame rate
547.content: Alignment brings the depth and color images into the same frame of reference, and decides the resolution of the point cloud: . | Color to depth (default): the point cloud has the depth resolution. This is usually the right choice for point clouds. | Depth to color: the point cloud has the color resolution, which is much heavier (about five times more points than measured on a Femto Mega). Use it when you need pixel-aligned color and depth images. | None: no alignment. A colored point cloud requires an alignment other than None. | . Choosing an explicit color resolution is the simplest way to reduce the cost of a depth to color point cloud.

548.title: Troubleshooting
548.content: | Symptom | Likely cause | . | No camera at all in the browser | The Depth cameras package is not installed, or score was not restarted after installing it. | . | One camera family is missing | Its udev rules are not installed (Linux), or for Azure Kinect, the Microsoft SDK is missing. | . | Kinect v2 or Azure Kinect missing, RealSense very slow | The camera is on a USB 2 port. | . | Network Orbbec cameras do not appear | A firewall drops the broadcast replies of the cameras (UDP source port 3956), or the camera is on another subnet: type its address instead. | . | Colored point cloud is greyed out | Alignment is set to None. | . | No controls node | The camera’s SDK offers no settings for this model. | . Set the environment variable SCORE_DEPTHCAM_DEBUG=1 to log, every second, how many frames each point cloud receives. More details are in the add-on’s README.

549.title: score development manual
549.content: This section of the manual gives an overview of the score development processes. It explains how to make a local build, create a plug-in, discusses the software architecture, etc.

550.title: Deployment targets
550.content: . | Building for WebAssembly covers the browser build, its assets and hosting requirements. | Custom applications covers packaging a score project as a branded, platform-specific application. | .

552.title: Device Examples
552.content: Choose an example by what the performer does: play notes, change sound or image continuously, or trigger a cue.

553.title: Play and shape sound
553.content: . | Gamepad control pairs button-triggered drums with stick-controlled degradation and echoes. Start here for a compact instrument with both discrete and continuous controls. | MIDI notes, controls and timeline triggers moves beyond playing notes: use a keyboard to start, stop and choose sections of a scenario. | Playing synths on channels 1 and 10 separates lead and drums so one MIDI source can address two instruments. | MIDI synth and drum effects patch explores contrasting treatments of those instruments, with a different saved drum sound. | Soundfonts, drum kits and a single-file sampler plays an instrument live and sequences and layers recorded sounds. | .

554.title: Perform visuals
554.content: . | MIDI controls for a shader turns wheels and notes into changes of scale, rotation and shape. | Sensors2OSC phone control uses phone rotation and touch to move a cube and distort its image. | OSC values controlling a native 3D scene offers the same kind of interaction for any sender that can produce the required OSC messages. | .

555.title: Connect a service to a cue
