656.title: External script languages
656.content: Shell command can launch code with an interpreter installed on the host computer. These are external programs, not additional embedded runtimes with access to Script, Score.Editor or score’s audio buffers. Use JavaScript/QML or a native process interface when the code needs to run inside score’s execution graph.

657.title: Choose the matching manual
657.content: | Interpreter selection | Language reference | Execution requirement | . | System | The host operating system’s command interpreter documentation | Syntax depends on the operating system. | . | Sh | POSIX shell command language | A sh executable; Bash-specific extensions are not portable POSIX shell syntax. | . | Bash | GNU Bash manual | Bash installed and discoverable. | . | Zsh | Zsh manual | Zsh installed and discoverable. | . | Fish | Fish language reference | Fish installed; its syntax differs from POSIX shells. | . | Python | Python language reference and standard library | The process invokes python3. | . | PowerShell | PowerShell language reference | powershell on Windows or pwsh elsewhere. | . | Cmd | Windows command reference | Windows command support; selecting Cmd does not install it on another platform. | . | Custom | The selected executable’s own documentation | Supply the executable and arguments in Custom command. | . A pipe, variable expansion or quoting rule belongs to the selected interpreter. For example, shell $name expansion is not Python variable syntax, and PowerShell pipelines pass objects rather than simply following POSIX text-pipeline conventions.

658.title: Passing the script
658.content: In Custom command, %s is replaced by the complete Script text. If %s is absent, score appends the script as a final argument. The executable must accept that invocation; many interpreters require an option to distinguish source text from a filename. Quote the command arguments according to the interpreter and avoid inserting untrusted input into source code.

659.title: Lifetime, communication and safety
659.content: Shell command starts the program when the process executes, including when used as a state cue. The program is detached: ending the interval does not terminate it. There are no stdout or exit-status output ports on this process. Use Process Launcher when the score needs managed process lifetime and communication. External scripts run with the current user’s permissions. They can read and modify files, make network requests or launch further programs. Inspect scripts before playing a downloaded score. Interpreter versions, installed libraries and executable paths are deployment dependencies; they are not bundled merely because the script text is saved in a score. Shell command is unavailable in the WebAssembly build.

660.title: Extract Attribute
660.content: A rotating goblet takes its colors from a generated image instead of its original material: the mesh keeps its positions and gets new per-vertex colors. The process labelled Extract attribute—now named Extract buffer—takes the loaded mesh’s position data. Texture to buffer turns Color Test Grid into a second data source, and Buffers to geometry pairs positions with colors, and native Model display renders the result to Window:/; this is native geometry processing, not Qt Quick 3D. Geometry Info supplies the vertex count so that the reconstructed geometry follows the source mesh. Here, the image is a palette of per-vertex RGBA values, not a texture wrapped around the goblet with UV coordinates. Buffer format and stride determine how its pixels become colors; see Geometry and buffer utilities when adapting this layout. The processing uses GPU buffers, but that does not guarantee that every extraction or conversion is zero-copy.

661.title: Try it
661.content: Open the ZIP directly in score and start playback; the goblet model is included. Change Color Test Grid’s color shift to cycle the goblet’s palette, then change its grid dimensions to change how quickly the colors vary across the shape. When substituting a color texture, provide at least one RGBA pixel per vertex. The score’s notes illustrate the sizing with 3,000 vertices and a 55-by-55 texture, which supplies 3,025 pixels. Use the Value displays to compare vertex count and buffer size, and keep the attribute format and stride consistent with the texture’s pixel format. Try this on web . Download this example .

662.title: Learn more
662.content: . | Object loader - Loading 3D models | Model display - 3D mesh rendering process | LFO - Low-frequency oscillator for animation | Graphics pipeline - How rendering works in ossia score | Geometry and buffer utilities - Current process names, byte layouts and conversion controls | .

663.title: Extract buffer
663.content: Extract buffer exposes data from incoming Geometry through a GPU Buffer outlet. Use it to feed a compute process or inspect data with Buffer to array from Geometry and buffer utilities. It does not output a complete mesh or scene.

664.title: Controls
664.content: Attribute selects what to extract: . | Position, TexCoord, Color, Normal or Tangent select a standard attribute semantic. | Attribute 0–8 select an attribute by its index in the geometry description. | Index selects the geometry’s index buffer. | Buffer 0–8 select a whole buffer by index. | . Attribute extraction and whole-buffer selection are different operations. An attribute can occupy only part of an interleaved vertex record; a whole buffer can contain several attributes. Use Geometry Info to inspect the source layout before choosing an index. Pad vec3 to vec4 requests four-component records when extracting a three-component attribute. Account for the changed record size in the downstream consumer; this is not a general format-conversion control for arbitrary whole buffers.

665.title: Workflow
665.content: Connect a geometry producer to Geometry, select a resource actually present in it, and connect Buffer to the consumer. Match the consumer’s element type and stride to the extracted data. For several attributes in one newly packed buffer, use Repack attributes instead. For custom attribute names and scene auxiliary resources, use the distinct Extract buffer (by name) process documented in Geometry and buffer utilities. That process has Mode and Name / index controls rather than this page’s Attribute selector. Neither process replaces Scene Preprocessor: preprocess a scene before extracting resources from its geometry output.

666.title: Frequently Asked Questions
666.content: Here is a list of (not necessarily) frequently asked questions. In case none of these answer yours, feel more than welcome to ask for help on the ossia.io forum or send a message on ossia score Gitter channel where you will most likely find a handful of score users and developers.

668.title: Faust language reference
668.content: Faust is a functional language for digital signal processing, developed at GRAME with an international community. A program describes a signal-processing graph rather than a sequence of per-sample imperative statements. score compiles this graph and uses it as an audio processor. For loading DSP files, editing and compiling them, import paths, portable projects and packages, see the Faust process. This page separates language constructs from the interface provided by score.

669.title: Definitions and program entry point
669.content: A runnable DSP defines process. Definitions end in ;; // and /* ... */ introduce comments. Definitions name expressions, not mutable variables. Functions can take named parameters: . // One input, one output: halve the incoming signal. half(x) = x * 0.5; process = half; . The identity block _ passes a signal unchanged; ! discards one. Numeric expressions can operate on signals. For example, process = _ * 0.5; describes the same gain operation. Local definitions can be grouped with with { ... };. Metadata such as declare name "My effect"; describes the program rather than adding a signal connection. See the authoritative Faust syntax manual for definitions, lexical environments, pattern matching, numeric operators and primitives.

670.title: Signal composition
670.content: Faust expressions are block diagrams with a known number of inputs and outputs. Wiring must match their arities; composition operators do not represent imperative statement order. | Operator | Meaning | Connection rule | . | A, B | Parallel composition | Place the blocks side by side; retain both sets of inputs and outputs. | . | A : B | Sequential composition | Connect each output of A to an input of B; their counts must match. | . | A <: B | Split composition | Repeat the outputs of A across the inputs of B; the input count of B must be a multiple of the output count of A. | . | A :> B | Merge composition | Sum groups of outputs of A into the inputs of B; the output count of A must be a multiple of the input count of B. | . | A ~ B | Recursive composition | Feed outputs back through B to inputs of A, with an implicit one-sample delay in the feedback connection; feedback arities must be compatible. | . Use parentheses to make grouping explicit. For example: . // Two independently processed channels: two inputs and two outputs. process = *(0.5), *(0.5); . // Duplicate a single input into two outputs. process = _ <: _, _; . The diagram-composition reference gives exact arity constraints, precedence, recursion and iteration forms such as par and seq. Explicit delay primitives and feedback are how signal state is represented; an ordinary definition is not an assignment to stored state.

671.title: Controls
671.content: Control primitives produce signals. Slider and numeric-entry arguments are a label, initial value, minimum, maximum and step: . level = hslider("level", 0.5, 0, 1, 0.01); process = _ * level; . Related primitives include vslider, nentry, button and checkbox. Labels name the controls; Faust also supports label metadata and grouping primitives. See the user-interface primitives for the language-level contract. A host chooses how to expose these controls: a Faust UI declaration does not itself create a score QML interface.

672.title: Standard library
672.content: Import the standard library to access its namespaced DSP functions: . import("stdfaust.lib"); level = hslider("level", 0.1, 0, 1, 0.01); process = os.osc(440) * level; . This is a mono generator with no audio input. os.osc comes from the oscillator library; the import provides library environments such as os rather than requiring every function to be defined in the DSP file. Common library families include: . | os — oscillators: periodic signal generators. | fi — filters: filtering building blocks. | en — envelopes: amplitude and control envelopes. | de — delays: delay-line functions. | ba — basics: common DSP utilities. | ma — maths: mathematical helpers and constants. | . Consult the full library index and standard functions reference for signatures and examples. Library functions and language primitives are different layers; available library versions depend on the installation and import search path.

673.title: score integration contract
673.content: . | The compiled DSP determines the process’s audio channel counts. A graph with no audio inputs is a generator; an effect consumes its declared input channels. | Faust sliders, numeric entries, buttons and checkboxes become score controls. Recompiling a different program can therefore change the process interface. | A synthesizer using the conventional freq, gain and gate controls is detected as MIDI-driven. These names are a score integration convention, not keywords required by the Faust language. | Editing the source in score does not immediately replace the running DSP: use Compile in the process editor. | score embeds the loaded DSP source, not the entire transitive set of imported libraries. An import("my-library.lib"); still requires that file to be available through the import search path. | Compilation requires a score build with Faust support and usable libraries. See the process page for FAUST_LIB_PATH, relative import directories and packaging; this is not a guarantee that every external Faust architecture or standalone compiler option is exposed in score. | . The process workflow and portability guide is the canonical guide to locating and distributing imported files. Ready-made score DSPs are available in the Faust user-library presets.

674.title: Upstream references
674.content: . | Faust documentation | Language syntax and primitives | Faust standard DSP libraries | Faust online IDE for experimenting with the language outside score; host integration remains different. | .

676.title: Faust Synthesis
676.content: . Ringing bells and bowls give way to buzzing, plucked strings in a small synthetic ensemble. The sounds come from physical models, not recordings: changing how a model is excited can alter the character of a strike or pluck as well as its pitch.

677.title: Structure
677.content: The timeline brings the instruments in and out, while modulation changes their excitation and resonance. Reverb connects the sections, and a later pitch-shifting layer transforms the plucked sounds. The return to the first section is cued by hand, not fixed in time. The Faust DSP code is embedded, so no samples or MIDI controller are needed. Use a build with Faust support and assign the root interval’s audio output before listening; the saved root has no output destination.

678.title: Try it
678.content: . | Start at a low listening level. Follow the bell and bowl section into Buzz, where sitar and guitar models take over. Listen for the difference between sustained resonance and the attack of a pluck. | Change the Step sequencer values driving the sitar’s Resonance. This changes the repeating timbral pattern without changing its MIDI notes. The bowl’s excitation is also modulated; adjust its LFO to hear a different pattern of excitation. | In Pitch, reshape the automation feeding Noisify. Draw a smooth contour, then one with abrupt steps, and listen to how the pitch-shifted layer moves against the source. | Trigger the end of Buzz to return to the bowl section. Try holding the plucked section longer before returning: the cue changes the form without rewriting the material. Freeverb and Pitch have independent end triggers; use Stop to finish everything. | Open a Faust process’s script editor to connect the audible controls with its model or effect. Replacing a model is a possible adaptation; the saved score already supplies the timeline and modulation around it. | . Download this example . Try this on web .

679.title: Learn more
679.content: . | Audio plugins - Complete guide to VST, VST3, CLAP, LV2, JSFX plugins | Faust - Writing and using Faust DSP code | Audio Effects - Built-in audio effect processes | Supported protocols and formats - All supported audio plugin formats | .

681.title: Faust
681.content: . Faust is a domain-specific programming language, tailored for writing digital signal processing code, for instance audio effects and synthesizers, super easily. It is mainly developed at Grame, with an international community of contributors. For syntax, signal composition, controls and the standard DSP library, see the Faust language reference. This page covers the score process workflow, setup and project packaging. Faust DSP files can be drag’n’dropped directly inside a score. This will compile the DSP and embed it as a signal processor in the score. Additionally, any .dsp file found recursively in the library folder will be detected and added under the Faust section in the process library. Faust code can be edited directly from within the user interface, by clicking on the small “window” icon on the node header. One must press “Compile” when the code is ready to update it to the audio engine.

682.title: Ports and controls
682.content: The DSP determines the number of audio channels. Faust sliders, numeric entries, buttons and checkboxes become score controls, so the process interface changes with the compiled program. A synthesizer using the conventional freq, gain and gate controls is detected as MIDI-driven; a normal effect processes its audio input instead. See the score integration contract and control syntax for the distinction between Faust language primitives and score’s host interface.

683.title: Imports and portable projects
683.content: When a .dsp file is loaded, score embeds its source text in the document and remembers the original file’s directory as an additional import search path. For example, an import("my-library.lib"); can resolve a library beside that DSP file. Editing the embedded code is not the same as editing the original file on disk. score saves this import directory relative to the score library or project where possible, and resolves it again when loading. This lets a project or library move without unnecessarily retaining the old machine’s absolute path. Imports still need the referenced files: embedding the DSP does not embed every imported .lib. Keep local Faust libraries with the project, or install them as a score package on every machine that opens it. The project media tools report the import folder as an external dependency, but do not automatically collect or rewrite the whole Faust library tree. When using Save as, verify imports still resolve if the destination no longer contains the same files. FAUST_LIB_PATH can override the bundled Faust library location; see command-line and environment options. Compilation requires a build with Faust support and a usable library search path, not just the presence of the .dsp file.

685.title: Video tutorial
685.content: Faust in ossia score: video tutorialPlay · loads YouTube

686.title: Faust packages
686.content: It is possible to provide new Faust libraries as score packages. This is done for instance with Alain Bonardi’s abclib which is packaged here : most importantly, the library folder in such a package will be added to the Faust library path so that new functions can be provided.

687.title: FFmpeg input and output streams
687.content: . Receive a live video stream, transform it in score and send a treated image to another application without recording an intermediate file. A separate local view shows a different treatment from the one your receiver sees.

688.title: Local and outgoing paths
688.content: The incoming UDP video splits into two paths. Hyperspace creates the scrolling treatment in score’s output window; Color Controls changes the image sent to the external receiver. Adjusting the local Hyperspace effect does not change the outgoing picture. The test runs entirely on your machine: input arrives on UDP port 5000 and output leaves on port 5001.

689.title: Run the stream
689.content: Use a score build with the FFmpeg device and an external FFmpeg installation with libx264 and AAC encoding. Keep ports 5000 and 5001 available. Start this local test source: . ffmpeg -re -f lavfi -i testsrc=size=1280x720:rate=30 -re -f lavfi -i sine=frequency=1000:sample_rate=44100 -c:v libx264 -preset ultrafast -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -b:a 96k -f mpegts udp://127.0.0.1:5000 . Open the score and start playback. Run a receiver for its processed output: . ffplay udp://127.0.0.1:5001 . Change Color Controls brightness or saturation: only the receiver’s image changes. Then change the LFO driving Hyperspace: only the local window changes. The saved output is video-only: MJPEG encoding with the MJPEG muxer at 1280×720, 30 fps. It is not MPEG-TS like the test input, and the test tone is not forwarded. Stop the external sender and receiver when finished. Try this on web . Download this example .

690.title: Files, strings and serialization
690.content: . Read a text at a musical pace, reshape its words, and capture changing device values for later replay. Displays show what each transformation produces. Try this on web . Download the example .

691.title: Read and transform text
691.content: Open the ZIP directly in score and use a writable project directory. Start playback, then try the two ways of bringing text into a patch: . | Press Read File’s Read control to load a complete sample. Inspect the data and status outputs together so you can distinguish content from a failed read. | Press Read File Line’s Open control to open the fables. The metronome advances through the text one line at a time; Rewind returns to the beginning. | . The line-by-line path turns stored text into a timed sequence. Each line is shown next to its split-and-joined version; change the join separator to recombine the words differently. The regular-expression branch selects fable headings and captures their Roman numerals; change the pattern to select another feature, using RE2 syntax. Write File saves transformed lines in the project directory using a timestamped filename. Its Write mode replaces the current target’s contents instead of appending a continuous transcript. Choose a new destination if you want to preserve an earlier result.

692.title: Exchange structured values
692.content: A pair of changing values can be kept as structured data or encoded as text for another system. Change Vec2f: the reconstructed result should match the value before serialization. The JSON branch builds an object, while the plain-text branch separates components with , ; the serializer and parser must agree on that delimiter. The object-building branch requires the Jk Object filter add-on. A separate string-to-bytes round trip shows the same text as bytes, the form a byte-oriented connection expects.

693.title: Record and replay control values
693.content: The device branch records generated control values, then replays them at different addresses, so what a recording controls can be chosen later. The downloadable archive has no recording for the saved CSV Playback mode. To make one, choose Record, set the pattern to OSC:/foo.*, and select a new writable file. Then switch to Playback with OSC:/bar.* and inspect the replayed values. Keep any earlier recording you want to retain in a different file. The text experiments work independently of this recording. To observe device values in another application, the OSC device listens on UDP 9997 and sends to 127.0.0.1:9996.

694.title: Gamepad Control
694.content: . Play a rhythm with the buttons and reshape it with the sticks. The buttons trigger drum attacks; the sticks change the sound continuously between them.

695.title: Prepare the controller and samples
695.content: . | Open the ZIP directly in score; the Fairlight drum kit and its samples are included. | Connect a gamepad. If Gamepad is disconnected in the Device explorer, right-click it and select your controller or choose Reconnect. Check that /button/a, /button/b and the stick axes change before starting playback. Physical button labels may differ from these standardized names. | Configure audio output and begin at a low level. This patch needs Deuterium, Faust and Airwindows. | .

696.title: Play the patch
696.content: Press A and B during playback to play two drum sounds. Alternate them until you have a repeatable rhythm, then keep that rhythm steady while moving one stick at a time. The left stick controls Bitcrush: horizontal movement changes Rate, and vertical movement changes Crush. Move along one axis first, then diagonally: the drums get grainier and rougher while the pattern stays the same. The right stick controls delay time and feedback. Begin with low feedback and try short repeats, then lengthen the delay to fill the space between hits. Raise feedback cautiously and leave pauses to hear the echoes decay; changing both axes at once can make a familiar rhythm much denser. There is no rumble mapping in this patch: the feedback to the performer is audible, not tactile. Download this example . Try this on web .

697.title: Learn more
697.content: . | Joystick device - Gamepad and joystick device configuration | MIDI utilities - Converting triggers to MIDI notes | Working with devices - General device setup guide | .

699.title: Grid-Based Amplitude Panning (GBAP)
699.content: . GBAP calculates weights for a rectangular grid of sinks. Cursor and sink sizes determine how a source overlaps the grid; RollOff shapes the distribution. The result is control data for processes such as Matrix Spatialization, not an audio signal.

700.title: Inputs and output
700.content: | Port | Value | . | Input Weights | List of incoming gains; System Number selects one entry | . | Input Multicursor | List of XY source positions | . | Output Weights | List of weight lists, one list per source | . When Input Multicursor contains positions, they replace the internal Position control. When it is empty, GBAP calculates one weight list from Position. Each list contains Sink X # multiplied by Sink Y # weights, with X varying first.

701.title: Controls
701.content: | Control | Purpose | . | Gain | Overall multiplier, from 0 to 1 | . | RollOff | Shapes the weight distribution, from 0 to 24; default 6 | . | Normalize | Scales each source’s largest weight to 1 before applying Gain and the selected input weight | . | Sink X # / Sink Y # | Grid dimensions, each from 1 to 12 | . | System Number | One-based index into Input Weights | . | Sink Size | XY size of each sink | . | Cursor Size | XY size of the source’s overlap area | . | Position | Internal source position in the 0–1 XY area | . Normalize is peak normalization, not constant-power normalization. Gain and the selected input weight are applied afterward. System Number must select an existing Input Weights entry. Otherwise the output is zero. For a standalone spatializer, send [1] to Input Weights and set System Number to 1.

702.title: Moving a source
702.content: Drag the cursor in the grid, click a new position, or automate Position. For external positions, connect Multi-Cursor Manager or Path Generator in XY output mode to Input Multicursor.

703.title: Applying weights to audio
703.content: For one source and four speakers: . | Set Sink X # and Sink Y # to 2. | Send [1] to Input Weights and set System Number to 1. | Leave Input Multicursor empty and move the internal Position. | Connect Output Weights to Array Flattener, then connect the flattened result to Matrix Spatialization’s Weights inlet. | Connect a mono audio source to Matrix Spatialization’s Input. Set Audio outs to 4 and Channel offset to 0. | Route its audio output to the four loudspeaker channels. | . For several sources, extract each nested weight list and send it to a separate Matrix Spatialization instance with the corresponding mono audio source. Flattening all source lists together does not create an audio mixing matrix.

704.title: Related processes
704.content: DBAP supports irregular speaker layouts. Multi-Cursor Manager supplies editable positions; Path Generator supplies moving positions. See Spatial audio techniques for a complete DBAP patch.

706.title: Generate Array
706.content: A sequence of numbers becomes a rotating line drawing in space. Glow and a long exposure turn its changing geometry into luminous traces. Arraygen evaluates an expression on the CPU, using i for each array element and pos for playback position. The 300 resulting values describe 100 XYZ vertices. Array to buffer transfers those values to the GPU, and Pointcloud to mesh makes geometry that Model display draws in Lines mode. A procedural sine warp gradient colors the drawing. An LFO rotates it, while bloom brightens its highlights and Long Exposure retains earlier images. The visible trail therefore contains previous rendered frames, not additional vertices in the current mesh.

707.title: Try it
707.content: Start playback and edit the expression to change the distribution of points. Keep complete XYZ triples and the Array to buffer type set to Float32; see Geometry and buffer utilities if you change the layout. Slow the LFO, then vary Long Exposure’s discharge rate. One changes how fast the drawing moves; the other changes how long the image remembers it. No external asset is required. This is native Model display rendering, not Qt Quick 3D. The saved Window uses an HDR swapchain format: use a compatible HDR output, or change the Window format and adapt the final image for an SDR display. Try this on web . Download this example .

708.title: Learn more
708.content: . | Math expressions - Expression-based value generation | ISF Shaders - Interactive Shader Format for GPU effects | LFO - Low-frequency oscillator for animation | Model display - 3D mesh rendering process | Graphics pipeline - How rendering works in ossia score | .

709.title: Generative arc sphere
709.content: . A sphere assembled from arcs bends and ripples under a swirling texture. Deformation, surface animation and viewpoint move independently, and none of them regenerates the geometry. Structure Synth builds the arc sphere on the CPU. Bend then changes its vertices during native Model Display rendering, while color automation and a moving camera alter how the structure is seen. Regenerating the grammar changes the underlying sculpture; it is not required for each frame of bending.

710.title: Try it
710.content: Start playback and turn off Bend’s animated bending to inspect a fixed deformation. Change its amount and radius, then re-enable animation and vary its speed. Move the pointer in the output window to change HypnoSwirl’s texture; the camera keeps following its own LFO. The geometry program and shaders are stored in the score. No external model is needed; allow time for CPU mesh generation when editing the Structure Synth program. Try this on web . Download this example .

711.title: Geo Zones
711.content: . Create interactive zones in 2D space where parameters change based on position within those zones. Define areas with different behaviors and interpolate smoothly between them as objects or people move through the space. Perfect for location-based installations, interactive floor projections, or any system where you want different behaviors in different areas of a physical or virtual space.

712.title: How it works
712.content: Geo Zones lets you define multiple zones in a 2D coordinate system, each with its own parameter values. As a position input moves through this space, the system interpolates between zone values to create smooth transitions. Position input - XY coordinates representing location in 2D space, in latitude / longitude. Zone definition - Create zones with shapes, positions, and parameter values Blur - Smooth blending between zone parameters Multiple outputs - Different parameters can have different zone configurations .

714.title: Geometry filter shaders
714.content: Geometry filter is another score-specific, ISF-derived shader format. It attaches a vertex transformation to incoming geometry for a downstream renderer. Unlike CSF, it does not ask you to dispatch a compute kernel; unlike raw raster, it does not require a complete vertex/fragment pipeline. Use it to deform a mesh or change vertex attributes before display. Connect a geometry source to Geometry In, then Geometry Out to a compatible renderer such as Model display. The Animated Sphere Geometry Filter is a working example.

715.title: Header and source file
715.content: Use a .glsl file with a JSON comment header. MODE selects the geometry-filter format, and INPUTS defines controls using the ISF input vocabulary. For example: . /*{ "ISFVSN": "2", "MODE": "GEOMETRY_FILTER", "DESCRIPTION": "Time-varying vertex displacement", "INPUTS": [ { "NAME": "intensity", "TYPE": "float", "DEFAULT": 0.01, "MIN": 0.0, "MAX": 0.1 } ] }*/ void process_vertex(inout vec3 position, inout vec3 normal, inout vec2 uv, inout vec3 tangent, inout vec4 color) { position += this_filter.intensity * 10.0 * sin(TIME * position); } . The body follows the deformation in the supplied sphere example. This is a callback, not a standalone main(): the renderer supplies the enclosing vertex shader. Keep the header and body together when saving a file or adding it to the user library.

716.title: Callback contract
716.content: | Argument | Type | Purpose | . | position | inout vec3 | Vertex position to transform. | . | normal | inout vec3 | Surface normal used for shading. | . | uv | inout vec2 | Texture coordinates. | . | tangent | inout vec3 | Tangent attribute. | . | color | inout vec4 | Vertex color. | . Arguments are mutable: leaving one unchanged preserves the value supplied to the callback. Displacing a position does not automatically give the corresponding deformed normal; update the normal as part of the transformation when the intended lighting requires it. The source mesh and renderer still determine which attributes are available and how they are used. Access header controls through this_filter, as in this_filter.intensity. TIME is available for animation. Do not copy ISF fragment output code into this callback: it changes vertex attributes, not a pixel color attachment. Do not add the raw-raster main() prologue or epilogue around it; that enclosing shader belongs to the renderer. For GLSL types and portable arithmetic, see the GLSL runtime reference. For explicit geometry buffers, generated topology or compute feedback, use the CSF geometry reference.

717.title: Implementation reference
717.content: The current Geometry filter process defines the callback and validates it inside a generated vertex shader. Its library handler identifies .glsl files with the GEOMETRY_FILTER mode. These host conventions are specific to score, not part of standard ISF.

718.title: Animated Sphere Geometry Filter
718.content: . A checkerboard sphere turns while its surface swells and distorts. One control rotates the whole object; another, independent one deforms its shape. Geometry filter displaces the sphere’s vertices with a time-varying sine function. One slow LFO changes the strength of that displacement; another rotates the sphere. The checkerboard makes surface changes easier to follow, and Model Display renders the result before a glow effect softens it.

719.title: Try it
719.content: Start playback and open the Window output. Disconnect the filter’s intensity cable and set intensity to zero: the sphere should keep rotating, but lose its deformation. Restore the cable, then change the deformation LFO’s rate without changing the rotation rate to see the two rhythms drift apart. Increasing the sphere’s subdivisions gives the filter more vertices to displace, at a higher rendering cost. The shape and texture are generated in the score; no mesh or image download is required. See the Geometry filter shader reference for the deformation callback and Model display for rendering the resulting geometry. Download this example . Try this on web .

720.title: Geometry Info
720.content: Geometry Info inspects one connected Geometry input. It reports the geometry description; it does not read back vertex values, render an image or pass the geometry through to another outlet.

721.title: Outputs
721.content: | Output | Type and contents | . | Vertices | Integer vertex count from the geometry description. | . | Indices | Integer index count from the geometry description. | . | Instances | Integer instance count. | . | Attributes | Structured list of attribute descriptors: semantics, formats, bindings and offsets. Not a count. | . | Bindings | Structured list describing record strides, step rates and per-vertex/per-instance classification. Not a count. | . | Inputs | Structured list mapping bindings to buffer indices and byte offsets. Not a count. | . | Readable | Text summary of the counts and layout descriptors. | .

722.title: Diagnosing a draw
722.content: Branch a geometry producer to this process and connect Readable to a value display. Check: . | Whether the reported counts match the intended draw. | Whether the expected position, normal, UV or color semantics exist. | Whether attribute formats and byte offsets agree with the producer’s layout. | Whether binding strides and per-instance classification agree with the consumer. | . The report describes metadata, not proof that all referenced buffer bytes are valid. For example, Buffers to geometry uses your explicit layout settings rather than deducing them from the data. Use Extract buffer and Buffer to array when you need to inspect actual values, or Buffer Info and Texture Info from Geometry and buffer utilities for those resource types.

723.title: Geometry and buffer utilities
723.content: Use these tools at the boundaries between value arrays, GPU buffers, geometry and textures. A buffer contains bytes, not a self-describing mesh. Its element type, stride, offset and count must agree with the consumer. Start with a small dataset and inspect the result before increasing counts.

724.title: Choose a conversion path
724.content: | Starting data | Goal | Process | . | XYZ value array | Geometry positions or reconstructed surface | Array to mesh | . | Numeric pixel array | Texture | Array to texture | . | GPU vertex/index buffers | Geometry with an explicit layout | Buffers to geometry | . | Geometry | One attribute or an existing buffer | Extract buffer | . | Geometry | A new interleaved attribute buffer | Repack attributes | . | Texture | Pixel bytes in a GPU buffer | Texture to buffer | . | Geometry | Counts and layout diagnostics | Geometry Info | . Keep resource boundaries explicit: value arrays live on the CPU, buffers contain typed-by-convention bytes, geometry adds a draw description, and scenes carry hierarchy and resources. The individual references above are the canonical control and port manuals; the sections below locate them within a workflow. To change vertex attributes in code rather than convert their representation, use the Geometry filter shader interface. For explicit GPU buffer processing, see the CSF language reference.

725.title: Array to buffer and Buffer to array
725.content: Array to buffer accepts a numeric array or string on Input and exposes it as Output buffer data. Type selects Float32, Float64, signed/unsigned 32-bit, 16-bit or 8-bit elements. Numeric values are converted to that type; strings supply bytes. Buffer to array performs the opposite boundary crossing. Set Type to the buffer’s actual element representation; Mode selects FloatArray, IntArray or String on Output. Reading GPU-produced data into a value array introduces a readback path: keep calculations on the GPU when a CPU array is not needed.

726.title: Array to mesh
726.content: See Array to mesh for the XYZ-array contract, placement controls and limits of its optional surface reconstruction. For explicit attribute layouts, use Buffers to geometry instead.

727.title: Pointcloud to mesh
727.content: Wrap a Buffer in a point-cloud geometry description. Buffer type selects XYZ, XYZ_RGB, XYZW or XYZW_RGBA; choose the format actually produced upstream. Position, Rotation and Scale control placement. Despite the name, this supplies renderable point geometry; it is not a surface-reconstruction algorithm.

728.title: Buffers to geometry
728.content: See Buffers to geometry for named-semantic attribute setup, indexed draws, instances and topology. Its reference also distinguishes the separately registered Buffers to geometry (v1), which uses numeric attribute locations.

729.title: Extract buffer
729.content: See Extract buffer for semantic/index selection and vec3 padding. Use the by-name variant below when selecting custom names or scene auxiliary resources.

730.title: Extract buffer (by name)
730.content: Mode selects Attribute or Buffer, and Name / index identifies the resource: . | Attribute mode accepts semantics such as position, normal, tangent, texcoord0, color0, a numeric attribute index or a custom attribute name. | Buffer mode accepts a numeric buffer index, index for the index buffer, an auxiliary-buffer name, or an attribute name to retrieve its containing buffer. | . Auxiliary names allow explicit access to resources carried by Scene Preprocessor output. Selecting a whole buffer is different from extracting one tightly packed attribute from an interleaved buffer.

731.title: Repack attributes
731.content: See Repack attributes for attribute selection, packing order and the byte-stride outlet. This creates a new layout rather than selecting a whole existing buffer.

732.title: Merge Geometries
732.content: Combine eight Geometry 1–8 inputs into Merged. This composes geometry draws and their transforms; it does not weld vertices, perform a boolean union or create a new scene hierarchy. Use Scene Group for hierarchy composition.

733.title: Array to texture
733.content: See Array to texture for pixel component counts, formats and numeric ranges. It uploads numeric pixels, not encoded image-file bytes.

734.title: Texture to buffer
734.content: See Texture to buffer for the pixel-byte transfer path and downstream layout requirements. It does not create mesh attributes and is not the direct inverse of Array to texture.

735.title: Inject Buffer and Inject Texture
735.content: Both take Scene In, a Buffer or Texture, and an Aux name, then emit Scene Out carrying the named auxiliary resource. Use these before Scene Preprocessor to pass custom resources alongside a scene. An unwired resource input leaves the scene unchanged. These tools do not replace material textures; use Material Override for that operation.

736.title: Extract Scene Buffer
736.content: Read a GPU-backed Buffer from Scene In. Kind selects Environment, Camera or Material. Index selects the camera/material entry and is ignored for Environment. This exposes existing scene resource storage, not an arbitrary serialization of the hierarchy; an absent or unavailable resource cannot produce usable bytes.

737.title: Extract texture (by name)
737.content: Read an auxiliary texture from Geometry, using Name (for example skybox), and output Texture. Use this after preprocessing when another consumer needs a scene-carried texture explicitly. A 2D texture, cubemap and texture array are different resource kinds: the receiving shader must agree with the extracted resource.

738.title: Geometry Info, Buffer Info and Texture Info
738.content: | Process | Input | Outputs useful for debugging | . | Geometry Info | Geometry | Integer counts, structured attribute/binding/input lists and a Readable layout report; see its reference for details. | . | Buffer Info | Buffer | Byte size, Byte offset, Handle, Changed and Readable summary. | . | Texture Info | Texture | Width, Height, Format, Handle and Readable summary. | . Handles are opaque resource identities for diagnostics, not stable values to save and reuse in another run. Connect Readable to a value display to troubleshoot an empty or incorrectly interpreted draw. See Compute Shaders, Render Pipeline, Mesh generators and splats and 3D scene pipeline for consumers and end-to-end workflows.

739.title: Gestures
739.content: These native processes use the Puara Gestures library. They produce continuous values, not named gesture events. Install or enable the Puara add-on if they are absent from the process library.

740.title: Leaky Integrator
740.content: Library: Control > Filtering > Leaky Integrator . The Leaky Integrator accumulates its input, retaining a fraction of the previous value on each leak step: . leak step: output = input + leak_factor * previous_output between steps: output = input + previous_output . | Port or control | Type / range | Default | Meaning | . | Input | Float | — | Value added on each evaluation. | . | Leak Factor | 0–1 | 0.5 | Fraction of the old accumulator retained at a leak step. | . | Leak Frequency (Hz) | 0–200 | 100 | Leakage frequency. Fractional values are truncated to an integer; at 0, every evaluation is a leak step. | . | Output | Float | — | Accumulated value; not constrained to 0–1. | . A factor of 1 disables decay: nonzero input keeps accumulating. A factor of 0 discards history on leak steps, but still accumulates between them. To observe decay, keep the process running with zero input and a factor below 1. For positive frequencies, the process checks elapsed wall-clock time on each evaluation and applies at most one leak step. It does not run a separate leakage timer or catch up missed steps. Lowering the frequency allows more input additions between leak steps. The output therefore depends on the evaluation rate; it is not a normalized moving average or an integral scaled by elapsed time. Example: accumulation and decay . Download the accumulation and decay score . Try this on web . Give a brief event a lingering control signal: a short pulse builds up in the Leaky Integrator, then leaves a fading trace in Signal display. This is a starting point for making a light or visual response outlast the gesture that caused it; the supplied patch plots the envelope rather than controlling an artwork. The generator uses if(pos < 0.1, 1, 0): it sends 1 during the first tenth of the interval, then keeps sending 0. The integrator has Leak Factor set to 0.99 and Leak Frequency (Hz) set to 0, so every evaluation is a leak step. Play from the beginning. The display rises during the pulse and decays during the zero-input phase. The peak depends on how many evaluations occur during the pulse and can exceed 1. Reopen the example to start with a fresh accumulator when comparing settings: . | Factor 1, frequency 0: the pulse accumulates, then the output holds its value while the input is zero. | Factor 0, frequency 0: the output follows the input, with no retained history. | Factor 0.5, frequency 10: input accumulates between timed leak steps, each of which retains half the previous value. | . The example is adapted from the tutorial and score contributed by yashtiwari9182.

741.title: Roll
741.content: Library: Analysis > Gestures > Roll . Roll estimates side-to-side orientation from three motion-sensor vectors. Inputs must use the same device axes, in x, y, z order. | Port or control | Type / units | Default | Meaning | . | Acceleration | Three components, g | — | Accelerometer including gravity. | . | Gyroscope | Three components, degrees/second | — | Angular velocity, not an orientation angle. | . | Magnetometer | Three components, gauss | — | Magnetic field. | . | Enable Unwrap | Toggle | On | Tracks crossings of the raw −π to π boundary. | . | Enable Smooth | Toggle | On | Averages a 50-value history. | . | Enable Wrap | Toggle | Off | Applies the fixed 0 to 2π wrapping range. There are no range controls. | . | Output | Float, radians | — | Roll after the enabled processing stages. | . The order is raw roll → optional unwrap → optional smooth → optional wrap. Enable Unwrap can produce angles beyond one turn only while final wrapping is disabled. With all three toggles off, the raw output is in −π to π. Smoothing is a sample-history average, not a user-adjustable time constant. Android physical-unit streams need explicit conversions: acceleration in m/s² ÷ 9.80665, gyroscope in rad/s × 180/π, and magnetic field in µT ÷ 100. A vector connection alone does not perform these conversions. Validation limit: a synthetic three-stream OSC check exercised Roll successfully, but the shared orientation implementation requires further investigation after the Tilt failure described below. The phone tutorial and downloadable orientation examples are withheld rather than presented as dependable tracking workflows.

742.title: Tilt
742.content: Library: Analysis > Gestures > Tilt . Tilt derives a tilt descriptor from all three sensor vectors. The native wrapper passes acceleration, gyroscope and magnetometer to the orientation algorithm on each evaluation; it does not expose a two-sensor mode. | Port | Type / units | Meaning | . | Acceleration | Three components, g | Accelerometer including gravity, x/y/z. | . | Gyroscope | Three components, degrees/second | Angular velocity, x/y/z. The current UI spells this inlet Gyrosocope. | . | Magnetometer | Three components, gauss | Magnetic field, x/y/z. | . | Output | Float | Scaled vertical component of the orientation’s rotated axis, not an asin-derived pitch angle. Do not rely on the nominal −π/2 to π/2 range; see the runtime limitation below. | . There are no unwrap, wrap or smoothing controls on this process. The implementation computes euler.tilt = c_temp.z * π/2, so it should not be treated as a calibrated pitch angle. Input units and conversions are the same as Roll. Runtime limitation: a Linux runtime check using three synthetic OSC streams produced unstable Tilt output outside the nominal −π/2 to π/2 range. The sensor-fusion constructor initializes its quaternion but leaves its Euler and gyro-bias fields uninitialized; the exact cause of the observed failure has not been established. The tutorial and download are withheld pending an application-side investigation, not hidden behind output clamping or a selected passing input. Source: score-addon-puara/Puara/Tilt.cpp, include/puara/descriptors/tilt.h and the vendored IMU_Sensor_Fusion/imu_orientation.{h,cpp}. Source inspection of the intended equations does not supersede the failed runtime check.

743.title: Shake
743.content: Library: Analysis > Gestures > Shake . Shake takes acceleration in m/s², unlike Roll and Tilt. For each axis, the algorithm adds abs(acceleration) / 10 to an accumulator when the absolute input exceeds its internal threshold; otherwise it adds zero and uses the slow leak. The output is the Euclidean magnitude of the three axis accumulators. | Port or control | Type / range | Default | Meaning | . | Acceleration | Three components, m/s² | — | x/y/z acceleration. Gravity is not removed internally. | . | Integrator Frequency (Hz) | 0–200 | 10 | Timed leakage cadence; truncated to an integer. At 0, every evaluation is a leak step. Not the sensor sampling rate. | . | Fast Leak | 0–1 | 0.6 | Old-state fraction retained on leak steps while that axis is above threshold. Lower values retain less accumulated activity. | . | Slow Leak | 0–1 | 0.3 | Old-state fraction retained on leak steps while that axis is at or below threshold. Lower values decay faster. | . | Activation Threshold | 0–1 | 0.1 | Currently ineffective: exposed in the UI, but not forwarded by the native wrapper. The internal per-axis threshold remains 0.1 m/s². | . | Output | Float, nonnegative | — | Magnitude, not a boolean trigger or a normalized 0–1 value. | . Current limitations: changing Activation Threshold does not change sensitivity. Raw phone accelerometer readings include gravity, so a stationary phone can still produce sustained output. For example, constant (0, 0, 9.80665) input with frequency 0 and the default fast leak tends towards a magnitude of about 2.45166, not zero. A motion-only application needs independently verified gravity-removed acceleration in m/s² before Shake. Learn that stream from the chosen device; do not assume the raw accelerometer address provides it. Add an explicit comparison downstream if a discrete trigger is required. The threshold-tuning / “stop moving to reach zero” phone exercise is not provided because the current wrapper and raw-gravity input do not support those claims.

744.title: Glossary
744.content: . | Automation | Branch | Condition | Device | Device explorer | Graph inspector | Interval | Process | Processes explorer | Project folder | Protocol | Slot | State | Timeline | Trigger | User library | . Automation . Branch . Condition . Device . Devices are pieces of equipment you want to use with score in your creative project. These can be hardware (a Midi controller, a synthesizer) or software running locally or on the network. Device explorer . The device explorer is the left panel. This is where devices involved in your project can be set up, browsed or monitored. Graph inspector . The Graph inspector available in score’s top right panel allows to inspect a temporal object and its context. For example, select an interval on the scenario to list all attached processes. Interval . Some block of time in the scenario. Process . A process is an action used in the scenario to control some devices’ parameter or other processes’ parameters. score includes a number of processes such as breakpoint function-based automation, sub-scenarios, LFO or modulators or custom scripts. Processes explorer . The processes explorer is accessible at the left panel in score main window. This is where you can browse and select some processes to use in your scenario. Project folder . This is where you can browse the content of the current project. Protocol . Slot . State . Timeline . Trigger . User library . The User library can be accessed in the left panel in score main window. It can contains various uer defined components such as devices setups, processes, presets.

745.title: GLSL runtime reference
745.content: GLSL is the language used for score’s GPU shader bodies. Author Vulkan-compatible GLSL, not a legacy OpenGL program. score combines your body with declarations generated from a JSON header and compiles shaders for its Qt RHI graphics backend. Running on OpenGL does not make OpenGL-only source portable to Vulkan, Metal or Direct3D.

746.title: Choose the shader contract
746.content: | Reference | Execution and interface | . | ISF | Fullscreen fragment shader; header controls, image/audio inputs, passes and outputs. Includes an explicit standard-versus-score extension boundary. | . | CSF | score compute format: dispatches, storage images, structured buffers and geometry. | . | Raw raster | score vertex/fragment pipeline: attributes, varyings, camera data, raster state and attachments. | . | Vertex Shader Art | Procedural vertex shader with a supplied fragment stage and VSA compatibility variables. | . | Geometry filter | process_vertex callback with mutable attributes, composed into a renderer’s vertex shader. | . These are not interchangeable GLSL profiles. Their headers describe what score must allocate and bind. Process setup belongs to ISF Shaders, Compute Shaders, Render Pipeline and Vertex Shader Art; Graphics pipeline explains the graph, and Shader cookbook gives worked recipes.

747.title: Core language
747.content: The authoritative language definition is the Khronos GLSL specification, with the Vulkan GLSL rules describing its Vulkan environment. These define language features, not a promise that every score backend exposes them. A shader entry point is void main(). Helpers are ordinary typed functions. Scalar types include float, int, uint and bool; vectors include vec2–vec4, ivec*, uvec* and bvec*; matrices include mat3 and mat4. Use constructors for conversion (float(i), vec4(rgb, 1.0)) and swizzles for components (position.xyz, color.rgb). A matrix multiplied by a vector transforms that vector; order matters, so projection * view * model * position is not interchangeable with its reverse. Arithmetic, if/else, bounded for loops, arrays, structs and functions work as in GLSL, not JavaScript. There are no dynamically growing arrays, strings, host objects or file I/O. sin, cos, length, dot, normalize, mix, clamp, step and smoothstep are built-ins. Avoid undefined numerical cases: normalize only nonzero vectors, guard divisors and indices, and pass increasing edges to smoothstep. For a reversed ramp, use 1.0 - smoothstep(low, high, value). // A helper that can be used in a shader body; no resource declarations needed. vec3 adjustContrast(vec3 rgb, float amount) { return (rgb - vec3(0.5)) * amount + vec3(0.5); } . const expresses an immutable value. uniform data is supplied by the host, not written by the shader. Vertex/fragment in and out values form stage interfaces; compute invocations instead read and write declared resources. Stage-specific built-ins are not available everywhere: derivatives such as dFdx and dFdy belong to fragment shading, not compute.

748.title: Vulkan-compatible source and generated declarations
748.content: Qt Shader Tools accepts Vulkan-style GLSL, compiles to SPIR-V and can translate it to backend languages. Its standalone examples explicitly declare #version, locations, uniform blocks and sampler bindings. Those standalone declarations are not a template to paste around a score shader. score’s current shader generator supplies a GLSL 460 prelude and the declarations required by the selected format. | Author supplies | score supplies | . | JSON metadata, named controls/resources and their types | Uniform blocks, samplers, images and buffers corresponding to the header | . | Shader functions and main() | Runtime uniforms and family-specific helper macros | . | Raw-raster VERTEX_INPUTS, VERTEX_OUTPUTS, FRAGMENT_INPUTS, FRAGMENT_OUTPUTS | Stage declarations and locations (or the requested explicit locations) | . | CSF LOCAL_SIZE and execution model | Compute workgroup declaration and runtime dispatch | . Do not declare uniform float gain; after declaring gain as a header control, or manually bind a sampler already described by INPUTS. Do not duplicate the generated output or stage interface. Use the header EXTENSIONS field where supported to request extensions; a request cannot add a missing backend capability. The generator uses bindings 0 and 1 for renderer/process uniform data. Graphics shaders normally use binding 2 for material controls and allocate resource bindings thereafter; compute allocation also depends on whether a control block exists. These are implementation details, not a stable binding-number API. Persistent resources, auxiliary data and additional images can consume bindings. Address resources by their header names and the documented macros, not by guessed descriptor numbers. Current generator source is useful when diagnosing generated-source errors. Important Vulkan differences: . | Non-opaque uniforms must be in blocks; score generates these blocks from controls. Legacy loose-uniform snippets are not directly portable. | Use modern texture functions (texture, textureLod, texelFetch) where direct sampling is appropriate; use score’s IMG_* helpers for portable image orientation. texture2D is not Vulkan GLSL. | Use gl_VertexIndex / gl_InstanceIndex in raw raster, not the OpenGL gl_VertexID / gl_InstanceID. VSA exposes its own vertexId compatibility variable. | Fragment outputs are explicit. score accepts and rewrites gl_FragColor for ISF compatibility; new single-output ISF code can write isf_FragColor. Multiple outputs use header-declared names. | Fixed-function OpenGL matrices, glBegin-style drawing and compatibility attributes are not the score shader interface. Use raw-raster attributes and camera macros. | .

749.title: Coordinates and stage conventions
749.content: Texture coordinates, framebuffer origins and clip coordinates are separate concerns. Do not fix a flipped result by adding an unconditional Y flip everywhere. | ISF fragments: isf_FragNormCoord is the current normalized coordinate. IMG_NORM_PIXEL takes normalized coordinates; IMG_PIXEL takes pixel coordinates; IMG_TEXEL takes integer texel coordinates. IMG_THIS_* samples at the current fragment. These helpers account for runtime texture orientation. See the full macro table. | Compute images: derive integer coordinates from gl_GlobalInvocationID, bounds-check against the resource size, then use IMG_LOAD, IMG_STORE or IMG_STORE_LAYER. These implement score’s image-origin convention; raw imageLoad/imageStore do not apply its fixups. The image contract covers dimensionality and access. | Raw-raster vertices: start main() with isf_vertShaderInit() and end with isf_vertShaderFinish(). Compute clip position with clipSpaceCorrMatrix * VIEWPROJECTION_MATRIX * MODEL_MATRIX * position for directly cabled geometry. The matrix and finish helper have complementary backend duties; do not call the helper twice or add another backend Y flip. Flattened scenes instead use per-draw transforms. | VSA: write the original OpenGL-style clip-space position; score maps the depth convention. Do not add raw-raster init/finish calls or a second depth correction. | . For texture lookup outside fragment shading, choose an explicit LOD where required, as in the cookbook’s compute audio recipe. Implicit fragment derivatives are not available to a compute invocation. Sampler filtering, wrapping and mip generation are separate choices described in the resource header.

750.title: Buffers, images and parallel execution
750.content: A sampled texture is read through a sampler; a storage image is accessed with image load/store operations and must have a compatible format and access mode. An SSBO carries structured data, not an image. score’s storage layouts use std430; uniform buffers use std140. Preserve the complete declared layout when consuming upstream buffers: a vec3 or an array does not imply tightly packed host bytes. See CSF storage buffers and custom types. Each compute invocation runs independently. Workgroup counts round up, so a valid dispatch can contain invocations outside the intended image or array range. Guard accesses even for a minimal example. A workgroup barrier() is not a global synchronization point between all workgroups; do not use it to coordinate an entire simulation. Do not let some invocations skip a barrier that others in the same workgroup must reach. Prefer separate passes or the documented persistent/snapshot resource model for cross-pass and previous-frame dependencies. Geometry gather access provides separate read/write snapshots for neighbour reads; it does not make arbitrary in-place races safe.

751.title: Portability and debugging
751.content: A shader can parse and still fail to render because an attachment format, compute feature, sample count, blend mode or resource limit is unsupported. Integer storage formats additionally require Qt 6.10 or newer in score; older fallback to RGBA8 does not retain integer semantics. Check Graphics pipeline for runtime limits. When adapting a shader, first establish a constant color or minimal geometry result, then add one resource at a time. Check header names, resource access, matching vertex/fragment varyings, output sizes and array bounds before changing coordinate math. Preserve the family’s initialization and finalization conventions. A successful render on one backend is not proof of portability to the others. Use the small corpus-linked Shader cookbook recipes to isolate the stage you are working on.

752.title: Authoritative references
752.content: . | Khronos GLSL 4.60 specification: types, expressions, stage interfaces, built-ins and memory rules. | Khronos Vulkan GLSL semantics: differences from OpenGL GLSL. | Qt Shader Tools QSB manual: Vulkan-style input, SPIR-V and target translation. | Qt RHI overview: graphics backend abstraction and capabilities. | ISF JSON and ISF GLSL: portable ISF declarations and functions, distinct from score extensions. | .

753.title: glTF Scene with Effects
753.content: Navigate a chess scene while a looping beat pushes its colors and glow and distorts the rendered image. The sound changes the image, not the camera. A JavaScript/QML scene loads A Beautiful Game through Qt Quick 3D’s RuntimeLoader. An HDR environment map, reflections and a moving light establish the scene before score’s shaders process its output. Peak analysis of the looping sound feeds smoothing, then color blowout and bloom intensity. Optical Flow Distort acts on the resulting image, with a separate beat-synchronised LFO periodically resetting it. Camera navigation and moving light are independent of the audio analysis.

754.title: Try it
754.content: Open the ZIP directly in score: the model, environment and sound loop are included, despite the older note inside the score saying otherwise. Use a desktop build with GPU JavaScript, Qt Quick 3D and its AssetUtils module. Start playback and focus the output window to navigate with the mouse and WASD. Begin with modest output volume. Raise Peak Gain or lower Gate for a stronger visual response; lower smoothing Alpha so the glow fades gradually after each hit. The color and bloom follow the audio; the distortion resets on its own beat-synchronised LFO. For a native scene-based adaptation, see Asset Loader and 3D scene pipeline: Qt cameras and environment objects cannot simply be cabled into that renderer. Try this on web . Download this example .

756.title: Temporal Patching (Glutton Mode)
756.content: . Build a changing sound texture by bringing effects in after the source has already begun. Each new effect hears the source playing now, not a replay from its beginning.

757.title: Overview
757.content: One generated source feeds three effect intervals with different start times. In glutton mode, their cables pass the available current signal; starting an effect does not retrieve audio from before that effect was active. The source and the effects can therefore have separate lifetimes without turning each entrance into a restart.

758.title: Try it
758.content: Configure audio output and start playback at a low level. Bytebeat supplies the sound, so no sample file or external controller is needed. The example requires Bytebeat, Faust and Airwindows support. Listen as the Low, Medium and High effect intervals join the source. End them one at a time and hear which part of the texture disappears. Then replay the score, end Source first, and listen to the remaining tails: stopping the sound’s input is different from stopping the effects themselves. All four ends are interactive; their drawn positions do not stop them automatically. Leave one effect running longer, then use its end trigger to decide where the passage closes. See the delayed example, where later effects receive earlier source material. Live input is optional through the saved audio input binding; use headphones if adding a microphone to avoid feedback. Download this example . Try this on web .

759.content: . | Audio routing - How audio propagates through the timeline | Audio plugins - VST, Faust, JSFX effect formats | Audio device - Configuring audio input/output | .

761.title: GPhoto2 DSLR device
761.content: GPhoto2 DSLR connects a camera supported by libgphoto2, exposing its live-view preview as a texture and its reported configuration as device parameters. It is distinct from a webcam/video-capture device.

762.title: Availability
762.content: This device is registered by the graphics plug-in in native builds, not the WebAssembly build. The integration dynamically loads libgphoto2 and libgphoto2_port: the device entry alone does not establish that these libraries or a compatible camera driver are installed. The loader has Linux, macOS and Windows library-name branches. Actual camera support, USB access and live-view capability depend on the installed libgphoto2 distribution and camera; this is not a guarantee that every supported still camera can provide a live preview on every platform. Close other applications holding the camera before connecting it to score.

763.title: Connection
763.content: . | Connect the camera and enable the camera’s appropriate remote-control/USB mode. | Open Add device in the Device explorer and select GPhoto2 DSLR. | Choose a detected camera, or Default DSLR to resolve the first detected camera when connecting. | Review Device Name, Camera Model and Port. The port is a libgphoto2 camera port identifier, not an OSC or TCP port. | Expand the resulting device to inspect the controls the camera actually reports. | . If no camera is detected, verify the runtime libraries, libgphoto2 camera support and operating-system device permissions. A default selection cannot provide an image when detection returns no camera.

764.title: Texture and controls
764.content: The device root carries the preview texture. Select that address as the source for a compatible texture input in your graphics patch. Configuration entries are children of the root, using the camera’s reported configuration names. Their value types follow the camera widgets: toggles become booleans, ranges become floats, menu/radio choices and text become strings, and dates become integers. Available numeric ranges and menu choices are attached to the parameters. Changing a supported configuration parameter queues the corresponding camera-setting update. The address names and available controls are camera-specific: do not assume that an aperture, ISO or shutter setting has a universal path. These controls are not a promise of continuous feedback for changes made directly on the camera.

765.title: Limitations
765.content: This integration uses libgphoto2’s preview capture path. It is not a documented still-photo download workflow, a full-resolution recording device, or a guarantee of a particular frame rate. A camera can connect successfully while refusing preview capture in its current mode. Test the actual camera configuration before relying on it in a performance. See also Camera device for ordinary capture devices and Working with devices.

766.title: GPS device
766.content: . ossia supports reading GPS data from gpsd servers. This can be used for instance to easily read the data of a GPS chip such as a BN-220 connected to a Raspberry Pi’s UART port. When connected to a GPSD instance, ossia will report latitude, longitude, number of satellites and GPS time.

767.title: GPU data bending
767.content: Make motion linger, smear or break into compression-like artifacts. Five shader treatments appear beside a corrected camera view. Try this on web . Download the example .

768.title: Try it
768.content: Select an available camera in the Camera device settings, grant capture permission where required, and start playback. The camera passes through Color Controls before splitting into the different treatments, giving them a common source. | Move, then hold still. Some effects only rearrange the current picture; others keep smearing or distorting it after you stop. | Change FastMosh’s update rate to set how often fresh imagery replaces retained material. | Adjust Sorting Smear’s adaptation or Optical Flow Distort’s amount, then repeat the same movement to see how much distortion it leaves behind. | Change the LFOs that reset or refresh effects to alter the rhythm of those changes. | . Use a GPU graphics backend. The shaders are saved in the score; to work without a camera, connect a movie or generated texture to Color Controls.

769.title: Gradient Scrubber
769.content: Scrub through color gradients interactively to extract colors and create dynamic color sequences. This process lets you define color gradients and then “scrub” through them with a position control, outputting the resulting colors for use in lighting, video effects, or other visual applications. Perfect for dynamic lighting control, color-based installations, or any project where you need smooth color transitions controlled by sensors, automation, or user interaction.

770.title: How it works
770.content: Gradient Scrubber creates a color gradient from your defined color stops, then uses a position parameter (0-1) to extract colors from any point along the gradient. Gradient definition - Set up your color gradient with multiple color stops and positions Position control - Scrub through the gradient (0.0 = start, 1.0 = end) Color output - Get RGB, HSV, or other color format outputs Interpolation - Smooth color blending between your defined stops .

771.title: Gradient creation
771.content: Color stops: Define key colors at specific positions along the gradient - you can have as many as needed for complex color schemes. Position mapping: Each color stop has a position value, allowing for non-uniform color distribution along the gradient. Interpolation modes: Choose between linear, cubic, or other interpolation methods for different color blending characteristics. Color spaces: Work in RGB, HSV, or other color spaces depending on your desired color transitions.

772.title: Creative applications
772.content: Dynamic lighting: Control LED installations, architectural lighting, or stage lighting with smooth color transitions based on musical content, sensor data, or user interaction. Video effects: Generate color sequences for video processing, background generation, or visual effect parameters. Interactive installations: Map user gestures, sensor readings, or other control data to color gradient positions for responsive color environments. Sunset/sunrise simulation: Create natural color progressions that follow environmental or temporal patterns. Mood lighting: Generate color sequences that respond to audio content, creating synchronized lighting and sound experiences.

773.title: Integration techniques
773.content: Sensor control: Map sensor data to gradient position using Mapping Tool - temperature sensors could control warm/cool color transitions, motion sensors could trigger color changes. Audio synchronization: Use audio analysis to drive gradient position based on music tempo, frequency content, or amplitude. Timeline automation: Automate gradient position over time for predetermined color sequences that sync with other timeline elements. Multi-gradient systems: Use multiple Gradient Scrubbers for different color aspects - one for hue, another for brightness, creating complex color evolution.

774.title: Technical features
774.content: Real-time processing: Fast color interpolation suitable for high-frequency control and smooth color transitions. Multiple outputs: Simultaneous RGB, HSV, and other color format outputs for different types of devices and applications. Smooth interpolation: Advanced color blending algorithms prevent harsh transitions and color banding. Preset management: Save and recall gradient configurations for different moods, scenes, or installation requirements.

775.title: Workflow tips
775.content: Color theory: Use complementary colors and natural color progressions for pleasing visual results. Position mapping: Consider using Mapping Tool to shape the position control response - ease-in/out curves can create more natural color timing. Multiple gradients: Layer different color aspects by using separate gradients for hue, saturation, and brightness control. Testing: Always test gradients with your actual lighting or display hardware, as different devices reproduce colors differently.

776.title: Integration with lighting
776.content: RGB LED strips: Direct connection to RGB color outputs for pixel-perfect color reproduction. DMX lighting: Convert color outputs to DMX values for professional lighting control. Smart bulbs: Control Philips Hue, LIFX, or other smart lighting systems through an HTTP device or another network protocol. Projection systems: Feed color data to video systems for large-scale color projection and mapping.

777.title: Related processes
777.content: Perfect companion to Mapping Tool for position control shaping, LFO for cyclical color movements, lighting device protocols for hardware control, or Video processes for visual color applications.
