885.title: Execution and build limitations
885.content: Ports are declared as children of Script: ValueInlet / ValueOutlet carry messages, AudioInlet / AudioOutlet carry audio buffers, and MidiInlet / MidiOutlet carry MIDI messages. Score controls declare stored control inlets; TextureInlet / TextureOutlet require GPU JavaScript support. GPU scripts use the graphics execution path; CPU scripts run with execution, not on the GUI thread. Do not open native dialogs or directly edit the document from tick. The current WebAssembly build does not insert Javascript processes into the execution graph: desktop examples should not be assumed to execute in the browser build.

886.title: General syntax
886.content: Every script must contain . import Score . somewhere at the top. A QML document defines a Script object with: . | Input and output ports | Callbacks that are called either regularly on every tick, or on special events (start, stop, pause, resume). | . The smallest valid empty script looks like this: . import Score Script { tick: function(token, state) { } } . The tick function’s two arguments give both timing and contextual information useful for writing algorithms. Please read Musical metrics for tempo and quantization, and the timing fields below for how model, physical and musical dates relate to each other. Callbacks and persistent state . Callbacks are function-valued properties on Script, as illustrated by the value-mapper example below. | Callback | Arguments and purpose | . | tick | (token, state): execute one tick, using the timing and execution objects documented below. | . | start | (): process starts. | . | stop | (): process stops. | . | pause | (): process pauses. | . | resume | (): process resumes. | . | uiEvent | (value): receive a message sent by ScriptUI.executionSend(value). | . | loadState | (savedState): initialize from the persisted key/value state object. | . | stateUpdated | (key, value): apply a persisted state change; removal is delivered with an undefined value. | . Script.uiSend(value) sends a message to the companion ScriptUI.executionEvent callback. These messages bridge separate objects/threads; they are not shared QML properties. See the custom UI API. Script.commitState(key, value) queues an undoable persistent state edit, including when no custom UI is open. Implement loadState and stateUpdated to restore that state. JavaScript presets include program code, companion UI and persisted script state; plain temporary QML properties are not automatically saved as document state. The state argument of tick is the execution environment, not this persisted state object. Available functions . A very simple API to read / write messages from the device explorer is provided: . // Reads the current value of an address in the device explorer let value = Device.read("an:/address"); console.log(JSON.stringify(value)); // Sends a value to the device explorer Device.write("an:/address", 123); . Note that some types (vec2, vec3, vec4) that may be returned from the equivalent types in the device explorer require an import of QtQuick to be useable. Token object . Important note: due to the way numbers work in Javascript (that is, double-precision floating point numbers), and due to the timing units, scripts can only be expected to be accurate for representing durations no greater than 147 days. That is, if a time interval lasts a year, after 147 days the timing values returned by previous_date, date, … may not be accurate anymore. This limit is pushed back to the hard limit of 414 years when using the C++ integer-based API instead. Note that this does not affect for instance, scores with normal durations which would loop back to the beginning - permanently running installations are safe. Properties . | previous_date: the model date at which the tick starts. | date: the model date at which the tick ends | parent_duration: the nominal model duration of the closest parent interval. | offset: the model date at which we must start reading from our input. | speed: current speed (a multiplicative factor). | tempo: current tempo. | musical_start_last_signature: what is the position in quarter notes of the closest previous musical signature change to previous_date. | musical_start_last_bar: what is the position in quarter notes of the closest previous bar change to previous_date. | musical_start_position: what is the position of previous_date in quarter notes. | musical_end_last_bar: what is the position in quarter notes of the closest previous bar change to date. | musical_end_position: what is the position of date in quarter notes. | signature_upper: 6 in “6/8”, at the start of the tick. | signature_lower: 8 in “6/8”, at the start of the tick. | . Methods . | model_read_duration(): how long are we reading from the model data. Older documentation called this logical_read_duration(); the current QML API exposes model_read_duration(). | physical_start(ratio): at which sample in the output must we start to write. | physical_read_duration(ratio): how many samples are we reading from the input ports. | physical_write_duration(ratio): how many samples are we writing to the output ports. | to_physical_time_in_tick(time, ratio): convert a model time into a physical time. | from_physical_time_in_tick(time, ratio): convert a time in physical dates, to a time in model dates. | in_range(time): check that the model time given is indeed in the range of this tick. | position(): where are we in relation to our parent interval. 0 is the beginning, 1 is the nominal duration. If an interval has a greater max, or is infinite, this will go beyond 1. | forward(): is the time going forward in this tick (speed > 0). | backward(): is the time going backward in this tick (speed < 0). | paused(): is the time going anywhere in this tick (speed == 0). Note that there is a difference between setting the speed to zero, and pressing the “pause” button - in the first case, processes will still keep being executed, just with no duration. | get_quantification_date(quant): get a model date if there is a quantification date for the requested quantification in this tick. -1 is returned if there isn’t any. | get_physical_quantification_date(quant, ratio): get a physical date if there is a quantification date for the requested quantification in this tick. -1 is returned if there isn’t any. | . State object . The state object contains global properties relevant for the whole score execution. Properties . | sample_rate: explicit. | buffer_size: explicit. | model_to_physical: the ratio to pass to the token functions going from model to physical dates. | physical_to_model: the ratio to pass to the token functions going from physical to model dates. | physical_date: how many samples have elapsed since the score has started playing. | start_date_ns: the date in nanoseconds when the score started playing. | current_date_ns: the current date in nanoseconds. | timings(token): given the token object, this gives back a timings object, which has the following properties: . | start_sample: at which index is the first sample to write in an audio buffer. | length: how many samples must be written. | . | . timings is most of the time what you need ! .

887.title: Example of a value mapper
887.content: // Necessary for the Script object. // It is also possible to import QtQml and QtQuick import Score // Create our script object Script { // Define the inputs & outputs - they are sub-objects of the script object ValueInlet { id: in1 } ValueOutlet { id: out1 } FloatSlider { id: slider; min: 10; max: 100; } // QML syntax for defining a floating-point constant readonly property real my_constant: 1.234 // This function is called on each tick. tick: function(token, state) { // has a message been received ? if (typeof in1.value !== 'undefined') { // print it in the console console.log(in1.value); // transform it with some math operations. var newValue = in1.value + slider.value * Math.random() + my_constant; // write it in the output out1.value = newValue; } } start: function() { console.log("I am called on start"); } stop: function() { console.log("I am called on stop"); } pause: function() { console.log("I am called on pause"); } resume: function() { console.log("I am called on resume"); } } . Note: it is also possible to access the list of messages with their precise timing, with values.

888.title: Example of an audio generator
888.content: import Score Script { // Declare our inputs & outputs FloatSlider { id: in1; min: 20; max: 800; init: 440; objectName: "Frequency" } AudioOutlet { id: out1 } // Index to keep track of the phase property real phase: 0; tick: function(token, state) { // Create an array to store our samples let arr = new Array(state.buffer_size); for (let i = 0; i < state.buffer_size; ++i) arr[i] = 0; // How many samples we must write in this array // (the process could run for e.g. only frame 17 through 24 in a 128-frame buffer) const tm = state.timings(token); if(tm.length > 0) { // Computer the sin() coefficient var freq = in1.value; // Notice how we get sample_rate from state. var phi = 2 * Math.PI * freq / state.sample_rate; // Fill our array for(var s = 0; s < tm.length; s++) { phase += phi; var sample = Math.sin(phase); sample = freq > 0 ? sample : 0; arr[tm.start_sample + s] = 0.3 * sample; } } // Write two audio channels, which will give stereo output by default in score. out1.setChannel(0, arr); out1.setChannel(1, arr); } } .

891.title: Properties common to all ports
891.content: FloatSlider { id: myVariableName // <- how you refer to it in the javascript Code objectName: "The name shown in the score UI" address: "foo:/bar/baz" // <- default address used when the object is created } .

892.title: Audio
892.content: Create an audio input: . AudioInlet { id: inputPort } ... var left = inputPort.channel(0); var right = inputPort.channel(1); console.log(left[0]); // print the first sample of the first channel for (var value of left) { ... } . Create an audio output: . AudioOutlet { id: out } ... // set the data of channel 0 to the following: out.setChannel(0, [0.1, 0.0, 0.2, 0.0, -0.1, 0.0]); .

893.title: Example of fetching various timings
893.content: This example shows how one can access both score-relative and global-time-relative timing information from a JS script. import Score Script { ValueInlet { id: in1 } ValueOutlet { id: out1; objectName: "logical" } ValueOutlet { id: out2; objectName: "physical" } property int samples_since_beginning: 0 tick: function(token, state) { // Logical time: this time is affected // by the speed sliders in score. // The unit is the Flick. out1.value = token.date; // Logical time in seconds: out1.value = token.date / 705600000; // Physical time: the time in real-world clock since the interval started playing. // The physical time unit is the audio sample. samples_since_beginning += state.buffer_size; out2.value = samples_since_beginning; // Physical time in seconds: out2.value = samples_since_beginning / state.sample_rate; } } .

894.title: MIDI
894.content: Create a MIDI input: . MidiInlet { id: inputPort } ... var messages = inputPort.messages(); for (var message of messages) { // Print the MIDI bytes console.log(message[0], message[1], message[2]); } . Create a MIDI output: . MidiOutlet { id: out } ... // push a new message out.add([144, 64, 127]); // set & replace all the messages to be pushed out.setMessages([ [144, 64, 127], [144, 68, 127], [127, 30, 0] ]); .

895.title: Messages
895.content: Receiving: . ValueInlet { id: inputPort } ... // Print the latest message received console.log(inputPort.value); // Iterate through all the messages received for this tick, with their timestamp for (var message of inputPort.values) { console.log(message.timestamp, message.value); } . Sending: . ValueOutlet { id: out } ... // Use either out.setValue(1.234); // or out.addValue(timestamp, 1.234); .

896.title: Controls
896.content: Controls behave exactly like ValueInlet but show up as actual UI controls. They have as such relevant properties: min, max, etc. FloatSlider { min: 0.0 max: 1.0 init: 0.5 } . IntSlider { min: 0 max: 127 init: 0 } . Enum { choices: ["foo", "bar", "baz"] index: 2 } . Toggle { checked: true } . LineEdit { text: "Hello world" } .

897.title: Generative graphics
897.content: TextureOutlet { item: Rectangle { } } . Adding a TextureOutlet ports turns the JS object into a GPU one - rendering will be performed by Qt Quick in the GPU thread. Note that it will not run if not connected to a graphical output! . Any QtQuick item can be put as item. Here is an example of a basic animated rectangle: . import Score import QtQuick Script { TextureOutlet { objectName: "out" item: Rectangle { id: rect color: "blue" width: 100 height: 100 } } tick: function(token, state) { rect.x = ((rect.x + 1) % 100) rect.y = ((rect.y + 1) % 100) } } . When using Qt Quick Controls, it is better to use explicit namespaces as some objects have the same type name between Score and QtQuick.Controls modules. It is possible to use reactive bindings: . import Score as Score import QtQuick import QtQuick.Controls as QQC Score.Script { Score.Toggle { id: show_text objectName: "Show text" } Score.TextureOutlet { objectName: "out" item: Item { id: self anchors.fill: parent QQC.Label { anchors.bottom: parent.bottom text: self.height color: "white" visible: show_text.value font.pointSize: 64 } } } } . As well as interactive widgets: . import Score as Score import QtQuick import QtQuick.Controls as QQC Score.Script { Score.TextureOutlet { objectName: "out" item: Item { id: self anchors.fill: parent QQC.Button { anchors.centerIn: parent text: "X" onClicked: text = text + "X" } } } } . The current GPU runtime keeps interactive QML state across output resizing and graph reconstruction instead of treating every resize as a fresh script. Editing the program still replaces its objects. For state that must survive save/load or be undoable, use the explicit state callbacks and commitState, not only temporary QML properties. Canvas2D . A Canvas can be the visual content of a texture outlet. This minimal QML draws a solid frame; connect its outlet to a graphical output and play: . import QtQuick import Score as Score Score.Script { Score.TextureOutlet { objectName: "Drawing" item: Canvas { anchors.fill: parent onWidthChanged: requestPaint() onHeightChanged: requestPaint() onPaint: { var ctx = getContext("2d"); ctx.fillStyle = "#204060"; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, height); } } } } . For animated drawing, change the data used by onPaint and call requestPaint() from tick. Canvas drawing is part of Qt Quick rendering; it is not an audio-rate drawing API. Texture input and render size . Declare TextureInlet { id: source; objectName: "Texture" }, cable a texture-producing process into it, then use source.item as the visual input (for example Texture.sourceItem in Qt Quick 3D). The item is owned by the inlet: do not destroy it yourself. See the Qt Quick 3D texture example. Rendering follows the connected output and texture-inlet resolution settings. To set an inlet’s override from an editor script, obtain its model with Score.inlet(process, index) and assign renderSize = Qt.size(width, height). This is distinct from an item’s logical QML width/height. Score.UI.TextureSource previews a process’s texture outlet in a custom UI; it does not declare a cable inlet. Source: QmlObjects.hpp, JSProcessModel.cpp and score_plugin_js.cpp. Timing declarations: ValueTypes.Qt6.hpp. State callback invocation: CPUNode.cpp and CPUNode.hpp.

899.title: JavaScript and QML
899.content: score embeds Qt’s JavaScript and QML engines for process execution, editor automation, custom interfaces and devices. The language is shared, but the host API depends on where the script runs. Importing a module does not give an execution script the editor’s document-editing context.

900.title: Choose a scripting context
900.content: | Context | Canonical reference | Entry point and purpose | . | Process execution | JavaScript Process API | A QML Script object from import Score; ports, tick(token, state), lifecycle callbacks, audio, MIDI and textures. See the Javascript process for installation into intervals or states and editing. | . | Editor automation | JavaScript Editor API | Scripts that inspect and edit a document through the editor’s Score context. Detailed references cover Score, devices, utilities, views and examples. | . | Custom process interfaces | QML custom UI API | A companion ScriptUI, controls and messages between UI and execution objects; the UI is not the execution object. | . | QML devices | QML device API | Device trees and JavaScript callbacks in a device context. | . | QML protocols | QML protocol API | Protocol-specific roots, configuration and message handling. | .

901.title: ECMAScript and QML are different layers
901.content: JavaScript is the programming language standardized as ECMAScript: expressions, functions, objects, arrays and built-ins such as Math and JSON. The ECMAScript specification defines the language; the MDN JavaScript reference explains its syntax and built-ins. Neither reference defines score’s ports or callbacks. QML is Qt’s declarative object language, with JavaScript expressions and functions embedded in it. Declarations such as Script { ... }, property real phase: 0, id: output and reactive property bindings are QML, not ordinary ECMAScript object syntax. A process program is a QML document, not a standalone browser or Node.js script. Consult the QML reference, QML syntax basics, and the QML Book. For example, this process declares a QML output object and assigns a JavaScript function to the execution callback: . import Score Script { ValueOutlet { id: output } tick: function(token, state) { output.value = token.position(); } } . Here Script, ValueOutlet, token.position() and the callback invocation are score APIs, not JavaScript built-ins.

902.title: Qt runtime and restrictions
902.content: Language features and installed QML modules follow the Qt version bundled with score, not the newest ECMAScript specification or the Qt version installed elsewhere on the computer. Qt documents its supported language baseline and version-specific additions in the JavaScript host environment and supported objects and functions. | This is not a web browser: do not assume window, document, an HTML DOM or browser APIs exist. Qt Quick’s Canvas is a QML item, not an HTML canvas. | This is not Node.js: Node’s require, filesystem/process APIs and npm package resolution are not supplied by the QML host. A package that relies on them is not made compatible merely by using JavaScript. | Qt supplies its own QML global object, including the Qt facilities, and QML-specific scope rules. JavaScript inside a .qml file cannot add undeclared globals; declare local variables or QML properties. Use explicit QML object IDs rather than assuming browser-like this behavior. | A Qt module must be available in the score build to be imported. Importing QtQuick supplies visual types; it does not move process execution onto the GUI thread. GPU ports require GPU JavaScript support. See execution and build limitations, including the current WebAssembly limitation. | .

903.title: Imports, modules and resource locations
903.content: A QML module import such as import Score makes QML types available. Process scripts require it for Script and ports; add import QtQuick when using Qt Quick items or types. Prefer qualified imports when names overlap, for example import Score as Score and import QtQuick.Controls as QQC, then use Score.Script and QQC.Button. A JavaScript helper is imported into a QML document with a namespace, for example import "helpers.js" as Helpers; its functions are then called as Helpers.functionName(...). The qualifier begins with an uppercase letter. This QML import syntax is not ECMAScript’s import { name } from ... syntax. Qt also supports ECMAScript modules in .mjs files; use ECMAScript import and export within that module context, not at the top of a QML object definition. Imported resources have scope rules of their own. In particular, a .pragma library helper does not inherit the importing QML document’s imports, and a JavaScript resource with its own imports also does not inherit them. Do not assume a helper has access to a particular process’s object IDs or host objects. See Qt’s JavaScript resource imports, JavaScript resources and scope and naming resolution for the exact rules. For file-backed processes, the source location supplies the QML base URL: neighboring imports and assets resolve relative to that source file. Qt.resolvedUrl("image.png") resolves a resource URL; the internal rootPath is not a JavaScript filesystem global. Keep companion files and imported modules with the source when moving a project. The companion name.ui.qml provides the custom UI for name.qml; see the process’s files, relative resources and presets workflow.

904.title: Execution reference contents
904.content: The complete process execution reference preserves the process API and examples: . | Script syntax, callbacks and persistence, and device read/write. | Token timing fields and methods and execution state. | Ports, audio, MIDI, messages and controls. | Value mapping, audio generation, MIDI transposition and timing examples. | Generative graphics, Canvas2D, and texture input and render size. | .

905.title: QML custom UI API
905.content: This reference covers score-provided QML interface types and their JavaScript APIs. For launching a whole-application UI, a downloadable score and a complete control-panel walkthrough, see the Custom UI tutorial. For core syntax, see JavaScript and QML and the QML language reference. Editor operations belong to the GUI-thread interface, not an audio execution callback. See the JavaScript editor API and the separate JavaScript execution API.

906.title: UI objects
906.content: Import Score.UI (for example import Score.UI as UI) for the following QML types. For editor operations, import Score as Score provides Score.Editor; this avoids confusing the Score QML module with the console’s global object. | Score.UI.PortSource reads execution updates from a control inlet and writes UI changes to its value. Live updates require playback. Identify the process by scripting name and the port by name or index, or pass the port object directly. These bindings set values directly; use Score.Editor.editValue / commitEdit if the UI gesture must become an undoable editor command. | Score.UI.PortSink allows to read and write output controls from the score. If read, the displayed value will be the current execution value, thus the score has to play. | Score.UI.AddressSource allows to read and write addresses from the device explorer. | .

907.title: Per-process interfaces and placement
907.content: A file-backed Javascript process can pair effect.qml (a Script) with effect.ui.qml (a ScriptUI). The .ui.qml companion is not a separate process-library entry. Edit code and UI independently in the script editor; the process’s custom-UI action opens the interface. import QtQuick import QtQuick.Controls as QQC import Score as Score import Score.UI as UI Score.ScriptUI { id: root width: 320 height: 100 QQC.Slider { anchors.centerIn: parent from: 0 to: 1 UI.PortSource on value { port: root.inlet(0) } } } . This companion assumes the process has a numeric control inlet at index 0. ScriptUI.inlet(indexOrName) and outlet(indexOrName) resolve that process’s own ports; PortSource and PortSink also accept port objects rather than a process name and port index. Custom UIs and script editors can each open in a Window, Side panel or Central area. The editor API exposes setProcessUIPlacement(process, placement) and setProcessScriptEditorPlacement(process, placement), followed by showProcessUI(process, true) or showProcessScriptEditor(process, true). An empty placement string uses the preference default. See View and interface API. Messages and persistent state . ScriptUI.executionSend(value) sends a message to the Script.uiEvent callback. In the other direction, Script.uiSend(value) reaches ScriptUI.executionEvent. These are message bridges between separate objects/threads, not shared QML properties. For persisted UI state, bracket a gesture with beginUpdateState(name), updateState(key, value) and endUpdateState(); cancelUpdateState() cancels it. replaceState(value) and clearState() replace or clear the state. Both Script and ScriptUI provide loadState and stateUpdated callbacks. An execution script can emit commitState(key, value) to queue an undoable state change even when no custom UI is open. This persisted state is included in the document and JavaScript presets.

908.title: Imported QML forms
908.content: Where the build includes imported-UI support, import Score.ImportedUi provides ImportedUi. It hosts trusted QML in its own engine and scales an exported content form to fit. Choose an Item-based .qml / .ui.qml file with positive width/height or implicit dimensions, not the project’s Window or ApplicationWindow bootstrap. Required Qt modules must be installed; add project module directories with importPaths. import QtQuick import Score.ImportedUi ImportedUi { width: 640 height: 480 source: Qt.resolvedUrl("Panel.ui.qml") mapping: [ { name: "level", object: "levelSlider", property: "value", direction: "both" } ] values: ({ level: 0.5 }) onEvent: function(name, value) { console.log(name, value) } } . Here the imported form must expose levelSlider as a public root object alias or a unique objectName; a private QML id is not enough. A mapping has a unique name, an object ("." means the root), and direction: input, output, both or event. Property mappings use property; event mappings can name a signal. Inputs arrive through the values map; outputs emit event(name, value). Inspect status, errorString, designSize and objects to diagnose a missing module, invalid root or mapping, and use reload() after changing the form. This is an integration mechanism, not a sandbox.

909.title: Graphics and texture previews
909.content: Use ordinary Qt Quick Controls for visual sliders, buttons and text fields. Score’s FloatSlider, FloatKnob, range, XY/XYZ, HSVSlider, MultiSlider and chooser types instead declare native process controls in a Script; they are not visual children to place in a custom layout. Qualify imports to avoid collisions such as Score.Button and QtQuick.Controls.Button. Qt Quick Canvas with getContext("2d") can paint inside a TextureOutlet, alongside other QML graphics. Request repaint with requestPaint() when changing drawing data. The output must reach a graphical sink and execution must be running. A Canvas is not a new score process type. Score.UI.TextureSource displays an existing process texture in a custom UI: . UI.TextureSource { width: 320 height: 180 process: "My shader" port: 0 } . The process and texture outlet must exist, and GPU JavaScript support must be compiled in. This is a preview/source for QML, unlike Score.TextureInlet, which declares a cabled texture input inside a Javascript process. See Texture Inlet in Qt Quick 3D.

910.title: Javascript support
910.content: For language syntax, imports and the different scripting contexts, see JavaScript and QML under Reference → Languages. The complete JavaScript Process API documents ports, callbacks, timing, persistent state and example programs.

911.title: Scripting in Javascript / QML.
911.content: score allows to write scripts using the JavaScript language. These scripts can be used to write specific processes such as value mappers, audio generators. score executes JavaScript through Qt’s QML engine. Language and Qt module availability follow the Qt version bundled with the application; this is not a browser or Node.js environment. See the JavaScript reference for language concepts. QML is Qt’s declarative object language with embedded JavaScript expressions and functions. Its object declarations and properties (property real, etc.) are not ordinary JavaScript syntax. See the language overview for the distinction and upstream language references. Enter QML code or a source-file path in the Javascript code editor. File-backed scripts keep their source location so that relative imports, images and companion UIs resolve correctly. JS can be used as a process both for intervals, and in states. | To add a JS process to an interval, simply drag’n’drop it from the Process Library to the interval. | To add a JS process to a state, right-click on the state in the Object Explorer, and choose “Add Process”. | . JS can also be used for generative graphics with Qt Quick. See the graphics examples; connect the texture outlet to a graphical output before playing.

912.title: Editing code
912.content: The editor validates QML before applying it to the process. Resolve reported compilation errors before expecting the new program or its ports to be used; keep substantial code in an external source file as well as in the document. Files, relative resources and presets . The source location (rootPath internally) supplies a QML base URL, not a new JavaScript filesystem global. Use Qt.resolvedUrl("image.png") and relative imports next to the source file. The companion name.ui.qml supplies a ScriptUI for name.qml; see the custom UI API. Source files are watched. If a saved/edited program differs from its external source, the inspector can offer an Update action rather than silently discarding the document’s copy. An unreadable source does not replace the saved program with empty text. See source update notices. When moving projects, retain the source’s neighboring assets and imported modules. JavaScript presets include program code, companion UI and persisted script state. Plain temporary QML properties are not automatically saved as document state: see the persistent state callbacks. Execution and build limitations . Declare the ports and controls required by the process, then apply the code and connect its inlets and outlets to other processes or device addresses. The port reference covers messages, audio, MIDI, controls and textures. GPU scripts use the graphics execution path; CPU scripts run with execution, not on the GUI thread. Do not open native dialogs or directly edit the document from tick. GPU ports need GPU JavaScript support, and the current WebAssembly build does not insert Javascript processes into the execution graph. See the canonical execution and build limitations.

913.title: Language and API reference
913.content: The detailed language and API reference is under Reference → Languages. Go directly to a relocated section: . | General syntax: import Score, the Script object and execution callbacks. | Available functions: Device.read and Device.write. | Token object: model, physical and musical timing. | Token properties. | Token methods. | State object: execution environment and audio-buffer timing. | Execution state properties. | Example of a value mapper. | Example of an audio generator. | Example of a MIDI transposer. | Port types. | Properties common to all ports. | Audio ports. | Example of fetching various timings. | MIDI ports. | Message ports. | Controls. | Generative graphics: texture output, reactive bindings and interactive widgets. | Canvas2D. | Texture input and render size. | .

915.title: Joystick device
915.content: The Joystick device exposes game controllers through SDL. Use it to map buttons, sticks or supported motion sensors to score parameters; compatible gamepads may also provide rumble outputs.

916.title: Connect a controller
916.content: . | Connect the controller to the operating system. | Choose Add device → Joystick in the Device explorer. | Choose a detected controller, or the Default entry to use the first controller not already opened by score. | Review Name and Gamepad API, then add the device. | . The picker rescans while the dialog is open. In a web browser, press a button or move an axis first: browsers do not expose an untouched controller to the page. Gamepad API requests SDL’s standardized game-controller mapping and additional features. score falls back to the generic joystick interface if opening the gamepad interface fails. Controller model, SDL mapping, operating system and browser determine which features are available.

917.title: Address trees
917.content: With the generic joystick interface, read-only addresses use one-based names: . | Address | Value | . | Joystick:/axis-1 | Float axis value in [-1, 1]. | . | Joystick:/button-1 | Boolean button state. | . | Joystick:/hat-1 | Two-component directional-hat value. | . The number of entries follows the hardware. With Gamepad API, names instead describe functions, for example stick/left/x, trigger/right, button/a and dpad/up. Sticks use [-1, 1]; triggers use [0, 1]. Supported sensors appear under sensor, and supported touchpads under touchpad. Do not assume that every gamepad provides these nodes or that generic joystick and gamepad address paths are interchangeable.

918.title: Rumble
918.content: When supported, rumble/main/low_frequency and rumble/main/high_frequency set motor strengths in [0, 1]. Set those values first, then write rumble/main/duration in milliseconds to start the rumble. Devices with trigger rumble similarly expose rumble/triggers/left, right and duration. Changing a strength alone does not start playback of the effect.

919.title: Reusing a project
919.content: A named device selection tries to resolve the saved controller identity on reload. A default device intentionally selects available hardware rather than guaranteeing a particular physical unit. For installations with several controllers, check identities and addresses on the target machine. If a controller is missing, reconnect it and use Reconnect while playback is stopped. Use a Mapper device to rescale axes, combine controls, or give controller-specific addresses stable names within a project.

921.title: jq and Jk
921.content: Object filter uses Jk, a C++ implementation of a subset of the jq query language. Use it to select a tracked point, route messages by a field, reshape a list or construct an object from incoming data. The jq manual is the upstream language reference. The Jk implementation and compatibility notes define the subset available in score. Object filter does not launch the jq executable, and installing jq does not extend Jk’s syntax. The reference below describes the current Jk implementation; older add-on versions may support fewer constructs.

922.title: Values and result streams
922.content: A filter consumes one value and produces zero, one or several results. Each result becomes a separate output event in score. This is different from returning one array: . | Filter | Input | Output events | . | . | [123, "foo"] | One event containing [123, "foo"]. | . | .[] | [123, "foo"] | Two events: 123, then "foo". | . | [.[]] | [123, "foo"] | One event containing [123, "foo"]. | . | [.] | [123, "foo"] | One event containing [ [123, "foo"] ]. | . | empty | Any value | No events. | . The dot means the current input. A pipe sends each result of the left-hand filter into the right-hand filter. Square brackets collect the enclosed filter’s results into one array. A comma produces multiple results from the same input. For example, [.[] | .name] turns [{"name":"Shashimi","age":6},{"name":"Flocky","age":3}] into one list, ["Shashimi","Flocky"]. Without the outer brackets, .[] | .name emits the two names separately. Inputs are score values: maps, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null-like values. A string containing JSON text is still a string; it is not implicitly parsed. Decode it upstream with Value serialization when an incoming protocol supplies serialized JSON rather than an object.

923.title: Navigation and slices
923.content: | Syntax | Meaning | . | .name, .a.b | Select a map field or a nested field. | . | .["odd key"] | Select a key that is not a simple identifier. | . | .[0], .[-1] | Select the first or last array element. Indices start at zero. | . | .[0, 2] | Emit the elements at indices 0 and 2 separately; [.[0, 2]] collects them. | . | .[] | Emit every array element or map value. Map traversal uses sorted keys in Jk. | . | .[start:end] | Return a slice as one value. The start is inclusive and the end is exclusive. | . | .[:end], .[start:] | Slice from the beginning or to the end. Negative and expression-valued bounds are supported. | . | .a?, .[]? | Suppress errors from the optional operation. This can produce no result, rather than a null placeholder. | . | .. | Recursively emit the input and its descendants. | . A missing map field or an out-of-range array index returns null; applying a field lookup to a number is a type error. Use optional navigation when that mismatch is expected. For input [123, 456, 789, 10]: .[1:3] → [456, 789] [.[1:3]] → [ [456, 789] ] [.[1:3][]] → [456, 789] . A slice does not emit its elements individually, and index 3 is not included in .[1:3]. For a nested input: . { "foo": [ {"bar": 1}, {"bar": 3}, {"bar": 4}, {"bar": 2}, {"bar": 5}, {"bar": 2} ] } . use [.foo[2:5][] | .bar] to obtain [4, 2, 5]. The [] after the slice is necessary before selecting .bar from each object. Similarly, .[6].test selects 123 from an array whose seventh element is {"test":123}, and .b[0].foo selects "x" from {"b":[{"foo":"x","bar":"y"}]}.

924.title: Construction, arithmetic and selection
924.content: | Construct | Example | Result or purpose | . | Literals | 42, "hello", true, false, null | Produce the literal independently of the input. | . | Array construction | [.x, .y] | Collect two fields into one array. | . | Object construction | {id, x: .position[0]} | Retain id and name a value extracted from position. | . | Computed key | {(.key): .value} | Use an input field as the output key. | . | Arithmetic | .position[0] * 4 | Scale a coordinate. Operators include +, -, *, / and %. | . | Comparison | .confidence >= 0.8 | Compare with ==, !=, <, <=, > or >=. | . | Selection | select(.state == "confirmed") | Keep the original input when the condition is true; otherwise emit nothing. | . | Alternative | .gain // 0.5 | Substitute when the left filter produces no non-false, non-null results. | . | Conditional | if .active then .value else 0 end | Choose a filter. elif is supported; an omitted else returns the input unchanged. | . | Interpolation | "x=\(.x)" | Insert a filter result into a string. | . + also concatenates strings or arrays and merges objects. Other operators likewise depend on operand types; combining a number and string with + is a type error, not implicit string conversion. Parentheses group expressions. A # starts a comment outside strings. Only false and null are false-like. Zero, an empty string, an empty array and an empty object are true-like. Logical operators are and, or and the not filter; do not assume JavaScript truthiness. A practical tracking query is: . [.[] | select(.confidence > 0.8) | .id] . For [{"id":1,"confidence":0.95},{"id":2,"confidence":0.42}], this produces [1]. Removing the collecting brackets turns the accepted IDs into individual events.

925.title: Supported built-ins
925.content: The following names and arities are supported by the current Jk evaluator. Function arguments are filters; separate multiple arguments with a semicolon, not a comma. | Group | Functions | . | Inspection | length, type, keys, keys_unsorted, has(key), to_entries | . | Type selection | values, nulls, booleans, numbers, strings, arrays, objects, scalars, iterables | . | Arrays and aggregation | add, min, max, sort, unique, reverse, flatten | . | Filtered collections | map(filter), select(filter), sort_by(filter), min_by(filter), max_by(filter), group_by(filter) | . | Conversion and strings | tostring, tonumber, join(separator), split(separator) | . | Mathematics | floor, ceil, round, fabs, sqrt | . | Logic | not, any, any(condition), any(generator; condition), and the corresponding three all forms | . | Stream access | first, last, first(filter), last(filter), nth(index), nth(index; filter) | . | Stream control | empty, isempty(filter), limit(count; filter), skip(count; filter) | . | Ranges | range(end), range(start; end), range(start; end; step) | . | Errors | error, error(payload), try expression, try expression catch handler | . values removes null inputs; it does not enumerate object values. Use .[] for that. In Jk, keys_unsorted uses the same sorted order as keys. first and last without arguments select array elements; their filter forms consume the beginning or end of a result stream. map(. + 1) on [1,2] returns [2,3]; [range(1;4)] returns [1,2,3].

926.title: Errors and compatibility limits
926.content: try expression catch handler sends the original error value into the handler. Without a handler, try expression suppresses the error. The // operator handles false, null or empty results, not errors; use try or optional navigation for potentially invalid operations. The current subset does not implement variables, user-defined functions, reduce, foreach, assignments or update assignments, modules, regex functions, or I/O. In particular, do not assume that an arbitrary query copied from the full jq manual or a command-line flag such as -r or --arg works in the Filter field. Use score’s Regex process for regular-expression processing. Object keys are sorted rather than kept in jq’s insertion order. Integer comparisons retain signed 64-bit precision, but general arithmetic uses binary64 floating-point numbers. UTF-8 slices and splitting on an empty separator operate on codepoints. Error wording need not match jq exactly. In score, an invalid program disables output until a valid filter is supplied. A runtime error stops the remaining results for that input, but does not retract results already emitted. Object filter has no separate error outlet. The current wrapper also ignores an empty-string input. Check the incoming type and test a simple . filter before troubleshooting a longer query. Keep work bounded during playback: a large recursive traversal or generated range can be expensive. Jk’s evaluation has no automatic work budget and is not guaranteed hard-real-time safe. first(filter) and limit(count; filter) avoid evaluating the unused remainder of a stream.

927.title: References and examples
927.content: . | jq manual: full language semantics, beyond Jk’s supported subset. | Jk language and compatibility notes: evaluator capabilities and limits. | Object filter add-on: score’s message-to-query integration. | Maths and structured objects: selecting and reshaping values in a working score. | Files, strings and data: preparing structured data and text for other processes. | .

928.title: Texture Inlet in Qt Quick 3D
928.content: A bouncing, rotating sphere carries a live shader pattern while a red cylinder and moving light give it a simple stage. The pattern travels from a score texture into a QML material; the same connection can put generated images or video onto any object in a scripted scene. Kaleidolines produces the pattern, and a JavaScript/QML process receives it through a texture inlet. Inside Qt Quick 3D, a Texture uses that inlet’s item as its sourceItem, then supplies the sphere’s base-color map. The image on the object can change independently of the object’s motion. The sphere’s bounce and rotation are scripted. A separate LFO controls the directional light and cylinder rotation.

929.title: Wiring the texture
929.content: . | Add a texture-producing shader or video process and the Javascript scene to an interval. | Cable the producer’s texture outlet to the scene’s TextureInlet. Do not use a value inlet for image data. | Connect the scene’s texture outlet to a graphical output and play the interval. | In the scene’s Qt Quick 3D material, use the inlet’s item, not the inlet QObject itself: | . // Inside a Score.Script using `import Score as Score`: Score.TextureInlet { id: incoming; objectName: "Texture" } // Inside the View3D scene carried by the script's TextureOutlet: // PrincipledMaterial { // baseColorMap: Texture { sourceItem: incoming.item } // } . These are the two relevant declarations, not a complete stand-alone scene. Texture and PrincipledMaterial come from QtQuick3D; TextureInlet comes from Score. The inlet owns its exposed item, so do not manually destroy it.

930.title: Resolution and availability
930.content: Use a desktop build with GPU JavaScript and Qt Quick 3D support; the current WebAssembly build does not execute JavaScript processes. No model file is needed because the sphere and cylinder are QML primitives. If the image is blank, check that the texture source, scripted scene and output are all executing. The texture’s render resolution is separate from the QML item’s logical dimensions. When adapting the patch, change the texture inlet’s render resolution rather than expecting a QML item resize to supply more image detail. An editor script can set it after looking up the right texture inlet: Score.inlet(process, index).renderSize = Qt.size(640, 360). Resizing preserves the interactive QML scene; persistent state across save/load still requires the script state API. To preview an already-rendered outlet in a custom control interface, use Score.UI.TextureSource instead. It selects an existing process and port; it does not replace the cabled texture inlet used here.

931.title: Try it
931.content: Start playback and change Kaleidolines’ controls to alter the pattern on the sphere. Then slow the LFO: the light and cylinder slow down while the sphere keeps its scripted bounce. Finally, replace Kaleidolines with another shader or video source to change the surface image without rebuilding the scene. Try this on web . Download this example .

933.title: JSFX and EEL2
933.content: JSFX effects are text programs for processing or generating audio and MIDI, optionally with a custom graphical interface. Their code is written in EEL2, not JavaScript. score hosts them through YSFX, which compiles and runs the scripts. Use the official JSFX programming reference for the file format and API, and the EEL2 reference for the underlying language. The links below lead to those existing references rather than duplicating their function tables here.

934.title: Language and API references
934.content: | Topic | Reference | . | Variables, expressions, operators, branching, loops and mathematics | EEL2 language reference and JSFX basic code reference | . | File headers, sliders, audio pins, imports and code sections | JSFX file structure | . | User-defined functions, local variables and namespaces | Functions and namespace pseudo-objects | . | Audio samples, sample rate, block size, sliders and transport variables | Special variables | . | Receiving and sending MIDI, including event offsets | MIDI functions | . | Data files and saving/restoring script state | File I/O and serialization | . | Memory operations, FFT and MDCT | Advanced functions | . | Strings and string operations | String reference | . | Drawing, images, mouse and keyboard interaction | Graphics reference | . | Slider notifications and other host calls | Host interaction functions | . For orientation, the code sections separate initialization (@init), parameter updates (@slider), block processing (@block), sample processing (@sample), persistent state (@serialize) and drawing (@gfx). Consult their individual descriptions before deciding where code belongs; drawing and audio processing are not the same callback. EEL2’s C-like appearance can be misleading: variable names are case-insensitive, parentheses group statements, and conditional expressions use ? and ?:. Its memory indexing and operator precedence also differ from JavaScript and C. Use the basic code and operator reference, not the JavaScript reference, when adapting a script.

935.title: Using JSFX in score
935.content: . | Loading, routing and opening the UI: follow Audio plug-in support. | Installing scripts and their dependencies: see Adding JSFX plug-ins. This covers the .jsfx extension, user-library discovery, the Effects / Data folder layout and existing effect collections. | Editing and saving: the same JSFX hosting section explains score’s script editor, saved script text and controls, presets, and keeping companion data/import files with the package. Saving the script in a document does not remove its external dependencies. | Playback position and tempo: see Transport and reverse playback. score supplies JSFX with time, tempo and signature information; reversing the timeline does not reverse an effect’s internal DSP history. | .

936.title: Host compatibility
936.content: The Cockos manual describes JSFX in REAPER. It is the language/API reference, not a guarantee that every REAPER-specific feature or recently added extension is available in score. Likewise, EEL2 is used in several applications: sharing the language does not make ReaScript or other host-specific APIs available to a JSFX effect. Compatibility depends on the YSFX version included in the score build and on score’s host integration. Use the YSFX project and usage notes for the runtime, the score hosting documentation for integration behavior, and the score YSFX integration source when checking a particular host feature. YSFX’s standalone plug-in instructions are not score’s installation instructions. Before relying on an imported effect, check its audio/MIDI routing, controls, custom graphics, required files and save/reload behavior in the target score build. A script compiling successfully does not establish that all of its host-dependent behavior works.

937.title: Kinect
937.content: Kinect v1 (Xbox 360), Kinect v2 (Xbox One) and the Azure Kinect DK are supported by the Depth cameras device, since ossia score 3.9.0. It provides their color, infrared and depth images, point clouds, inertial sensors and, on the Kinect v1, the tilt motor and LED.

939.title: Languages
939.content: Find the syntax and runtime contract for code used in score. Each reference separates the underlying language from the objects, ports, variables or shader resources supplied by score. Process and device pages explain how to insert, connect and operate the corresponding component.

Choose the API for the place where the code executes; a console script and an audio-process callback do not have the same responsibilities. | Process API: Script, ports, callbacks, timing, audio, MIDI and textures. | Editor API: document editing, transport, devices, utilities and view automation. | Custom UI API: control bindings, ScriptUI, persistent state and texture previews. | QML device API: device trees, mappings and protocol-specific callbacks. | QML transport API: sockets, framing, HTTP, OAuth, OSC and MIDI payloads. | . For editor workflow and examples, see Scripting and Custom UI. These are Qt-hosted scripts, not a browser or Node.js environment.

941.title: Audio languages
941.content: | Language | Use in score | Reference | . | Faust | Compiled signal-processing graphs for synthesis and effects | Syntax, composition, libraries and controls | . | JSFX / EEL2 | Source-based audio and MIDI effects hosted through YSFX | Language, API references and host compatibility | . | Pure Data | Visual dataflow patches hosted through libpd | Patch language and score interface | . | Bytebeat | Short arithmetic and bitwise expressions that generate sound | C++ expression dialect and formula collection | . Their timing and buffer contracts differ; use the reference for the selected process rather than transferring a callback from another language.

942.title: GPU languages and shader formats
942.content: Start with GLSL and Vulkan compatibility for types, shader stages, standard functions and the distinction between user code and declarations generated by score. The formats below combine GLSL with a header that defines controls, resources and execution. | Format | Execution model | Reference | . | ISF — Interactive Shader Format | Fullscreen fragment passes for images and video | ISF and score extensions | . | CSF — score’s compute extension | Compute dispatches over images, buffers and geometry | CSF headers, resources and functions | . | Raw raster pipeline | Vertex and fragment stages for custom geometry rendering | Raster interfaces and pipeline state | . | Vertex Shader Art | Procedural points and lines generated in a vertex shader | VSA inputs and shader contract | . | Geometry filter | Vertex-attribute callback applied by the downstream renderer | Geometry-filter shader contract | . The Graphics pipeline explains how these processes connect. The Shader cookbook gives recipes that use the references. A Vulkan-compatible shader language does not mean that every GPU or rendering backend supports every resource or extension.

943.title: Rule-based graphics
943.content: . | EisenScript: transformations, recursive rules and weighted alternatives for Structure Synth geometry. | Context Free / CFDG: shape grammars for image generation. | . These languages build geometry or images from rules; they are not per-sample audio languages or per-frame GPU shaders.

944.title: External interpreters
944.content: External scripts links the Python, POSIX shell, Bash, Zsh, Fish, PowerShell and Cmd references used with Shell command. These interpreters must be installed separately: invoking them is not the same as embedding their language runtime in score.

Installed Qt modules, compiler support, plug-ins and graphics capabilities determine what is available in a particular build. See Add-ons for optional capabilities and Live coding for the shared code-editor workflow.

946.content: . ossia supports using the Leapmotion. Right now only one sensor at a time is supported, this limit will soon be lifted. Every UltraLeap device recognized by the Gemini or Hyperion drivers are supported. | On Windows and macOS the UltraLeap drivers (Gemini or Hyperion) must be installed : https://leap2.ultraleap.com/downloads/. Both AppleSilicon and Intel Macs are supported. | On Linux, ossia will be looking for the following Ultraleap binaries: . | . /opt/ultraleap/LeapSDK/lib/libLeaC.so.5 /opt/ultraleap/LeapSDK/lib/libLeaC.so.6 .

947.title: Combine shader LED arrays
947.content: . Build a longer lighting pattern from three distinct animations. Each shader supplies one section of the strip, previewed on screen before any physical LEDs are assigned. Download the example . Try this on web .

948.title: Run the preview
948.content: Start playback in nodal view. Lightness computer samples each shader on a 10×10 grid and converts the image to color values. Array Combiner appends the three lists end to end; it does not blend corresponding pixels. LED View displays the resulting sequence in RGB01 mode because these samples use the 0–1 range, not 8-bit values. Change one sampler’s Size and watch that section occupy more or less of the sequence. Use an Array tool on the second or third branch to vary its brightness independently of the other sections. Padding also changes where colors fall. The third branch starts with 130 padding elements, which is not a whole number of RGB pixels. Try 129 instead: padding now occupies complete triples, preserving the red/green/blue alignment of the following values. Use triplet-aligned spacing when adapting the pattern to a physical strip. The shaders require a graphics backend but no external media. This score provides a preview, not a configured hardware output. For device addressing and a shader-to-output patch, see LED design. SilverMaze’s embedded source credits Florian Berger (flockaroo), 2017, under CC BY-NC-SA 3.0; retain its attribution and consider that license when reusing the shader.

949.title: LED device
949.content: ossia supports talking to NeoPixels over a bitbang-based SPI protocol.

950.title: Generated RGB LED Strip
950.content: . Watch a strip of colors evolve from a single expression, without an image source or physical LEDs. Arraygen calculates 127(1+sin(i*t/1e10)) for every element of a list. Time changes the values, while the element index gives each one a different rhythm. LED View reads consecutive groups of three as red, green and blue: 192 values become 64 colored pixels.

951.title: Try it
951.content: Start playback and watch the preview in the process UI. Increase the divisor 1e10 to slow the changes, or decrease it to accelerate them. Remove the i* factor to make all channels move together: the strip turns a uniform gray that brightens and darkens as one. To extend the pattern, change Size to another multiple of three; 384 values provide 128 complete RGB pixels. This score only previews those values. Sending them to physical LEDs requires a separately configured output; see LED View for preview modes. Download this example . Try this on web .

952.title: LED View
952.content: . Visualize control signals in real-time for monitoring, debugging, and performance feedback. LED View previews a numerical array as colored cells. Mode selects RGB, RGBW, RGB01, Lightness01 or Lightness8bit. RGB01 and Lightness01 use normalized values; the corresponding 8-bit modes use 0–255 values. RGBW’s fourth component is white, not alpha. It is useful for instance for visualizing arrays of LEDs, or arrays with large numbers of elements where Signal Display becomes impractical.

953.title: Grid sizing
953.content: The Size pair requests an explicit layout. Set both components above zero to enable it; the first component determines how many cells are drawn before wrapping to a new row. With the automatic size, wrapping follows the process width instead. Match the grid width to the row width of your incoming pixel data. LED View only visualizes the values. It does not send data to LEDs, correct colors, or enforce electrical limits. Pixel Utilities can extract values from a texture, and Array utilities can rearrange their channels.

954.title: Example
954.content: The Generated RGB LED Strip walkthrough includes a patch for inspecting a 192-value array without LED hardware.

955.title: Related processes
955.content: score comes with multiple processes for monitoring input data LED View, Signal Display, Value display.

956.title: Generate LED arrays with expressions
956.content: . Create a changing color strip from numbers instead of images, without a shader-rendering stage. Three sine expressions produce related patterns with different phases and lengths; joining them makes a sequence whose sections develop differently over time. Download the example . Try this on web .

957.title: Try it
957.content: Start playback and watch LED View. Each Arraygen calculates values from time and position in its list, while the Array tool stages provide places to reshape the values before and after joining. Change a phase offset in one expression: its section shifts out of step with the others. Then increase that generator’s Size by three: it contributes one more complete RGB triple to the sequence. The generator names R, G and B can be misleading here: Array Combiner is in Append mode, joining whole lists end to end, and the preview reads each consecutive triple as a pixel. The generators do not independently control red, green and blue. To explore that alternative, give all three generators the same Size and switch to Intersperse. Each pixel can then take one value from each generator. This changes the relationship between the expressions and the colors, not just the strip’s length. The expressions can produce negative values. Before adapting the patch for hardware, map or clamp them to the receiver’s legal range and keep the final array aligned to complete RGB triples. This score only previews the values; it does not transmit to LEDs. See LED design for device-side setup.

958.title: LFO
958.content: . The LFO generates a control value at its Out port: connect it to a parameter to make that parameter oscillate. It does not generate an audio signal. This page describes LFO version 3. Older scores may contain LFO (old) or LFO (v2), which retain their own controls rather than automatically becoming v3.

959.title: Period and synchronization
959.content: Period is the duration of one cycle, not its frequency: free range 0.01–60 seconds, default 1 second. A one-second period corresponds to 1 Hz; a two-second period to 0.5 Hz. Use the time chooser readout to select straight, dotted or triplet note values. Lock to bars affects synchronized mode only: . | Off: cycles accumulate from the playback start or the last Retrigger. | On: cycles are calculated from the timeline’s musical position, keeping their alignment through tempo changes, jumps and loops. Retrigger establishes a new origin at the current musical position. | . Retrigger restarts the cycle; Phase still applies to its starting position. Musical periods are whole-note fractions: a 1/1 cycle is four quarter notes, not necessarily one bar in a different time signature.

960.title: Waveform and shape
960.content: The waveform selector offers sine, triangle, rising saw, falling ramp, square, sample-and-hold, three noise variants and drift. Square and sample-and-hold each have an every-tick and an on-change variant. Choose on-change when a downstream process should receive only the steps, rather than repeated copies of the held value. Sample-and-hold chooses a new random value at each of the cycle’s two steps. Shape ranges from 0 to 1 (default 0.5). It changes the rise/fall balance of sine and triangle, the step width of square and sample-and-hold, the curve of the ramps, and the roughness of drift.

961.title: Output range and phase
961.content: | Control | Range; default | Meaning | . | Ampl. | 0–2; 0.5 | Multiplies the waveform, whose base range is −1 to 1. | . | Offset | −1–1; 0.5 | Added after amplitude scaling. | . | Phase | 0–360 degrees; 0 | Constant phase offset. 0 and 360 represent the same point; values outside the range wrap. | . | Jitter | 0–180 degrees; 0 | Adds a random phase offset within ±this amount on each execution tick. This is phase variation, not output-amplitude noise. | . The default amplitude and offset produce values from 0 to 1. For a bipolar modulation around zero, set Offset to 0. The destination’s own range still determines which values are useful.

962.title: Older saved LFOs
962.content: The earlier variants remain separately registered for saved scores and are marked deprecated. Their frequency-based timing and phase controls must not be interpreted using the v3 units above. To use the new Period, Shape or Lock to bars controls, add a current LFO and deliberately re-create the desired modulation and connections.

963.title: Libav device
963.content: The Libav device opens media through FFmpeg or encodes score’s output to a file or URL. The Direction setting selects Input or Output. Available demuxers, protocols, encoders and muxers depend on the linked FFmpeg build.

964.title: Input
964.content: Set Path / URL to a file, network stream such as RTSP, or an image-sequence pattern such as /path/to/frames_%05d.png. Options accepts key=value entries, one per line, passed to the input. For an image sequence, options such as framerate=30 and start_number=0 describe how the files form a stream. Select the resulting device as a texture inlet’s source. Unlike a timeline Video process, this is a streaming input; placing the consuming process on an interval does not make a live source seekable. If the input contains audio, its /Audio endpoint can feed an audio inlet independently of the texture. A /path parameter also exposes the source path for control.

965.title: Output
965.content: Choose Path / URL, Width, Height, Rate, and Audio Channels. Then select the Muxer, Video Encoder, Audio Encoder, Pixel Format and Sample Format appropriate for the destination. The encoder and format lists are derived from FFmpeg capabilities; an encoder being listed does not prove its hardware or runtime dependencies are available. Assign the device’s video endpoint to the final texture outlet. When audio channels and an audio encoder are configured, route audio to /Audio as well. Video pixels and audio samples are converted for the selected encoders before muxing; GPU pixel conversion is not the same as hardware codec encoding. Use Options and Show options… for additional encoder/muxer configuration. Input Transfer describes the incoming graph texture: sRGB (default), Linear, HDR10 (PQ), HLG or Passthrough. Match this to the preceding processes rather than using it as a substitute for correct source metadata. The dialog checks named muxers and encoders, but destination permissions, network connectivity and format compatibility can still fail at runtime. Test the intended output and inspect the resulting media before a performance. See Video formats and color, GStreamer for explicit pipelines, and Livestreaming.

966.title: Libmapper client
966.content: libmapper connects named signals between applications and devices. score’s source contains an optional LibmapperClient protocol, distinct from the Mapper device, which builds a device tree using QML.

967.title: Availability
967.content: Compilation and registration require OSSIA_PROTOCOL_LIBMAPPER and the linked mapper dependency. The integration has an interface mismatch: its factory header declares getEnumerators, while the implementation defines getEnumerator. This mismatch must be resolved for a libmapper-enabled build to work; enabling the build option alone is insufficient.

968.title: Intended device model
968.content: The source describes a client for a discovered libmapper device: . | The enumerator observes libmapper devices joining or leaving the graph. | Selecting a discovered device supplies its identifier; the client uses that identifier to obtain its signal tree. | The settings widget exposes a local Name, not a manually editable remote identifier or host/port pair. Merely typing a name into an empty configuration does not provide the required discovery identifier. | The device advertises tree refresh, but not adding, removing or renaming remote nodes or editing their properties from score. | . The underlying client builds parameters for remote input signals, intended for sending values from score. Its observe operation returns false; do not infer support for subscribing to remote output signals or bidirectional device synchronization. This does not make the QML Mapper device a libmapper client. For a script-defined namespace and mappings inside score, use Mapper device instead.

969.title: Source references
969.content: The build guard and registration are in score-plugin-protocols/CMakeLists.txt and score_plugin_protocols.cpp. The factory, discovery and client behavior are in Protocols/Libmapper/LibmapperClientDevice.hpp and .cpp.

970.title: Library
970.content: The library is split across multiple panels: . | The Process library: Ctrl+Shift+P(Win / Linux) or⌘+Shift+P(Mac) | The system library: Ctrl+Shift+B(Win / Linux) or⌘+Shift+B(Mac) | The project library: Ctrl+Shift+L(Win / Linux) or⌘+Shift+L(Mac) | .

971.title: Process library
971.content: This pane shows the processes available to add to the score: automations, audio effects, etc. Everything is there ! . The top part shows the list of available processes, grouped by category. Processes there can be dragged to the score. The middle part shows available presets for the selected processes. Presets can also be dragged to the score. The bottom part shows information on the selected process. Categories and preset descriptions . File-backed process entries can be grouped into nested categories derived from their containing folders. Expand the category tree to find related shaders, scripts and other supported library files; the exact entries depend on the installed packages and process plug-ins. Files in a process’s default preset folder can appear directly beneath that process rather than beneath another wrapper. The preset list remains associated with the selected process. A preset may carry an optional Description in its .scp JSON metadata; hover over that preset to read it as a tooltip. A missing description does not prevent a preset from loading. See Presets for saving and reusing presets. Package and source updates . When an installed package has an update, the Process library can display a notice with an Update link to the Packages settings page. This is separate from the inspector’s Update button for a process taken from an external file. For process types that support source refresh, that button appears when the source is out of date and replaces the process with the current file version. It is an undoable edit, not an automatic rewrite of every existing process when a package changes. Review the result before continuing playback. Fast creation of effect chains . To allow easy experimentation, double-clicking on a process or preset will add it and connect it, if possible, to the currently selected process in the score, or to the currently selected port if a port is selected. If nothing is selected, the process will be added to the currently displayed interval. Note: that means that by default, if nothing is selected, the processes may go at the bottom slot and won’t be visible without scrolling to the bottom of the score.

972.title: System library
972.content: This pane displays content shared across all scores. In a normal installation its folder is <Documents>/ossia/score/packages. The Library settings change the root directory above packages. On first interactive launch, score offers to download the User Library, containing pre-existing presets and other content. It is installed in packages/default. Personal content belongs in packages/user. Content installed through the package manager also appears here. SDKs and native support packages are stored separately and are not ordinary library items. The process-library scan is asynchronous, so large packages may take time to appear. Restart if manually copied content is not discovered. A library rescan does not replace running native libraries: restart after installing or changing native support packages. Various actions are possible: . | Dragging and dropping one or multiple files to the score. | Double-clicking on files. For instance, double-clicking on a .score will open it. | Right-click allows to open a folder in the system file explorer. | Dragging and dropping processes from the score: one can save a preset at a specific place by dragging from the folder preset icon. | . Here is an example of saving and loading a whole score as a preset, to embed it recursively in itself. Important folders in the default library . | Skins: contains skins which can be changed in the settings. The currently provided screens are adaptations for various color-blindness schemes. | Util/metro_tick.wav and Util/metro_tock.wav: replace these if you want to change the sound of the metronome. | .

973.title: Project library
973.content: This pane displays the content of the current project folder: this is simply the folder in which the edited score is saved. Otherwise, it behaves exactly like the system library.

974.title: Preview
974.content: For now, sound files are previewed when clicking on them ; playback can be started and stopped with the little play / stop button at the bottom-left.

975.title: Basic configuration
975.content: Some basic steps are usually required on Linux systems to make the most out of ossia. For instance, a lot of Linux capabilities are by default accessible only to the root user, e.g. through sudo for instance. It is generally not feasible to run score as for instance sound daemons such as JACK or PipeWire are per-user ; thus running score under another user would prevent access to sound output. The way capabilities are granted to non-root users is through the groups system. We recommend to be in the following groups (and creating them if they aren’t with groupadd "name_of_the_group": . | uucp and / or dialout depending on the distribution for serial port access (including access to DMX devices such as an ENTTEC USB-DMX for instance). | audio for raw access to sound and MIDI devices (usually this one is by default). | video for cameras and anything in /dev/video. | render to be able to use direct rendering through EGLFS, without e.g. X11 or Wayland. | realtime for enabling low-latency support with e.g. JACK or PipeWire. | gpio to access GPIO pins, etc. | i2c to access other raw devices. | bluetooth to use the Bluetooth support. | input to use the raw evdev input device and for some BLE devices (Bluetooth gamepads). | power if you want to be able to control e.g. turning off a computer through score directly. | . This can be done in one command: . $ sudo usermod -a -G dialout,uucp,audio,video,render,realtime,gpio,i2c,bluetooth,input,power $USER . Note that it is necessary to log-out and log-in again after it as this command does not affect the current user session.

977.title: Livecoding processes
977.content: . Change the rules of a running composition and observe the result without rebuilding the patch. Three independent sections let you reshape a control signal, edit a generated image and interact with a custom interface. Try this on web . Download the example .

978.title: Try it
978.content: Start playback and release the start triggers for JS, Shaders and JSui. Each section also has an interactive end, so you can run and stop the experiments independently. | Reshape a signal. Open JS with its terminal-shaped editor button. An LFO passes through Math.sin(10. * in1.value) before reaching Signal display. Change the multiplier, then press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on macOS) to apply it. A larger multiplier puts more oscillations across the same incoming sweep. | Change an image. Open SpaceSpore’s shader editor and find the ray-marching step t += 1.8 * d;. Change its multiplier and apply the edit: the generated form changes on the next frame. Right-click the editor button to choose a panel, separate window or central editor, including the background-render option. | Perform through an interface. Open ui-example’s external interface and move its controls while watching the adjacent Signal display, which also shows the incoming LFO. | . Use a build with JavaScript/QML, Qt Quick UI and ISF shader support. These processes come from the default library, but the saved JS code has already been edited: it applies a sine function instead of averaging values.

979.title: Using score OSCQuery device
979.content: score exposes its scenario execution parameters through OSCQuery protocol so they can be monitored and controlled locally or from any device on the network. For example, using score’s own Device explorer, you will see when browsing available OSCQuery devices the score application and its address and port. Exposed parameters include: . | ‘exit’: close current scenario | ‘global_play’: play score’s current scenario | ‘play’: play score’s current scenario | ‘reconnect’: reconnect a device | ‘reinit’: stop score execution and recall init state | ‘running’: report whether score is playing | ‘stop’: stop scenario execution | ‘transport’: set scenario main playhead at a particular point (in ms.) | . Below is a simple Max patcher provided in ossia-max package illustrating remote control of score’s transport.

980.title: More parameters in the local tree
980.content: In the preferences of the software, it is possible to enable the extended tree. This tree will create nodes for every interval, process, etc. This means that it will become possible to control any parameter in your score from OSC / OSCQuery.

981.title: Local device
981.content: While score can synchronise and automate your media softwares and hardware, it can also be remote-controlled, should you need to control your scenario execution using some hyper advanced next generation IA software, a custom sensor interface or whatever fits your needs.

982.doc: Live audio looper with drum backing
982.title: Live audio looper with drum backing
982.content: . Play a short phrase once, then hear it return over a drum backing. The timeline switches the Looper from stopped to recording to playback, so the moment a live phrase becomes a repeating part is composed in advance. The Looper captures the main audio input, not the internally generated drums, so the accompaniment stays out of your recording.

983.doc: Live audio looper with drum backing
983.title: Prepare and record
983.content: . | Open the ZIP directly in a score build with Kaboom support. The current score uses synthesized drums and needs no sample kit. Configure a working audio input and output. | Use headphones or isolated monitoring to avoid feeding loudspeaker output back into a microphone. Begin at a low listening level. | Start playback and supply audio to the input. The initial cue requests Stop, the cue at 4 seconds requests Record, and the cue at 12 seconds requests Play. | Listen for the captured phrase repeating against the drums. Quantize is set to one bar, so mode changes wait for the next bar line instead of switching freely between beats. | Trigger the end of Loop, drawn at 14.5 seconds, or stop the transport. The end is interactive: its position is not an automatic stop. | .

984.doc: Live audio looper with drum backing
984.title: Shape the phrase
984.content: Record a phrase with a clear attack and a little silence at the end. Listen to the join between repetitions, then move the Record or Play cue to change what falls inside the capture window. Because of quantization, the audible switch can come slightly after the cue. Try a sustained sound next. A capture window that works for a rhythmic phrase may cut a sustained note differently; this makes the recording boundary part of the composition. The cues address the Looper through the Local device, so no remote client is required. Download this example . Try this on web .

985.title: LSL device
985.content: The LSL device connects score to Lab Streaming Layer streams. It can subscribe to external streams and create separate outgoing streams. These are distinct directions: an incoming sensor channel is read-only, not a remote control for the sensor.

986.title: Availability and dependencies
986.content: LSL is provided by the optional score-addon-lsl add-on. If LSL is absent from the device protocol list, the running score installation does not expose this add-on; installing a sensor driver or Python package alone does not add the protocol. For a source build, include the add-on and its 3rdparty/liblsl submodule. Its CMake configuration builds liblsl statically and links LSL::lsl and score’s Device explorer plug-in. The bundled liblsl requires CMake 3.23 or newer, thread support and Boost headers; this add-on disables liblsl’s private bundled Boost. Pugixml is bundled by default. The Windows build targets Windows 10 APIs. These build settings do not establish availability in every score package or on every platform. At runtime, receiving requires an application or hardware bridge that publishes an LSL outlet, not merely a connected instrument. Sending requires an external LSL receiver if you want another application to consume score’s values. The static build above does not require a separately installed shared liblsl for score; an external publisher or receiver may have its own liblsl installation requirements. Python and pylsl are only needed for Python-based publishers or receivers, not for the score device itself.

987.title: Receive a stream
987.content: . | Start the source application or instrument’s LSL bridge and enable its outlet. | In the Device explorer, choose Add device → LSL. | Set Name: to the name you want for the score device, for example LSL. | Wait for the Inbound Streams table to populate.
