Each scale root then lasts longer, making the changing tonal centre easier to hear. | Reduce Drive’s Dry/Wet for a cleaner synth sound. Listen for the amplitude-decay modulation as well as the small oscillator-pitch changes. | . Finally, edit the source pattern: the transformation chain applies the same treatment to the new notes. Download this example . Try this on web .

1121.title: MIDI Humanize
1121.content: MIDI Humanize processes a MIDI input into a MIDI output with controlled variation. Insert it between a sequencer and an instrument. Timing controls use the shared Time Chooser. | Timing sets the timing deviation. Colour chooses uncorrelated white noise (0), correlated 1/f variation (1), or Brownian drift (2). | Early permits apparently early deviations by adding a real baseline delay of Early × 3 × Timing. It cannot send notes before they arrive. | Velocity controls velocity deviation; Vel. range bounds resulting velocities. | Length varies durations. Shortening is limited by available lookahead because duration is only known when note-off arrives. | Chance is the probability of playing a note. Pitch adds random transposition in semitones; note-offs follow the transposed note. | Chord groups nearby notes under one timing deviation. Spread adds delay between successive chord notes for a strum. | Channel (0 means all) and Key range restrict affected notes. | Seed 0 runs freely. A nonzero seed makes a reproducible take and resets its random sequence when transport rewinds. | . Timing, Chord and Spread use time choosers. Begin with small deviations and Early at zero when live latency matters. Use a nonzero Seed when comparing repeated renders or rehearsing a fixed variation.

1122.title: MIDI controls for a shader
1122.content: . Perform an abstract image from a MIDI keyboard. The modulation wheel zooms a line pattern, pitch bend couples rotation with amplitude, and notes reshape and twist the drawing. The image is generated by the native ISF shader Triangle Square Twist. No video or model file is needed, and the patch produces no sound.

1123.title: Connect and play
1123.content: . | With playback stopped, right-click MIDI In, choose Edit and select your actual MIDI input. The saved default port may not exist on your machine. | Use Learn on that device and move your controls if their addresses are not present. Confirm values change in the Device explorer before starting playback. | Start playback and send channel 1 CC1 (MIDI In:/1/control/1) to control zoom. Channel 1 pitch bend changes rotate and amplitude together. | Send note 36 on channel 10 with different velocities to change the shader’s triside1 control. This percussion-style input uses a different channel from the wheels. | Play a run of notes to change twist. Note values are normalized and smoothed, so the image travels between settings instead of simply snapping from one to the next. | .

1124.title: Try it
1124.content: Alternate low and high notes while leaving the wheels still. Raise Exp Smoothing’s Alpha from its saved 0.01 toward 1: the pattern stops flowing between notes and starts following individual attacks. Then combine pitch bend with the modulation wheel to rotate and zoom at once. To try a different physical control, learn its address and drag it onto the relevant shader inlet, or edit the inlet’s address. A direct mapping like this has no conversion or smoothing; the note-to-twist chain uses conversion to set the range and smoothing to set the timing. Download this example . Try this on web .

1125.title: Midi Quantify
1125.content: The process named Midi quantify receives MIDI notes at in and schedules their starts and endings before sending them to MIDI out. Put it between a live MIDI source and an instrument to constrain note timing. Non-note MIDI messages pass through unchanged. This page describes version 2.

1126.title: Grid and Tightness
1126.content: Grid sets the spacing between possible note starts. Its free range is 0–4 seconds, default 0.125 seconds. Zero lets notes start as they arrive. Use the time chooser for straight, dotted or triplet note values. | A free grid is measured from the playback origin in samples. | A synchronized grid follows the timeline’s musical position, so it remains aligned to the beats when playback starts elsewhere in the score. | . Tightness ranges from 0 to 1, default 0.8. At 1, an off-grid note waits for the next grid point. Reducing it allows a note played just after a grid point to start immediately: the acceptance window is (1 − Tightness) × half a grid step. At the default 0.8, this is 10% of a step. This is causal processing: it never moves a live note backwards in time.

1127.title: Length and Duration
1127.content: Length determines how note endings are handled: . | Choice | Behavior | . | UntilNoteOff (default) | End on the incoming note-off. If a note is released before its delayed start, it still plays for the duration it was originally held. | . | FixedDuration | End after Duration measured from the scheduled start, regardless of the input note-off. | . | EndOnGrid | End at the next point of the Duration grid after the scheduled start, regardless of the input note-off. | . Duration has a free range of 0–8 seconds, default 0.25 seconds, and its own independent time chooser. For example, synchronize Grid to 1/8, choose FixedDuration, and set Duration to 1/16 for eighth-note starts with sixteenth-note lengths. Duration is not used in UntilNoteOff mode. A repeated note-on for the same channel and pitch replaces a waiting note and ends an already sounding one before rescheduling it. Transport discontinuities release sounding notes and discard pending starts rather than leaving them queued for a later position.

1128.title: Older saved processes
1128.content: Midi quantify (old) remains available to load existing scores with its earlier quantification and duration controls. It is not automatically replaced with v2. Re-create the intended settings and connections in a new Midi quantify process to use Grid, Length and the two time choosers. See MIDI Utilities for other note transformations.

1129.title: MIDI Sync Out
1129.content: MIDI Sync Out, in Timing/Midi, sends synchronization from an executing score interval to external MIDI equipment.

1130.title: Setup
1130.content: . | Add a MIDI output device. | Add MIDI Sync Out to the interval whose tempo/time should drive the receiver. | Assign MIDI output to that device. The process resolves the addressed MIDI device stream directly; an ordinary cable to a MIDI-processing node is not a substitute for this device assignment. | Enable the message families the receiving hardware expects, and configure the receiver to follow that external clock or timecode. | .

1131.title: Controls
1131.content: | Input | Purpose | . | MIDI Clock | Enable the 24-pulses-per-quarter-note clock derived from the interval tempo | . | MIDI Start/Stop | Enable MIDI transport messages | . | MIDI TimeCode | Enable MIDI timecode (MTC) | . | MTC offset (s) | Add an offset in seconds to the transmitted time | . | MTC rate | Select the displayed 24, 25, 29.97 or 30 fps mode | . Clock expresses musical tempo; MTC expresses a time position. They are different protocols, so enabling both is only useful when the receiver understands both. The output controls start disabled until enabled by the user. When playback starts on a clock pulse, the first clock goes out together with Start, so that the receiver counts its first beat from there.

1132.title: Limitations
1132.content: This process sends synchronization; it does not make score a slave to an external transport. Use MIDI Sync In to extract incoming timing values. MIDI transmission and receiver behavior add latency and jitter; test the actual devices rather than assuming sample-accurate lock.

1133.title: Seeking and looping
1133.content: After a seek, a loop or a resume in the middle of the score, MIDI Sync Out sends Stop, a Song Position and Continue. A Song Position counts 16th notes, so the clock starts again on the first 16th note at or after the new position, and nothing is sent until then: the receiver’s first clock is where the score is. With a clock rate other than x1, the 16th notes are the receiver’s: at x2, a score quarter is two quarters for the receiver. Positions past 1024 bars of 4/4 cannot be sent as a Song Position. In the current implementation the displayed 29.97/30 choices use the opposite numerical rates for frame calculation; use 24 or 25 fps when possible, and do not rely on the two higher-rate modes for frame-accurate synchronization.

1134.title: MIDI Sync In
1134.content: MIDI Sync In, in Timing/Midi, decodes incoming MIDI Time Code (full-frame and quarter-frame messages) and MIDI clock into control values. Assign a MIDI input device to MIDI in, or cable a MIDI source to it. Keep the containing interval executing while receiving messages. Connect the resulting values to the controls or synchronization logic that should follow the source.

1135.title: Inputs
1135.content: | Control | Purpose | . | Sync Mode | MTC only, clock only, or MTC with clock interpolation | . | Offset (seconds) | Offset the decoded time | . | Output Format | Seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, nanoseconds or flicks | . | Framerate | Auto, 24, 25, 29.97 or 30 fps | . | Base Tempo | Starting tempo for clock-derived timing before estimation stabilizes | . | Clock filter | Smoothing for the clock-based tempo estimate | . | Song Position | Initial MIDI song-position value, in sixteenth notes | .

1136.title: Outputs
1136.content: . | Timecode: position in the selected Output Format. | Tempo: estimated clock tempo. | Song Position: MIDI song-position value. | Valid: whether the process has a valid timing result. | Frame Rate, MTC Active, Clock Active: status of the decoded timing source. | . Use the status outputs to decide whether downstream logic should follow the position. A MIDI clock stream alone does not convey SMPTE timecode: clock-only position is derived from tempo, transport messages and song position. Adding this process does not automatically slave score’s global transport, start playback or select a master clock. It produces values for an explicitly constructed synchronization workflow. For sending score’s timing to equipment, see MIDI Sync Out.

1137.doc: Playing synths on MIDI channels 1 and 10
1137.title: Playing synths on MIDI channels 1 and 10
1137.content: . One MIDI connection carries two independent parts: channel 1 plays a layered synth lead, while channel 10 plays drums. Each note reaches only the instrument on its channel, and each part has its own effects. Choose the channel on your keyboard or software MIDI source. Starting score’s transport does not generate notes: this patch is an instrument for incoming performances, not a sequenced piece.

1138.doc: Playing synths on MIDI channels 1 and 10
1138.title: Setup and sound
1138.content: . | Stop playback, edit MIDI In in the Device explorer and select a connected keyboard or MIDI source. Configure score’s audio output. | Start playback at a low volume. Send notes on channel 1 to play Synthimi’s layered, detuned saw oscillators. | Send drum notes on channel 10 to play Kaboom. Begin with note 36; other notes follow Kaboom’s drum assignments. Alternate between channels to confirm which instrument receives each note. | Hold a lead note and listen for IronOxide5’s coloration and Vibrato’s pitch movement. These are parallel treatments of the original synth, combined before a shared chorus, not two effects applied one after another. | Keep a drum pattern steady and lower ZLowpass2’s cutoff, then change Compresaturator’s Drive. The filter removes brightness and the drive adds saturation; both change the drums’ apparent weight without changing the rhythm. | . Play a sustained channel-1 phrase against short channel-10 attacks, then adjust the drum filtering: the lead is unaffected. The build needs Synthimi, Kaboom and Airwindows; no sample files or external plug-ins are required. If your MIDI device is not listed, select a suitable API in Settings and choose the input again. Enable the MIDI device’s velocity-zero-as-note-off option if your controller uses that convention. Download this example . Try this on web .

1140.title: Arpeggiator
1140.content: . The classic arpeggiator effect. Play a chord on your keyboard and let the process create new notes from it. Some of its patterns: . | Forward: plays the notes in order (1-2-3-1-2-3) | Backward: plays the notes in reverse order (3-2-1-3-2-1) | F->B: first forward then backwards (1-2-3-3-2-1) | B->F: first backwards then forward (3-2-1-1-2-3) | Chord: repeats the chord currently being held | . See Arpeggiator for all its patterns and its timing, velocity and latch controls.

1141.title: Chord
1141.content: . This process transforms an input note into a chord. For instance, if “Major” is selected: C3 -> C3 E3 G3 . Its Mode picks where the chord comes from: . | Chord: the chord type chosen in the list, with up to Num. Notes notes. | Harmonizer: the Intervals list, in semitones from the played note. | Memory: a chord of its own for each key, from the Memory list. | . The Memory list has one row per key: the key, then the semitones of each note from that key, e.g. C4: 0 4 7 (C4 is MIDI note 60; 60: 0 4 7 works too). Rows are added with “+”, removed with “x”, and edited by double-clicking them; a key without a row plays itself. To fill it from a keyboard, turn on Learn, play a chord, release it, then press the key that will trigger it: the row for that key appears in the list.

1142.title: MIDI scale
1142.content: . This process allows to transpose and make the input MIDI fit into predetermined scales, to prevent wrong notes for instance. Lowest and Range limit it to part of the keyboard: only the notes from Lowest to Lowest + Range are scaled and transposed, the others pass unchanged. For instance the preset “Fifth up above C4 only” has Lowest at 60 (C4) and Transpose at 7: C4 plays G4 and E4 plays B4, while every key below C4 plays itself.

1143.title: Quantifier
1143.content: . This process quantifies input MIDI onto the musical grid. See Midi Quantify for the distinction between onset and release quantization.

1144.title: MIDI pitch
1144.content: . This process allows to extract the pitch of a MIDI note as a simple value.

1145.title: Pulse to note
1145.content: . This process allows to convert input signals into MIDI. | If the input is of type impulse, then the default velocity and default pitch are used. | If the input is of type int, then it is used as pitch and the velocity is set with the default velocity. | If the input is of type vec2, then the first element is the pitch, the second is the velocity. | .

1146.title: Midi Glide
1146.content: Midi Glide makes a stream monophonic: one note sounds at a time, chosen among the keys held as a monophonic synthesizer does. | Control | Meaning | . | Priority | The held key that sounds: Last pressed, Lowest or Highest. A key that does not win is remembered. | . | On release | When the sounding key is released while others are held: Stop ends the note and forgets the keys still held; Return goes back to the held key that wins, at the velocity it was played with. | . | Transition | Retrigger ends a note before starting the next. Legato starts the next one first, which a synthesizer in legato (“fingered”) mode plays as a slide: glide, and no new attack. | . | Latch | Toggle: the note keeps sounding when its key is released, until another key takes over. Momentary: the same while Hold is pressed; the latched note ends when Hold is let go. | . The defaults (Last, Stop, Retrigger, no latch) are a plain monophonic legato.

1147.title: Midi transform
1147.content: Midi transform turns one kind of MIDI message into another. Its Value outlet gives the value of each message it produces, at the time of the message: . | note on and note off: the velocity; CC: the controller value; poly pressure: the pressure (0 to 127); | program change, channel pressure, MTC quarter frame, song select: the data byte (0 to 127); | pitch bend: -1 to 1, 0 at the center; | song position: 0 to 16383, in sixteenth notes; | tune request and real-time messages: no value. | . Messages that pass through untransformed have no value. With Into set to Note on, the note-off that ends a produced note gives 0.

1148.title: Midi value shaper
1148.content: Midi value shaper reshapes velocities, controllers, pitch bend or pressure. Its Value outlet gives each shaped value as it is sent, at its time: 0 to 127 for velocities, controllers and pressure, -1 to 1 for pitch bend.

1149.title: Midi sustain
1149.content: Midi sustain holds notes after their key is released, like a sustain pedal: CC 64 of each channel, or the Pedal button, which holds every channel while it is pressed.

1150.title: MIDI Envelope
1150.content: MIDI Envelope turns note-on/off events into control envelopes. Choose staged or drawn shapes, mono/poly voicing and a voice-combination mode, then connect Out to the parameter to animate.

1151.title: MIDI Humanize
1151.content: MIDI Humanize varies note timing, velocity, length and pitch. Chord grouping preserves chord timing, while a nonzero Seed makes a repeatable take. Early timing adds real latency.

1152.title: Entity To MIDI
1152.content: Entity To MIDI maps tracked positions and identities to sustained or triggered notes, including MPE expression. Feed it Point Tracker records when detections are not already in a stable order.

1153.title: Example: using the step sequencer to drive MIDI inputs

1154.title: MIDI communication
1154.content: MIDI communication is provided by two kind of devices, available from the Device explorer: . | MIDI input device can be used to plug a MIDI keyboard to score. | MIDI output device can be used to send MIDI data from score to an external sequencer. | .

1155.title: MIDI processes
1155.content: MIDI processes can write to a specific channel or directly to the root device through addresses. Simply drop either the MIDI node corresponding to the MIDI device, or the channel, to the port you want to connect to. The most important processes are: . | Piano roll | Patternist | MIDI utilities | .

1156.title: MIDI file support
1156.content: . | The Piano roll process supports MIDI files. | . Simply drag’n’drop a MIDI file in the score, either on a scenario or on the interval, from the user library or from your file explorer ! . A MIDI file is placed by its beats: a file of two bars lasts two bars of the score whatever tempo it was saved at, and plays at the tempo of the score.

1157.title: MIDI processing
1157.content: . | See MIDI utilities for a list of processes that can alter MIDI data: arpeggiator, etc. | You can write your custom MIDI processors, for instance with the Javascript or the [[C++ JIT]] process. | . # RTP MIDI / AppleMIDI To access MIDI devices over the network, it is recommended to use a custom RTP MIDI daemon. | On Linux: rtpmidid | On macOS: support is built-in to the operating system. | On Windows: rtpmidi | .

1159.title: MIDI Looper
1159.content: . The process named Looper (MIDI) records the notes, controllers, pitch bend and pressure it receives at in into a loop, and plays them back at out. It shares its transport, timing, undo, capture and timeline features with the audio looper and the value looper; this page describes what is particular to MIDI. The recording keeps its own timing: quantize, transpose and channel changes only apply on playback, and can be changed at any time without losing anything. A take is what the loop plays with the quantize of the moment, but not transposed and on the recorded channels, see Takes and the timeline.

1160.title: Passes and overdubs
1160.content: Each recording or overdub is a pass, kept as a layer of its own. Undo hides the last pass, Redo shows it again, Clear forgets everything; Undo or Clear during a recording starts it again at once, its bars counted from there. Start from is in the Play tab; Follow tempo is in the Speed tab. Overdub mode, in the Overdub tab, chooses what a pass does to the notes of the passes under it: . | Choice | Behavior | . | Merge (default) | Every pass is heard. | . | Replace | A pitch played in a pass silences that pitch in earlier passes, over the part of the loop the pass went through. The rest of the loop is untouched. | . Controllers always replace their own earlier values over the part of the loop a pass went through: a pass that moves CC 74 replaces the earlier CC 74 curve there, and leaves CC 1 and pitch bend alone. Two curves of one controller never fight.

1161.title: Record, Overdub and the Switches tab
1161.content: Mode, the Switches, Layers and Speed tabs and the settings Quantize, After record, After overdub, Start from and Stop at work as for the audio looper: Mode is the state of the looper, Play, Stop, Record and Overdub set it, and Rec / Play / Dub, Play / Stop, New layer, Retrigger and the layer actions do what no value of Mode can. Record on a loop that has something in it overdubs it, as on a looper pedal: Clear the loop first to record a new phrase. See there for what each one does and when it is taken up. |   | What it is for | What it does to the loop | How layers are cut | . | Record | Making a phrase. | Makes the loop: it is as long as the recording, or Record bars bars. On a loop that has something in it, Record overdubs: Clear first to make the phrase again. | The recording is the first layer. | . | Overdub | Playing over the phrase. | Adds what is played, replacing earlier controllers, and notes with Replace, where it goes; with Past the end on Extend, makes the loop longer. | One layer from where it starts to where it stops, made when its first event comes in; with Passes on Per cycle, one each time round that gets something; New layer cuts one where it is pressed. | . | Play, Stop | Listening, or not. | Nothing. | None. | . With After record set to Overdub, or with Overdub on an empty loop, the overdub starts on the very frame the recording ends on. A note held across the end of the recording is one note of the recording, which wraps round the end of the loop to where it was let go; a note played on the first frame of the overdub is the first note of the new layer. An overdub pass becomes a layer when its first note or controller comes in, not when the overdub starts: until then the overdub runs, the playhead going round as it records nothing, but there is no new layer, no lane for it in the view, and Undo still takes out the last layer there is. The layer starts where the overdub began, and goes as far as the overdub went. An overdub that gets nothing writes no take, adds no layer, and merges nothing; with Passes on Per cycle, a round that gets nothing is no layer either. Past Max layers, the room for the new layer (merging the oldest, or setting a muted layer aside) is made when its first event comes in, and Merge into newest merges only a layer there is. Max layers, 2 to 32, default 8, and At max layers, in the Overdub tab, work as for the audio looper: past Max layers, a pass is merged into the newest layer when it ends (the default, which undo can take out again until the next pass), the two oldest layers are merged, or the pass replaces the oldest muted layer, else the newest (which undo puts back, and redo replaces again, until the next pass). Merging moves the notes and controllers of a layer into the other; what either of them replaced stays replaced, muted or erased as the merged layer.

1162.title: The view
1162.content: The view shows one lane per pass, as the audio looper does: up to 32 lanes, sharing the height of the view, the oldest passes sharing the first lane when there are more. A lane is added when a pass gets its first event; until then the header shows the overdub running. Each lane is a small piano roll of its own pass, over the pitches that pass played. Notes a later pass replaced are drawn dimmed.

1163.title: Erasing a pass
1163.content: As with the audio looper, any pass can be erased while the loop plays, with the x of its lane or with Layer and Erase layer, on the grid. Layer is on the newest layer unless it was stepped back. Its notes and controllers go; the passes over it stay where they are, and the loop keeps its length. Erasing the pass being overdubbed is the same as Undo, and erasing the only pass empties the loop. The notes the loop was playing end, as with Undo. What only the erased pass replaced is heard again. What a later pass replaced as well stays replaced: if the second pass and the third both played a C over the C of the first one, erasing or muting the second leaves the first one’s C silent, because the third still replaces it.

1164.title: Notes at the edges of the loop
1164.content: Held notes chooses what a note held across the end of the loop does: Wrap (default) carries it on from the start of the loop, Truncate ends it with the loop. Grace (ms), default 60, is for a note played slightly before a recording or an overdub starts: it is recorded on the first beat instead of being lost. The other way round, a recording asked to stop a little after a grid point, within Late stop (ms), ends on that point; when it gives way to an overdub, the notes played since the point are the overdub’s, where they were played. A note held on the input is never sent twice when the loop plays the same note.

1165.title: Quantize and Note grid
1165.content: Quantize is when a mode change is taken up: a time, a note value, a number of bars, or the loop itself, as for the audio looper. With Loop, a change waits for the loop to come round to its start, wherever that falls in the bar; before there is a loop, it waits for Record bars bars, or one bar when Record bars is 0. The rest of this section is about the notes, not the mode changes. Note grid (default a quarter note, 1/4) and Strength (default 0), in the Note grid tab, pull the notes towards a note value when they are played back. Note grid is a note value only, straight, dotted or triplet: it waits for nothing, and only says where the notes go. At a Strength of 0 the notes play as recorded; at 1 they play on the grid. Note ends pulls the ends of the notes too. A note sounding when one of them changes ends where it was going to: the change applies from its next start, and a note moved to where the playhead has yet to go plays there once it has ended.

1166.title: Notes and channels
1166.content: . | Transpose moves the notes of the loop by semitones. | In channel chooses the channel recorded; 0 records them all. | Out channel plays the loop on one channel; 0 keeps the recorded ones. | Passthrough chooses when the input is heard, as for the audio looper. It is Full by default. | . Changing the transposition or the output channel, stopping, undoing, erasing a pass or clearing ends the notes the loop was playing. Overdubbing an empty loop records it, as with the audio looper.

1167.title: Tempo changes
1167.content: With Follow tempo, on by default, the loop plays at the tempo of the score: a loop recorded over two bars lasts two bars whatever the tempo becomes. Off, it keeps the speed it was recorded at. Either way the quantize grid stays on the loop’s own beats, and its takes have the tempo it was recorded at. Past the end works as for the audio looper: an overdub can make the loop longer, the passes under it repeating.

1168.title: Takes and the timeline
1168.content: When a recording or an overdub ends, what is heard of the loop is written to a Standard MIDI File, at the tempo and in the time signature it was recorded in, and ending exactly at the end of the loop. score places a MIDI file by its beats, so a take of two bars is a clip of two bars whatever its tempo. A click on Send in the looper’s view, or a drag from that button, places it in the timeline as a MIDI clip that holds the notes, where the take was recorded. Dragging a lane drops that layer alone, as a clip in a box of its own, muted or not. A take is a loop wherever it goes: its clip loops at the length of the loop, so that a take of four bars is a box of four bars, and making the box longer plays it round again. Dropped on a box that is already there, the looper’s own box for instance, the clip is as long as that box and plays the loop round over it. A MIDI file dragged from a file browser is not a take, and is not looped. When the take has no file of the layer dragged, it is written when the drag starts, the lane saying Preparing until it is there, as for the audio looper. The file can also be opened in any other MIDI editor. Export chooses what Send, and a drag from its button, place, and the files the take written when a recording or an overdub ends has: what is heard of the whole loop (Mix, the default), each pass in a file of its own (Layers), or both; the files go in one box, a looping clip each, the mix first. A take that Send or a drag asks for, or that the score’s stop leaves, has all of them, so that Export can be changed afterwards, as for the audio looper. A take has the notes where the loop plays them: Note grid, Strength and Note ends are applied to it, and so is Held notes. Transpose and Out channel are not: the notes are at the pitch and on the channel they were played, so that the clip can be transposed or routed again in the timeline. While a recording or an overdub goes on, Send or a drag from it asks for a take of the loop as it is heard at that moment, the pass in progress included, a key still held lasting up to the playhead; the Send button says Saving until it is written, as for the audio looper. When the score stops while a pass is taken in, the pass is closed as any; Mode then shows Play, and playing the score again plays the loop without recording over it. The score’s stop leaves a take with the mix and a file for each layer whenever the last take does not have them all as the loop is, even though the looper is gone by then: the view, saying Stopped with the score, still drags each lane’s layer, and Send still places what Export says, Export being changed once the score is stopped too.

1169.title: Reverse and speed
1169.content: Reverse and Speed, in the Speed tab, work as for the audio looper. | Played backwards, a note plays where it ended: a note over the first quarter of a one-bar loop plays over its last quarter. A note held across the end of the loop wraps or is truncated as it was forwards: truncated, what was heard of it at the end of the loop is heard at its start. A controller, pitch bend or pressure goes back the way it came: going back over a point where it changed, it takes the value it had before, so a sustain pedal held over a part of the loop is held over that part backwards. | Speed plays the loop at x1/4 to x4: at x2, a phrase takes half as long. With Follow tempo, Speed applies on top of the tempo. | . An overdub records where the playhead goes. A phrase played over the reversed loop plays reversed when the loop goes forwards again, its notes starting where they were let go; a phrase played at x1/2 plays twice as fast at x1. A recording is always made forwards at x1. The notes the loop was playing end when it turns round.

1170.title: Comping
1170.content: As for the audio looper, there is no comp mode: overdub, cut the takes into layers with New layer, with Passes on Per cycle (in the Overdub tab) or with After overdub on New layer, then step through them with Previous layer and Next layer, hear one with Solo layer, and keep the best with Mute layer and Erase layer, or the m and x of the lanes. A note held across the start of the loop belongs to the round it started in. Each layer cut is closed like any, and written in a take. A muted layer’s notes and controllers are not heard, and it replaces nothing, so with Replace the notes it replaced are heard again while it is muted, unless another layer replaces them as well. Muted layers are left out of the mix of a take, and still have their own file in a take written as layers. The notes the loop was playing end when a layer is muted or unmuted.

1171.title: Start from In phase
1171.content: Start from set to In phase keeps the loop in phase with the timeline, as for the audio looper. With Follow tempo, on by default, the position is counted in quarter notes, so the loop comes back on its bars after a tempo change.

1172.title: Capture
1172.content: Record starts taking in when it is pressed, or on the next grid point. Capture, in the Length tab next to Capture bars, works backwards: it takes what was already played, recorded or not. You play first, and decide afterwards that it was worth keeping. | With no loop, the last Capture bars bars played become the loop, and it plays at once; Mode shows Play. | Over a loop, what was played over the last round of the loop becomes a new layer on top, as if that round had been an overdub pass: each note lands where it was played in the loop, and the loop keeps its length. Capture bars does not apply, one round is taken. A stopped loop is taken as going round where it would be had it kept playing, as In phase has it, and it plays from there. Max layers and At max layers make room for the layer as for an overdub pass, muted layers stay muted, Overdub mode applies to what it plays over, and a take is written as for any pass that closes. When nothing was played over that round, no layer is made, as for an overdub that gets nothing. | . Undo takes the captured layer out and Redo brings it back, as for any pass. On an empty loop, Undo empties the loop as it does after a first recording. Pressed shortly after a point of the grid, within Late stop, Capture ends on that point, as a late stop would: a note held across that point ends there. Capture does nothing while a recording or an overdub is going on. The MIDI looper always keeps the last 8192 messages it received, so there is nothing to set up; a busy input only lets Capture look back as far as those messages go.

1173.title: Presets
1173.content: As for the audio looper, each preset sets every setting, quantized to the bar unless said otherwise, and what is played is always heard. | Preset | What it is for | . | Song form | Record, Play, Overdub and Play again. Quantize is Loop: the first recording ends on a bar, then every change waits for the loop to come round, and a stop lets it play to its end. | . | One footswitch, song form | The same from Rec / Play / Dub alone, a stop also letting the loop play to its end, with a Late stop of 250 ms. | . | One footswitch, layering | Rec / Play / Dub records, goes straight on overdubbing, and each press after that starts a new layer. | . | Comping, a layer per press | Each press of Rec / Play / Dub while overdubbing starts a new take in a layer of its own; once there are 16, a new take replaces a muted one; takes are written as a mix and as layers. | . | Comping, a layer per round | One overdub, a layer each time round the loop; takes are written as a mix and as layers. | . | Four bars, then play | A recording of four bars, then plays it. | . | Four bars, then overdub | A recording of four bars, then goes on overdubbing: a chord held across the end of the loop is not cut. | . | Free loop | No grid, no Record bars, no Late stop: the loop is as long as it was played for. | . | Overdub drums | Two bars, then overdubbing; notes end with the loop. | . | Drum pattern on channel 10 | Records channel 10 only, two bars then overdubbing; a hit replaces the hits of that pitch under it, notes end with the loop, and play back on the sixteenth. | . | Replace as you play | Four bars, then overdubbing, a layer each time round the loop: a pitch played replaces that pitch in the rounds before it, so each round played over replaces the one before. | . | Sixteenths, 70 percent | Notes pulled 70 percent of the way to the sixteenth on playback; mode changes on the quarter note. | . | Octave up | The loop plays an octave above what was played. | . | Half speed | The loop plays twice as slow; what is overdubbed plays twice as fast at x1. | . | Grows as you overdub | A bar long recording, and Past the end on Extend: overdubbing over several bars makes the loop that long. | . | In phase with the timeline | Start from In phase: a loop played again after a stop, or when the score starts or jumps, is where it would be had it kept playing. | . | Takes for editing | Export on Both: takes are written as a mix and as a MIDI file for each layer. | .

1174.title: Older scores
1174.content: A score or a preset made with an older MIDI looper loads with the settings it had, as for the audio looper: Loop is now Mode, Quantif is now Quantize, Bars is now Record bars, and Sync is gone. The settings of the notes have new names as well: . | Grid is now Note grid. Its list of note values gives the same note value; its None did what a Strength of 0 does, and gives the default note value, a quarter. | Quantize, the strength, is now Strength, with the same value. The control now named Quantize is the grid of the mode changes, which was Quantif. | Quantize ends is now Note ends. | . Record on a loop that has something in it now overdubs it, and stopping the score during a recording or an overdub leaves Mode on Play, as for the audio looper.

1175.title: Capacity
1175.content: A loop holds up to 4096 notes and 8192 controller values. When it is full, the view says so and further events are not recorded.

1177.title: MIDI input device
1177.content: To receive MIDI, select MIDI Input in the Protocols column of the Add device window. In the Devices column, select the desired input. The list separates hardware, software and network inputs and includes Default MIDI In. The default selector resolves to the first available input reported by the backend; it is not a guarantee that a particular keyboard will be selected. Choose a named port for a performance setup. Optionally, you can set a custom name (or use the default one). On platform that support it (macOS and Linux), you can create a virtual MIDI device.

1178.title: Create whole tree option
1178.content: The Create whole tree setting creates the complete MIDI namespace where available. In the current input settings widget this checkbox is disabled for editing; use Learn to build the namespace interactively. A whole-tree namespace uses addresses of the following form: . <device name>/<channel number>/<message type>/message number> . Should you want not to automatically create a whole Midi namespace (i.e. and use Midi learn instead), just leave the option unset.

1179.title: Use Midi learn
1179.content: You can use the learn function to build your Midi input namespace with only the needed Midi message (rather than setting up the whole Midi namespace). To do so, once added the Midi device with the Create whole tree option off, in the Device explorer, right-click on your Midi input device name and select Learn from the contextual menu. This opens score Midi learn window. From then, score will monitor any incoming Midi message and store it under an address following the pattern mentioned above. When you are done sending the needed Midi message, click Done on the Midi learn window. All received Midi messages should now appear under your Midi input device name in the Device explorer.

1180.title: Note-on with zero velocity
1180.content: Velocity = 0 -> Note Off interprets incoming zero-velocity note-on messages as note-offs. It is off by default in newly created settings. Enable it for a controller that uses this MIDI convention, particularly when driving note-lifetime tracking. This is an input policy, separate from the output device’s inverse conversion and the MIDI Filter controls.

1181.title: Reopening on another machine
1181.content: Saved MIDI ports are matched against available ports when reopening a document, including name-based recovery when backend identifiers change. A missing backend or device can still leave the connection unavailable: edit the device and select the actual input instead of assuming the saved mapping is portable. For named controls from a manufacturer/model description, use MIDI Controller rather than this raw MIDI Input protocol. Device maps describe controls; they do not install a driver or make an absent hardware port available.

1182.title: MIDI output device
1182.content: To send MIDI, select MIDI Output in the Protocols column of the Add device window. In the Devices column, select the desired output. The list groups hardware, software and network outputs and offers Default MIDI Out. The default selector chooses the first available output reported by the backend, not a guaranteed synthesizer. Select a named port when the destination matters. Optionally, you can set a custom name (or use the default one). On platform that support it (macOS and Linux), you can create a virtual MIDI device.

1183.title: Routing and note-off policy
1183.content: Assign the device to the MIDI outlet of a Piano roll, sequencer or MIDI process. The Create whole tree option exposes channel/message addresses when individual messages need to be sent from states or controls. Note Off -> Velocity = 0 sends note-offs as zero-velocity note-on messages. It is off by default in newly created settings. Enable it only when the receiving device expects that representation; it is independent of the input device’s Velocity = 0 -> Note Off option. When moving a document between machines or MIDI backends, score attempts to match the saved port against available ports. Check and, if necessary, edit the selected output before playback: device names and installed backends may differ. MIDI Controller is the separate protocol for manufacturer/model device maps with named controls. Raw MIDI Output remains appropriate for note streams and devices without a description.

1184.title: Minuit device
1184.content: . Connect to other creative coding applications and automatically discover their parameter trees. Minuit enables rich bidirectional communication between score and other software, sharing not just values but complete parameter hierarchies with metadata like types, ranges, and descriptions. Perfect for collaborative setups, distributed installations, or any project where multiple applications need to share parameter data seamlessly. Note that Minuit has been superseded by OSCQuery.

1185.title: Setting up a Minuit device
1185.content: . | Add device in the Device explorer and choose “Minuit” | Configure network settings - set host IP and ports for communication | Set device name - choose a unique identifier for this score instance | Connect to remote - the device automatically discovers the remote parameter tree | Monitor synchronization - watch as remote parameters appear in your device explorer | . Both applications need to support the Minuit protocol for full bidirectional communication.

1186.title: How Minuit works
1186.content: Minuit builds on OSC and adds automatic device-tree discovery and metadata exchange. Tree discovery - Applications broadcast their parameter hierarchies Metadata exchange - Share parameter types, ranges, units, and descriptions Real-time sync - Changes in one application instantly appear in others Bidirectional control - Both applications can control each other’s parameters .

1187.title: Network configuration
1187.content: Host address: IP address of the remote application (use 127.0.0.1 for same computer) . Remote port: Port where the remote application receives data (default 9998) . Local port: Port where score listens for incoming data (default 13579) . Device name: Unique identifier for this score instance (default “score”) . Rate limiting: Optional throttling to prevent network flooding during rapid parameter changes .

1188.title: Automatic discovery features
1188.content: Zeroconf integration: Minuit devices can automatically discover each other on the network without manual configuration. Dynamic tree updates: When the remote application adds or removes parameters, your score device tree updates automatically. Metadata synchronization: Parameter types, value ranges, units, and descriptions sync automatically from the remote application. Connection monitoring: The device detects when remote applications connect or disconnect.

1189.title: Parameter types and metadata
1189.content: Minuit handles rich parameter information beyond simple values: . Data types: Integers, floats, strings, booleans, vectors, and complex data structures . Value ranges: Minimum and maximum bounds with different clipping behaviors (clamp, wrap, fold) . Units and dataspaces: Physical units like frequencies, distances, colors with automatic conversion . Descriptions: Human-readable parameter descriptions for better interface understanding . Access modes: Parameters can be read-only, write-only, or bidirectional based on their function .

1190.title: Creative applications
1190.content: Multi-app performances: Connect score with Max/MSP, Pure Data, TouchDesigner, or other creative tools for complex multi-system performances. Collaborative composition: Multiple composers can work with the same parameter set simultaneously, seeing each other’s changes in real-time. Distributed installations: Spread an installation across multiple computers while maintaining centralized parameter control. Educational environments: Students can connect their projects to shared parameter spaces for collaborative learning experiences. Cross-platform integration: Bridge different creative coding environments regardless of their native parameter systems.

1191.title: Integration advantages
1191.content: Automatic setup: No need to manually create parameter addresses or configure complex routing - Minuit handles discovery automatically. Rich metadata: Unlike plain OSC, Minuit exchanges parameter types, ranges and descriptions. Bidirectional control: Both applications can control each other’s parameters, enabling true collaborative workflows. Network resilience: Built-in error handling and reconnection logic keeps distributed systems running smoothly.

1192.title: Advanced features
1192.content: Listen subscriptions: Subscribe only to parameters you actually need to reduce network traffic and improve performance. Tree exploration: Explore large parameter trees efficiently with asynchronous discovery and lazy loading. Connection management: Robust handling of network disconnections, timeouts, and reconnections. Multi-device support: Connect to multiple Minuit-enabled applications simultaneously for complex distributed setups.

1193.title: Integration with score
1193.content: Minuit devices appear in the Device explorer just like any other device, but with automatic parameter discovery. Parameter mapping: Use discovered parameters with Mapping Tool or Automation just like local parameters. Real-time control: Control remote application parameters in real-time during performances. State management: Parameter values and ranges are preserved in score projects for consistent setups.

1194.title: Troubleshooting
1194.content: Discovery failures: Check that both applications are on the same network and using compatible Minuit protocol versions. Port conflicts: Ensure the specified ports aren’t used by other applications - try different port numbers if connections fail. Firewall issues: Network firewalls may block UDP communication - configure firewall rules to allow Minuit traffic. Network latency: High network latency can affect real-time parameter control - use local networks for best performance.

1195.title: Mixing busses
1195.content: Intervals can become mixing busses for all their child process. To use that feature, mark an interval as a bus in its inspector. The Audio panel then allows to change its volume / pan. Things with more than 2 channels will be available once we figure a proper UI for it - designers welcome as the code already supports it ! .

1199.title: Model Display
1199.content: Model Display is the quick renderer for geometry ports. Connect geometry from Object loader, a primitive generator, Structure Synth, Compute Shaders or a geometry filter, optionally connect a texture, and render the result to a texture output. Native scenes from Asset Loader first need Scene Preprocessor; Model Display does not implement the complete imported scene material/lighting workflow. Use Render Pipeline instead when you need custom vertex / fragment shaders, custom raster state, scene auxiliary buffers, cubemaps, multiview, or advanced material logic.

1206.title: Modular workflow
1206.content: ossia score is built upon an entirely modular foundation. At any point during edition, it is possible to switch from the temporal view, to the modular view, in order to patch processes together as easily as possible. The mode switching is operated by the buttons at the bottom of the software: . Some processes will always appear in patch view: audio effects, generators, and more generally any process for which the effect does not depend on time-relative data. Here is a small score viewed in temporal mode (the default): . Here is the same score viewed in modular mode: . It is also possible to disable the cables when the patching has been done and one wants to focus on the controls, the automations, etc: . This functionality is accessible through Alt+Shift+G.

1207.title: Interactions
1207.content: Outside of simply drag’n’dropping or double-clicking from the process library, there are multiple interactions available to add a process directly at a specific position in the data flow.

1208.title: Adding a process in the middle of a cable
1208.content: If a cable is selected, and one doubles-clicks in the process library, the object is if possible inserted in the middle of the cable.

1209.title: Adding a process before a specific port
1209.content: If an input port or control is selected, and one doubles-clicks on a process in the process library, if the process’s first output is compatible with the port’s type then the process will be connected before the port. If there is an address in the port, it will be moved to the first input port of the newly-created process. Likewise for the “Propagate” attribute on audio ports. For instance, if a score contains an LFO object, with the address foo:/bar assigned to the LFO amplitude, and one selects the amplitude port and doubles-clicks on the Micromap object in the process library, the Micromap’s input will be set to foo:/bar, a cable will be created from the Micromap’s output to the LFO’s amplitude and the LFO’s amplitude won’t have the foo:/bar address set anymore.

1210.title: Adding a process after a specific port
1210.content: The same than above applies for output ports.

1211.title: Adding a process after another
1211.content: If an entire process is selected in the score, and one doubles-clicks on a new process to add in the library, score will try to connect to the first port. This is useful for instance when creating audio or video effect chains as one can quickly connect new effects as they always have an audio or video input and output as first port by convention. To make this workflow even faster, when a new process is created, it is selected, meaning that one does not even have to go to the score to add new objects.

1212.title: Device Modulation
1212.content: Give a parameter a repeating pulse, a stepped phrase or an irregular drift without drawing every change by hand. The score only displays the values; connect one to a sound, a light or another application to use it.

1213.title: Choose the motion and its delivery
1213.content: LFOs provide periodic movement, step sequences repeat a set of levels, and noise expressions produce less predictable variation. Interactive ends let you stay with one source, then cue the next. Two displays show the same source through a direct cable and through an OSC device parameter. A cable carries individual emissions; the address-bound display reads the parameter’s stored value each tick. The difference is easiest to see when a source sends values only occasionally. Use the parameter when a destination needs a continuous current value instead of isolated updates.

1214.title: Try it
1214.content: . | Start playback and watch the displays during LFO. Change the rate or waveform of each source: a sine gives a smooth cycle, a square an abrupt pulse. | Trigger the LFO interval’s end to reach Step. Edit a few values in both step sequences, keeping them alike, then watch what each display does between emissions. | Trigger again to reach Math expression and vary the noise parameters. The two noise generators have slightly different saved settings, so their curves do not match. | Trigger the expression interval’s end to return to LFO. The saved example only visualizes data and makes no sound. | . Keep Display running while switching sections; it has its own end trigger. No media files or external receiver are needed. To try the OSC output in another application, configure its receiver for UDP port 9996 on the same computer. The saved device listens on port 9997 and sends /some_address to 127.0.0.1:9996. Change the destination host and port for another computer, and allow the connection through any firewall. The internal displays do not require a network round trip. Download this example . Try this on web .

1217.title: How to monitor messages ?
1217.content: With Logging option activated in score preferences, you can for example check messages coming in and out of a selected process in the Messages log panel (Ctrl+Shift+G(Win / Linux) or⌘+Shift+G(Mac)) .

1219.doc: Monitoring values, MIDI, audio and textures
1219.title: Monitoring values, MIDI, audio and textures
1219.content: . When a patch does not produce the expected sound or image, look at the signal before changing the artwork. This score places displays beside generated signals so you can distinguish a missing event, an unexpected range and a value interpreted in the wrong way.

1220.doc: Monitoring values, MIDI, audio and textures
1220.title: Overview
1220.content: A meter answers “how strong is the sound?”, a plot answers “how does this value move?”, and a point view answers “where does this pair of values place something?”. The LED and texture previews make color and image data visible. These are observation tools you can reuse inside a performance patch, not additional media outputs to compose.

1221.doc: Monitoring values, MIDI, audio and textures
1221.title: Try it
1221.content: Start playback in nodal view. No physical controller, sound file or network destination is needed. | Watch the MIDI note display next to the converted MIDI values, then the synth’s VU meter and plotted RMS envelope: a note event is instantaneous, while the resulting sound level rises and decays. The saved audio branch is not routed to speakers. | Change an automation in the scalar, list or 2D examples. The same change appears as a curve or a moving point. | Look at RGB01 and Lightness01 in the LED Views. One groups components into colors; the other treats them as separate intensities. An unexpected preview may be an interpretation problem, not bad input. | Press Bang, then hold Button. Pulse View shows a single impulse for Bang and repeated messages for the held Button. | Inspect the generated LED patterns and shader texture preview. Use the previews to check the result before adapting these signals to physical lights or a projection. | . Synthimi is required for the audio-analysis branch. The texture preview uses the default library’s GLSL_shaders/sophia-digital-art/colors.fs shader and score’s native graphics processing; no separate Window device is needed. Download this example . Try this on web .

1222.title: Sequencing audio effects
1222.content: . A repeating drum part moves from clear attacks to crushed, echoing and distorted versions of itself. The rhythm stays in place while its treatment changes.

1223.title: One interval per effect
1223.content: The drum generator runs across the piece, but each effect lives in its own interval. As the timeline activates successive intervals, the same source receives a different treatment, without any change to the drum part. After the final section, playback returns to the ring-modulation section and repeats the last two treatments. The drum source has its own interactive end, so the score is not a fixed-length export.

1224.title: Listen and edit
1224.content: Use a build with Kaboom, BarrVerb and Airwindows. No samples or external device are required. Configure audio output and start at a low volume. | Watch the active effect interval while listening. Which treatments leave the drum attacks recognizable, and which turn the pattern into a texture? | Lower Bitcrush’s Rate to change the grain of the sound, or cautiously vary Echo’s Feedback to change how much one hit spills into the next. The opening section is unprocessed, for reference. | Move an interval boundary. The same effect can feel like an accent or a sustained section depending on when it arrives and how long it lasts. | Trigger the end of Drums to stop the source, or stop the transport to finish. Its drawn 68-second endpoint does not fire automatically. | . Download this example . Try this on web .

1225.title: MQTT Device
1225.content: . MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport) is a lightweight messaging protocol designed for IoT and embedded systems. ossia score’s MQTT device enables seamless integration with IoT ecosystems, smart home systems, and industrial automation networks.

1226.title: Overview
1226.content: MQTT support in score enables: . | Publish/subscribe messaging patterns for distributed systems | IoT device integration with smart home and industrial networks | Cloud service communication (AWS IoT, Google Cloud IoT, Azure IoT) | Low-bandwidth, high-reliability messaging for resource-constrained devices | Real-time data collection from sensor networks | .

1227.title: Supported Transports
1227.content: TCP (Default) . | Standard MQTT over TCP (port 1883, or 8883 for TLS) | Reliable, ordered message delivery | Most common deployment method | . WebSocket . | MQTT over WebSocket protocol | Browser compatibility and firewall-friendly | Useful for web-based integrations and cloud services | .

1228.title: Device Setup
1228.content: Basic Configuration . | Add MQTT Device: Right-click Device Explorer → Add Device → MQTT | Configure Connection: . | Host: MQTT broker address (e.g., mqtt.broker.com or 127.0.0.1) | Port: Broker port (1883 for TCP, 8080 for WebSocket) | Transport: Select TCP or WebSocket | Client ID: Unique identifier (auto-generated if empty) | . | . Authentication & Security . | Parameter | Description | Example | . | Username | MQTT username | user123 | . | Password | MQTT password | secret456 | . | Keep Alive | Heartbeat interval (seconds) | 60 | . | Clean Session | Start with clean state | Enabled | . | Use TLS | Enable encryption | For secure connections | .

1229.title: Topic Structure & Discovery
1229.content: MQTT uses hierarchical topics separated by forward slashes. Unlike OSC, MQTT has no automatic discovery mechanism - you must use the “Learn” feature or create topics manually. Topic Patterns & Wildcards . | Single level wildcard (+): home/+/temperature matches home/kitchen/temperature | Multi-level wildcard (#): sensors/# matches all topics under sensors/ | Examples: . | home/livingroom/lights/brightness | industrial/sensor01/pressure/value | score/performance/cue_state | . | .

1230.title: Usage Examples
1230.content: Smart Home Integration . Control smart home devices from score: . [Score Automation] → [MQTT: home/lights/living_room] → [Smart Bulb] [Sensor Input] → [MQTT: home/thermostat/target] → [HVAC System] . IoT Sensor Networks . Collect data from distributed sensors: . [MQTT: sensors/+/temperature] → [Score Processing] → [Visualization] [MQTT: sensors/+/humidity] → [Data Analysis] → [Environmental Control] . Cloud IoT Platforms . Connect to major cloud services: . AWS IoT Core . Host: your-endpoint.iot.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Port: 8883 (TLS required) Topics: $aws/things/device-name/shadow/update . Google Cloud IoT . Host: mqtt.googleapis.com Port: 8883 (TLS required) Topics: /devices/device-id/events .

1231.title: Getting Started Example
1231.content: To try MQTT locally, use Mosquitto: . 1. Start MQTT Broker . $ mosquitto . 2. Test with Command Line Tools . Publish test data: . $ mosquitto_pub -t /sensors/temperature -m 23.5 -h 127.0.0.1 . Subscribe to responses: . $ mosquitto_sub -t /controls/# -h 127.0.0.1 . 3. Configure in ossia score . | Add MQTT Device with host 127.0.0.1, port 1883 | Use “Learn” feature to discover /sensors/temperature topic | Add child node to send to /controls/lighting topic | Test bi-directional communication | .

1232.title: Important Considerations
1232.content: Loop Prevention . Warning: Many MQTT brokers cannot handle loops (publishing and subscribing to the same topic). Unlike OSC, avoid creating feedback loops between publish and subscribe on identical topics. Message Persistence . | Use retained messages for state information | Configure QoS levels based on reliability needs: . | QoS 0: At most once (fire and forget) | QoS 1: At least once (acknowledged) | QoS 2: Exactly once (guaranteed) | . | . Performance Tips . | Batch updates for high-frequency data | Use appropriate keep-alive intervals (60-300 seconds) | Organize topics hierarchically for efficient wildcards | Consider message size limits (typically 256KB max) | .

1233.title: Related Documentation
1233.content: . | OSC Device - Alternative real-time protocol | HTTP Device - REST API communication | WebSocket Device - Real-time web communication | Serial Device - Direct hardware communication | .

1234.title: Multi-choice
1234.content: Multi-choice chooses among numeric inputs after smoothing, useful for selecting a gesture or classification result without immediately reacting to every fluctuation. Input count creates the In ports. Smooth sets the smoothing coefficient: smaller values respond more slowly. A winner must exceed Threshold, and exceed the runner-up by more than Margin. Output index is zero-based and announces a newly accepted winner. An ambiguous frame clears the accepted choice internally and sends no index; it does not send a special “none” number. Current Weights provides the smoothed values for monitoring. Connect Current Weights to LED View while tuning Threshold and Margin. For an immediate minimum/maximum and softmax probabilities from one array, use Array Best Match in Array utilities.

1235.title: Multi-Cursor Manager (X-Y point arrays)
1235.content: The Multi-Cursor manager is a process for generating an array of XY points in 2D space by modifying their position, adding new ones and deleting others.

1236.title: Modifying points.
1236.content: . | Points can be dragged with the mouse. | To create a new point, click on an empty space. | To delete a point, right-click on it. | .

1238.title: Multiple shader render targets
1238.content: . Watch a generated 3D form as an image, a surface-like normal view and a set of edges. A four-view grid shows them next to the original image.

1239.title: Render targets
1239.content: A textured generative mesh is rendered to an image. A shader then produces color, image-derived normals and detected edges in a single pass, displayed alongside the original. The normal view estimates changes from the image; it does not expose the original mesh’s geometric normals.

1240.title: Try it
1240.content: . | Start playback and watch the four views as Structure Synth periodically regenerates the mesh: each regeneration shows up in all four at once. | Change normalStrength in mrt-gbuffer to alter the image-derived normal view without changing the mesh. | Raise edgeThreshold to keep only sparse outlines, or lower it until texture features become edges as well as the object’s silhouette. | . The mesh, texture and shaders are generated in the score. Rendering uses native Model Display and ISF multiple render targets, with no external model or Qt Quick 3D scene required. Try this on web . Download this example .

1241.title: Musical metrics
1241.content: Processes and elements of a score can be quantized on musical metrics, and have independent tempo curves, & time signatures. Musical metrics are propagated hierarchically: . | The tempo, and musical position in an interval is either relative to this interval (if the 4/4 button in the inspector is pressed) or it’s taking the musical information from its closest parent (recursively). | Processes take the quantization and metrics information from their parent. | . This means that polyrhythmic scores are possible: the root can be in 4/4 with a child interval in 3/4, 7/8. At interval level, the musical controls are time signatures, tempo curves and quantization. Individual processes can also expose their own timing controls.

1242.title: Musical signatures
1242.content: They are set on intervals and are used to delimit the start and end of bars, for quantization purposes. To change the musical signatures, go into an interval in full view and mark the interval as having its own metrics in the inspector if it does not already have some.

1243.title: Quantization
1243.content: The quantization setting on an interval allows to say at which musical interval child elements will be triggered if they rely on hierarchy for synchronization. For instance, if the quantization setting is set at one bar, it means that the event will be processed at the start of the next bar. Most places that can be quantized thus have a choice of quantization intervals (bars, quarter notes, …), plus the Parent (uses the parent quantization setting, recursively) and Free (no quantization, things start directly) settings.

1244.title: Tempo
1244.content: Likewise, by default the tempo is the global one. Intervals support tempo curves, which can give them a different speed behaviour. The interval’s children will all take this tempo unless another more precise tempo is given at a deeper nesting level by adding a tempo process to the interval.

1245.title: Usage
1245.content: . | Processes which use tempo and metrics information (audio plug-ins, LFO, arpeggiator, etc.) receive that information from their interval. Whether a particular parameter follows tempo depends on its synchronization mode. | Triggers and intervals can be quantified to fall on the next quantification date from when they are triggered. | .

1246.title: Process durations and the time chooser
1246.content: Processes use the Time Chooser for parameters that can be free durations or musical note values. Click the readout beneath the knob to cycle free → straight → dotted → triplet. Free durations do not follow tempo; note values do. This control is distinct from an interval’s Parent or Free quantization setting: . | Kind of timing | Example | What is synchronized? | . | Event quantization | Trigger quantized to a bar | When an event is allowed to happen. | . | Process grid | Free Metronome, Midi Quantify | Impulses or note starts are placed on a process’s selected grid. | . | Stage duration | ADSR Attack or Release | How long a stage takes after it starts; the trigger itself is not moved onto a beat. | . | Cycle duration | LFO Period | How long an oscillation takes. Enable Lock to bars for synchronized cycles aligned to musical position. | . | Quiet-time duration | Rate Limiter in Debounce mode | How long to wait after the last input; even a synchronized duration does not make its output grid-aligned. | . Note fractions refer to a whole note, not the current bar. 1/4 is a quarter note and 1/1 is four quarter notes. Thus 1/1 matches a bar in 4/4 but not a bar in 3/4. At 120 BPM a quarter note lasts 0.5 seconds; changing tempo changes synchronized durations accordingly. For a rhythmic control pattern, give the parent interval its intended metrics, select 1/8 on Free Metronome’s Period, and connect its output to ADSR’s Trigger. The metronome determines the grid; ADSR’s Attack and Decay determine the shape and length after each trigger. Older saved variants may still expose a frequency, millisecond or quantification selector instead of a time chooser. They remain distinct process types, not an automatic migration to the newer controls. Consult each process page before transferring settings.

1247.title: GPU particle forces
1247.content: . A cloud of particles swirls and gathers under competing forces. You set the forces, not the path of each point. RandomScatter initializes 1,024 particles. Vortex, basic and gravitational forces contribute to their motion, then Integrate updates the simulation over time. The resulting points are converted to sphere splats for native rendering, not Qt Quick 3D.

1248.title: Try it
1248.content: Start playback and lower Integrate’s timeScale to inspect the motion. Raise vortex strength to make the cloud swirl, then raise gravitationalConstant to pull it into clumps. Increase drag to damp the motion. RandomScatter has once enabled: changing a force during playback is not the same as initializing a different cloud. This is a visual simulation, not a reference scientific integrator. It requires compute-shader support but no external particle data or model. Try this on web . Download this example .

1249.title: NDI
1249.content: NDI is a network protocol for sharing video frames across applications. It requires the NDI add-on and an available NDI runtime. The device supports several raw RGB/YUV receive and send formats; the runtime, source and receiver determine which are usable. NDI HX additionally depends on the appropriate HX decoding runtime.

1250.title: NDI input device
1250.content: This device allows receiving a video stream directly from a NDI-compatible input. Choose the wanted Source, use the input dialog’s Preview, and assign the device to a texture inlet. Route the receiving process to a window or other texture output. Color space selects the assumed conversion matrix. An NDI received frame does not reliably communicate the matrix used by the sender, so match both ends when colors disagree. Receive format offers 8-bit (SDK de-interlaces) and Best available (16-bit, fields). The latter can receive 16-bit sources (including P216 and alpha-bearing PA16), but interlaced sources may then arrive as individual fields. Deinterlace chooses Weave (more vertical detail, possible motion combing) or Bob (less vertical detail, smooth field-rate motion). It applies to separate fields, not already-woven full frames.

1251.title: NDI output device
1251.content: This device allows to create a NDI stream that other NDI-compatible software will be able to display or modify. Choose the output name, width, height, rate, Format and Color space, then assign the device as the destination of the final texture outlet. The format choices include RGBA, RGBX, BGRA, BGRX, UYVY, P216, NV12, I420 and YV12. Use RGBA or BGRA when sending transparency; RGBX/BGRX and the listed YUV output formats do not carry alpha. Receiving alpha-bearing formats and choosing an alpha-preserving output are distinct requirements. The downstream application must also retain/composite alpha. NDI video availability does not imply audio routing through these texture ports. Test the complete sender/receiver chain, including range and matrix choices. See Video formats and color.

1252.title: PTZ support
1252.content: A camera exposing PTZ controls will be able to get controlled by ossia. The following parameters are available if the camera provides access to them: . /ptz/zoom (float) /ptz/pan (float) /ptz/tilt (float) /ptz/pan/speed (float) /ptz/tilt/speed (float) /ptz/preset/store (int) /ptz/preset/recall (int) /ptz/focus/auto (impulse) /ptz/focus/manual (float) /ptz/focus/speed (float) /ptz/wb/auto (impulse) /ptz/wb/indoor (impulse) /ptz/wb/outdoor (impulse) /ptz/wb/oneshot (impulse) /ptz/wb/manual (rgb) /ptz/exposure/auto (impulse) /ptz/exposure/manual (float) .

1254.title: Nodes

1255.title: Usage
