1398.title: Processes
1398.content: score processes generate, transform and route control values, audio, MIDI, images and 3D data. Place them on intervals for continuous processing, or on states for instantaneous actions.

1399.title: Find a process
1399.content: The reference pages below are grouped by task. Some cover a family of processes. Optional add-ons and platform requirements are listed on the individual pages. | Task | Starting points | . | Timeline and parameter control | Scenario, Automation, Mapping, LFO, Tempo | . | Audio and MIDI | Sound files, Audio effects, Audio utilities, Audio plug-ins, MIDI utilities | . | Video and images | Video, Images, ISF shaders, Text, Sprite Reader | . | Native 3D and GPU processing | Geometry Loader (Object Loader reference), Asset Loader, Model Display, Render Pipeline, Compute Shaders | . | Data and routing | Array utilities, Control utilities, Mapping utilities, Value Filter | . | Scripting and synthesis | JavaScript / QML, Expressions, Faust, Pure Data, C++ JIT | . For video capture, streaming and display outputs, start with Devices. The supported protocols and formats page distinguishes file support from platform-dependent device backends. Timing, routing and utility tools . | Generate and reshape musical events: Free Metronome, Arpeggiator and Midi Quantify. | Choose when values leave a patch: Buffer queue, Value delay, Rendezvous, Switch and Multi-choice. | Convert and parse data: Regex, String / byte conversion, Value serialization and Array utilities. | Record or annotate: Audio recorder, CSV recorder and Text Box. Text Box is a document annotation; use Text to generate an image. | Store and select data: Tables provide editable data tables; availability depends on the compiler/build. | Accumulate statistics: Accumulator provides running statistics with selectable output timing. | Turn observations into music: Point Tracker, Beat Tracker and Entity To MIDI. | Shape MIDI expression: MIDI Envelope and MIDI Humanize. | Follow an external time position: Timecode Synchronizer. | Send or decode synchronization: MIDI Sync Out and MIDI Sync In. | Decode audio timecode: LTC Input and XWax DVS; generate it with LTC Generator. These require the optional LTC add-on. | Describe sensor gestures: Puara Gestures covers Leaky Integrator, Roll, Tilt and Shake. | Inspect signals: MIDI display, VU Meter and Signal display. | Run external tools: Shell command and Process Launcher. | . Native scenes and graphics . Use Scene tools to select and organize imported scenes, Scene animation to drive them over time, and Scene Preprocessor to prepare them for GPU rendering. This native scene path is distinct from QtQuick3D hosted inside a JavaScript / QML process. Continue with Instancing and materials, Cameras and lighting, and Environments and cubemaps for scene composition. For procedural content and data conversion, see Mesh generators and splats, 3D text, and Geometry and buffer utilities. For choosing media decoding, pixel formats, color conversion and HDR output, see Video formats and color. Sink runs an upstream graphics chain at a chosen rate without displaying its image, useful when only a data result is needed. Optional synthesis and image generation . Synthimi is a MIDI-driven synthesizer provided by an optional add-on. StreamDiffusion / LibreDiffusion provides image generation; its reference includes runtime setup and engine-building instructions.

1400.title: General description
1400.content: score allows to handle a number of actions evolving either through some amount of time, or at a single instant. These processes can either be actions evolving during a given duration, such as automation of a given device’s parameter, or actions activated only in a defined duration, such as mapping or LFO modulations. Processes are attached to an interval in the scenario when they represent an evolving behaviour, and to a state when they are instantaneous.

1402.title: Create processes on intervals
1402.content: Using drag & drop . From the Device explorer . Processes can be created by drag & dropping parameters from the Device explorer onto an existing interval in the scenario. The interval to which processes will be attached turns to yellow as the mouse with selection hovers it. The Device explorer selection may contain one or several parameters. When multiple parameters are dropped, processes get stacked in different layers. From the libraries . Processes can also be created by drag & dropping the desired process from the Process library or the User library in the scenario. When doing so, score automatically creates the interval to which process will get attached. You may as well drop a process onto an existing interval. Note that both namespace selection and processes selection can be dropped onto an interval to which some processes are already attached. Depending on the type of processes, these may be created on top of processes already in place or at a slot below. Audio, video and script files (Faust DSP, GLSL fragment shader, JS script…) can also be drag’n’dropped inside a scenario from your desktop’s file manager. By default, dropping several processes at the same time stacks them in the same interval. Holding the Maj key while dropping will create sequential intervals for each item in the selection. If a process is currently selected in the score, it is also possible to create a new process afterwards by double-clicking on it in the library. This will only work if the processes are compatible: the first output port of the selected process must be of the same type than the first input port of the process double-clicked in the library. A connection between the two ports will automatically be made. This allows to easily chain effects: . Likewise, if an output port is currently selected in the score, double-clicking on a process in the list will create and connect it afterwards if compatible.

1403.title: Create processes on a state
1403.content: Adding processes on a state is a way to run a computation at a single, precise point in the timeline. The processes will not be directly visible in the timeline ; the state has to be selected to edit their properties through the inspector. It is done by right-clicking on the state in the object inspector, and selecting the Add process option.

1404.title: Remove existing processes
1404.content: Using keyboard . To remove a process, select it (for example by clicking on the slot background) and choose Remove from the Object menu (Suppr/Backspace key). Make sure the process you want to remove is properly selected when bringing it to front (for example, check the inspector) ! . From Graph inspector . Processes can also be deleted from the Graph inspector at the top of score’s right panel. In the scenario, select the interval the process to remove is attached to. In the Graph inspector, browse through the attached processes and select the one to remove. Right-click to open the contextual menu and choose Remove (or use Suppr/Backspace key).

1406.title: Fullsize edit
1406.content: Processes can be edited in full size. This is especially handy when you want to precisely edit a process such as an automation or mapping function. To display the process in full size, double-click on the interval the process is attached to. Process is now displayed using score central panel full width. Note that if several processes are attached to an interval, open them in full size will display all at once juxtaposed as shown below (see the Multiple processes interval). To exit full size mode (go back to parent scenario), click the desired node of the path displayed at the top or use the Ctrl+Alt+↑(Win / Linux) or⌘+Alt+↑(Mac) shortcut.

1407.title: Process Loops
1407.content: Time-based processes such as automations, media and sub-scenarios can be looped for as long as their parent interval is active. When selecting a process, either from the object panel or by clicking on process header, the loop option will appear in the Inspector.

1409.title: Fold/unfold attached processes
1409.content: Processes attached to an interval can easily be fold/unfold. This comes up especially usefull when working with a lot of processes while still maintaining some screen space and the scenario readable. To do so, click the blue arrow on top of the processes to fold/unfold. When selecting an interval, attached processes can also be fold/unfold using the Show processes & Hide processes entries from the Object menu.

1410.title: Stacked slots
1410.content: Time-based processes (that is, processes whose x represents time, such as automations, media files) can be stacked on a same slot. This is the default presentation when dragging some parameters onto an interval or dragging a process from library onto an interval. In that case, top-most process is displayed in full color while processes in other layers or displayed in semi transparent color. You can of course re-arrange them as you want. Bring to front . To change which process to display top-most, mouse over to the top of the process slot displaying the destination address. Clicking the address bar opens up a contextual menu listing all layered processes. Selecting one in the menu brings it to front. Move to new slot . Processes can also be juxtaposed in several slots rather than stacked on top of the other. Grab the handle at the top left corner of the slot and drag & drop it on another slot to move it above another process or between different slots to insert it. Processes can also be dragged & attached to a new interval .

1411.title: Project files
1411.content: File → Project files provides commands for managing files referenced by the open document. Save each project in its own folder before collecting or cleaning media. These commands inspect dependencies reported by processes and devices; they are not a search through arbitrary script text or a replacement for a backup.

1412.title: Paths and moving a project
1412.content: The project folder is the folder containing the saved document. References can be absolute, project-relative (<PROJECT>:Audio/kick.wav), or user-library-relative (<LIBRARY>:...). See Media management for resolution rules. When Save As changes folders and the document has project-relative references, score asks whether to copy its media to the new folder. Yes collects into the new folder; No leaves files in place and changes these references to absolute paths. No therefore preserves playback on this machine, not portability. Scripted saves without a window use the latter behavior.

1413.title: Consolidate project
1413.content: Choose Consolidate project…, inspect the report, then press Consolidate. The dialog previews files, destinations and problems before writing. | Method → Copy the files makes independent copies. Originals are not moved or deleted; existing destinations are not overwritten. Identical content can be reused and conflicting names receive distinct destinations. | Symbolic links depend on the original location. Hard links require a compatible filesystem and share file contents. Prefer copies for handoff; do not treat links as an independent backup. | Also collect files from the user library is off by default. Enable it if the receiving computer will not have the same library content. | Sort into Audio/, Video/, Images/… groups files by kind and is on by default. Other categories include MIDI, models, shaders, scripts and data. | Keep the name of the source folder retains an extra directory level, useful for similarly named samples from different collections. | . Supported kit references can declare companion samples. These are collected with their relative layout instead of copying only the kit description. This depends on the process exposing those dependencies: it does not discover every file a script or external plug-in might open. The reference changes form an undoable document command, and score saves after consolidation. Disk copies remain if the reference changes are undone. Missing files and unsupported dependencies are reported; failed copies keep their old references. Plug-ins and folder dependencies may still need installing or transferring separately. Remote streams are not local media to collect.

1414.title: Locate missing files
1414.content: Locate missing files… also opens automatically after loading a document with missing dependencies. The document remains open while you repair it. | Choose Search a folder… to search that directory and its descendants for matching filenames. The search can be cancelled. | Inspect Used by, Missing file and Found at. Multiple candidates can have the same name: check the location rather than assuming the first match is correct. | Select a row and use Locate… to choose its replacement explicitly. | Press Relink to apply the candidates, then save the document. | . Searching alone changes nothing. Network URLs are not reported as missing local files. A relink can only update a reference that the owning process or device exposes for rewriting.

1415.title: Remove unused files
1415.content: Remove unused files… finds files in the project folder that the current document no longer references. By default it searches only the media folders created by consolidation, not every render, note or collaborator’s file alongside the score. Review the list and untick anything to keep. The default Move them to the Unused folder preserves their relative layout under Unused/; restoring them requires moving them back with a file manager. Delete them is permanent and prompts for confirmation: score’s Undo does not restore deleted files. The whole-project-folder option broadens the search and needs extra care. The operation refuses files outside the project folder and score documents. Nevertheless, “unused” means unused by dependencies score knows about in this document. Read warnings about missing references and other documents sharing the folder; resolve missing media and back up shared projects before cleanup.

1416.title: Shorten media files to what is played
1416.content: Shorten media files to what is played… is different from removing unused files: it shortens media that is still in use. The current audio trimmer writes a new 32-bit floating-point WAV at the source sample rate, beside the original under a new name, and adjusts references and offsets together. | Keep extra retains handles on either side of the used region (two seconds initially). | All known readers of a file contribute to the retained span. Unbounded readers, references that cannot be rewritten, companion samples and files within a referenced folder can prevent trimming. | Only files inside the project folder qualify. Consolidate external media first. | Files that are almost entirely used, have unknown duration or would not save enough space are left alone. Decoding compressed audio to WAV can increase its size; this is not a general audio/video compression command. | Delete the untrimmed files afterwards is off by default. Leave it off to retain recovery and Undo’s source files. Unreferenced originals do not travel in the project archive and can be cleaned up later. | . Inspect the per-file reasons and estimated saving before pressing Trim. References are undoable and the document is saved afterwards; deletion of original media is not reversible through Undo.

1417.title: Archive project
1417.content: Archive project… consolidates with the default copy settings, saves the document, then writes a ZIP containing the document and its known referenced files within the project folder, including declared companion samples. It is not a ZIP of every file in the folder: unrelated material and unused originals are omitted. Library collection is off in the archive command’s default consolidation. For a portable handoff, first consolidate manually with Also collect files from the user library, repair missing files and review external dependencies. The archive completion message warns about missing files and dependencies such as plug-ins or folders that must be installed separately. In the browser, archiving produces a download and can include an unsaved document. It can only include media available to the browser’s filesystem; it does not gain access to the desktop’s files. See Using score in the browser. Downloaded example archives . Open downloaded project ZIPs directly in score, which opens the enclosed document with its bundled media. Project names, descriptions and documentation links do not replace required add-ons, model packages or external files. The online-example installer can initially open a nested score but its installed-file lookup searches only the archive’s top-level directory. Selecting that example again may therefore download it again. The preserved nested project is not necessarily broken or missing media; this is a separate installed-example lookup limitation.

1418.title: Operating systems
1418.content: score works on Linux, macOS, Windows, and partially on the web platform. Its development mainly happens on an ArchLinux system. As score is built with Qt, it should be portable to any system where Qt runs.

1419.title: Network protocols
1419.content: . | OSC (Open Sound Control): the standard intermedia protocol. It is implemented through a heavily modified version of Ross Bencina’s oscpack library. | Documented here. | . | OSCQuery: . | Documented here. | . | Minuit. | Documented here. | . | HTTP. | Documented here. | . | WebSockets. | Documented here. | . | CoAP. | Documented here. | . | MQTT. | Documented here. | . | LSL (Lab Streaming Layer), through the optional LSL add-on. | Documented here. | . | Bitfocus Companion modules expose supported module controls through a device; the module’s own dependencies and configuration still apply. | Spatialization, provided by the SpatGRIS add-on, is a device integration for external spatial-audio software. | . Support is implemented through libartnet, which has been integrated inside libossia. score is able to load fixtures definitions in the open-fixture-library format. | Documented here. | . | LED Strip Support: Comprehensive support for LED strips including NeoPixel (WS2812), individual LED control, and strip/pane/volume layouts through Art-Net. Supports RGB, RGBW, and specialized diode configurations (Warm/Cold White, Amber, UV). | s.ACN / E1.31 is supported. | ENTTEC DMX USB Pro devices are supported (Mk1 and Mk2). | DMX input and output are both supported. | .

Most gamepads and joysticks should work without issue. | Documented here. | . | Wiimotes: they are supported through the WiiUse library. | Documented here. | . | LeapMotion / UltraLeap: they are supported through the UltraLeap SDK (Gemini / Hyperion) which must be installed on the target computer. | Documented here. | . | GPIOs, ADCs, PWMs etc.: they are supported through the SimpleIO library which is a simple wrapper over the raw kernel access. This feature is only available on Linux with the relevant hardware, for instance on Raspberry Pi. | Documented here. | . | BLE: Bluetooth Low Energy devices are supported through the SimpleBLE. Both reading advertisments / beacons / manufacturer data and GATT services is supported. | Documented here. | . | GPS: score can connect to a gpsd server and expose the GPS data. | Documented here. | . | Phidgets has an optional Phidget22 integration in libossia. The wrapper contains a stale include path that must be corrected for a Phidgets-enabled build to work. See the reference for channel activation and input/output limitations. | CAN / DBC receives and decodes CAN signals through Linux SocketCAN. It is receive-only and requires a DBC database; it does not provide CAN transmission or CANopen control services. | .

1422.title: Audio systems
1422.content: . | JACK: support is implemented in libossia. | PulseAudio: support is implemented in libossia. | PipeWire: implemented in libossia and in score. | ALSA, the native Linux backend, supported through PortAudio. A direct implementation is also provided for instance for working with as low latency as possible on embedded devices, but it only supports output, not duplex / input. | CoreAudio: the native macOS backend, supported through PortAudio. | MME, WASAPI, WDMKS: the native Windows backends, supported through PortAudio. | ASIO: the low-latency pro-audio Windows backend developed by Steinberg, supported through PortAudio. | SDL: support is implemented in libossia. It is mainly used to provide audio for the WebAssembly build of score. | .

1423.title: Video protocols
1423.content: . | Spout is supported on Windows. | Documented here. | . | Syphon is supported on macOS. | Documented here. | . | Shmdata is supported on Linux and macOS. | Documented here. | . | Sh4lt provides shared-memory video input and output when built with the Sh4lt backend. See the Sh4lt device; the wider Sh4lt library’s data types are not a promise that every type is exposed by this device. | NDI video input and output require the NDI add-on and a loadable NDI runtime. Platform and format support depend on that runtime and build. | See the NDI device, including PTZ controls for compatible cameras. | . | PipeWire video provides input and output on Linux builds with that backend. It is distinct from the PipeWire audio and MIDI backends. | GStreamer bridges user-defined media pipelines; capabilities depend on the GStreamer runtime and installed elements. | FFmpeg / libav provides media-device input and output for supported files and streams. Available codecs, muxers and network protocols depend on the FFmpeg build. | Camera and screen capture use platform-specific capture backends. | GPhoto2 DSLR provides camera live-view preview and device-reported configuration when libgphoto2, its camera driver and suitable hardware are available. | .

1424.title: Transport synchronisation
1424.content: . | JACK transport: score can act as a master or a slave. | Timecode Synchronizer follows an incoming time position. Musical pulse generation and timestamp synchronization are different operations; choose the process appropriate to the source. | MIDI Sync Out sends MIDI clock, transport messages and timecode. MIDI Sync In decodes incoming synchronization into control values; it does not automatically make the whole score follow an external transport. | .

1425.title: MIDI
1425.content: All the MIDI support in score comes from the libremidi library: . For real-time communication, the following implementations are provided: . | ALSA, through either the raw or sequencer API. | JACK. | PipeWire. | The native operating systems MIDI API: MME for Windows, CoreMIDI for macOS. | WebMIDI. | . In addition, score is able to load Standard MIDI files (SMF). Use MIDI input and MIDI output for MIDI streams. MIDI Controller additionally provides named device-map controls and a Mackie Control surface mode; these are two modes of one protocol, not separate processes.

1426.title: Audio file formats
1426.content: score uses FFMPEG for its audio needs. It should support most codecs and formats listed at this page. Every standard format (WAV, W64, AIFF, MP3, OGG Vorbis, FLAC, etc.) are supported without issues. score handles WAV files in a specific way, through the dr_wav library, to allow for memory-mapping the data for large files. score is able to read ACID tags to devise for instance BPM info from sound files. See the sound file process documentation for more information.

1427.title: Video file formats
1427.content: score uses FFmpeg to read video files. Available demuxers and codecs depend on the FFmpeg build; common choices include H.264, H.265, ProRes and transport streams (.ts). HAP and supported DXV variants have specialized GPU texture-decoding paths. This differs from hardware video decoding: compressed texture blocks can be sampled on the GPU, while the file still needs to be read and unpacked. The Video process provides Auto, Direct (seek) and Frame queue playback modes. Auto selects the playback path using the stream’s keyframe layout. Direct playback is useful for independently decodable frames; inter-frame codecs generally need the frame queue.

1428.title: Hardware decoding
1428.content: The video decoder can use FFmpeg hardware-acceleration backends, including Direct3D / DXVA on Windows, VideoToolbox on macOS, and Linux options such as VAAPI, V4L2-M2M, CUDA or QuickSync where available. Vulkan decoding is also build- and driver-dependent. Selecting a graphics renderer does not by itself guarantee hardware video decoding. Support depends on the codec, pixel format, FFmpeg version, driver and GPU. Use the video decoding preference to select a backend; unsupported streams may still need software decoding.

1429.title: Hardware rendering
1429.content: score can convert many decoded pixel formats with GPU shaders rather than converting every frame to RGB on the CPU. This reduces conversion work; it does not make file decoding or transfer free. Supported paths cover packed and planar RGB / RGBA, grayscale, YUV and YUVA; common examples include NV12, P010 / P016, planar 4:2:0 / 4:2:2 / 4:4:4, YUYV / UYVY, high-bit-depth and floating-point images, and DCI XYZ12. The precise path depends on the source format and graphics backend; other formats can require a software conversion.

1430.title: Color and HDR
1430.content: The video pipeline interprets source color metadata, including BT.601, BT.709, BT.2020, P3, PQ and HLG. The Video inspector’s Format and Tonemap (HDR) controls choose conversion to SDR, HDR passthrough or linear output, and the tone-mapping operator. Decoding an HDR file is not the same as displaying HDR. The output window format, graphics backend, operating system and display must also support the requested output. For SDR displays, use tone mapping rather than assuming passthrough will produce the intended image. See Video, Window and the graphics pipeline for the processing and output controls. For detailed choices and limitations, see Video formats and color.

1431.title: Image file formats
1431.content: The Image process reads raster images through Qt’s image readers and handles SVG through a scalable SVG renderer. Common formats include PNG, JPEG and GIF; additional formats depend on installed Qt image-format support.

1432.title: 3D file formats
1432.content: Native 3D processes are separate from QtQuick3D content embedded in a JavaScript / QML process: . | Geometry Loader (Object Loader reference) imports geometry for mesh-oriented processing. | Asset Loader imports scenes from glTF / GLB and FBX, as well as OBJ, PLY, STL, OFF, SPLAT and SPZ assets. It preserves scene data where the format and importer support it; USD-family files require the optional parser add-on. | Scene data can be processed and rendered through the native Render Pipeline. A simple geometry path can use Model Display. | JavaScript / QML can host QtQuick3D scenes when the required Qt modules are installed. This is a separate rendering path, not a requirement for native glTF / FBX import. | .

1433.title: Graphics APIs
1433.content: score uses Qt RHI to target OpenGL, Vulkan, Metal, Direct3D 11 and Direct3D 12. Available backends depend on the platform and build. Advanced features such as compute shaders, storage buffers and particular texture formats additionally depend on GPU and driver support. The shader processes cover several jobs: . | ISF shaders generate and filter images. | Compute Shaders work with GPU data, textures and geometry. | Render Pipeline provides custom raster rendering for geometry and scenes. | Vertex Shader Art generates visuals from a vertex shader. | . See the graphics pipeline for how these processes connect.

1434.title: Audio plug-ins
1434.content: Desktop builds support the following audio plug-in and embedded-language systems when the corresponding backend is included. A plug-in binary must match the operating system and architecture; desktop plug-in support does not imply availability in the browser build. | AirWindows. | Documented here. | . | CLAP. | Documented here. | . | Steinberg VST3. | Documented here. | . | LV2 on Linux. Note that currently this requires building score on your own computer or use a Linux distro package. | Documented here. | . | JSFX is embedded in score through ysfx. | Documented here. | . | Faust, the Faust programming language developed by GRAME. score embeds the Faust compiler and libraries. | Documented here. | . | Pure Data is embedded in score through libpd. | Documented here. | . | It is possible to write simple audio instruments and effects with the various math-expression processes. | It is possible to write simple audio instruments and effects with the JavaScript process. | It is possible to write more advanced instruments and effects in C++ with the C++ JIT process. | .

1435.title: Supported protocols and formats
1435.content: This page summarizes the systems and file formats that score can interoperate with. Availability depends on the operating system, build options, installed add-ons and external runtimes.

1436.title: Pure Data patch language
1436.content: Pure Data is a visual dataflow language. Object and message boxes, joined by patch cords, describe message processing and audio signal processing. A .pd file stores this graph; it is normally authored in Pure Data rather than typed into score’s script editor. score hosts the patch through libpd.

1437.title: Language and object reference
1437.content: . | Pure Data manual: the upstream language and environment manual. | Theory of operation: boxes, messages, signal connections, scheduling, abstractions and arrays. | Messages and evaluation order: message types, hot/cold inlets and right-to-left outlet ordering. | Audio signals: tilde objects, DSP blocks and conversions between signals and messages. | Externals: abstractions, compiled objects and their dependencies. | . For an individual object, open its Help patch in Pure Data. A library installed in your standalone Pd environment is not automatically available in score’s embedded runtime; keep that distinction in mind when choosing externals.

1438.title: Audio, MIDI and message ports
1438.content: The Pure Data process maps these Pd objects to score’s host interface: . | Pd objects | score interface | . | [adc~], [dac~] | Audio input and output ports. Set the required channel counts in the inspector; channels share a single audio port in each direction. | . | [midiin], [notein], [ctlin] | MIDI input. | . | [midiout], [noteout], [ctlout] | MIDI output. | . | [r] / [receive], [s] / [send] | Value input and output. | . A Pd audio connection and a message connection are not interchangeable. Use Pd’s signal/message conversion objects when crossing that boundary; changing a score port’s destination does not change the semantics inside the patch.

1439.title: Receive annotations and controls
1439.content: Receive names can use the libossia parameter annotation syntax to describe a control. This integration remains work in progress: not every annotation combination is implemented. The documented widget names are intslider, floatslider, logfloatslider, intspinbox, toggle, button, lineedit, xyslider and hsvslider. The existing examples of annotations are: . [r myInput @type float @range -1 1] [r myInput @widget intslider @min 0 1000] [r myInput @type impulse] [r myInput @type bool @default true] [r myInput @unit color.hsv] . These are host annotations on receive objects, not new built-in Pd object classes. Check the resulting score controls before relying on a particular annotation in a performance.

1440.title: Execution and editing
1440.content: Do not use score’s Parallel execution mode with Pd patches. For loading patches, opening their external editor and closing that editor safely, see Pure Data integration. For a working sound patch, see Pure Data integration example.

1442.title: Pure Data support
1442.content: ossia score supports running Pure Data patches as processes. Simply drop a patch in the score to add it. This is done thanks to libpd. The Pure Data language reference links the patch-language and object manuals and documents score’s audio, MIDI, message and control-annotation interface.

1443.title: Example
1443.content: The following Pure Data patch: . Will look like this when loaded in score: . This particular example can be downloaded in the user library. Feel free to contribute your own useful patches here ! .

1444.title: Limitations
1444.content: For now do not use the “Parallel” execution mode when running Pd patches.

1445.title: Usage
1445.content: Patch objects determine the audio, MIDI and value ports exposed in score. Set the required audio channel counts in the inspector, then connect the resulting process ports to the rest of the score. See Audio, MIDI and message ports for the recognized Pd objects, and Receive annotations and controls for the optional control metadata. Annotation support is still work in progress.

1446.title: Editing the patch
1446.content: If a Pure Data binary is detected on the host computer (by looking into their default installations folders and in the PATH), then it will be possible to open the patch directly from score. Do not close the main Pd UI window by quitting it like other OS windows. Instead, the window should be closed by pressing the “window” button in the score node.

1448.title: QML device API
1448.content: QML device definitions combine JavaScript functions with a QML root object imported by import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia. This page documents score’s device runtime, not browser JavaScript or Node.js. For core syntax, see the Qt QML reference, JavaScript in QML and the JavaScript language overview.

1449.title: Root types
1449.content: | Root | Purpose | Setup and worked examples | . | Ossia.Mapper | Persistent parameter mappings, generators and script-managed values; can use Device and raw Protocols sockets. | Mapper device | . | Ossia.HTTP | Parameter writes issue outgoing HTTP requests. | HTTP device | . | Ossia.WebSockets | Connect to an existing WebSocket server and map its messages into a parameter tree. | WebSocket device | . | Ossia.Serial | Map a custom serial-port protocol into a parameter tree. | Serial device | . These root types are not interchangeable with the Protocols transport API. A raw socket does not create a device tree. In particular, Protocols.http has a different callback contract from Ossia.HTTP, and Protocols.serial uses a different framing configuration from Ossia.Serial. Neither the HTTP nor WebSocket device is score’s remote-control server.

1450.title: Device trees
1450.content: createTree() returns an array of node descriptions. children nests nodes; a node can be a container or a typed parameter. A Mapper parameter does not need a binding to exist. For example: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { function createTree() { return [{ name: "node", children: [{ name: "sensor", type: Ossia.Type.Float }] }]; } } . With a device named Mapper, the parameter is Mapper:/node/sensor. Common metadata and types are below; bind, read, write and interval are Mapper-specific, while the other roots add their own request and receive callbacks. Tree node properties . Node descriptions use the following properties. The binding and generator fields apply to Ossia.Mapper, not automatically to the HTTP, WebSocket or Serial roots: . | Property | Type | Description | . | name | string | Required. The name of the parameter node. | . | type | Ossia.Type.* | The value type (see below). | . | children | array | Child nodes to create a tree hierarchy. | . | bind | string or array | Address(es) of other parameters to bind to. | . | read | function | Callback when a bound parameter changes, or when interval fires. | . | write | function | Callback when this parameter is written to. | . | interval | number | Polling interval in milliseconds (for generator use). | . | value |   | Default value for the parameter. | . | min |   | Minimum value for the domain. | . | max |   | Maximum value for the domain. | . | access | Ossia.Access.* | Access mode: Bi, Get, or Set. | . | bounding | Ossia.Bounding.* | Bounding mode: Free, Clip, Wrap, Fold, Low, High. | . | repetition_filter | Ossia.Repetitions.* | Unfiltered or Filtered. | . | unit | string | Unit, e.g. "color.rgba", "position.cart2D". If set, type is inferred. | . | description | string | Human-readable description of the parameter. | . | tags | array | Array of string tags. | . | extended_type | string | Extended type information. | . | disabled | bool | If true, the parameter is disabled. | . Value types . The Ossia.Type constants are: . | Constant | Description | . | Ossia.Type.Float | Floating-point number. | . | Ossia.Type.Int | 32-bit integer. | . | Ossia.Type.Bool | Boolean. | . | Ossia.Type.String | String. | . | Ossia.Type.Vec2f | 2D float vector. | . | Ossia.Type.Vec3f | 3D float vector. | . | Ossia.Type.Vec4f | 4D float vector. | . | Ossia.Type.Impulse | Impulse (no value). | . | Ossia.Type.List | List of values. | . | Ossia.Type.Map | Key-value map. | .

1451.title: Mapper callbacks
1451.content: Mapper runs continuously, even when timeline playback is stopped. Bindings are rebuilt when other devices become available or reconnect. Source updates change the Mapper value without automatically writing the same value back to the source; explicit writes to the Mapper follow its write rule or binding. Missing sources do not provide live values. Callback signatures . The read and write callbacks receive values as JS objects with a .value property: . // read: called when a bound address changes // - orig: the OSC address string of the source that changed // - v: an object with a .value property read: function(orig, v) { return v.value / 127.; } // read (generator mode, no bind): called on each interval tick // - no arguments read: function() { return new Date().getSeconds(); } // write: called when this mapper parameter is written to // - v: an object with a .value property write: function(v) { return v.value * 127.; } // write returning address-value pairs (for unbound parameters): write: function(v) { return [ { address: "foo:/bar", value: v.value } ]; } . A single bind address aliases that source parameter. An array of bindings makes orig identify the source that changed, for example "/1/control/45", while write(v) returns one value per binding in order. With no bind or read, write(v) can return an array of { address, value } pairs to route a write to addresses chosen at runtime. Lists contain typed elements: a list argument’s first element is accessed as v.value[0].value; vector elements are bare numbers such as v.value[0]. For a generator, omit bind, set interval in milliseconds, and return the generated value from read(). A QML property var can hold state shared between callbacks, such as two source values combined into a vector. See the Mapper tutorials for aliases, scaling, multiple bindings, dynamic destinations, XY combinations and clock generators.

1452.title: Available context objects
1452.content: Mapper scripts have access to Device for parameter reads, writes and tree edits, and Protocols for raw transport connections. The complete socket, framing, encoding, HTTP, OAuth, OSC and MIDI contract lives in the QML transport API.

1453.title: Device object
1453.content: The Device object allows reading and writing values to any parameter across all devices in the current score document. // Read the current value of a parameter let val = Device.read("OSCdevice:/sensor/x"); // Write a value to a parameter Device.write("OSCdevice:/sensor/x", 0.5); // Add a new parameter node to the mapper device Device.addNode("/my/new/parameter", "float"); // Remove a parameter node Device.removeNode("/my/new/parameter", "float"); . Value conversion helpers: . Device.asArray(v) // Convert a value to an array Device.asColor(v) // Convert a value to a color (RGBA) Device.asVec2(v) // Convert a value to a Vec2 Device.asVec3(v) // Convert a value to a Vec3 Device.asVec4(v) // Convert a value to a Vec4 Device.toValue(v) // Unwrap a typed { type, value } object into a plain JS value . toValue recursively unwraps typed list and map elements; an impulse becomes undefined, while an already unwrapped value is returned unchanged. Device.read(address) reads a current parameter value; Device.write(address, value) writes one. In a Mapper, an unqualified address such as "/foo" refers to that Mapper’s own tree; use "DeviceName:/path" for another device. Device.addNode(address, type) and Device.removeNode(address, type) edit only the script’s own device tree. The second argument is a type string, as in the "float" examples above. Writing to the mapper’s own nodes . This is useful when incoming network data or a timer should update a parameter exposed by the mapper itself: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { property var udpIn: Protocols.inboundUDP({ Transport: { Port: 9000 }, onMessage: function(bytes) { // Parse the raw bytes and write the result to the mapper's own node var val = parseInt(bytes); Device.write("/parsed_sensor", val); } }) function createTree() { return [ { name: "parsed_sensor", type: Ossia.Type.Int } ]; } } . Writing to other devices . The mapper can push values to any device parameter known to score: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { function createTree() { return [ { name: "trigger", type: Ossia.Type.Float, // When Mapper:/trigger is written to, forward the value // to two different devices at once write: function(v) { Device.write("Lights:/dimmer/1", v.value); Device.write("OSCdevice:/fx/intensity", v.value * 100); } } ]; } } . Reading from other devices . Use Device.read to query the current value of any parameter: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { function createTree() { return [ { name: "snapshot", type: Ossia.Type.Float, interval: 500, read: function() { // Poll a parameter from another device every 500ms return Device.read("OSCdevice:/sensor/temperature"); } } ]; } } . Combining Device reads and writes . A common pattern is to read several parameters, combine them, and write the result somewhere: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { function createTree() { return [ { name: "average", type: Ossia.Type.Float, interval: 100, read: function() { var a = Device.read("SensorA:/value"); var b = Device.read("SensorB:/value"); var avg = (a + b) / 2.0; // Write the computed average to a light controller Device.write("Lights:/master", avg); // Also expose it on this mapper node return avg; } } ]; } } . Reacting to incoming network data and dispatching to multiple devices . This example listens for OSC messages over UDP and routes them to different devices depending on the OSC address: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { property var oscParser: Protocols.osc({ onOsc: function(address, args) { if(address === "/sensor/x") Device.write("Millumin:/millumin/layer/x/instance", args[0]); else if(address === "/sensor/y") Device.write("Millumin:/millumin/layer/y/instance", args[0]); else if(address === "/sensor/button") Device.write("/button_state", args[0]); // write to the mapper's own node } }) property var udpIn: Protocols.inboundUDP({ Transport: { Port: 7000 }, onMessage: function(bytes) { oscParser.processMessage(bytes); } }) function createTree() { return [ { name: "button_state", type: Ossia.Type.Bool } ]; } } .

1454.title: HTTP device API
1454.content: Use Ossia.HTTP and createTree(). A parameter’s request is a URL string or a function returning a URL; pushing a value to that parameter sends the request. answer(body, value) receives response text and the parameter’s current value, then returns an array of device-local { address, value } updates. | A string request may contain $val, replaced by the sent value. A function request(value) receives a typed object such as { type: Ossia.Type.Int, value: 123 }; construct a URL using value.value and escape query components with encodeURIComponent. | Requests are GET by default. Set method: "post" and requestData (a string or function) for a POST body. This device’s tree API is not a generic arbitrary-method/header client. | onRead(bytes) or onReadString(text) receives chunks as they arrive. Chunk boundaries are not message boundaries, and these callbacks consume reply data; do not assume a subsequent answer also receives the complete body. | No automatic polling interval is implied by a tree entry. Schedule requests from the score or your script when required. | . For arbitrary HTTP methods, custom headers, status codes or bearer authorization, use the object form of Protocols.http, for example in a Mapper. Keep credentials out of shared scores. See the HTTP setup example for a complete request/answer tree.

1455.title: WebSocket device API
1455.content: Use Ossia.WebSockets and createTree(). The root host property can supply the server address, for example property string host: "ws://127.0.0.1:8080". | Callback / property | Contract | . | onConnected() | Called on connection; returns device-local { address, value } updates. | . | onDisonnected() | Called on disconnection; returns tree updates. The spelling deliberately preserves the implementation’s missing “c”. | . | onMessage(message) | Receives a server message; return an array of { address, value } updates. Parse JSON explicitly if needed. | . | Parameter request(value) | Receives a typed object such as { type: Ossia.Type.Int, value: 123 }; its return value is sent when not undefined. | . | Parameter request string | Sends text, replacing $val with the parameter value. | . | Parameter openListening() / closeListening() | Called when score starts / stops listening on the node; return a remote message when needed, or undefined to send nothing. | . | Root processFromJson: true | Match incoming JSON against the declared tree and update parameters in C++; replaces manual onMessage handling for that path. It does not discover an API or create the tree. | . A function-valued request currently sends a binary WebSocket message, whereas a string-valued request sends text. The peer must accept the corresponding message kind. The connection, disconnection and receive callbacks return local updates, not arbitrary remote commands. For explicit text/binary receive callbacks or a listening server, use Protocols WebSockets. The WebSocket device tutorial includes a complete road-traffic server/client and the user-library script for generating a tree from sample JSON.

1456.title: Serial device API
1456.content:
Use Ossia.Serial and createTree() to define the initial tree. Select the actual port and baud rate in the Serial device dialog. The root callbacks below return arrays of device-local { address, value } updates. Receiving serial data . Choose one receive callback rather than declaring all three: the implementation gives onMessage precedence over onBinary, and onBinary over onRead. | Callback | Input and behavior | . | onMessage(message) | A framed text message as a string. | . | onBinary(message) | A framed binary message as an ArrayBuffer. | . | onRead(bytes) | Raw available bytes as an ArrayBuffer, with no framing; reconstruct messages in the script. Incoming chunk boundaries are not message boundaries. | . For example, a text callback can parse a sensor value: . function onMessage(message) { console.log(message); return [{ address: "/sensor", value: parseInt(message) }]; } . A binary or raw callback instead reads the bytes of its buffer, for example new Uint8Array(message) or new Uint8Array(bytes), and returns the same update shape. Do not install a text callback when choosing the raw receive path. Serial framing . Framing is configured on the root, not in a Protocols configuration object: . property string framing: "delimiter" property string delimiter: "
" . Recognized names are: . | framing | Meaning | . | "delimiter" | Delimiter-terminated messages; set delimiter explicitly, e.g. "
" or "

". | . | "slip" | SLIP framing. | . | "osc-slip" | SLIP framing with OSC message handling. | . | "size" | Each message starts with a big-endian 32-bit size prefix. | . Do not use "none" or "cobs" as an assumed raw-framing mode: unrecognized names take the parser’s fallback branch. For raw input and output, choose onRead without onMessage or onBinary; the parser then disables framing. The OSC device’s serial COBS transport and the raw Protocols.serial factory are separate configuration paths. Serial requests and listening . A tree node’s request customizes outgoing data: . | A string is sent when the parameter receives a message from score; $val is textually replaced with the value. | A function with no arguments can generate a request, e.g. request: () => Math.random() + " foo ". | A function request(val) receives { value, type }, for example request: (val) => val.value + " foo ". | Without request, a numeric parameter is written textually to the port. | . The root also accepts openListening(address) and closeListening(address), called when score needs to start or stop actively listening for changes on an address. Writing binary data . By default, the values returned from request in the device tree are treated as strings and will be written to the serial port in textual, ASCII format. For instance, an “int” parameter with value 123 will cause the actual integer to be written textually in the serial port: 123 as the bytes 0x31 0x32 0x33, and not the single-byte value for 123, 0x7B. If one wants actual binary data to be written, it is necessary to use a Javascript Typed Array, such as Uint8Array. Note that in this case the framing also must be handled manually, to enable for more control. Here is an example which will write a single byte delimited by 
. { name: "request", type: Ossia.Type.Int, access: Ossia.Access.Set, min: 0, max: 127, request: (val) => { let auint8 = new ArrayBuffer(3); let uint8 = new Uint8Array(auint8); uint8[0] = val.value; // An integer between 0 and 127 uint8[1] = 0x0D; // CR uint8[2] = 0x0A; // LF return auint8; } } . OSC support . If the target device reads OSC natively on its serial port, it is possible to implement support for it quite easily: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Serial { function createTree() { return [ { name: "foo", type: Ossia.Type.Int, access: Ossia.Access.Set, osc_address: "/foo" }, { name: "foo_but_as_list", type: Ossia.Type.List, access: Ossia.Access.Set, osc_address: "/foo" } ]; } } . In the above case, sending messages to foo and foo_but_as_list will both be translated directly as OSC messages, for instance /foo 1 or /foo 10 "blah" True. If setting extended_type to for instance u8Blob then a list would be translated in a blob containing a sequence of u8 values. Coalescing messages . In case the serial port is too slow and overflows, one can add the property: . property real coalesce: 15 . to the Serial object, to coalesce messages every 15 milliseconds for instance. If a specific parameter must not be coalesced, but always sent, one can simply set critical: true on the node. One will generally want to use coalescing on parameters such as lights, drives, or anything that more-or-less maps to an electrical voltage, and not for parameters that would trigger the start of an action. In case messages use the OSC feature, then non-critical messages will get coalesced as a single bundle.

1457.title: Sources and runtime scope
1457.content: The device roots are Qt/QML integrations; available backends depend on score’s build and platform. QML validation only proves that the component can load, not that an external device or API is reachable. The setup pages above cover connection diagnostics and hardware requirements. Source: libossia’s qml_engine_functions.hpp, qml_context.hpp, qml_plugin.cpp, http_protocol.hpp, ws_generic_client_protocol.cpp, and serial_protocol.cpp.

1458.title: QML transport API
1458.content: Use Protocols in the console or a Mapper device when an external API cannot be expressed by a standard device. Mapper QML declares the device tree, then translates transport messages into Device.write calls. The HTTP device and WebSocket device have their own Ossia.HTTP / Ossia.WebSockets tree conventions; do not mix their callbacks with raw socket callbacks below. Backends depend on the platform and compile-time features. Keep the returned socket in a variable/property for as long as it is needed, and implement onError to diagnose connection failures. Opening is asynchronous; send initial data from onOpen(socket), not immediately after calling the factory.

1459.title: Transport selection
1459.content: Factory names below are members of Protocols; transport keys are case-sensitive. | Factory | Configuration / receive path | . | outboundUDP(config) | Transport: { Host, Port, Broadcast }; call write(data). Set Broadcast: true to enable broadcast sends. | . | inboundUDP(config) | Transport: { Bind, Port }; onMessage(bytes). | . | outboundTCP(config) | Transport: { Host, Port }; onMessage(bytes) for received data. | . | inboundTCP(config) | Transport: { Bind, Port }; onConnection(connection), then connection.receive(callback) and connection.write(data). | . | outboundWS(config) | Transport: { Host, Port }; onTextMessage(text) and onBinaryMessage(bytes). | . | inboundWS(config) | Transport: { Bind, Port }; handle connections with onConnection. | . | outboundUnixDatagram, inboundUnixDatagram, outboundUnixStream, inboundUnixStream | Transport: { Path }; require local-socket support, normally Linux/macOS. | . | serial(config) | Transport: { Port, Baud, DataBits, FlowControl, Parity, StopBits }; Port is a device path/name, not a UDP port. | . Common socket lifecycle callbacks are onOpen, onClose and onError. onError is the preferred spelling; older UDP/TCP/Unix/WebSocket configurations may use onFail. If both are supplied, onError wins. var connection = Protocols.outboundTCP({ Transport: { Host: "127.0.0.1", Port: 5000 }, Framing: { type: "line", delimiter: "\r\n" }, onOpen: function(socket) { socket.write("STATUS"); }, onMessage: function(bytes) { console.log(bytes.toString()); }, onError: function(error) { console.log(error); } }); . This example expects a server with a CRLF-delimited command protocol on port 5000. The framing layer adds/removes the delimiter; do not append it a second time.

1460.title: Framing and encoding are different
1460.content: TCP and serial are byte streams: one received chunk is not necessarily one message. Framing determines message boundaries; Encoding converts payload bytes to/from text. Use the settings required by the other endpoint, not an arbitrary combination. Framing configuration uses lower-case keys: . | { type: "line", delimiter: "\r\n" }: delimiter-terminated messages; omitted delimiter means newline. | { type: "slip" }, { type: "cobs" }, { type: "stx_etx" }: protocol-specific byte framing. | { type: "size_prefix", bytes: 4, endian: "big" }: length prefix. Supported widths are 1, 2 and 4 bytes; 4-byte big-endian is the default, and "little" selects little-endian where applicable. | { type: "fixed_length", size: 64 }: fixed-size receive frames, particularly useful for serial protocols. | Omit Framing for raw chunks; your code must then accumulate/parse partial messages. | . Encoding: { type: "base64" } supports Base64; alternatives are ascii85, hex, intel_hex (alias ihex) and srec (aliases s_record, motorola). Encoding is optional and is not encryption. UDP already supplies datagram boundaries; WebSocket already distinguishes complete text and binary messages. Do not assume every framing option applies to these transports.

1461.title: HTTP requests
1461.content: Use the object form for methods, headers, JSON bodies and status codes: . Protocols.http({ url: "http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/level", verb: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify({ level: 0.5 }), onResponse: function(status, body) { console.log(status, body); }, onError: function(message) { console.log(message); } }); . The endpoint must exist and accept this request. Headers can carry service-specific authentication such as Authorization: "Bearer " + token. Do not print or embed production tokens in shared scores. The older Protocols.http(url, callback, "GET") form provides a simpler body callback; use the object form when you need a complete request contract.

1462.title: OAuth
1462.content: import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia exposes Ossia.OAuth only when score is built with Qt NetworkAuth and a Qt version newer than 6.10.0. It implements an OAuth2 authorization-code flow, not a universal credential store. Configure clientIdentifier, optionally clientIdentifierSharedKey, authorizationUrl, accessTokenUrl and requestedScopeTokens for the actual service. Call grant() to start authorization, react to granted or requestFailed(error), and use the accessToken property. Registration with the service and its redirect requirements remain necessary; a client ID from a different application is not a portable example. The object also exposes send(verb, url, config, callback): config.headers supplies custom headers and a string config.body supplies a raw body; authorization is added by the OAuth object. Its callback is function(result, error), not the Protocols.http status/body callback. Errors expose code, message and body. This implementation evaluates successful response text to convert structured data, so use it only with trusted services and responses.

1463.title: Socket callbacks
1463.content: Socket factories return objects, not parameter trees. Keep the object alive in a QML property or JavaScript variable. Callback availability depends on the transport: . | Callback | Receive contract | . | onOpen(socket) | Connection established; outbound TCP/WS provide the socket for initial writes. | . | onClose() | Connection closed. | . | onError(error) | Connection or transport error; preferred over the older onFail spelling. | . | onMessage(bytes) | Received bytes for UDP, TCP, Unix, serial and MIDI receive paths. | . | onConnection(connection) | Accepted TCP, WS or Unix stream client. | . | onTextMessage(text) | Outbound WebSocket text message. | . | onBinaryMessage(bytes) | Outbound WebSocket binary message. | . Outbound sockets expose write(data). For accepted TCP and Unix stream clients, register connection.receive(callback) and send with connection.write(data); see the server example below. Do not substitute the device-tree callbacks of Ossia.WebSockets, Ossia.HTTP or Ossia.Serial for these callbacks: those root types are documented in the QML device API.

1464.title: Transport examples
1464.content: These QML examples use Ossia.Mapper to keep their sockets alive. Add a Mapper device to run them; the remote endpoint or hardware must implement the corresponding protocol. UDP sockets . Send raw bytes over UDP: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { // Open an outbound UDP socket as a QML property property var udpSocket: Protocols.outboundUDP({ Transport: { Host: "127.0.0.1", Port: 9000 } }) function createTree() { return [ { name: "send", type: Ossia.Type.String, write: function(v) { udpSocket.write(v.value); } } ]; } } . Listen for incoming UDP messages: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { property var udpIn: Protocols.inboundUDP({ Transport: { Bind: "0.0.0.0", Port: 7000 }, onMessage: function(bytes) { console.log("Received:", bytes); } }) function createTree() { return []; } } . TCP sockets . Connect to a TCP server: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { property var tcpSocket: Protocols.outboundTCP({ Transport: { Host: "127.0.0.1", Port: 5000 }, onOpen: function(socket) { console.log("Connected!"); socket.write("hello"); }, onClose: function() { console.log("Disconnected"); }, onError: function(error) { console.log("Connection failed:", error); } }) function createTree() { return []; } } . Create a TCP server and accept connections: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { property var tcpServer: Protocols.inboundTCP({ Transport: { Bind: "0.0.0.0", Port: 5000 }, onOpen: function() { console.log("Server started"); }, onConnection: function(socket) { console.log("New client connected"); socket.onClose = function() { console.log("Client disconnected"); }; socket.receive(function(bytes) { console.log("Received:", bytes); }); }, onClose: function() { console.log("Server closed"); } }) function createTree() { return []; } } . WebSockets . Connect to a WebSocket server: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { property var ws: Protocols.outboundWS({ Transport: { Host: "127.0.0.1", Port: 8080 }, onTextMessage: function(msg) { console.log("Text:", msg); }, onBinaryMessage: function(msg) { console.log("Binary:", msg); } }) function createTree() { return []; } } . Create a WebSocket server: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { property var wsServer: Protocols.inboundWS({ Transport: { Bind: "0.0.0.0", Port: 8080 }, onConnection: function(socket) { console.log("Client connected"); } }) function createTree() { return []; } } . Unix sockets . On systems that support Unix domain sockets (normally Linux/macOS), datagram and stream variants are available: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { // Outbound datagram property var unixOut: Protocols.outboundUnixDatagram({ Transport: { Path: "/tmp/my_socket" } }) // Inbound datagram property var unixIn: Protocols.inboundUnixDatagram({ Transport: { Path: "/tmp/my_socket" }, onMessage: function(bytes) { console.log(bytes); } }) // Outbound stream property var unixStreamOut: Protocols.outboundUnixStream({ Transport: { Path: "/tmp/my_stream" } }) // Inbound stream (server) property var unixStreamIn: Protocols.inboundUnixStream({ Transport: { Path: "/tmp/my_stream" }, onConnection: function(socket) { socket.receive(function(bytes) { console.log("Unix stream:", bytes); }); } }) function createTree() { return []; } } . Periodic HTTP requests . The older Protocols.http(url, callback, verb) form invokes callback(body) without a status argument. This Mapper example schedules a request every five seconds; the asynchronous callback logs the response rather than returning it as the parameter value: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { function createTree() { return [ { name: "fetch", type: Ossia.Type.String, interval: 5000, read: function() { Protocols.http( "http://api.example.com/data", function(response) { console.log(response); }, "GET" ); } } ]; } } . The third argument is the HTTP verb ("GET", "POST", etc.). OSC message parsing . Protocols.osc({ onOsc: function(address, args) { ... } }) only creates a parser: processMessage(bytes) feeds a packet into it and does not itself open an OSC socket. The Protocols.osc function creates an OSC message processor that can decode raw OSC bytes received from a UDP or other socket: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { property var oscParser: Protocols.osc({ onOsc: function(address, args) { console.log("OSC:", address, args); } }) property var udpIn: Protocols.inboundUDP({ Transport: { Port: 9000 }, onMessage: function(bytes) { oscParser.processMessage(bytes); } }) function createTree() { return []; } } . MIDI . List available MIDI ports and open them directly: . import Ossia 1.0 as Ossia Ossia.Mapper { // List available MIDI input and output ports property var midiInputs: Protocols.inboundMIDIDevices() property var midiOutputs: Protocols.outboundMIDIDevices() // Open the first available input (if any) property var midiIn: midiInputs.length > 0 ? Protocols.inboundMIDI({ Transport: midiInputs[0], onMessage: function(bytes) { console.log("MIDI in:", bytes); } }) : null // Open the first available output (if any) property var midiOut: midiOutputs.length > 0 ? Protocols.outboundMIDI({ Transport: midiOutputs[0] }) : null function createTree() { // midiOut.write(...) can be used to send MIDI bytes return []; } } . MIDI 2.0 (UMP) equivalents are also available: Protocols.inboundUMPDevices(), Protocols.outboundUMPDevices(), Protocols.inboundUMP(...), and Protocols.outboundUMP(...). Pass the port identifier returned by enumeration as Transport. Backend support and connected hardware determine which ports exist; never assume element zero is available. Serial sockets . Protocols.serial(config) opens a low-level serial socket. Transport accepts Port, Baud, DataBits, FlowControl, Parity and StopBits; Port is a device path/name rather than a network port number. Use onMessage(bytes) for received payloads and write(data) for sends. Match these settings to the hardware and configure stream boundaries with the Framing object. This is not the Ossia.Serial root’s framing string: its separate Serial device API has different recognized names and tree callbacks. See Serial device setup for port ownership and permissions.

1465.title: Troubleshooting and scope
1465.content: Validate QML first, then check the host/bind address, port permissions, framing and payload encoding independently. A valid QML component proves neither a reachable server nor a correct external API. Prefer loopback while developing, and avoid exposing listeners to untrusted networks. These are client/device integration APIs; for an operator’s browser controlling score, see Remote Control. Source: qml_protocols.hpp, qml_protocols.cpp and qml_oauth.hpp.

1466.title: QML protocols
1466.content: Custom QML transports let a script communicate with an API that cannot be represented by a standard device. The complete runtime reference now lives under Reference → Languages: . | QML transport API: Protocols factories, socket callbacks, framing, encoding, HTTP, OAuth, OSC and MIDI. | QML device API: root types, parameter trees, Device operations and device-specific callbacks. | . Use a Mapper device for custom sockets and persistent mappings. Use the HTTP, WebSocket or Serial device when its tree-oriented API matches your hardware or service. These roots have their own callback contracts; do not copy raw socket callbacks into them.

1467.title: Transport selection
1467.content: Start with the transport factory table, then the socket lifecycle and worked examples. Backend availability depends on the platform and build.

1468.title: Framing and encoding are different
1468.content: TCP and serial need explicit message-boundary handling. Use the framing and encoding reference to match the other endpoint. The Serial device root has its own framing names.

1469.title: HTTP requests
1469.content: For arbitrary methods, headers, JSON bodies and response status codes, see Protocols.http. For parameter-driven requests with local tree updates, see the separate HTTP device API.

1470.title: OAuth
1470.content: The OAuth reference documents the build requirements, authorization-code flow, callback shape and trusted-response caveat. Register your own service application and keep tokens out of shared scores.

1471.title: OSC and MIDI payloads
1471.content: See OSC packet parsing and MIDI / UMP enumeration and ports. An OSC parser does not open a socket; a MIDI port must exist before it can be opened.

1472.title: Troubleshooting and scope
1472.content: Validate QML first, then diagnose addresses, permissions, framing and encoding independently using the transport troubleshooting guide. Begin with loopback and avoid exposing listeners to untrusted networks. For an operator’s browser controlling score rather than a client/device integration, see Remote Control.

1473.title: Quick start
1473.content: ossia score 3.8.0 . This is the ossia score quick start manual. The following pages will guide you through score interface and general workflow. They also cover some of the basic elements available to author advanced scenarios such as snapshots saving and recalling, automations, as well as using audio and video files. These will get you started with the various ways score can be used to author flexible and structured scenarios for live performances, art installations or other media-based works. To try score without installing the desktop application, see Using score in the browser. That guide explains browser requirements, permissions, project archives and desktop-only limitations. Enjoy advanced scenario authoring for your intermedia creation ! .

1474.title: Qwen LLM
1474.content: The Qwen LLM process enables local inference of Qwen language models for text generation, conversation, and creative applications within score.

1475.title: Overview
1475.content: Qwen (通义千问) is a series of large language models that can be run locally for: . | Text generation and completion | Interactive conversations | Code generation | Creative writing | Real-time text processing in performances | .
