The same rules apply everywhere. They hold when a process reads an address from the network, when it reads an address that another process wrote earlier in the same tick, when two processes are connected with a cable, and when a process writes to an address. On the way out, the value is converted to the unit of the device’s parameter, and the parameter’s own clip mode decides what happens if it is out of range: score does not clip it beforehand. | Written by | To | Sent to the device | . | a port in distance.m writing 1.5 | /height, declared in distance.mm | 1500 | . | a port in distance.m writing 1.5, ranged [0; 2] | /height, declared in distance.m, ranged [0; 10] | 1.5: the clip mode of /height applies | . | a port without a unit writing 1.5, ranged [0; 2] | /x, ranged [0; 10] | 7.5 | .

1897.title: Using score in the browser
1897.content: Open score for the web to work without installing the desktop application. Only features supported by web browsers can be used in the WASM builds of score.

1898.title: Before starting
1898.content: Use an up-to-date browser with WebAssembly JavaScript Promise Integration (JSPI). The loader checks for WebAssembly.Suspending and WebAssembly.promising and explains which APIs are missing if it cannot start. The threaded build needs shared WebAssembly memory and a cross-origin-isolated page. Use the hosted HTTPS application rather than opening a downloaded HTML file directly. Audio uses Web Audio (MiniAudio) and an AudioWorklet; camera capture also needs getUserMedia, MediaStreamTrackProcessor and WebCodecs video frames. Allow time for the application and its bundled library to download. The application, imported media and decoded media consume browser memory: start with a small project before trying a large desktop session.

1899.title: Open a document and bring in media
1899.content: . | Use File → Open to select a .score, .scorejson, .scorebin or project .zip file. The browser grants access to the selected file, not its entire surrounding folder. | Drop supported media files into the timeline as on desktop. score copies the dropped bytes into its virtual filesystem; it cannot follow arbitrary paths on your computer. | For an existing project with media, prefer a project ZIP archive rather than a bare score file. Absolute desktop media paths are not accessible to the web application. Package the project on desktop with Archive project…, then open the ZIP in the browser. | . The application includes a snapshot of the user library. Presets requiring desktop-only processes, devices or external files need adapting for the browser. Opening a shared URL . The page accepts ?open= followed by a document or project ZIP URL, for example: . https://ossia.io/score-web/?open=/path/to/project.zip . Replace /path/to/project.zip with a document served from the same origin as the application (same scheme, host and port). For a file on another site, download it first and use File → Open. The URL importer accepts stored or deflated ZIPs, but not ZIP64. Downloads are limited to 256 MiB and total extracted file data to 512 MiB. Playback memory requirements depend on the project’s media and processing.

1900.title: Audio and camera permissions
1900.content: Interact with the page before starting playback: browser autoplay policies can suspend audio until a user gesture. The Web Audio backend requests microphone input, so the browser may show a microphone permission prompt even when you first intend to play a score. Captured input remains silent until permission is granted. Check the site’s permissions if input is missing. Camera discovery may request permission to read device names. Allow camera access, select the camera in score, and check the browser’s camera indicator. Capture requires HTTPS and the camera APIs listed above.

1901.title: Save outside the tab
1901.content: Save / Save As downloads a JSON .score document through the browser. This file contains the score, not its media. Use Archive project… to download a ZIP containing the document and its collected project media. Relink missing media before archiving, and save the download before closing or reloading the tab. Preferences and crash-recovery data use the site’s local storage. Clearing site data or using private browsing can remove them. Imported media lives in memory, so download a project archive to keep it.

1902.title: When to use the desktop application
1902.content: . | JavaScript processes do not execute in the web build. | Desktop VST/LV2 plug-ins and native hardware drivers require desktop score. | Browser networking supports browser-compatible transports and endpoints, rather than raw desktop OSC/UDP and TCP sockets. | Keep the tab in the foreground for interactive work. Use desktop score for unattended installations and native device access. | . See Installation for desktop options, or Building for WebAssembly for hosting and build details.

1903.title: Files and utilities API
1903.content: This reference now lives under Reference → Languages. Open the complete Files and utilities API for API details, examples and runtime restrictions. For console setup, library scripts and menu actions, use the Scripting tutorial. Go directly to a relocated section: . | Files and paths | Asynchronous native dialogs | Time | Other helpers | .

1904.title: JavaScript files and utilities API
1904.content: Back to the JavaScript editor API · Examples . Util is available to console and JavaScript process engines. Availability does not make blocking file access, shell commands or GUI dialogs appropriate inside an audio callback. Perform setup outside tick; use native dialogs from GUI-thread code.

1905.title: Files and paths
1905.content: | Function | Behavior | . | fileExists(path), isFile(path), isDir(path) | Test existence and kind. | . | canReadFile(path), canWriteFile(path) | Check filesystem access. | . | readFile(path) | Read bytes. Convert textual results with .toString() where needed. | . | writeFile(path, bytes) | Write file content; this is not an undoable operation. | . | makeDir(path) | Create a directory and missing parents; return whether it exists afterwards. | . | removeFile(path) | Remove a file; true if it is gone, including if absent already. Does not remove directories. | . | listFiles(path, filters) | Absolute paths of files matching glob filters, e.g. "*.scp;*.json"; "" includes all files. | . | listDirectories(path) | Absolute paths of immediate child directories. | . | urlToLocalFile(url) | Convert a local-file URL into a filesystem path. | . | imageSize(path) | Return image dimensions. | . | environmentVariable(name) | Read an environment variable. | . File helpers resolve score’s <LIBRARY>: and <PROJECT>: prefixes. For document-aware conversion, Score.locateFilePath(path) resolves a stored path and Score.relativizeFilePath(path) converts an absolute path for storage. Score.readFile(path) returns text rather than the utility’s byte array. var files = Util.listFiles("<PROJECT>:/", "*.json"); for (var i = 0; i < files.length; ++i) console.log(files[i]); console.log(Util.environmentVariable("HOME")); . Do not confuse these prefixes with a QML component’s base URL. A file-backed JavaScript process keeps its source location for relative imports and resources; see Javascript.

1906.title: Asynchronous native dialogs
1906.content: Util.openFileDialog("Choose data", "JSON files (*.json)", "", function(path) { if (path !== "") console.log(Util.readFile(path).toString()); }); . | openFileDialog(title, filters, folder, onAccept) selects a file. | saveFileDialog(title, filters, folder, defaultName, onAccept) selects a save path; the callback must write the file. | openColorDialog(title, initialColor, onAccept) selects an RGBA color and returns #AARRGGBB on acceptance. | . Callbacks receive "" on cancellation. Dialogs are owned by the active editor/output window, with the main window as fallback. If the owner is destroyed, the dialog is removed without calling back. Keep the script engine alive until completion; these functions do not synchronously return the chosen value.

1907.title: Time
1907.content: Util.toSeconds(value), toMilliseconds(value) and toTime(value) convert model time values; isInfinite(value) tests infinity. timevalFromMilliseconds(ms) constructs a time value. Raw model dates and durations use flicks (705,600,000 per second), while Score.scrub and Score.playFromHere use milliseconds. timestamp() returns seconds from a monotonic clock, useful for measuring elapsed time; it is not the position of score’s transport or a calendar timestamp.

1908.title: Other helpers
1908.content: . | uuid() generates a UUID string. | layoutTextLines(text, font, pointSize, maxWidth) inserts line breaks using a simple text-layout algorithm. | imagePixelColor(image, x, y) reads physical-pixel coordinates from a captured QImage; invalid coordinates or null images return transparent. A path string is not an image object. | shell(command, onFinish) launches a shell command and invokes its completion callback. Only use trusted command text; it runs with the application’s permissions. | settings(uid) accesses an installed settings object’s properties by its UID; settings are build-dependent. | . The console’s Library object provides installedPackages(), refreshAvailablePackages(), availablePackages() and installPackage(uid). Refresh and installation are asynchronous; a refresh call does not mean the package list has already arrived. System exposes isDeviceMDMEnrolled(), availableCudaDevice() and availableCudaToolkitDylibs(major, minor) for platform-dependent capability queries, not guarantees that a process can use those capabilities. Source: Utils.hpp and Utils.cpp.

1910.title: Value delay
1910.content: Value delay retains the history of In and produces Out, a list of delayed taps, plus Mix, a blend of the current input and first echo. It accepts control values, not audio. See Time Chooser for entering absolute or tempo-relative Time values. | Count sets the number of taps. | Mode: Ticks spaces taps by Length processing ticks; this depends on execution settings. | Mode: Messages spaces taps by Length received messages rather than elapsed time. | Mode: Time uses the Time chooser for spacing; musical durations follow the tempo. | Feedback mixes echoes back into the delay line. Mix ranges from current input (0) to first echo (1). | Freeze stops recording new input and repeats the retained delay segment. Clear empties history. | Smooth interpolates between recorded values in Time mode. | . Numbers, matching vectors and numeric lists can be blended. Other values, such as strings, are delayed without numeric interpolation. Use Buffer queue instead when explicit push/pop and output triggers are needed.

1911.title: Value Display
1911.content: Visualize control signals in real-time for monitoring, debugging, and performance feedback. Value Display shows you the current value being ouput from a given node, or an input OSC or network message. Simply connect it to an output and watch the result. The inspector allows to select how many recent values are retained. The small light above the input port flashes on value arrival, including repeated values whose displayed text does not change. It remains lit while messages keep arriving and fades when they stop. Use it to distinguish a constant stream from a source that sent one value and then became silent.

1912.title: Related processes
1912.content: score comes with multiple processes for monitoring input data Signal Display, LED View, Point2D View.

1913.title: Delayed value feedback
1913.content: . Create variation without drawing a long automation curve. Each value in this patch becomes the seed of the next calculation, producing a trace that keeps changing even though the rule stays the same. The signal is shown in a display; nothing is heard or rendered. Try this on web . Download the example .

1914.title: Try it
1914.content: Start playback and watch the Signal display. Micromap repeatedly applies 3.68 x (1-x), beginning with the Float value as a seed. The result returns through Float and becomes the next input: the system’s recent state drives its future. | Set a new seed strictly between zero and one. The trace never repeats like an LFO. Try a nearby seed: after a few steps the two traces diverge completely. | Change the coefficient from 3.68 to 2.5. The values settle to a resting point instead of continuing their irregular motion. | Restore 3.68 to bring back the continuous movement. | . The return cable is delayed by one tick. This makes the loop an iteration using the preceding result instead of an immediate dependency cycle. Keep that delay when replacing the expression with another recurrence. No external files or devices are needed. If you connect the result to sound, light or motion in your own work, map it to an appropriate range first; the numerical experiment alone does not establish safe limits for a destination.

1915.title: Value Filter
1915.content: Value filter is a toolkit for letting incoming values go through according to multiple parameters: . | Is the value repeating or close to the last incoming value? (Noise gate) | . For instance, to turn the following input: . 0 1 1 1 0 1 0 0 1 . Into . 0 1 0 1 0 1 . or, with some margin: . 0.1 0.8 1.1 -0.1 -0.08 1.02 . into . 0.1 0.8 -0.1 1.02 . | Is the value close in time to another value? . | Do we want to clamp this value ? . | If clamped, do we want to filter the repetition of the clamped values too? (Repetition filter) . | .

1916.title: Value serialization
1916.content: Serialize converts Value to a raw string on Bytes. Deserialize converts Bytes back to Value. Both provide Success and Error outlets; Error is empty on success, and a failure clears the result rather than leaving the previous result valid.

1917.title: Formats
1917.content: . | JSON: strict UTF-8 JSON. Impulses become null, lists and vectors become arrays. Serialize’s Pretty print indents JSON without reducing precision. | CBOR: the JSON-compatible subset, with UTF-8 text map keys. Tags, byte strings and undefined values are not supported. | Text: Plain writes raw strings, delimited flat lists/vectors, and JSON for nested containers. Set Delimiter and Line ending to agree at both ends. Deserialize’s Interpretation can be Auto, String, Integer, Float, Boolean or List. Use List when a one-field list must remain a list. String preserves text and line endings. | Binary: FreeFlow serializes untagged scalar bytes and flattens lists/vectors; decoding uses the chosen Scalar type and returns a list. Layout specifies explicitly typed fields. Byte order selects little or big endian unless overridden by the layout. | . A binary Layout uses a subset of Python’s struct notation: for example <B H I f 4s 2x means little-endian packed fields, a four-byte string, and two padding bytes. Ns requires an exact-size raw string; it does not pad or truncate it. Sender and receiver must agree on the layout.

1918.title: Limits and round trips
1918.content: Values must fit score’s int32 and finite float32 representation. The converters enforce limits of 8 MiB, 65,536 nodes and 64 nested containers. Vectors decode as lists, not their original vector type. Text Pretty is a human-readable display with rounded floats, not a lossless archive; use JSON for structured interchange instead. Binary FreeFlow is not self-describing and does not encode maps or impulses. Use String / byte conversion when the next process expects a list of byte integers rather than a raw string.

1919.title: Value Looper
1919.content: . The process named Looper (values) records the values it receives at in into a loop, and plays them back at out: numbers, booleans, vectors, text, lists, maps and impulses, from any source, such as an LFO, a sensor, a controller or another process. It shares its transport, timing, undo, capture and timeline features with the audio looper and the MIDI looper; this page describes what is particular to values.

1920.title: Held values and impulses
1920.content: A value is held until the next one, as a parameter keeps the last value it was sent: playing the loop sends each value where it came, and nothing in between. At the end of the loop, the value held carries on into its start; nothing is sent again unless it changes. An impulse is not held: it fires where it came, as a note would, every time round. Only a new value is recorded: a value equal to the one before it is left out, so a source that sends the same value over and over takes no room in the loop. Two values of the same type are equal when they hold the same thing, a list or a map element by element; an int and a float are never equal. Of several values that come on the same sample, the last one is kept. Every impulse counts, one a sample. A recording starts with the value the input held when it starts: a value that does not move during the first beat is in the loop all the same.

1921.title: Passes and overdubs
1921.content: Each recording or overdub is a pass, kept as a layer of its own. Undo hides the last pass, Redo shows it again, Clear forgets everything; Undo or Clear during a recording starts it again at once. An overdub holds the value from its first new value to its end: before it is touched, the passes under it are heard; from the first new value on, what the overdub recorded is heard instead, and the value it holds while nothing new comes in is the last one it recorded; after the end of the pass, the passes under it are heard again, from the value they hold there. An overdub that only listens, without the input moving, leaves the loop as it was. Impulses of every pass are heard: an overdub adds its impulses to the ones under it. An overdub that goes round the loop more than once writes over what it recorded the round before, as a tape would: the second time round, the value it holds is the value of the input, whether it moves or not. With Passes on Per cycle, each round is a layer of its own instead. An overdub pass becomes a layer when its first value comes in, not when the overdub starts: until then the overdub runs but there is no new layer, no lane for it in the view, and Undo still takes out the last layer there is. The layer starts where the overdub began. An overdub that gets nothing writes no take, adds no layer and merges nothing; with Per cycle, a round that gets nothing is no layer either. Past Max layers, the room for the new layer is made when its first value comes in. Max layers, 2 to 32, default 8, and At max layers, in the Overdub tab, work as for the other loopers. Two merged passes are heard as they were: the newer one still holds the value where it did, and the older one elsewhere.

1922.title: Chasing
1922.content: Whenever what the loop holds where the playhead is changes for another reason than a value of the loop, the value now held is sent at once: . | playing the loop, retriggering it, or the playhead jumping, e.g. with Start from on Loop start or In phase; | muting, unmuting, soloing or erasing a layer, Undo and Redo: a layer that held the value hands it back to the ones under it, and the other way round; | the end of an overdub, where the layers under it are heard again. | . When nothing changes, nothing is sent: stopping and playing again from where it was sends nothing if the value held is the same.

1923.title: Record, Overdub and the Switches tab
1923.content: Mode, the Switches, Layers and Speed tabs and the settings Quantize, After record, After overdub, Start from and Stop at work as for the audio looper. Record on a loop that has something in it overdubs it: Clear the loop first to record a new one. Late stop (ms) works as for the other loopers: a recording asked to stop a little after a grid point ends on that point, and what came in since belongs to the overdub that follows.

1924.title: Passthrough
1924.content: Passthrough, in the Play tab, chooses when the input goes out as well as the loop: never, while recording or overdubbing only, or always (Full, the default). With Full, the input wins while it moves: a value that comes in goes out, and the loop does not send anything of its own for the next 0.2 seconds; once the input has stopped moving, the loop takes over again from the value it holds there.

1925.title: The view
1925.content: The view shows one lane per pass, as the other loopers do: up to 32 lanes, sharing the height of the view, the oldest passes sharing the first lane when there are more. Each lane draws what its pass holds: . | numbers and booleans as steps, scaled to the numbers that lane holds; a vector, or a list of numbers, by its first number; | text, lists and maps as a line across the middle of the lane, a tick where each one starts; | impulses as ticks across the lane. | . What the loop does not play there, e.g. what a later pass holds over, is dimmed. The m and x of each lane mute and erase it, on the grid.

1926.title: Takes and the timeline
1926.content: When a recording or an overdub ends, what is heard of the loop is written to a small file of its own, a .values file, which keeps every value where it is heard, with its type. Export chooses what Send, and a drag from its button, place, and the files the take written when a recording or an overdub ends has: what is heard of the whole loop (Mix, the default), each pass in a file of its own (Layers), or both, a box for each file. A take that Send or a drag asks for, or that the score’s stop leaves, has all of them, so that Export can be changed afterwards. When every value of a take is a number, a boolean, a vector, or a list of numbers and booleans, a click on Send in the view, or a drag from that button, places it in the timeline as automations: one for each number of the values, so three for a vector of three, four for lists of four floats such as Arraygen sends, in one box, where the take was recorded. Values of different sizes can be mixed: the take has as many automations as the longest value has numbers, at most 32. A value that has fewer numbers leaves the others where they were, and before an index first has a number, its first number holds. The automations of a vector are named by its axes, x, y, z and w; those of lists by their index, from 0. Each automation holds each value until the next, in steps, its minimum and maximum those of the take; the box is as long as the loop, in bars, whatever the tempo it was played at, and the automations loop as the box is made longer; dropped on a box that is already there, they are as long as that box and play the loop round over it. They can be edited, given an address or cabled as any automation. One undo removes the box. Dragging a lane places that layer alone, as automations in a box of its own, when its values are all numbers as above; its file is written when the drag starts if the take has none, the lane saying Preparing meanwhile. A take with impulses, text, maps, lists holding anything but numbers and booleans, or more than 32 numbers, is kept as a file only: the button of the view says File instead of Send, nothing is placed in the timeline, and its lanes drag nothing. The file is plain JSON, and can be read by any other tool. While a recording or an overdub goes on, Send or a drag from it asks for a take of the loop as it is at that moment; the Send button says Saving until it is written. When the score stops while a pass is taken in, the pass is closed as any. The score’s stop leaves a take with the mix and a file for each layer whenever the last take does not have them all as the loop is, even though the looper is gone by then: the view, saying Stopped with the score, still drags each lane’s layer, and Send still places what Export says, Export being changed once the score is stopped too.

1927.title: Reverse and speed
1927.content: Reverse and Speed, in the Speed tab, work as for the other loopers. Played backwards, a value goes back to the one it had before: going back over a point where the value changed, the loop sends the value it held before that point. Impulses fire where they came. At Speed x2, the values come twice as often. An overdub records where the playhead goes: what is played over the reversed loop plays reversed when it goes forwards again.

1928.title: Tempo changes
1928.content: With Follow tempo, on by default and in the Speed tab, the loop plays at the tempo of the score: a loop recorded over two bars lasts two bars whatever the tempo becomes. Off, it keeps the speed it was recorded at. Past the end works as for the other loopers: an overdub can make the loop longer, the passes under it repeating.

1929.title: Capture
1929.content: Record starts taking in when it is pressed, or on the next grid point. Capture, in the Length tab next to Capture bars, works backwards: it takes the values that already came in, recorded or not. You move things first, and decide afterwards that it was worth keeping. | With no loop, the last Capture bars bars of values become the loop, and it plays at once; Mode shows Play. The loop starts with the value the input held just before those bars. | Over a loop, the values that came in over the last round of the loop become a new layer on top, as if that round had been an overdub pass: each value lands where it came in the loop, and holds from its first new value to where the round ended. The loop keeps its length: Capture bars does not apply, one round is taken. A stopped loop is taken as going round where it would be had it kept playing, as In phase has it, and it plays from there. Max layers and At max layers make room for the layer as for an overdub pass, muted layers stay muted, and a take is written as for any pass that closes. When no new value came in over that round, no layer is made, as for an overdub that gets nothing. | . Undo takes the captured layer out and Redo brings it back, as for any pass. On an empty loop, Undo empties the loop as it does after a first recording. Pressed shortly after a point of the grid, within Late stop, Capture ends on that point, as a late stop would. Capture does nothing while a recording or an overdub is going on. The value looper always keeps the last 4096 values it received, so there is nothing to set up; a busy input only lets Capture look back as far as those values go.

1930.title: Comping and Start from In phase
1930.content: Comping with New layer, Passes on Per cycle, Solo layer, Mute layer and Erase layer, and Start from on In phase, work as for the audio looper.

1931.title: Presets
1931.content: Each preset sets every setting; mode changes wait for the bar unless said otherwise, and the input always goes out. | Preset | What it is for | . | Two bar gesture | A recording of two bars, then plays it. | . | Free gesture | No grid, no Record bars, no Late stop: the loop is as long as it was played for. | . | A layer per round | Two bars, then one overdub, a layer each time round the loop; once there are 16, a new layer replaces a muted one. | . | Takes for automation | Four bars; Export on Both: takes are written as a mix and as a file for each layer, to place them in the timeline as automations. | .

1932.title: What it does not have
1932.content: The value looper loops one stream of values. It has no Feedback, no Held notes, Note grid, Strength or Note ends, no Transpose and no channels, which are about sound or notes, and no Overdub mode: impulses always merge, other values are always held by the pass that last moved them. It has no Grace either: a recording starts with the value held, which is what a value played just before it is.

1933.title: Capacity
1933.content: A loop holds up to 8192 values, whatever their type. When it is full, the view says so and further values are not recorded. Numbers, booleans, vectors and impulses take no other memory; text, lists and maps take what they hold.

1935.title: Vertex Shader Art reference
1935.content: This is the canonical shader contract for the Vertex Shader Art process. For GLSL syntax, generated declarations and portability, see GLSL runtime reference. For worked tasks, see Shader cookbook. This integrates the Vertex Shader Art convention into score’s shader runtime. The JSON MODE and ISF-style input declarations are score’s integration contract, not a standard ISF rendering mode. Vertices are procedural; score supplies the fragment stage that displays v_color. Use raw raster when you need to author both stages.

1936.title: Header
1936.content: A VSA shader is an ISF-style shader with MODE: "VERTEX_SHADER_ART". "MODE": "VERTEX_SHADER_ART" . Common VSA fields: . | Field | Description | . | POINT_COUNT | Number of vertices to generate. | . | PRIMITIVE_MODE | POINTS, LINES, LINE_STRIP, or compatible VSA primitive mode. | . | LINE_SIZE | Line / point sizing policy used by imported VSA shaders. | . | BACKGROUND_COLOR | Clear color. | . | INPUTS | ISF-style controls, textures, and audio inputs. | . The process also supports the standard ISF metadata fields such as DESCRIPTION, CREDIT, CATEGORIES, and ISFVSN.

1937.title: Shader variables
1937.content: The shader writes the normal vertex outputs: . gl_Position = vec4(...); // clip-space position gl_PointSize = ...; // point size when drawing points v_color = vec4(...); // color passed to the fixed fragment stage . Typical VSA examples also use: . vertexId // current vertex index time // playback time resolution // render size . ISF-style controls declared in INPUTS are available as uniforms. VSA clip-space depth follows its original OpenGL-style convention; the runtime maps it to the backend’s clip range. Do not add the raw-raster isf_vertShaderInit() / isf_vertShaderFinish() sequence or a second backend depth correction to a VSA shader. To understand how individual vertices make an image, start with the triangle recipe in Shader cookbook. It places three vertices and gives them one color; changing a vertex position changes the silhouette without loading a mesh. Point and line sizes remain GPU/backend-dependent.

1938.title: Example
1938.content: Build a rotating, colored spiral from points rather than an image texture. Each vertex’s index determines its angle and distance from the center; playback time rotates the pattern. In the code below, try reducing radius to gather the points toward the center, then change the 0.05 angle increment to alter how tightly the spiral winds. /*{ "DESCRIPTION": "Simple VSA spiral", "CREDIT": "ossia score", "ISFVSN": "2", "MODE": "VERTEX_SHADER_ART", "CATEGORIES": ["Geometry", "Animated"], "POINT_COUNT": 20000, "PRIMITIVE_MODE": "POINTS", "BACKGROUND_COLOR": [0, 0, 0, 1], "INPUTS": [ { "NAME": "radius", "TYPE": "float", "DEFAULT": 0.8, "MIN": 0.1, "MAX": 2.0 } ] }*/ void main() { float i = vertexId; float a = i * 0.05 + time; float r = radius * sqrt(i / 20000.0); vec2 p = vec2(cos(a), sin(a)) * r; gl_Position = vec4(p, 0.0, 1.0); gl_PointSize = 2.0; v_color = vec4(0.5 + 0.5 * cos(a + vec3(0.0, 2.0, 4.0)), 1.0); } .

1939.title: Video Manipulation
1939.content: A looping cat movie leaves traces and breaks into a circular pattern as sound changes its treatment. The movie file itself is never modified.

1940.title: Audio analysis to shader controls
1940.content: The movie passes through Echo Trace, which retains parts of earlier images, and Circular Screen, which adds a patterned surface. A microphone-analysis branch filters the sound with YBandpass and measures its level with RMS; those changing values control the visual effects. The Bass pattern sequencer is not the source of this response. The same footage reacts differently to a voice, an instrument or a recording. The ISF shaders expose their parameters as inlets, so audio analysis can be replaced by automation when a composed sequence is more appropriate.

1941.title: Setup
1941.content: Open the ZIP directly in score and select a working microphone input. Use a build with the Airwindows YBandpass process. To work without a microphone, connect a sound-file process in place of the live analysis source. The movie is credited to Andrew Kota on Pexels and is converted to HAP for looping and scrubbing.

1942.title: Try it
1942.content: . | Start playback, make sound, and adjust RMS sensitivity until quiet and loud sounds produce visibly different treatments. Move YBandpass’s frequency to choose which part of the sound drives that response. | Change the Video inspector’s stretch mode to either preserve the movie’s proportions or fill the output. | Double-click the time ruler and drag while holding the mouse button to scrub. Drag smoothly, then jump, and watch how Echo Trace’s trails differ. | . The main interval has a manual ending time-sync: the movie keeps looping until you trigger it. Try this on web . Download this example .

1943.title: Learn more
1943.content: . | Video - Video playback process and supported formats | ISF Shaders - Interactive Shader Format effects | Graphics pipeline - How rendering works in ossia score | Supported protocols and formats - Complete list of supported video codecs | .

1945.title: Video Examples
1945.content: Start with the kind of image you want to make: footage that reacts to a performer, patterns that grow from their own history, or a composition that spans a physical space. Each patch isolates one technique.

1946.title: Make an image respond
1946.content: For a first patch, open Video manipulation: a looping movie becomes patterned traces controlled by sound. Then choose where your image and its control should come from: . | Camera input keeps a live subject visible while sound changes its color, blur and distortion. | Audio-reactive visuals combines generated percussion and live sound to animate a geometric pattern. | Camera blobs, contours and tracking reduces the camera view to regions, outlines and tracked positions for camera-based interaction. | .

1947.title: Compose motion and timing
1947.content: . | Video transforms and fitting separates moving an image from fitting it to a display’s proportions. | Scrubbing video and scenario time makes speed, reversal and jumps through an arrangement playable controls. | Timed sound and image effects composes image distortion and changing reverberation with independently editable audio and video. | FFmpeg input and output streams sends a treated image to another application while retaining a separate local treatment. | .

1948.title: Let patterns develop
1948.content: Begin with Delayed shader texture feedback to see how repeatedly processing an earlier frame turns a moving dot into a complex trail. | Layered analog-style effects mixes fresh procedural patterns with distressed image history. | Reaction-diffusion geometry feedback grows organic structures by retaining simulation state instead of an image. | Compute-rendered Clifford attractor accumulates points into a slowly changing mathematical form. | Multiple shader render targets produces color, image-derived normals and edges from the same changing source. | .

1949.title: Fit the work to a space
1949.content: Mapping textures to editable shapes composes images within quads, polygons and freehand outlines. Use it when the shapes themselves are part of the composition. Multi-projector output mapping aligns and blends an already composed image across displays. The two techniques can be combined.

1950.title: Reference and setup
1950.content: See Video for playback modes, HDR conversion and pixel formats, ISF shaders for image effects, and Compute Shaders for GPU computation. Capture, streaming and output backends are listed under Devices; availability depends on platform and build. Each example notes its particular camera, package or output requirements.

1951.title: Video formats and color
1951.content: This reference describes score’s graphics/media pipeline. Features depend on the score build, FFmpeg version, graphics API, drivers and optional devices; it is not a universal codec or hardware support matrix.

1952.title: Container, codec and pixels are different
1952.content: A .mov, .mkv, .mp4, .mxf or transport-stream (.ts, .mts, .m2ts) file is a container. Its video codec must first be decoded. The resulting pixel format describes how samples are laid out: RGB or YUV, packed or planar, bit depth, chroma subsampling and possibly alpha. For example, software-decoded HEVC can produce 10-bit YUV which score uploads and converts to RGB on the GPU. This does not make the HEVC codec hardware-decoded. Conversely, a hardware decoder may still need to copy its decoded frames through CPU memory if its surfaces cannot be imported by the selected graphics backend.

1953.title: Choosing footage and playback
1953.content: The Video process offers Auto, Direct (seek) and Frame queue playback. Auto chooses Direct for HAP/DXV and streams classified as having every frame independently accessible; other streams use buffered playback. Long-GOP files remain expensive to scrub even when the codec is hardware-accelerated. | HAP and DXV have dedicated compressed-texture paths. HAP variants include alpha and higher-quality variants; their use still depends on the GPU’s block-compression support. They are not equivalent to H.264 hardware decoding. | CineForm, ProRes, DNxHD, MJPEG and other production codecs are decoded through the available FFmpeg implementation. The decoded format, not the codec name alone, selects the subsequent GPU conversion. | Transport streams can be imported as files. A live URL is better handled by a Libav device or GStreamer device; live sources do not acquire arbitrary timeline seeking. | Image sequences are understood by FFmpeg’s image-sequence demuxer when supplied a sequence path, such as frame%04d.png. This is different from dropping several images into an Image process, where Index chooses the image. A Libav input can supply the sequence path and demuxer options; dragging a still image uses the Image process instead. | .

1954.title: Hardware decoding
1954.content: In graphics preferences, Hardware Video Decoding controls codec acceleration, independently of the Video process’s Playback setting: . | None uses software codec decoding. GPU upload, pixel conversion and effects still run normally. | Auto chooses candidates using the platform, codec and graphics API. The direct renderer attempts viable candidates before software fallback; the frame-queue decoder has its own platform-preferred selection. | Explicit choices request a particular backend. Depending on build and platform, the list can include CUDA, Intel QuickSync, VDPAU, VA-API, Windows DXVA2, Direct3D 11 / Direct3D 12, macOS Video Toolbox, ARM Linux V4L2-M2M, and Vulkan Video. Only choices exposed by the installed build should be expected. | . A backend being listed does not guarantee that it can decode a particular profile, bit depth or resolution. Failed hardware setup can fall back to software decoding. Failed direct surface import can instead fall back to hardware decoding followed by CPU transfer and upload. Vulkan Video in particular needs compatible FFmpeg, Qt, driver and device capabilities; not every Vulkan renderer can decode video. Decoding threads configures software decoders. Auto selects the thread model and count per codec; a numerical choice limits the pool, not the codec’s threading model. More threads are not always better when several videos run together.

1955.title: Pixel formats and precision
1955.content: The current conversion paths cover common 8-bit YUV 4:2:0, 4:2:2 and 4:4:4; planar 10-, 12- and selected 16-bit YUV; alpha-bearing YUV; NV12/NV21 and other semi-planar formats; packed RGB/RGBA; planar RGB and floating-point RGB. Additional paths handle palettes, grayscale, packed bit-field RGB and raw Bayer images. These are conversion capabilities, not a promise that every input protocol exposes every format. Important distinctions: . | P010 is 10-bit 4:2:0 with 16-bit storage lanes; P210 is 10-bit 4:2:2; P216 uses all 16 bits of its 4:2:2 samples. They are not interchangeable with 8-bit NV12. | V210 packs groups of 10-bit 4:2:2 samples into words with padded rows. Dedicated wire-format conversion serves compatible capture paths. FFmpeg can also decode V210 files to planar frames. This does not imply that video/x-raw,format=v210 is accepted by every GStreamer input. | XYZ12 is the DCI X′Y′Z′ representation used by some digital-cinema material. The xyz12le path applies its own code-value normalization and XYZ-to-RGB conversion rather than treating it as ordinary YUV. | Alpha must survive both the source format and the destination. A texture can contain alpha while a chosen encoder, wire format or receiving application discards it. | .

1956.title: HDR and color output
1956.content: Correct appearance depends on more than bit depth: color primaries, matrix coefficients, transfer function and full versus limited range all matter. score’s conversion uses available metadata to select YUV matrices and range handling, including BT.601, BT.709 and BT.2020 paths. Incorrect or missing source metadata can produce wrong brightness, contrast or hue; choosing a different decoder does not repair mislabeled footage. The Video inspector’s Format setting controls the texture sent downstream: . | Format | Purpose | . | SDR | Convert HDR content for an SDR-oriented chain, with the selected tone mapper. | . | Passthrough | Preserve the HDR-oriented representation rather than applying SDR tone mapping. The next stage must understand it. | . | Linear | Convert into linear light for processing. | . | Normalized | Linear light normalized by peak luminance. | . Tonemap (HDR) offers Clamp, BT.2390, BT.2446, Reinhard, Hable, ACES2, AgX, PBR Neutral and Auto. Auto resolves PQ/HDR10 to BT.2390 and HLG to Clamp in the existing SDR conversion pipeline. Tone mapping is a rendering choice, not a change to the source file. For an SDR projection workflow, begin with SDR output and assess highlights on the actual destination. For HDR, agree on the representation through every effect and output stage. The Window device separately selects its swapchain format; the operating system, monitor and graphics backend must support that mode. A floating-point texture or an HDR file alone does not establish end-to-end HDR display. Libav and GStreamer outputs expose Input Transfer: this describes the texture arriving from the graph (sRGB, Linear, PQ, HLG or Passthrough), not the transfer function to arbitrarily assign to the source footage. Match it to the upstream process to avoid double conversion.

1957.title: Interlacing
1957.content: Distinguish a full frame with two fields already woven together from sources delivering one half-height field at a time. The latter require reconstruction. In NDI input, Weave retains vertical detail but can show combing on movement; Bob avoids combing by sacrificing vertical detail and displaying at field rate. These controls apply to separately delivered fields, not automatically to every interlaced file.

1958.title: Troubleshooting order
1958.content: . | Check the file or live source’s actual codec, pixel format, rate and color metadata. | Route directly to a known output, without effects, and compare range, colors and alpha. | Try software codec decoding to separate codec/driver problems from texture conversion. | Check the output device’s format and transfer settings independently of the input. | For shared GPU surfaces, try the documented CPU/shared-memory route to isolate interop or DMA-BUF problems. | .

1959.title: Multi-projector output mapping
1959.content: Extend one animated image across several displays or projectors, then align the portions so they read as a continuous composition. The image is composed first; the mapping only fits it to the physical displays.

1960.title: Output mapping
1960.content: The Window device’s Multi-window mode divides a procedural texture into output regions. Each region can be positioned, warped and edge-blended independently. Because this happens at the output, the source could instead be a movie or a texture composed with the rectangle mapper.

1961.title: Set up your displays
1961.content: Before playback, open the Window device settings and assign each output to a screen on your machine. Replace the saved desktop positions and screen indices with your own arrangement. Use the device’s test cards to align the source regions. Double-click a region to edit its perspective transform; use the dashed border controls to adjust edge blending. Adjacent projections need both overlapping source regions and physically aligned images: a soft edge alone cannot repair a misaligned projection.

1962.title: Try it
1962.content: Start playback and follow a feature of the animated source across the configured outputs. Adjust one region’s perspective until the feature lines up across the seam, then its blend border until the overlap is no brighter than its surroundings. No external media or Qt Quick 3D is required. More outputs and larger render sizes increase GPU and display-system requirements; establish a working alignment at a modest resolution before increasing it. Try this on web . Download this example .

1963.title: Mapping textures to editable shapes
1963.content: . Fit moving patterns to a set of shapes instead of filling a rectangular screen. Editable corners, polygons and freehand outlines let you sketch a projection composition around objects or architectural details, with soft edges and blending where shapes overlap.

1964.title: Mapping interface
1964.content: Three generated patterns feed a mapping interface that places them within one viewport. One source rotates and another responds to the pointer, so you can see how motion behaves inside a deformed shape. The mapper produces a composed texture; splitting that image across physical displays is a separate output step.

1965.title: Setup
1965.content: Use a build with JavaScript/QML and Qt Quick 3D, and install the default preset package containing rect-mapper. Keep the preset’s helper scripts and material shaders together: the saved interface still relies on its relative imports. No movie is required.

1966.title: Try it
1966.content: . | Start playback and click rect-mapper’s Show/hide UI button in its process header. Assign a texture to a quad and move its corners; use the checkerboard to see where the image stretches. | Soften a shape’s edges, then change blend or mask settings where shapes overlap. | Double-click the background to start a polygon, or hold Alt/Option while drawing in the background for a freehand shape; both can follow outlines a four-corner quad cannot. | . Reduce Subdivisions from 32 if deformation is too costly; strongly deformed shapes show visible facets at low values. For projection across several displays, send the composed texture to the Window device’s Multi-window mode. Try this on web . Download this example .

1967.title: Video transforms and fitting
1967.content: . See how the same movie changes when it is moved and rotated, then fitted into a different-sized output. Placement and fitting are controlled separately, so a composition can be adapted to a tall screen or a wide projection without changing its motion.

1968.title: Placement versus fitting
1968.content: The first section shows the looping movie unchanged. Transform then animates its translation and rotation. Scale and Fit follows with an animated zoom and a sequence of fitting modes. Continuous automation creates movement, while timeline states switch between discrete ways of occupying the viewport.

1969.title: Try it
1969.content: Open the ZIP directly in score and start playback. The animated transform begins at four seconds. Trigger the manual time-sync at the end of Transform to enter Scale and Fit. | Change the Window render size or aspect ratio, then watch each fitting mode: some preserve the whole image, some crop it, some stretch it. | Alter a Transform automation curve to change the movie’s motion without changing the output proportions. | Watch the zoom animation, then a fitting-mode change: the zoom evolves continuously, while the mode switch changes the rule used to place the image at once. | . Keep the movie and Scale and Fit intervals running to observe the mode sequence; their ending time-syncs are manual. No camera or network source is required. Try this on web . Download this example .

1970.title: Scrubbing video and scenario time
1970.content: . Speed up, reverse and jump through footage as part of a performance. Four manually triggered sections demonstrate a composed tempo curve, rhythmic speed changes, jumps in movie position and scrubbing a whole arrangement of clips and effects.

1971.title: Time-control processes
1971.content: The time-control processes run separately from the media they affect. Their rhythm can therefore keep going while the target clip reverses or jumps. Position is measured in milliseconds; a tempo of 120 corresponds to normal speed. The Cat FX section extends this idea to a nested scenario: changing its time moves through the arrangement, not just through one movie. Sequenced clips and feedback treatments become material to revisit and interrupt. Generated percussion provides an accompanying rhythm.

1972.title: Setup
1972.content: Open the ZIP directly in score. Use a build providing Kaboom and Airwindows for the audio branches, and begin at a low listening level. The cat footage is credited to Andrew Kota on Pexels. For responsive reverse playback and jumps, use an all-intra format such as HAP and the Video inspector’s Direct/Seek mode. Buffered forward playback prioritizes a different use and can lag when scrubbing.

1973.title: Try it
1973.content: . | Start playback and trigger one branch-start time-sync at a time. Watch the target interval’s progress line to see whether time moves continuously or jumps. | Change the LFO driving speed, then a position sequencer’s steps. Watch whether the movie reverses through nearby frames or cuts to a distant point. | Trigger Cat FX and change its time modulation. Notice how this changes which clips and effects are active; move the pointer in the output window to influence its pointer-controlled feedback graphics. | . Try this on web . Download this example .

1974.title: Video
1974.content: The Video process plays a video file into a texture output, which can feed effects or a video output device. FFmpeg decodes the media; score then converts its pixels for the graphics pipeline. These are separate operations: GPU YUV-to-RGB conversion does not mean that the codec itself is hardware-decoded. See Video formats and color for format, hardware-decoder and HDR details.

1975.title: Usage
1975.content: To add a video to a score, the simplest is to drag’n’drop it from the user library to the score. Videos loop by default to facilitate VJ use-cases. Otherwise a black screen would be shown when reaching the end. Do not forget to set a trigger at the end, though ! . The simplest way to play a video is as follows: . | Add a window device | Drop the video | Select the output port of the video process and assign it to the window device. | . See the example: . The Video process exposes a texture output, not an audio output. Extract the soundtrack and place an audio process on the same interval when sound is needed: . The following ffmpeg command can be used to extract audio track from a given input file : . $ ffmpeg -i <input_file> extracted_audio.wav .

1976.title: Inspector controls
1976.content: The video inspector allows to set a stretch mode and the timing behaviour: . | Scale offers Original size, Expand (Black bars), Expand (Fill) and Stretch. | Tempo is used to map the video to the score tempo, and to enable time-stretching with the Tempo process. If Enable tempo is not set, then the video will play at its internal rate. Otherwise, it will assume that the video is at the given tempo, and play it faster / slower depending on the difference between that tempo and the score’s actual playback speed: a video set at 120 will play twice as slow if the score tempo is at 60. | . Playback mode . Three modes are available: . | Auto selects Direct playback for HAP/DXV and streams classified as having a keyframe at every frame; other streams use the frame queue. Selection follows the actual stream layout, not simply its filename extension. | Direct (seek) requests the frame containing the current timeline time. It suits scrubbing and independently decodable frames, but forcing it on long-GOP footage can be expensive. | Frame queue is the normal buffered playback path: frames are decoded ahead and selected according to playback time. Prefer this for sequential playback of inter-frame codecs. | . This setting is independent of Hardware Video Decoding in graphics preferences. None uses software codec decoding; Auto attempts available hardware backends. Hardware and graphics-backend compatibility can require a CPU transfer even when decoding is accelerated. Color output . Format offers SDR, Passthrough, Linear and Normalized. Tonemap (HDR) offers Clamp, BT.2390, BT.2446, Reinhard, Hable, ACES2, AgX, PBR Neutral and Auto. These controls prepare the texture for downstream effects; they do not configure a monitor or turn an SDR window into an HDR output. See Video formats and color before combining HDR sources, shaders and output devices.

1977.title: Limitations
1977.content: Support depends on the FFmpeg build, codec profile and graphics backend. HAP, DXV and intra-frame formats are useful for interactive seeking; H.264 or HEVC footage with long groups of pictures may require decoding from an earlier keyframe when seeking. The importer recognizes transport-stream files including .ts, .mts and .m2ts, as well as common containers such as MOV, MP4, MKV and MXF. A container extension does not identify its codec. To re-encode a video into HAP, use an FFmpeg build with the HAP encoder: . $ ffmpeg -i source.mov -c:v hap <OPTIONS> output.mov $ ffmpeg -i source.mov -c:v hap -format hap_alpha outputName.mov $ ffmpeg -i source.mov -c:v hap -format hap_q outputName.mov $ ffmpeg -i source.mov -c:v hap -compressor none outputName.mov $ ffmpeg -i source.mov -c:v hap -format hap_q -chunks 4 outputName.mov . The (optional) HAP-related options can be: . | -format hap_alpha for alpha-channel support | -format hap_q for HAP Q codec support | -compressor none slightly reduces playback CPU usage at the cost of larger file sizes. | -chunks <N> with N a number between 1 and 64: optimizes the file for a specific multi-core decoding configuration. | .

1978.title: View and interface API
1978.content: This reference now lives under Reference → Languages. Open the complete View and interface API for API details, examples and runtime restrictions. For console setup, library scripts and menu actions, use the Scripting tutorial. Go directly to a relocated section: . | Navigate and capture | Process editors and custom interfaces | Prompt forms | .

1979.title: JavaScript view and interface API
1979.content: Back to the JavaScript editor API · Examples . View operates on score’s editor, not on a process’s texture output. It is available in the console and process UI engine. With no GUI, view navigation has no effect and captures requiring a view fail.

1980.title: Navigate and capture
1980.content: | Call | Action | . | View.zoom(x, y), View.scroll(x, y) | Zoom or scroll the current scenario view. | . | View.setZoomRatio(ratio) | Set the timeline zoom ratio. | . | View.centerOn(process) | Center on a process. | . | View.goToInterval(interval) | Navigate into an interval. | . | View.fit(), View.recenter() | Fit or recenter the view. | . | View.setNodal(enabled), View.isNodal() | Set or query dataflow view mode. | . | View.grabScene(path) | Save the currently visible scene region, respecting scroll and zoom, without main-window panels. | . | View.grabMainWindow(path) | Save the main application window. | . | View.grabScreen(path) | Capture the primary screen, subject to platform capture permissions. | . | View.grabWidget(widget, path) | Capture a particular QWidget. | . Capture functions return a boolean indicating success. They save to disk; they do not return a texture or a QImage. For a stable frame, navigate first and capture after the GUI has processed the update. var panel = View.panel("Device Explorer"); if (panel) console.log(View.grabWidget(panel, "/tmp/devices.png")); . View.panels() lists panel display names and widget class names. View.panel(name) accepts either, case-insensitively; class names avoid translated-label differences. View.child(parent, className) finds the first descendant of a Qt class, for instance a QTreeView. Returned widgets belong to score: do not destroy them. Only Qt-exposed slots/properties are callable from JavaScript.

1981.title: Process editors and custom interfaces
1981.content: var process = Score.parentProcess(Score.selectedObject()); if (process && Score.hasProcessScriptEditor(process)) { Score.setProcessScriptEditorPlacement(process, "Side panel"); Score.showProcessScriptEditor(process, true); } . setProcessScriptEditorPlacement(process, placement) and setProcessUIPlacement(process, placement) accept exactly "Window", "Side panel", "Central" or "" for the user’s default. They configure the script editor and custom UI independently. The side panel docks in the editor; central placement uses the center area; window placement detaches it. Use hasProcessUI(process) / showProcessUI(process, visible) for custom interfaces and hasProcessScriptEditor(process) / showProcessScriptEditor(process, visible) for code editors. A process must actually supply the corresponding interface. See QML custom UI API for ScriptUI, port bindings and imported forms, and Editing workflow for interactive placement controls.

1982.title: Prompt forms
1982.content: Score.prompt(configuration) opens a form and returns an array in widget order, or undefined if cancelled: . var answer = Score.prompt({ title: "Create controls", widgets: [ { name: "Name", type: "lineedit", init: "Control" }, { name: "Count", type: "spinbox", min: 1, max: 16, init: 4 }, { name: "Enabled", type: "checkbox", init: true } ] }); if (answer !== undefined) console.log(answer); . The form also supports textfield and floating-point slider widgets. For file and color pickers use the asynchronous Util dialogs instead. Source: ViewContext.hpp, ViewContext.cpp and EditContext.ui.cpp.

1984.title: Heat volume to point cloud
1984.content: . A moving heat source leaves a field that diffuses and cools over time. Sampling that field as points makes the source’s path visible as a trace that lingers and spreads. The heat simulation writes a three-dimensional texture. Noise warps that texture before VolumeToVoxels samples it into point geometry, which Model Display views from an orbiting camera. The motion of the source, deformation of the field and motion of the viewpoint are separate parts of the image.

1985.title: Try it
1985.content: Start playback and bring the warp amount toward zero to see the underlying heat field. Increase it again to distort the form, then vary VolumeToVoxels’ threshold to reveal different parts of the field. Lower resolution for coarse sampling or raise it for a denser cloud; higher values increase the workload. Use the heat shader’s clear control to reset accumulated state and watch a new trace form. No voxel file is needed, but the simulation and conversion require compute-shader support. The points render with native Model display. Try this on web . Download this example .

1986.title: Volumetric texture viewers
1986.content: . Look inside a fractal as well as around it. Three cross-sections and three raymarched views share the same Mandelbulb volume. The generator writes a three-dimensional texture. Slice viewers read individual planes through it, while raymarching viewers sample through its depth or reveal a surface at a chosen threshold. A grid places the results together, so changing the source has a visible effect across all six views.

1987.title: Try it
1987.content: Start playback and change the Mandelbulb’s power or zoom: all six views update together. Move just one sliceZ control to explore a different cross-section without changing the source. Then vary an isosurface viewer’s iso threshold. This chooses a different boundary within the same field; it does not generate a new volume. No mesh or volume file is required; the embedded generator needs a graphics backend with compute-shader support. This uses native volume textures, not a Qt Quick 3D scene. Try this on web . Download this example .

1988.title: Voxels with procedural sky
1988.content: A voxel model sits beneath a changing sky, with volumetric clouds above it and depth-based lighting giving the foreground shape. The clouds come from a generated volume, while the model is rendered as geometry. Depth keeps the sky behind the foreground in score’s reverse-Z rendering system. Depth-based shadows, shading and a moving light treatment add detail before bloom, grain and chromatic aberration finish the image. The sky and depth effects need the same viewpoint as the voxel renderer. Shared Eye and Target controls drive both paths; keep them aligned when adapting the composition.

1989.title: Try it
1989.content: Open the ZIP directly in score; the voxel model is included. Start playback and vary the cloud settings, then the depth-effect strengths. Adjust Bloom last: it adds glow to the finished image without changing the sky or the surface shading. To use your own supported voxel asset, select it in Voxel file and adjust the loader’s transform to frame it. Rendering is native, and compute-shader support is required. The depth shaders also include depth_helpers.glsl: install the csf-examples package with its shaderlib/depth directory intact, even though the main shader code is stored in the score. Try this on web . Download this example .

1990.title: Deforming a voxel model
1990.content: . A block-built model takes on a gentle, fluid movement while colored outlines emphasize its edges. Voxel loader converts the asset to geometry. A compute shader deforms it under LFO control, then the renderer, outline effect and tone mapping shape the final image. Geometry changes and image treatments remain independently adjustable.

1991.title: Try it
1991.content: Open the ZIP directly in score; the voxel model is included. Start playback and vary the LFO’s amplitude to change the driven deformation amount, then adjust Deform’s radius. Outline color and opacity change the edges; Tonemap exposure changes the brightness of the whole image. Change the loader’s Mode and switch to point rendering to see how each mode builds the geometry. The outline effect has no camera buffer connected in this score, so do not treat it as the camera-aware depth setup used by the other scene examples. Rendering is native; use a compute-capable graphics backend. The outline shader is embedded but still includes depth_helpers.glsl; install the csf-examples shader package with its shaderlib/depth directory intact. Try this on web . Download this example .

1992.title: Vertex Shader Art
1992.content: . The Vertex Shader Art process runs shaders based on the Vertex Shader Art convention. A VSA shader generates vertices procedurally in the vertex stage; the fragment stage only displays the color produced by the vertex shader. Use VSA for lightweight point clouds, line art, particle-like procedural visuals, and imported Vertex Shader Art examples. Use Render Pipeline instead when you need custom fragment shading, geometry inputs, buffers, depth / blend state, or scene rendering.

1993.title: Authoring a visual
1993.content: Use the Vertex Shader Art reference for header fields, vertex outputs, time and resolution variables, and a complete rotating spiral. Begin with the three-vertex recipe in Shader cookbook to see how positions and colors form the image. Connect the resulting texture to a video output. Point and line sizes depend on the GPU/backend. Go directly to a relocated section: . | Header | Shader variables | Example | .

1994.title: Related Processes
1994.content: . | ISF Shaders: Fullscreen fragment shaders. | Compute Shaders: Compute shaders for images, buffers, and geometry. | Render Pipeline: Raw vertex / fragment raster pipeline. | Model Display: Built-in 3D geometry renderer. | Lightness Computer: Convert rendered textures to LED pixel arrays. | .

1995.title: Try it
1995.content: For a more elaborate moving point cloud, download the example score. Its shader calculates the points’ positions and colors and sends the resulting image directly to a window. Reduce the vertex count from the saved 99,999 to see how a sparser set of points changes the image. This download uses a point-cloud-and-spheres shader, not the simpler spiral from the reference example. Try this on web .

1996.title: VU Meter
1996.content: VU Meter, in Monitoring, displays the level of each channel of an audio bus, with peak, RMS and peak-hold indications.

1997.title: Connections
1997.content: Connect the signal to Audio. The channel count follows the incoming bus. To listen and meter at the same time, branch the source to both the meter and the normal audio destination. There is no audio-through outlet: inserting only a meter at the end of a chain does not route sound to the speakers. Levels is a value-list output containing three linear-amplitude numbers per channel: peak envelope, RMS envelope and held peak. For two channels its order is [peak0, rms0, hold0, peak1, rms1, hold1]. These are not dB values; the graphical meter converts them for display. The envelopes include release smoothing, so Levels is not a list of instantaneous audio samples.

1998.title: Workflow
1998.content: Place the meter before or after an effect to compare signal levels, or monitor a multichannel Audio device bus. Keep the containing interval executing while observing it. The meter measures levels; it does not attenuate, limit or prevent clipping. Adjust gain in the source, effect or destination when a signal is too loud.

1999.title: Building for WebAssembly
1999.content: The browser target builds score with Emscripten and Qt for WebAssembly. Only features supported by web browsers can be used in WASM builds of score. For application use and platform restrictions, see Using score in the browser.

2000.title: Reproduce the CI environment
2000.content: The CI workflow runs on Ubuntu 24.04, matching the SDK’s host tools. In an Ubuntu 24.04 container or build machine, run from a recursive source checkout: ./ci/wasm.deps.sh ./ci/wasm.build.sh . These scripts install system packages, extract the SDK into /opt/ossia-sdk-wasm, build in /build, and replace the user-library checkout selected by SCORE_LIBRARY_DIR. ci/wasm.deps.sh downloads sdk42. Its version definitions select Qt’s 6.12 branch, emsdk 5.0.5 and FFmpeg 9.0; the WASM FFmpeg recipe uses that shared FFmpeg version. The dependency script also downloads the user library and add-ons. ci/wasm.build.sh sources emsdk_env.sh and configures with qt-wasm/bin/qt-cmake, Ninja, C++23, a release unity build and no precompiled headers. The target uses SIMD, pthreads, Wasm exceptions and JSPI, with a 16-thread pool, an 8 MiB main stack and memory growth up to 2 GiB. Audio uses Emscripten AudioWorklet and Wasm Worker support. Configuration entry points: . | Setting | Purpose | . | SCORE_EXTRA_CMAKE_ARGS | Additional CMake arguments passed by the build script. | . | SCORE_CMAKE_CACHE | Initial CMake cache file, supplied with -C. | . | SCORE_LIBRARY_DIR | Library source directory used by the CI scripts; defaults to $HOME/score-user-library. The dependency script replaces this checkout. | . | SCORE_WASM_PRELOAD_LIBRARY | CMake directory to embed as the default library. The build script supplies it when SCORE_LIBRARY_DIR exists. | . The library is embedded in the .data payload at /home/web_user/Documents/ossia/score/packages/default in the application’s virtual filesystem. Rebuild to update it.

2001.title: Add-ons and feature availability
2001.content: The WASM configuration in ci/common.deps.sh includes the network, Synthimi, JK, GBAP, LTC, Granola, Bendage, Airwindows, computer-vision, ONNX, Puara and Deuterium add-ons. Desktop-only add-ons are excluded, including BLE, Context Free, HDF5, LED, Libav filter graphs, LSL, NDI, OpenZen, SpatGRIS, Ultraleap, system information, tracking protocols, Video I/O, Carto TCP and Orbbec. Native VST/LV2 binaries cannot run in the browser. JavaScript processes are disabled because the QML execution engine’s thread synchronization is incompatible with AudioWorklet execution. Native UDP/TCP sockets are also unavailable to web pages; use browser-supported transports such as WebSocket.

2002.title: Bundle and deployment layout
2002.content: ci/wasm.deploy.sh assembles site/ from /build and cmake/Deployment/WASM. It initializes a deployment Git repository, so use it as a packaging reference rather than a generic local server command. Keep the generated files together: . | ossia-score.js and generated JavaScript helpers, including worker/worklet files; | the application binary, either ossia-score.wasm or the deployed ossia-score.wasm.gz; | ossia-score.data when generated, containing Qt resources and the preloaded library; | the supplied index.html, qtloader.js, JSPI check, URL importer, gzip loader and cross-origin-isolation service worker. | . The published website uses a gzipped binary to avoid the hosting repository’s per-file size limit. score-wasm-gz.js uses DecompressionStream and streaming WebAssembly compilation; it also handles a server that already decoded Content-Encoding: gzip. A deployment containing only the compressed binary therefore needs this browser API. When the compressed resource is absent, the loader falls back to the normal plain .wasm path. CI also publishes a WASM ZIP (ossia.score-<version>-wasm.zip, or ossia.score-master-wasm.zip). It contains the plain .wasm binary and its accompanying JavaScript and data files. See Custom applications to package a custom browser application.

2003.title: Serve with browser isolation
2003.content: Serve over HTTPS or localhost, rather than file://. The threaded target needs cross-origin isolation and shared memory. Configure the server with: . Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp . The supplied page also loads coi-serviceworker.min.js, which can establish isolation on static hosting by intercepting requests and adding headers. Service workers require a secure context and may trigger an initial reload. Keep the worker in the application’s deployment scope. Cross-origin subresources must satisfy the chosen isolation policy; co-hosting the application assets avoids many such failures. Serve a plain .wasm resource as application/wasm. At startup, the page checks JSPI before calling Qt’s qtLoad(). Its entry function is score_entry (derived from the CMake target name), not a function guessed from ossia-score.js. The loader installs URL-imported files during preRun and passes the document path to the application as a command-line argument. The ?open= importer accepts same-origin HTTP(S) documents and stored/deflated ZIP projects. ZIP64 is unsupported. Use project-relative media references and include media in the project archive.

2004.title: Diagnose a deployed bundle
2004.content: Check the browser’s developer console and network panel when the page does not start: . | Confirm WebAssembly.Suspending and WebAssembly.promising are functions. The supplied page explains a missing JSPI capability. | Confirm crossOriginIsolated is true and shared memory is available; inspect isolation headers and service-worker scope if not. | Check that JS helpers, the selected binary and .data all load from the same deployment. A cached loader paired with a different binary is not a valid bundle. | If audio or camera input fails, check secure-context status, user interaction and site permissions. Camera support additionally requires MediaStreamTrackProcessor on the thread used by the implementation. | For missing media after a reload, remember that imported files are in MEMFS. Local-storage preferences and crash recovery do not persist the imported filesystem. | .

2005.title: Wavecycle
2005.content: . Draw your own waveforms and hear them immediately. Wavecycle turns hand-drawn curves into audio oscillators, letting you sculpt sound by sculpting waves. Perfect for creating custom timbres, experimental synthesis, or when you want total control over your oscillator’s harmonic content. Draw harsh sawtooths, smooth sines, or impossible shapes that only exist in your imagination.

2006.title: How it works
2006.content: Wavecycle reads the curve you draw and uses it as a wavetable - cycling through your waveform at audio rate to generate sound. The faster the frequency, the higher the pitch. The curve inlet allows to click and drag to draw any shape you want. The horizontal axis is one complete cycle, the vertical axis is amplitude. Sharp corners create harsh harmonics, smooth curves sound gentle. The frequency inlet is how fast to cycle through your waveform. Low frequencies for bass tones, high frequencies for piercing leads. The frequency parameter includes smoothing to prevent clicks when adjusting. To plug for instance MIDI notes, one needs to take the MIDI pitch and convert it to frequency values: . Try it ! . Try this on web .

2007.title: What is score ?
2007.content: ossia score offers advanced tools to ease the authoring of time exigent projects involving medias: flexible score for a live performance, interactive scenario for an intermedia installation, game-like state machine scenarios, etc. It thus provides a unified place to write automations for the parameters of the devices involved in the project, provides means to author efficient mappings from device A to device B or to modulate some devices parameters using generative processes and so on.

2008.title: Advanced time sequencing environment
2008.content: When having to author scenarios for interactive art, music and sound performances, one often has to rely on two approaches: . | DAW / timeline-based software offering tools for fine time editing and parameters automation | cue-based software offering great flexibility in live situation | . While both approaches have numerous advantages, they also draw some limits in some advanced media-based productions: First type hardly offers (if any) flexibility in live situation regarding how events actually evolve in time. Second type makes it hard if possible at all to control precisely processes evolving over time. score thus aims at bridging the gap between these two models in a unified environment. By combining a flexible timeline with a patch-like authoring process, it allows to write precisely timed processes such as automations or more fancy parameters control and modulation while still maintaining some variations as the scenario is executed. But it also allows authoring open and non-linear scenarios yet still including some time-dependent processes.

2009.title: Interoperability-based
2009.content: ossia score aims to fully integrate with the favorite tools of artists and musicians involved in advanced media authoring. It allows to remotely control various commercial or custom software and hardware as well as to work with audio or video medias right from the app. While score itself offers some audio and video features, it does not aim at being an “All in one” super software (hence forcing intermedia authors to give up their personal toolset expertise). On the contrary, score was built from the ground up to be as interoperable as possible. Users remain thus free to use their tools of choice, be it their favorite VJing software, custom audio synthesis app or any specialized toolset. score 3.0.0 supports a number of protocols such as MIDI, Open Sound Control, OSCQuery or serial port making it easy to use score as the central hub of a project and thus author fine relationships between medias.

2010.title: Wiimote device
2010.content: . Turn Nintendo Wii Remotes into expressive wireless controllers for your score projects. Get 3D motion sensing, IR pointing, button input, and extension support through Bluetooth connectivity. Perfect for gestural control, spatial audio manipulation, interactive installations, or any project where you want natural, wireless interaction without complex sensor setups.

2011.title: Setting up a Wiimote device
2011.content: . | Put your Wiimote in pairing mode - Press and hold the 1 and 2 buttons simultaneously until the LEDs flash | Add device in the Device explorer and choose “Wiimote” | Wait for connection - The device will automatically discover and pair with available Wiimotes | Test the connection - Press buttons and move the remote to see parameter updates | . For IR pointer functionality, set up an IR sensor bar or use candles as IR reference points.

2012.title: Available inputs
2012.content: Motion sensing . Accelerometer - 3-axis tilt and motion detection X, Y, Z axes - Raw acceleration values for gesture recognition Tilt angles - Processed roll and pitch for precise orientation control Shake detection - Built-in gesture recognition for sudden movements . Button interface . D-pad - Four-way directional control A and B buttons - Primary action buttons 1 and 2 buttons - Secondary controls Plus and Minus - Menu/settings buttons Home button - Special function button . IR camera . IR pointing - 10-point infrared tracking with sensor bar X/Y coordinates - Screen-relative pointing position Distance sensing - Rough distance estimation from IR sources Multi-point tracking - Track up to 4 IR sources simultaneously . Extension support . Nunchuk - Additional analog stick and motion sensing Classic Controller - Traditional gamepad layout Motion Plus - Enhanced gyroscope for precise rotation Other extensions - Guitar Hero controllers, balance boards, etc.

2013.title: Creative applications
2013.content: Gestural composition: Map Wiimote movements to musical parameters - tilt for pitch bend, shake for rhythm triggers, pointing for spatial audio control. 3D spatial control: Use accelerometer data for positioning sounds in 3D space with DBAP or GBAP spatialization. Interactive performances: Wireless freedom lets performers move naturally while controlling audio, video, or lighting parameters. Installation interaction: Provide intuitive, game-like interfaces for gallery visitors - everyone knows how to use a Wiimote. Multi-user systems: Connect multiple Wiimotes for collaborative control or performance systems.

2014.title: Integration with score processes
2014.content: Mapping Tool: Shape accelerometer data into musical curves - add dead zones for steady holding, create response curves for natural gesture feel. Spatial audio: Connect motion data directly to DBAP positioning for sound that follows your movements through 3D space. Audio Effects: Map tilt and rotation to effect parameters - shake the remote to add distortion, tilt for filter sweeps. Video processing: Control visual effects with gesture - point to control projection mapping, shake for visual intensity.

2015.title: Advanced techniques
2015.content: Gesture recognition: Combine multiple axis data to recognize complex gestures - figure-8 movements, specific pointing patterns, or choreographed sequences. Sensor fusion: Use accelerometer and IR data together for more robust tracking and control. Distance-based interaction: Use IR distance sensing for proximity-based effects - sounds that change as you approach or move away from reference points. Multi-controller orchestration: Create ensemble pieces where multiple performers with Wiimotes contribute to a unified musical or visual experience.

2016.title: Technical considerations
